title: an identifier may begin with a Unicode letter
rule: An identifier begins with a Unicode letter or underscore (`_`) and continues with letters, digits, or underscores.

title: identifiers are case-sensitive
rule: Identifiers are case-sensitive: `Foo`, `foo`, and `FOO` are distinct.

title: string and String name the same type
rule: The lowercase keyword `string` and the standard-library type name `String` name the same type — they are interchangeable in source.

title: the bare underscore cannot be declared as a local's name
rule: The bare underscore `_` is not an identifier — never declarable and never readable as a name; `var _ := e;` is a compile error.

title: an identifier merely containing an underscore is ordinary
rule: Identifiers merely containing underscores (`_camelCase`, `snake_case`, `_f`) are ordinary identifiers; only the bare single-character token is reserved.

title: a parameter cannot be named the bare underscore
rule: The bare underscore `_` is never declarable as a name; every declaration named `_` — including a method parameter — is a compile error naming the sanctioned forms (§17.13).

title: a named parameter is an ordinary declaration
rule: An identifier merely containing an underscore is ordinary; a properly named parameter is unaffected by the discard rule.

title: a bare underscore cannot be read as a value
rule: The bare underscore is never readable as a name; a bare `_` in expression position is a compile error — `_` is not a value, so no such read can resolve (§17.13).

title: reading an ordinary local in expression position is legal
rule: A bare underscore cannot be read as a value; an ordinary literal read in the same position is unaffected.

title: a reserved keyword cannot be used as an identifier
rule: Reserved words may not be used as identifiers, except for the contextual keywords listed in Appendix B which have meaning only in specific syntactic positions.

title: an identifier that merely resembles a keyword is legal
rule: Reserved words may not be used as identifiers; a spelling that is not itself a reserved word is unaffected.

title: a contextual keyword is an ordinary identifier outside its position
rule: Contextual keywords have meaning only in specific syntactic positions; used elsewhere they are ordinary identifiers.

title: Exception is a PascalCase name, not a keyword
rule: Type identifiers like `Object`, `Array`, and `Exception` are not keywords; they are PascalCase names defined in the standard library.

title: block comments do not nest
rule: `/* ... */` — block comment, does not nest.

title: a method's end label matching its name is accepted
rule: Named constructs — method bodies included — take the identifier as the optional end label: `end methodName;`.

title: a method's end label that mismatches its name is rejected
rule: The optional label is the identifier: `end methodName;`. A mismatch is a compile error.

title: a constructor closed with the wrong introducing keyword is rejected
rule: Keyword-labelled constructs are labelled by the keyword that introduced the block (`end constructor;`, `end destructor;`); a label that does not match the construct's introducing keyword is a compile error.

title: a constructor closed with its own introducing keyword is accepted
rule: Keyword-labelled constructs are labelled by the keyword that introduced the block: `end constructor;`.

title: a labeled loop closed with the unlabeled keyword form is rejected
rule: A loop carrying a loop label is a named construct; the keyword closer (`end for;`) is rejected once the loop is labeled.

title: a labeled loop closed with its own label is accepted
rule: A loop carrying a loop label is a named construct; its closer is `end label;` or the unlabelled `end;`.

title: a nested loop cannot reuse an enclosing loop's label
rule: A loop label duplicates no loop label in scope at its declaration (Appendix C.5).

title: a nested loop with a distinct label is accepted
rule: A loop label duplicates no loop label in scope at its declaration; a distinct inner label is unaffected.

title: a dotted module name is one unnested identifier
rule: A module name is a single identifier or a sequence of identifiers separated by dots. The dotted form is a single name; it does not establish nesting.

title: an import alias is usable as a type qualifier
rule: An import may bind a file-scoped alias: `import BankingApp.Transactions as Tx;` — thereafter `Tx.Ledger` names that module's public `Ledger`.

title: naming a type requires importing its declaring module
rule: All other library modules require explicit `import` — importing `System.Threading` is required to name `CancellationTokenSource`.

title: naming a type is admitted once its module is imported
rule: All other library modules require explicit `import`; once imported, naming the type is admitted.

title: a duplicate plain import of the same module is idempotent
rule: A duplicate plain `import` of a module already imported in the same file is idempotent: the later occurrence adds nothing and is not diagnosed.

title: a current-module declaration shadows a same-named auto-imported name
rule: A declaration in the current module shadows any same-named import for bare-name purposes (the import stays reachable by qualifier) — the same shadowing already specified for auto-imported names.

title: an import alias cannot collide with a type declared in the module
rule: An alias may not collide with another alias, an imported module's name segment in qualifier position, a type declared in the file's module (a top-level declaration ... ), or an unambiguously imported public bare name.

title: an alias with no colliding declaration is accepted
rule: An alias may not collide with a type declared in the file's module; a distinctly-named type is unaffected.

title: a CancellationToken reached through an import alias is accepted
rule: `import` makes the public names of the named module visible in the current file (v0.338, §2.2).

title: a Mutex reached through an import alias is accepted
rule: `import` makes the public names of the named module visible in the current file (v0.338, §2.2).

title: an always-available name of the reference's arity is selected over an inherited nested type
rule: Arity selects among the types rule 1 of §2.7 finds for an identifier: a reference resolves to the first, in that rule's order, whose arity its type-argument list fixes; where none has that arity, it resolves to the first of them and is Appendix C.1's arity error, never an alias, a member or a module prefix (§2.2, v0.343). The reference `Task` fixes arity 0. Rule 1 of §2.7 finds the enclosing type's accessible members first, and `K` inherits the nested type `Task<T>` — but that candidate's arity is 1, so it does not end the search. The always-available names "stand in those rules where an imported bare name does" (§2.3, v0.343), and §2.3's table lists the Task family `Task`, `Task<T>`, `OwningTask<T>`: the non-generic `Task` has arity 0 and is the first candidate the reference's arity fixes, so `Take(t: Task)` names it and the program runs.

title: a bare reference whose arity no candidate fixes is the arity error
rule: Arity selects among the types rule 1 of §2.7 finds for an identifier: a reference resolves to the first, in that rule's order, whose arity its type-argument list fixes; where none has that arity, it resolves to the first of them and is Appendix C.1's arity error, never an alias, a member or a module prefix (§2.2, v0.343). The reference `IAsyncEvent` fixes arity 0. Rule 1 of §2.7 finds `K`'s inherited nested type `IAsyncEvent<T>` — arity 1 — and the always-available `IAsyncEvent<out T>` (§2.3's table, arity 1) stands where an imported bare name does; no candidate has the arity 0 the reference fixes, so the reference is Appendix C.1's arity error, "a bare name and a miscounted list are both compile errors naming the declared arity".

title: a bare name exported by two imported modules is ambiguous
rule: When two imported modules export the same public name, the **bare** name is ambiguous: using it unqualified is a compile error citing both origins; the fix is qualification (full module name or alias) (§2.2, v0.343). Both `LA` and `LB` export a public type `N` of arity 0, and the file imports both, so the bare `N` in the annotation `using var n: N` names two origins at once. The inherited nested type `N<U>` of `K` does not settle it: rule 1 of §2.7 finds the enclosing type's accessible members first, but a candidate is only reached when its arity the reference fixes, and `N<U>` has arity 1 while the bare reference fixes arity 0 (§2.2, v0.343) — so the search reaches the two imported names, and they collide.

title: several always-available names are usable with no import
rule: The following names are visible in every source file without import — including `System`'s `Console`, `System.Text`'s `StringBuilder`, and `System.Collections.Generic`'s `Array<T>`.

title: a non-auto stdlib type is not visible without its import
rule: All other library modules require explicit `import`. `CancellationTokenSource` is NOT auto — it needs `import System.Threading;`.

title: importing System.Threading makes CancellationTokenSource visible
rule: All other library modules require explicit `import`. `CancellationTokenSource` needs `import System.Threading;` — supplying it makes the name resolve and the file compile.

title: a user module's export collides with an auto-imported bare name
rule: A user module exporting one of the §2.3 always-available bare names makes the bare name ambiguous in a file importing both, and no opt-out exists.

title: qualifying the colliding name resolves the ambiguity
rule: A user module exporting an always-available bare name makes the bare name ambiguous; qualification (the module name or an alias, §2.2) is the remedy — no opt-out exists, but qualifying reaches the intended declaration.

title: naming Ptr<T> requires importing System.Interop
rule: `System.Interop` — `Ptr<T>` and the `Interop` intrinsics — is deliberately not auto-imported, so *naming* `Ptr<T>` or `Interop` requires the `import System.Interop;` line.

title: importing System.Interop makes Ptr<T> nameable
rule: `System.Interop` — `Ptr<T>` and the `Interop` intrinsics — is deliberately not auto-imported, so *naming* `Ptr<T>` requires the `import System.Interop;` line; supplying it makes the name resolve.

title: a System.Exception parameter type is qualified without import
rule: The following names are visible in every source file without import; the standard exception types are among them (v0.338, §2.3).

title: a System.Exception local annotation and constructor are qualified without import
rule: The following names are visible in every source file without import; the standard exception types are among them (v0.338, §2.3).

title: a System.Exception owned return type is qualified without import
rule: The following names are visible in every source file without import; the standard exception types are among them (v0.338, §2.3).

title: a non-always-available System type needs an import
rule: `import` makes the public names of the named module visible in the current file (v0.338, §2.2).

title: an auto-imported System.Text name is accepted
rule: The following names are visible in every source file without import; the standard exception types are among them (v0.338, §2.3).

title: an auto-imported System.Collections.Generic name is accepted
rule: The following names are visible in every source file without import; the standard exception types are among them (v0.338, §2.3).

title: a qualified CancellationToken without import is rejected
rule: `import` makes the public names of the named module visible in the current file (v0.338, §2.2).

title: a qualified CancellationToken with import is accepted
rule: `import` makes the public names of the named module visible in the current file (v0.338, §2.2).

title: a qualified Mutex with its module imported is accepted
rule: `import` makes the public names of the named module visible in the current file (v0.338, §2.2).

title: a qualified Mutex with the wrong import is rejected
rule: `import` makes the public names of the named module visible in the current file (v0.338, §2.2).

title: A user enum named DayOfWeek shadows the System one
rule: Language spec §2.3 (v0.350): the auto-imported `System` names, DayOfWeek and DateTimeKind (stdlib §2.5) among them, "may be shadowed by local declarations under the normal name-resolution rules". A module that declares `enum DayOfWeek: byte Alpha, Beta` therefore resolves `DayOfWeek.Beta` to its own constant; its underlying value is 1 and `nameof(d)` is the identifier "d".

title: Shadowing DateTimeKind by a class leaves the System DayOfWeek reachable
rule: Language spec §2.3 (v0.350): the auto-imported `System` names, DayOfWeek and DateTimeKind (stdlib §2.5) among them, "may be shadowed by local declarations under the normal name-resolution rules". The shadow is per name: a user class `DateTimeKind` hides only that name, and `DayOfWeek.Friday` still names the System enum constant (stdlib §2.5: Sunday is 0, so Friday is 5).

title: A library method taking and returning the System DayOfWeek is callable from an importer
rule: The auto-imported System DayOfWeek (§2.3, v0.350; stdlib §2.5) is one type across modules: Lib3.L3.Id(DayOfWeek) called with Wednesday returns Wednesday, byte value 3.

title: A user record named TimeSpan shadows the System one including its operator and members
rule: Language spec §2.3 (v0.350): an auto-imported System name such as TimeSpan "may be shadowed by local declarations under the normal name-resolution rules". The module's own `record TimeSpan(N: long)` with its own Add, Negate and `operator *` is what `a.Add(b)` and `a * 3.0` use: 5+7=12, Negate(5)=-5, and the declared `*` returns N*3 = 15.

title: A user class named TimeSpan shadows the System one including Add and Subtract
rule: Language spec §2.3 (v0.350): an auto-imported System name such as TimeSpan "may be shadowed by local declarations under the normal name-resolution rules". The module's own `class TimeSpan` with Add, Subtract and Negate is used for `a.Add(b)` etc.: 12, 5-7=-2, -5.

title: a chain head resolves to a reachable type over a same-named member
rule: Chain head — name followed by `.`: enclosing-type members rank last, after aliases — a reachable type outranks a same-named member. No warning fires because the member's declared type is the resolved type (the `property Color: Color` idiom).

title: a bare value read resolves to a same-named member over a type
rule: Bare value read: enclosing-type members rank between local scope and module declarations — a member outranks a same-named top-level type.

title: chain head resolving to a type warns when the shadowed member's declared type differs
rule: Warning row — chain head resolves to a type, or to an import alias (§2.2), while a same-named accessible member, a nested type included, exists: warn, *unless* the member's declared type is the resolved type (or an instantiation of the resolved generic). `Status` the member is declared `string`, not `Status` the type, so the carve-out does not apply.

title: a dotted prefix matching no import is an error at the leftmost segment
rule: Otherwise, match the longest dotted prefix of the chain against an imported module's full name. A prefix matching *no* import is an error at `A` (naming the unresolved segment).

title: the longest dotted prefix matching an imported module's full name resolves the chain
rule: Otherwise, match the longest dotted prefix of the chain against an imported module's full name. The remainder then resolves against that module's public declarations. `Data.Store` is the imported module's full (dotted) name; `Item` is the remainder.

title: a type named A shadows an imported module-name prefix A for chain purposes
rule: Consequences worth stating — a type named `A` in scope **shadows** a module-name prefix `A.…` for chain purposes (the compiler warns when both readings exist). `Data` the locally-declared type wins over `Data` the imported module's prefix.

title: an unimported module's presence in the build does not satisfy rule 2's prefix match
rule: Match the longest dotted prefix of the chain against an *imported* module's full name. A prefix matching no import is an error at `A`, even when a module of that name is known to the build — `Data.Store` is compiled as part of this build but never `import`ed by this file, so `Data` does not resolve.

title: an unknown qualifier before a type name is still rejected
rule: A prefix matching no import is an error at the leftmost segment (v0.338, §2.7 rule 2).

title: a misspelled System qualifier is still rejected
rule: A prefix matching no import is an error at the leftmost segment (v0.338, §2.7 rule 2).

title: a user type named System shadows the module prefix
rule: A prefix matching no import is an error at the leftmost segment (v0.338, §2.7 rule 2).

title: a local named like a collection type is a value, so a dotted access on it is member access
rule: If it resolves to a *value* (a local, field, or property), the chain is member access.

title: a chain head in a type position warns when the enclosing type declares a same-named nested type
rule: Chain head — name followed by `.`: enclosing-type members rank last, after aliases — a reachable type outranks a same-named member, and the shadowed member stays reachable by qualifying (`this.Data.W()`; the enclosing type's name for statics), which for a nested type is `Outer.Choice`. Warning row — chain head resolves to a type while a same-named accessible member exists: warn, *unless* the member's declared type is the resolved type (or an instantiation of the resolved generic).

title: A user class named DateTime shadows the always-available DateTime for member lookup through a chain
rule: Every always-available name other than the first row may be shadowed by local declarations (spec 2.3, 2.7 rule 1), so a chain off a user DateTime resolves members on the user class, not on the stdlib type.

title: a module cannot import itself
rule: An `import` naming the enclosing file's own module is rejected ("a module cannot import itself").

title: importing a distinct module is accepted
rule: An `import` naming the enclosing file's own module is rejected; importing a distinct module is unaffected.

title: declaring an implementation-provided module name is a build error
rule: The standard-library modules are implicit members of every build's artifact set; they participate in duplicate-name detection — a root compilation declaring a module name the implementation provides (`module System;`, `module System.Threading;`, …) is the rule-3 build error.

title: the root compilation may not declare a dependency's module name
rule: A build whose artifact set — the root compilation plus the dependency closure — contains two distinct artifacts declaring the same module name, or a dependency artifact declaring a module name the root compilation also declares, is ill-formed; the diagnostic names both origins.

title: a root module name distinct from every dependency is accepted
rule: A build's artifact set is ill-formed only when two distinct artifacts declare the same module name; a distinct root module name alongside a dependency is unaffected.

title: an aliased import of the file's own module is still a self-import
rule: An `import` naming the enclosing file's own module is rejected ("a module cannot import itself"); the self-loop is not a cycle, it is a mistake. An `as` alias renames the binding, it does not change which module is named.

title: an implementation-provided module resolves with no artifact supplied
rule: The standard-library modules are provided by the implementation, not by any presented artifact: implicit members of every build's artifact set, exempt from §2.8.3 rule 1's presentation requirement, resolvable by `import` with no artifact supplied.

title: a public generic works across modules even when its body reaches an internal helper
rule: Visibility inside a generic body is judged at the definition site: a public generic's body may reference its own module's `internal` declarations, and an external instantiation binds to them; the artifact interface must be sufficient for the consumer to type-check and instantiate the public generic with no access to `Helper`.

title: purity carries across the module boundary into a contract clause
rule: The artifact interface carries the purity modifier of every member it describes; a `requires` clause may call only `pure` members (§22.16), and that obligation is checkable against an imported member exactly as against a local one.

title: a default argument value crosses the artifact boundary
rule: The artifact interface must be sufficient for a consumer to type-check every well-formed use of the module's public surface, with full signatures — including default argument values.

title: a constraint violation at an external instantiation is diagnosed
rule: The artifact interface carries generic parameters with their variance and constraints; the consumer may instantiate a public generic only at type arguments satisfying them, so a type argument failing a declared constraint is diagnosed at the external instantiation.

title: a public generic instantiates at a consumer-declared type argument
rule: The artifact interface must be sufficient for a consumer to instantiate every public generic type at arbitrary module-external type arguments satisfying the declared constraints; an external instantiation behaves identically to a same-module instantiation at the same arguments.

title: a contract record carried in the interface is enforced at the consumer
rule: For every member the interface describes, it carries one contract record per contract clause — kind, `static` qualifier, canonical clause text, recorded tier; a `requires` clause runs in every build mode, so an imported member's precondition is enforced at the consumer's call site.

title: an importer reconstructs a generic type's nested type and instantiates it
rule: The interface of a compiled artifact must be sufficient for a consumer, given only the artifact, to type-check every well-formed use of the module's public surface, with full signatures. A nested type is one type whatever the instantiation of its enclosing type, and is identified by its declaring module, its qualified name with the enclosing-type path, and its own generic arity — so `Box<int>.Item<int>` is one type the importer reconstructs, and `Item<int>` is a distinct instantiation of it.

title: an importer reconstructs a nested type of a non-generic enclosing type
rule: The interface of a compiled artifact must be sufficient for a consumer, given only the artifact, to type-check every well-formed use of the module's public surface, with full signatures. A nested type is a member of its enclosing class, and a nested type none of whose enclosing types is generic is referenced from outside as `Outer.Nested` — so the consumer reconstructs `Holder.Cell`, calls its instance member, and passes it to an imported method whose parameter is that nested type.

title: an importer reconstructs a type nested two levels deep in a generic enclosing type
rule: The interface of a compiled artifact must be sufficient for a consumer, given only the artifact, to type-check every well-formed use of the module's public surface, with full signatures. Nested types may themselves contain nested types (§11.6), and the enclosing path is part of a nested type's qualified name — so the consumer reconstructs `Tree<int>`'s `Node.Leaf` and reaches it through the enclosing type's static member.

title: an importer reconstructs a nested type of a generic enclosing type with two type arguments
rule: The interface of a compiled artifact must be sufficient for a consumer, given only the artifact, to type-check every well-formed use of the module's public surface, with full signatures. A nested type is a member of its enclosing class, and the enclosing type's own type arguments are written at the chain head — so the consumer reconstructs `Pair<int, string>`'s `Item` and reaches it through the enclosing type's static member.

title: a type ascription naming a transitive type requires its own import
rule: Naming the type in source — in a type ascription, parameter or return type, `new` expression, cast, `is`/pattern type test, `catch` clause, explicit generic type argument, or extension declaration — requires importing its declaring module, even though `Money` reaches `App`'s compilation only transitively through `Lib1`.

title: importing a transitive type's own declaring module admits naming it
rule: Naming a transitively-reachable type in source requires importing its declaring module. Once `Base` is imported, `Money` may be named in a type ascription exactly as any other visible type.

title: use without import — an inferred binding needs no import of a transitive type
rule: A file that imports module `A` may freely use values of any public type reachable through `A`'s public surface — receive them into `using var` bindings with inferred types, call their public members, and dispose them — without importing the type's declaring module.

title: a new expression naming a transitive type requires its own import
rule: Naming the type in source — including in a `new` expression — requires importing its declaring module, even though `Money` is otherwise reachable through `Lib1`'s surface without one.

title: an is type test naming a transitive type requires its own import
rule: Naming the type in source — including a pattern/`is` type test — requires importing its declaring module.

title: an explicit generic type argument naming a transitive type requires its own import
rule: Naming the type in source — including an explicit (source-spelled) generic type argument — requires importing its declaring module.

title: the same type reached through two import paths is one type
rule: A type is identified program-wide by its declaring module name, qualified type name, and generic arity. `App` imports `Lib1` and `Lib2`, both of which import `Base`, and `App` imports neither `Base` nor presents it twice by hand — `Money` arrives via both `Lib1`'s and `Lib2`'s interfaces and is one type: a value `Payroll.Net` produces flows into `Invoices.Total`'s parameter with no conversion.

title: the dependency closure reaches an arbitrarily deep transitive chain
rule: A build must present the artifacts of the root compilation's direct imports and, transitively, of every module those artifacts' interfaces reference. `App` imports only `Outer`; `Money` is two hops further away (`Outer` -> `Mid` -> `Base`), and using it needs no import at any level.

title: two modules each declaring a public type of the same name declare two unrelated types
rule: A type is identified program-wide by its declaring module name, its qualified type name, and its generic arity. Two modules each declaring a public type of the same name declare two unrelated types (distinguished in diagnostics by module qualification) — so `L1.Box` and `L2.Box` are two types, and no value of one converts to the other.

title: a value of one module's type of a name is not convertible to another module's type
rule: A type is identified program-wide by its declaring module name, its qualified type name, and its generic arity. The two `Box` types of `L1` and `L2` are two types, so a value of one is not convertible to a target of the other.

title: nested types of the same name under different enclosing types are three unrelated types
rule: A type is identified program-wide by its declaring module name, its qualified type name (including any enclosing-type path, each enclosing type in it keyed with its own generic arity), and its generic arity. The three nested `N` types — `L1.G<T>.N`, `L2.K<A, B>.N` and `L2.J.N` — are three unrelated types, and the consumer reaches each of them.

title: a module's body reference to a transitive type pulls that artifact into the build
rule: The build supplies the transitive closure. A build must present the artifacts of the root compilation's direct imports and, transitively, of every module those artifacts' interfaces reference — where an interface's references include those made by the declaration bodies it carries, not only its public signatures. `App` imports only `B`; `B`'s body names `G<int>.N`, so `A`'s artifact must be presented to `B`'s compilation.

title: a generic instantiation's static state is one copy across independently compiled artifacts
rule: A process contains exactly one copy of each module's code and, for each type — including each generic instantiation — exactly one static state and one runtime identity, regardless of link mode and regardless of how many compilations emitted code for the type.

title: a qualifying Main in a library compilation is an ordinary method
rule: A library build has no entry point; a qualifying `Main` in a library compilation is an ordinary method — it is declared, compiled, and callable like any other static method.

title: a non-generic type has one static state across three artifacts
rule: A process contains exactly one copy of each module's code and, for each type, exactly one static state and one runtime identity, regardless of link mode and regardless of how many compilations emitted code for the type.

title: an interface variable may hold a boxed record value
rule: An interface variable is a reference; its underlying value may be a class instance, a boxed record, a boxed enum, or a boxed primitive.

title: an interface variable may hold a boxed int value
rule: An interface variable is a reference; its underlying value may be a class instance, a boxed record, a boxed enum, or a boxed primitive.

title: the unit type has exactly one value
rule: The unit type `()` — exactly one value, also written `()`.

title: value-typed assignment copies an independent value
rule: A value type is copied on assignment; each variable holds an independent value.

title: reference-typed assignment aliases the same heap object
rule: A reference type is shared on assignment; multiple variables may refer to the same heap-allocated object.

title: a record this appended to an Array with Add reads back its field values
rule: A **value type** is copied on assignment

title: a record this passed to an indexer set reads back its field values
rule: A **value type** is copied on assignment

title: a reference type is non-nullable by default
rule: A reference type is non-nullable by default.

title: a nullable reference type variable may hold null
rule: A reference type is non-nullable by default. A trailing `?` produces its nullable form.

title: a nullable value type is an optional with a value or null
rule: Value types may also be wrapped in ? to produce an optional.

title: a null-tested nullable reference is narrowed in the true branch
rule: A reference type is non-nullable by default. A trailing `?` produces its nullable form.

title: a user type may not be named after a reserved primitive alias
rule: The PascalCase standard-library names of the primitive value types and String are reserved type names: a program may not declare a user type whose name is one of them.

title: a non-reserved type name compiles
rule: The PascalCase standard-library names of the primitive value types and String are reserved type names; any other name is unaffected.

title: an ordinary library type name such as Stream may be shadowed by a user type
rule: This does not reserve other standard-library type names — only the PascalCase aliases of the primitive value types and String; an ordinary library type such as Array or Stream may still be shadowed by a user type.

title: the keyword and PascalCase forms of a primitive name the same static members
rule: Static members of the standard library type are accessible through either form: int.Parse, int.MaxValue, double.IsNaN.

title: a user class named like a library collection keeps its own static member
rule: This does not reserve other standard-library type names — only the PascalCase aliases of the primitive value types and `String`; an ordinary library type such as `Array` or `Stream` may still be shadowed by a user type under the normal name-resolution rules.

title: the keyword string and the standard-library name String name one type
rule: Each primitive keyword aliases a standard library type, and the two forms are interchangeable: the lowercase keyword `string` and the standard-library type name `String` (`System.String`) name the same type, and the dual-form rule makes the PascalCase form interchangeable with the keyword everywhere a type is named. So a local declared `String` takes a `string` literal and reaches the standard library's `String` members — `Length`, the number of code points (stdlib §9.6).

title: a user type may shadow a library collection type and keeps its own members
rule: Language spec §3.4 (v0.345): "This does not reserve other standard-library type names — only the PascalCase aliases of the primitive value types and String; an ordinary library type such as `Array` or `Stream` may still be shadowed by a user type." A user `Array` therefore names the user's own type, and that type's own member is the one a call on it reaches.

title: the ordering operators on bool operands are a compile error
rule: Ordering (<, <=, >, >=) on every primitive except bool — the ordering operators on bool operands are a compile error.

title: the ordering operators on int operands compile
rule: Ordering (<, <=, >, >=) on every primitive except bool.

title: bitwise operators on bool operands are a compile error
rule: Bitwise (&, |, ^, ~) ... Not valid on bool, char, or floating-point types. Boolean operations use and/or/not, which short-circuit and have boolean-only semantics.

title: bitwise operators on int operands compile
rule: Bitwise (&, |, ^, ~) on byte, sbyte, short, ushort, int, uint, long, ulong.

title: default(int) is defined as the zero value
rule: defaultable classifies types for which default(T) is defined: every non-nullable value type whose components are recursively defaultable — the primitives among them.

title: default of a non-nullable reference type is a compile error
rule: Not defaultable: non-nullable reference types.

title: default of the nullable form of a reference type is null
rule: defaultable classifies types for which default(T) is defined: every nullable type T?.

title: a constructor-only record is not defaultable
rule: constructor-only classifies records declaring a constructor carrying a contract clause; such a record is not defaultable.

title: a record with no contract clause on its constructor is defaultable
rule: a record all of whose declared fields are defaultable and which is not constructor-only is defaultable.

title: auto-hashable records get a synthesized structural equality operator
rule: auto-hashable classifies records and value-like choices for which =, GetHashCode, and ToString are synthesized.

title: a function type is not hashable, so a Set over a function type is rejected
rule: hashable ... every type except ... (e) a function type (§27.7.1: a lambda equals only itself, so a hash container of function values would hold every lambda evaluation apart; a function value's hash agrees with that equality, and at `Object` it is an ordinary key)

title: a borrow-bearing choice declaring user equality is still not hashable
rule: hashable ... every type except ... (b) a choice that is not value-like, or is value-like and neither auto-hashable nor declares user equality (§35.7 — owning and borrow-bearing choices are not hashable, user equality declared or not

title: a value-like choice outside auto-hashable only through its declared equality is hashable
rule: hashable ... every type except ... (b) a choice that is not value-like, or is value-like and neither auto-hashable nor declares user equality (§35.7 — ... a value-like choice outside auto-hashable through its own declared equality — `Equals(other: C)` with `GetHashCode`, with or without a homogeneous `=`/`<>` overload beside them — is hashable on the strength of those members)

title: the nullable form of a non-hashable record is not hashable
rule: hashable ... every type except (a) a record that is neither auto-hashable nor declares user equality, ... (c) a nullable type `T?`, or an inline array of any §15.1 form whose element type is `T` or `T?`, where `T` is itself not hashable

title: a nullable hashable type is a hash-container element and null hashes to one value
rule: (c) a nullable type `T?` ... where `T` is itself not hashable — such a type's `Equals` and `GetHashCode` are `T`'s, through §8.4's null-safe wrapper — which hashes `null` to one fixed implementation-defined value

title: a T? field at a borrow-bearing substitution holds borrows and rejects the store
rule: For borrow-bearing, holds-borrows, ... a nullable type `V?` is read as `V`, nullability stripped ... A rule that reads one of these properties off a declared, component or substituted type — §9.7's borrow-lifetime bullets ... — reads `V?` as it reads `V`, whether the nullable form is written or manufactured by substitution (`T?` at `T = Pair`, or `T` at `T = Pair?`)

title: the same T? field store is admitted at a substitution that holds no borrows
rule: For borrow-bearing, holds-borrows, ... a nullable type `V?` is read as `V`, nullability stripped ... A rule that reads one of these properties off a declared, component or substituted type — §9.7's borrow-lifetime bullets ... — reads `V?` as it reads `V`

title: T at T = Pair? holds Pair's borrows, so returning Id<Pair?> past its source is rejected
rule: A rule that reads one of these properties off a declared, component or substituted type — §9.7's borrow-lifetime bullets, §28.3's bare-type-parameter clauses, §30.14's rules — reads `V?` as it reads `V`, whether the nullable form is written or manufactured by substitution (`T?` at `T = Pair`, or `T` at `T = Pair?`)

title: the Id<Pair?> result used within its source's scope is admitted
rule: A rule that reads one of these properties off a declared, component or substituted type — §9.7's borrow-lifetime bullets, §28.3's bare-type-parameter clauses, §30.14's rules — reads `V?` as it reads `V`, whether the nullable form is written or manufactured by substitution (`T?` at `T = Pair`, or `T` at `T = Pair?`)

title: a Set of records with a declared Equals and GetHashCode holds one element for two keys
rule: A value-like choice outside auto-hashable through its own declared equality, `Equals(other: C)` with `GetHashCode`, is hashable on the strength of those members (v0.338, §3.6 hashable row).

title: a Dictionary keyed by a record with a declared Equals treats the keys as one
rule: A value-like choice outside auto-hashable through its own declared equality, `Equals(other: C)` with `GetHashCode`, is hashable on the strength of those members (v0.338, §3.6 hashable row).

title: a Set of choices with a declared Equals and GetHashCode holds one element for two values
rule: A value-like choice outside auto-hashable through its own declared equality, `Equals(other: C)` with `GetHashCode`, is hashable on the strength of those members (v0.338, §3.6 hashable row).

title: a declared Equals that is false for every pair keeps both elements in a Set
rule: A value-like choice outside auto-hashable through its own declared equality, `Equals(other: C)` with `GetHashCode`, is hashable on the strength of those members (v0.338, §3.6 hashable row).

title: a record without user equality keeps structural equality in a Set
rule: A positional record's default Equals is field-by-field value equality over its admissible component fields (v0.338, §8.3 default table).

title: a constrained type parameter reads its constraint's CauseChain, one entry per cause
rule: A generic body type-checks under the weakest assumption its constraints establish ([§3.6]). "copies its type name, message, stack-trace text, and its own `CauseChain` into the new exception's `CauseChain` (outermost cause first, flattened)" ([§31.4]), and `CauseChain` is "empty when no cause" ([§31.4]). So `x.CauseChain` on `T: Exception` yields the one cause of `outer` and nothing for `plain`.

title: a generic instance method reads its constraint's Message and an owned field's Message in one result
rule: A generic body type-checks under the weakest assumption its constraints establish ([§3.6]). The body of `Read<T>` with `where T: Exception` reads `x.Message` through that constraint, and `this.item.Message` reads the same member through the owned field's class type, so the result is the two messages joined.

title: a member read on a constrained type parameter type-checks through its where-constraint
rule: A generic body type-checks under the weakest assumption its constraints establish ([§3.6]). With `where U: ArgumentException`, `y.ParamName` reads through that constraint. `ParamName` is "`string?`" ([§31.4]) and `??` supplies `"-"` only when it is null, so the supplied name `pp` is used.

title: bool renders as True or False
rule: bool has two values, true and false.

title: an if condition of a non-bool type is a compile error
rule: Conditions of if/elif and while, and a case/catch arm's when guard, require bool.

title: an if condition of type bool compiles
rule: Conditions of if/elif and while require bool.

title: byte.MaxValue is 255
rule: byte | 8, unsigned | 0 to 255.

title: an out-of-range unsuffixed integer literal in an untyped context is a compile error
rule: In an untyped context, an unsuffixed integer literal exceeding int's range is a compile error directing to a suffix.

title: the same literal at a declared long target is a target-typed integer constant
rule: an unsuffixed integer literal whose value exceeds int's range is admitted at a declared integer target whose range contains it, taking that target's type.

title: a suffixed literal exceeding its suffix's range is a compile error
rule: A suffixed integer literal whose value does not fit the suffix's type is a compile error.

title: the same value under the ulong suffix fits
rule: A suffixed integer literal whose value fits the suffix's type is admitted (5000000000U exceeds uint's range — write 5000000000UL).

title: the boundary carve-out admits int.MinValue's magnitude as unary minus's immediate operand
rule: The decimal literal of magnitude 2^31 (unsuffixed) is admitted only as the immediate operand of unary -, denoting int.MinValue.

title: the same magnitude without the immediate unary-minus position overflows int's range
rule: Anywhere else those magnitudes remain errors — the magnitude alone overflows before the - applies.

title: an out-of-int-range literal is rejected at a generic parameter explicitly bound to double
rule: In an untyped context (var x := 3_000_000_000;), and at a non-integer target (var d: double := 3_000_000_000;), the literal is a compile error directing to a suffix (3_000_000_000L, which then converts by §5.1).

title: the same value with an L suffix converts to an explicitly bound double parameter
rule: In an untyped context (var x := 3_000_000_000;), and at a non-integer target (var d: double := 3_000_000_000;), the literal is a compile error directing to a suffix (3_000_000_000L, which then converts by §5.1).

title: floating-point division by zero produces infinity rather than raising
rule: floating-point division by zero produces one of these [Infinity, -Infinity, NaN] rather than raising an exception.

title: zero divided by zero produces NaN
rule: floating-point division by zero produces one of Infinity, -Infinity, or NaN rather than raising an exception.

title: a floating-point literal whose IEEE rounding is not finite is a compile error
rule: A literal whose value, so rounded (as IEEE 754 rounds to nearest, a tie to the even significand), is not finite is a compile error: its magnitude is at least its type's largest finite value plus half a unit in that value's last place — 1e999 and 1e40f are out of range.

title: a floating-point literal within range compiles
rule: A floating-point literal denotes the nearest representable value of its type: its value rounded as IEEE 754 rounds to nearest, a tie to the even significand. A literal whose value, so rounded, is not finite is a compile error.

title: NaN equals NaN under reflexive equality
rule: NaN = NaN is true.

title: negative zero equals positive zero
equality on a decimal is plain value equality, so 1.50m equals 1.5m
rule: Language spec §4.3.1 (v0.345): "`decimal` has no `Infinity`, `NaN`, or signed zero, so the question does not arise: `=` on `decimal` is straightforward value equality."

title: decimal division by zero raises DivideByZeroException
rule: Division by zero raises DivideByZeroException.

title: decimal arithmetic exactly represents finite decimal fractions
rule: High-precision decimal floating-point ... Exact representation of finite decimal fractions.

title: char values compare by code-point value
rule: Character values compare by code-point value: 'A' < 'B'.

title: a surrogate code point is not a valid char value
rule: Surrogate code points (U+D800 to U+DFFF) are not valid char values.

title: a non-surrogate char literal compiles
rule: A single Unicode scalar value, 32 bits wide; surrogate code points are not valid char values, other code points are.

title: string Length returns the number of code points
rule: s.Length returns the number of code points in s. O(1).

title: string indexing returns the char at a zero-indexed code-point position
rule: s[i] returns the char at code-point position i, zero-indexed. O(1).

title: out-of-range string indexing raises IndexOutOfRangeException
rule: s[i] ... Out-of-range raises IndexOutOfRangeException.

title: a closed range slice includes both endpoints
rule: s[r] ... a closed s[a..b] includes both ends.

title: a half-open range slice excludes the upper endpoint
rule: s[r] ... a half-open s[a..<b] excludes the upper.

title: an open-ended range slice extends to the end of the string
rule: s[r] ... the open-ended forms (s[..b], s[a..], s[..]) extend to the start or end of the string.

title: string ordering requires non-nullable operands
rule: Ordering requires non-nullable operands: an operand of static type string? is a compile error.

title: string ordering with non-nullable operands compiles
rule: Ordering requires non-nullable operands.

title: the + operator performs no implicit ToString conversion
rule: The compiler does not implicitly convert other types to string; use interpolation or .ToString().

title: interpolation is the correct way to embed a non-string value
rule: The compiler does not implicitly convert other types to string; use interpolation or .ToString().

title: a string is accepted where IEnumerable<char> is expected
rule: `string` implements `IEnumerable<char>`, so strings may be iterated with `for`:

title: a range value indexes a string slice
rule: `s[r]` for a `Range<int>` value `r` returns the substring spanning `r`. O(k) for a result of length `k`.

title: an empty range slice produces the empty string
rule: Out-of-range endpoints raise `IndexOutOfRangeException`; an empty range produces the empty string.

title: an out-of-range slice endpoint raises IndexOutOfRangeException
rule: Endpoints follow the standard rules for `Range<int>` over `s`'s indices: ... Out-of-range endpoints raise `IndexOutOfRangeException`.

title: a negative slice endpoint is out of range over the string's indices
rule: Endpoints follow the standard rules for `Range<int>` over `s`'s indices: ... Out-of-range endpoints raise `IndexOutOfRangeException`; a string's indices are zero-based code-point positions, so a negative endpoint is out of range.

title: a string has no Dispose() member
rule: Language spec §4.6 (v0.345): "A string has **no `Dispose()` member** — `s.Dispose()` is a compile error ([§8.7])".

title: a string's Length is its number of code points, not its byte count
rule: Language spec §4.6 (v0.345): "`s.Length` returns the number of code points in `s`. O(1)." The user-visible model is "a sequence of code points indexed in O(1)", so a string holding one two-byte code point beside one ASCII character has length 2.

title: IsAscii is true iff every code point of the string is below 128
rule: Language spec §4.6 (v0.345): "A pure-ASCII string (every code point in U+0000–U+007F) is identical in memory layout to a UTF-8 byte sequence. Implementations expose this through the runtime predicate `s.IsAscii: bool`" (standard library §9.6). A string holding a non-ASCII code point is therefore not ASCII.

title: a method with no declared return type has the unit-type result
rule: () is the type with exactly one value, also written (). It is the return type of methods declared without an explicit return type.

title: IntPtr is available without an explicit import
rule: IntPtr and UIntPtr are compiler intrinsics ... These types live in the auto-imported System module.

title: sbyte does not implicitly convert to byte (same-width signed/unsigned)
rule: The following are never implicit: between signed and unsigned types of the same or narrower width (e.g. int -> uint, uint -> int, short -> ushort).

title: sbyte implicitly converts to short (admitted widening)
rule: sbyte implicitly converts to short, int, long, float, double, decimal (the §5.1 implicit-conversion table). Twin of s5_1_0001: same source type, a target the table admits instead of one it excludes.

title: int does not implicitly convert to uint (same-width signed/unsigned)
rule: The following are never implicit: between signed and unsigned types of the same or narrower width (e.g. int -> uint, uint -> int, short -> ushort).

title: int implicitly converts to long (admitted widening)
rule: int implicitly converts to long, float, double, decimal (the §5.1 implicit-conversion table). Twin of s5_1_0003: same source type, a target the table admits instead of one it excludes.

title: ushort implicitly converts to int (unsigned widens to a strictly larger signed type)
rule: Widening from unsigned to a strictly larger signed type (e.g. byte -> short, ushort -> int) is permitted because no value is lost.

title: float implicitly converts to double
rule: float implicitly converts to double (the §5.1 implicit-conversion table).

title: double does not implicitly convert to float
rule: Implicit conversions occur only as listed in §5.1's table; double to float narrows and is not among the table's rows. Twin of s5_1_0006: same pair, direction reversed.

title: char implicitly converts to int
rule: char implicitly converts to int, uint, long, ulong, float, double, decimal (the §5.1 implicit-conversion table).

title: decimal does not implicitly convert from double
rule: The following are never implicit: between decimal and binary floats (float, double).

title: decimal converts from double only through an explicit conversion
rule: decimal and binary floats are never implicit (§5.1); decimal(x) for binary-float x yields the value of x's shortest round-trip form under an explicit conversion (§5.2). Twin of s5_1_0009: the same pair, spelled through the admitted explicit form.

title: an enum does not implicitly convert to its underlying integer type
rule: The following are never implicit: between an enum and its underlying integer.

title: an integer does not implicitly convert to bool
rule: The following are never implicit: between integers and bool.

title: comparing an int to zero is the legal spelling the rejected int-to-bool conversion needs
rule: Between integers and bool, conversion is never implicit (§5.1); a comparison such as n <> 0 produces bool directly. Twin of s5_1_0012: same source, the comparison in place of the rejected conversion.

title: a compile-time-constant int narrows implicitly to byte when its value fits
rule: An expression of integer type that is a compile-time constant implicitly converts to any integer type whose range contains its value: var b: byte := 50; is exactly such a conversion.

title: a compile-time constant whose value does not fit the target's range is a compile error
rule: A constant whose value does not fit the target's range is a compile error at the conversion site — never a silent truncation. Twin of s5_1_0014: same target, a value outside byte's range.

title: constant narrowing crosses signedness when the constant's value fits the target's range
rule: The rule is value-based, not type-based: the source may be a compile-time constant of any integer type, and the target any integer type whose range contains the value, across signedness: const N: long := 8; var b: byte := N; is well-typed.

title: a run-time int value does not implicitly narrow to byte even when it would fit
rule: The [constant-narrowing] rule applies to constants only; a run-time int value still requires the explicit byte(x) narrowing of §5.2. Twin of s5_1_0014: the same target, a non-constant source.

title: a non-nullable value implicitly converts to its nullable form
rule: For any type T, T implicitly converts to T? — for a value type, the present-value wrapping.

title: a derived class reference implicitly converts to its base class
rule: Reference conversions are implicit: class to base class, transitively, up to Object.

title: a base class reference does not implicitly convert to a derived class
rule: Implicit conversions occur only as listed in §5.1; a downcast from a base to a derived class is not among the listed reference conversions. Twin of s5_1_0019: same pair, direction reversed.

title: a value type implicitly converts to Object by boxing
rule: Reference conversions are implicit: any type to Object — value types (primitives, records, enums, choices, non-owning inline arrays, the unit type) by boxing.

title: a call applicable through two co-equal reference conversions is an ambiguous compile error
rule: For overload resolution, reference conversions rank co-equal with the other implicit conversions: given M(a: Animal) and M(o: Object), the call M(dog) is ambiguous — upcast explicitly.

title: a base class reference does not implicitly convert to a derived class (downcast)
rule: A base-to-derived (downcast) conversion is NOT implicit per §5.1. The diagnostic wording must identify this as a downcast and cite §5.2 for the explicit cast syntax. The target type name in the diagnostic must be the real target type (Dog), not a hardcoded placeholder.

title: an unrelated class reference does not implicitly convert to another unrelated class
rule: Unrelated classes have no inheritance relationship; implicit reference conversions are only those listed in §5.1 (class to base class, transitively). This is NOT a downcast — there is no base/derived relationship at all — so the generic "not implicitly convertible" message applies.

title: an int argument to Convert's string parameter is rejected
rule: stdlib §2.3 declares `ToInt32(value: string): int` - one parameter, of type `string`. §5.1's implicit-conversion table admits no conversion from `int` to `string` (a `string` is not a numeric type and no reference conversion reaches it), so the sole candidate of §22.6 is inapplicable and the call is a compile error: the `value` argument must be a `string`.

title: a string argument to Convert's string parameter is admitted and converted
rule: stdlib §2.3 declares `ToInt32(value: string): int`. §5.1's identity reference conversion - every type converts to itself - makes the `string` parameter match exactly, so the call is admitted and §2.3's conversion produces the int 42. This is the accepting counterpart of the `int` argument the conversion table does not reach.

title: a lone Object operator overload is applicable to a class operand by reference conversion
rule: A reference conversion of a reference-typed value is representation-preserving, the same reference viewed at a wider static type (v0.338, §5.1).

title: a class reference converts implicitly to a base class two levels up
rule: §5.1 (reference conversions): "class to base class, transitively, up to `Object`". C derives from B, which derives from A; the conversion of a C reference to A is implicit, and the call through A reaches A's method.

title: an interface reference converts implicitly to an interface it transitively extends
rule: §5.1 (reference conversions): "interface to extended interface, directly or transitively". H extends J and J extends I; a K reference converts to I, and the call through I reaches K's P.

title: a class does not convert implicitly to an interface it does not implement
rule: §5.1 (reference conversions) lists the implicit conversion "a type to an interface it implements or conforms to". K declares Q, not the interface member P, so K does not implement I and the conversion of a K reference to I is not among the listed implicit conversions.

title: a class that implements the interface converts to it: the twin
rule: §5.1 (reference conversions): "a type to an interface it implements or conforms to". K declares P, so K implements I and the conversion is implicit.

title: a class implementing IEnumerable<int> converts to IEnumerable<V> under an explicit list
rule: **a type to an interface it implements or conforms to**: classes by declaration or inheritance

title: a decimal value does not implicitly convert to int
rule: A value of one type implicitly converts to another when no programmer-visible information is lost ([§5.1]). The `decimal` result of `Math.Abs(-2.5m)` has a fractional part that an `int` cannot hold, so the conversion is not implicit.

title: a decimal result binds to a decimal local without conversion
rule: every type converts to itself ([§5.1]), and "public static pure method Abs(x: decimal): decimal;" (stdlib §2.2) returns a decimal, so the `decimal` binding is accepted. The product is exact ("The result of `+`, `-`, `*`, and `/` is the exact result when" [§6.4]), and the stdlib fixes its rendering: "`0m` renders `0`" (stdlib §9.3), so the printed line is `0`.

title: a negative hex literal that does not fit uint is rejected at the conversion site
rule: uniformly with the target-typed constant's check against its declared target
check: does not fit the target's range

title: a reference element converts to its nullable view inside a covariant interface
rule: `S?` implicitly converts to `T?` whenever `S` implicitly converts to `T` ([§5.1]). For a reference type the conversion is "the same reference viewed as nullable" ([§5.1]): the non-null ArgumentException element array converts to IEnumerable<Exception?>, and the nullable-element array with one null converts the same way, so the count of null elements is 1 and the empty array adds nothing.

title: a covariant interface does not convert from a base element type to a derived one
rule: A value of one type implicitly converts to another when no programmer-visible information is lost ([§5.1]). The reference conversions admitted are "class to base class, transitively, up to `Object`" ([§5.1]); IEnumerable<Exception> to IEnumerable<ArgumentException> would narrow the element type, which needs an explicit cast.
check: not implicitly convertible to the target type

title: an int constant narrows to byte at an explicitly bound generic parameter
rule: An expression of integer type that is a compile-time constant (§17.14) implicitly converts to any integer type whose range contains its value.

title: an int constant that does not fit byte is rejected at an explicitly bound generic parameter
rule: A constant whose value does not fit the target's range is a compile error at the conversion site — never a silent truncation.
check: does not fit the target's range

title: an int constant operand narrows to uint beside a uint variable in arithmetic and comparison
rule: Constant narrowing at a ulong site. "An expression of integer type that is a **compile-time constant** implicitly converts to any integer type whose range contains its value" (§5.1, Constant narrowing, v0.340). The mixed-operand promotion of §6.2 uses §5.1, so `const K: int := 7` is admissible beside a `uint` operand and the operation is typed `uint`.

title: two integer constants of types uint and int fold with the int constant narrowed to uint
rule: Constant narrowing in a comparison. "An expression of integer type that is a **compile-time constant** implicitly converts to any integer type whose range contains its value" (§5.1, Constant narrowing, v0.340). Both operands are constants, so the narrowing applies and the expression is typed `uint`; a `uint` sum is exact (§6.1).

title: a negative int constant does not narrow to uint beside a uint constant operand
rule: A constant whose value does not fit the target's range is a **compile error** at the conversion (§5.1, Constant narrowing, v0.340). `-7` is outside `uint`'s range, and `uint` and `int` have no non-constant implicit conversion either way (§5.1), so there is no common operand type (§6.2). The twin with `const V: int := 7` is the accepting case before this one.

title: a negative int constant does not narrow to uint beside a uint variable in a comparison
rule: A constant whose value does not fit the target's range is a **compile error** at the conversion (§5.1, Constant narrowing, v0.340). `-1` is outside `uint`'s range, so the comparison `u > K` has no common operand type (§6.2).

title: every integer type and char converts to decimal preserving its value
rule: The conversion table lists `decimal` among the implicit targets of `sbyte`, `byte`, `short`, `ushort`, `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong` and `char` (§5.1, v0.340). `Math.Max<decimal>` binds its type argument explicitly, so each argument converts to `decimal`; a `decimal` renders its exact digits (stdlib §9.3).

title: a double argument does not convert to decimal at an explicitly bound Math.Max
rule: The never-implicit list in §5.1 (v0.340) includes "Between `decimal` and binary floats (`float`, `double`)". `Math.Max<decimal>(dd, 2.5)` passes a `double` literal where `decimal` is required. The twin is `2.5m`.

title: an argument not implicitly convertible to the element type is rejected at a constraint head
rule: A value of one type implicitly converts to another when no programmer-visible information is lost — the §5.1 conversions are the only ones admitted at an argument position, so an argument whose type does not convert to the parameter's type is not applicable to the candidate (§22.6).

title: an index argument of a type not implicitly convertible to int is rejected at a constraint head
rule: A value of one type implicitly converts to another when no programmer-visible information is lost — the §5.1 conversions are the only ones admitted at an argument position, so an argument whose type does not convert to the parameter's type is not applicable to the candidate (§22.6).

title: the same argument-type check applies at a user interface's inherited member
rule: A value of one type implicitly converts to another when no programmer-visible information is lost — the §5.1 conversions are the only ones admitted at an argument position, so an argument whose type does not convert to the parameter's type is not applicable to the candidate (§22.6). Inside the generic body, T's surface includes IFoo's members, regardless of which conformance category T belongs to (§14.2).

title: a returned expression whose type does not implicitly convert to the declared return type is rejected
rule: Between signed and unsigned types of the same or narrower width (e.g. `int -> uint`, `uint -> int`, `short -> ushort`). Widening from unsigned to a strictly larger signed type ... is permitted because no value is lost. (§5.1, v0.340). "The top-level operand of `return expression;` in a body with a declared return type is a **declared-result position**" (§21.7, v0.340) — the returned expression must convert to the declared return type. `1 + u` is a uint (§6.2's "the result has the larger type"), and uint does not convert to int.

title: the same returned expression is admitted where the declared return type is long
rule: Widening from unsigned to a strictly larger signed type (e.g. `byte -> short`, `ushort -> int`) is permitted because no value is lost. (§5.1, v0.340). The returned expression is a uint (§6.2's "the result has the larger type"), and uint widens to long, so the declared-result position (§21.7) is satisfied.

title: a byte index widens to an int parameter and keeps its value
rule: A value of one type implicitly converts to another when no programmer-visible information is lost, and the conversion table lists `int` among the implicit targets of `byte`; widening from unsigned to a strictly larger signed type is permitted because no value is lost. The stdlib declares the parameter as `int`: `Substring(startIndex: int)`, so the byte 128 reaches the call as the int 128 and the substring starts at the byte's own value.

title: a uint argument is not implicitly convertible to an int parameter
rule: Between signed and unsigned types of the same or narrower width (e.g. `int → uint`, `uint → int`, `short → ushort`) is never implicit; a `uint` is the same width as `int`, and the stdlib declares the parameter as `int`: `Substring(startIndex: int)`.

title: a type-parameter value does not implicitly convert to a primitive
rule: The §5.1 conversion table lists the implicit conversions, and a type parameter is not one of its source rows; §14.2 gives a type parameter the surface its constraints establish — a generic body converts a type-parameter value only to `Object` and to the bounds its constraints guarantee, never to a primitive.

title: a constant long index narrows to an int index parameter by value
rule: The rule is value-based, not type-based: the source may be a compile-time constant of any integer type — not only `int` — and the target any integer type whose range contains its value, across signedness.

title: a char index converts to an int index parameter
rule: The conversion table lists `int` among the implicit targets of `char`.

title: a double index at a user-defined indexer is rejected
rule: An indexer is a property whose name is replaced by `[parameters]`, and the index argument must convert to the indexer's parameter type: a value of one type implicitly converts to another when no programmer-visible information is lost — `double` is not among `int`'s implicit sources.

title: a long argument at an int parameter is rejected
rule: A value of one type implicitly converts to another when no programmer-visible information is lost — the conversion table lists no `long` → `int` row, and a `long` does not fit an `int` without loss.

title: a string index at a generic indexer is rejected
rule: An indexer is a property whose name is replaced by `[parameters]`, and the index argument must convert to the indexer's parameter type: a value of one type implicitly converts to another when no programmer-visible information is lost — a `string` is not among `int`'s implicit sources.

title: a byte startIndex reaches an int parameter as its unsigned value
rule: A value of one type implicitly converts to another when no programmer-visible information is lost; the conversion table lists `int` among the implicit targets of `byte`, and `byte` is an UNSIGNED type, so the widening is a zero-extension and the byte 200 is the int 200 — not the -56 a sign-extension would give. stdlib §9.6's own contract for the member reads the bound at that widened value: "code-point index of the first occurrence at or after startIndex, or -1; 0 <= startIndex <= Length (IndexOutOfRangeException otherwise)". The receiver here is 220 code points long, so a startIndex of 200 is inside the bound and the first '5' at or after it is at 205.

title: a uint constant is admitted at an int parameter by value
rule: spec §5.1: "An expression of integer type that is a **compile-time constant** (§17.14) implicitly converts to any integer type whose range contains its value ... The rule is **value-based, not type-based**: the source may be a compile-time constant of **any** integer type — not only `int` — and the target any integer type whose range contains the value, **across signedness**". The `uint` constant 16 has a value that fits `int`, so the radix parameter admits it.

title: a nullable value does not implicitly convert to a non-nullable parameter
rule: spec §5.1: "For any type `T`, `T` implicitly converts to `T?` ... Each implicit conversion of this section also **lifts** to the nullable forms: `S?` implicitly converts to `T?` whenever `S` implicitly converts to `T`". The lifting runs one way only: there is no `S?` → `T` conversion, so an `int?` reaches no `int` parameter. The local is never narrowed — §7.4 narrows a declaration only from a non-nullable initializer, and this one is nullable-typed.

title: a nullable value lifts to the nullable form of the target
rule: spec §5.1: "Each implicit conversion of this section also **lifts** to the nullable forms: `S?` implicitly converts to `T?` whenever `S` implicitly converts to `T` — a present value converts by the underlying conversion, `null` converts to `null` (`int?` → `long?`)". The `int?` argument reaches a `long?` parameter. The local is never narrowed — §7.4 narrows a declaration only from a non-nullable initializer — so the argument's static type is `int?` and the lifting is what admits it.

title: A DayOfWeek property value is not implicitly convertible to int in a variable initializer
rule: DateTime.DayOfWeek has type DayOfWeek; an enum never converts implicitly to its underlying integer (spec 5.1, 5.4).

title: A DayOfWeek reached through a chained call is not implicitly convertible to int
rule: The chained read d.AddDays(3).DayOfWeek has type DayOfWeek; an enum never converts implicitly to its underlying integer (spec 5.1, 5.4).

title: An int property reached through a chained call is not implicitly convertible to string
rule: The chained read d.AddDays(3).Year has type int, which is not implicitly convertible to string (spec 5.1).

title: A DayOfWeek value is not implicitly convertible to int as a return value
rule: DateTime.DayOfWeek has type DayOfWeek; an enum never converts implicitly to its underlying integer, so returning it from an int method is rejected (spec 5.1, 5.4).

title: a nullable DateTimeKind? bound to the non-nullable kind parameter by name is rejected
rule: A nullable `T?` is none of these kinds: by the lifting rule above it converts at most to `Object?`, never to `Object` ([§7.1](#sec-non-nullable-and-nullable-types)), so an un-narrowed `Animal?` is rejected at an `Object` parameter as it is at an `Animal` one

title: a nullable int? bound to the non-nullable millisecond parameter by name is rejected
rule: A nullable `T?` is none of these kinds: by the lifting rule above it converts at most to `Object?`, never to `Object` ([§7.1](#sec-non-nullable-and-nullable-types)), so an un-narrowed `Animal?` is rejected at an `Object` parameter as it is at an `Animal` one

title: a byte argument widens to int at a positional TimeOnly parameter without sign extension
rule: | `byte` | `short`, `ushort`, `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` |

title: byte and sbyte arguments widen to int at DateOnly's positional parameters
rule: | `byte` | `short`, `ushort`, `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` | ... | `sbyte` | `short`, `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` |

title: byte arguments widen to int at named and positional constructor parameters on every iteration
rule: | `byte` | `short`, `ushort`, `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` | ... Named arguments may appear in any order after positional arguments.

title: string Insert given a nullable string? as its named value argument is rejected
rule: A nullable `T?` is none of these kinds: by the lifting rule above it converts at most to `Object?`, never to `Object` ([§7.1](#sec-non-nullable-and-nullable-types)), so an un-narrowed `Animal?` is rejected at an `Object` parameter as it is at an `Animal` one

title: string PadCenter given a nullable char? as its named paddingChar argument is rejected
rule: A nullable `T?` is none of these kinds: by the lifting rule above it converts at most to `Object?`, never to `Object` ([§7.1](#sec-non-nullable-and-nullable-types)), so an un-narrowed `Animal?` is rejected at an `Object` parameter as it is at an `Animal` one

title: a long argument at the DateTime int day parameter is not implicitly converted: rejected
rule: | `long` | `float`, `double`, `decimal` |
check: not implicitly convertible to the target type

title: a long argument at a shorthand new(...) of a DateTime-typed local is rejected
rule: | `long` | `float`, `double`, `decimal` |
check: not implicitly convertible to the target type

title: a uint argument at the DateTime int day parameter is rejected
rule: Between signed and unsigned types of the same or narrower width
check: not implicitly convertible to the target type

title: an enum argument at the DateTime int day parameter is rejected
rule: Between an enum and its underlying integer.
check: not implicitly convertible to the target type

title: a bool argument at the StringBuilder constructor is rejected
rule: Between integers and `bool`.
check: not implicitly convertible to the target type

title: a long argument at the TimeOnly int second parameter is rejected
rule: | `long` | `float`, `double`, `decimal` |
check: not implicitly convertible to the target type

title: a uint argument at the Semaphore int initialCount parameter is rejected
rule: Between signed and unsigned types of the same or narrower width
check: not implicitly convertible to the target type

title: explicit int-from-double conversion truncates toward zero
rule: var i: int := int(d); // truncates toward zero.

title: a checked integer narrowing that does not fit raises OverflowException
rule: Integer narrowing raises OverflowException if the value does not fit.

title: an explicit conversion from int to bool is rejected
rule: bool(n) remains an error in both the implicit and explicit forms — a numeric-to-bool reading is partial and truthiness-shaped; write the comparison (n <> 0) instead.

title: casting a negative int to uint raises OverflowException
rule: A conversion between a signed and unsigned integer type of the same width is a checked narrowing: it raises OverflowException when the value is not representable in the destination type — a negative value cast to an unsigned type.

title: narrowing a double beyond float's finite range yields Infinity and never raises
rule: float(d) for double d rounds d's value to the nearest float, a tie to the even significand; a value whose rounding is not finite yields +/-Infinity and never raises — floating-point narrowing follows floating-point arithmetic's own overflow behavior.

title: an explicit conversion from bool to an integer yields 1 and 0
rule: An explicit conversion from bool to any integer type is admitted: int(b) yields 0 for false and 1 for true (total, never fails).

title: an explicit conversion from bool to double is rejected
rule: A bool source likewise does not convert to float/double/decimal (no blessed numeric reading) or char (a code point, not a number).

title: casting an integer in the surrogate range to char raises OverflowException
rule: Casting an integer to char requires the integer to fall in U+0000–U+10FFFF excluding the surrogate range; otherwise OverflowException.

title: casting an integer in the code-point range to char yields that code point
rule: Casting an integer to char requires the integer to fall in U+0000–U+10FFFF excluding the surrogate range; var c: char := char(n); // n must be a valid code point.

title: converting an out-of-range binary float to decimal raises OverflowException
rule: decimal(x) for binary-float x yields the value of x's shortest round-trip form, rounded as §4.4 states where that value is not in decimal's set; NaN, +/-Infinity, and a value out of decimal's range as §4.4 states it raise OverflowException.

title: converting decimal to double never fails
rule: double(m) and float(m) for decimal m round to the nearest representable binary value and never fail (float's and double's finite ranges exceed decimal's).

title: a constant operand the conversion would reject is a compile error at the site
rule: Where the operand of an explicit conversion is a compile-time constant whose value would raise `OverflowException` under any rule of this section — integer narrowing, the same-width signedness change, the integer-to-`char` code-point range, and the floating-point and `decimal` conversions — the conversion is a **compile error at the conversion site**, never a deferred runtime fault: `uint(-1)` is rejected where it is written.

title: the constant-operand rejection holds in unreachable code
rule: A faulting constant operand is rejected **where it is written** — the posture §5.1's constant narrowing, §5.4's constant enum cast, §6.5's constant shift count and §17.14's constant evaluation all take, which reject a faulting constant whatever its reachability.

title: a constant operand that fits converts at compile time and is admitted
rule: The rule reads the **operand**: a compile-time constant whose value the conversion admits is not rejected, and the conversion keeps its ordinary semantics — the rejection reaches only a constant whose value would raise `OverflowException`.

title: a nullable-to-nullable cast maps a null operand to null
rule: A null operand yields null; var y: long? := long?(x); // nullable to nullable; null stays null.

title: casting a null nullable to its non-nullable form raises NullReferenceException
rule: var m: int := int(n); // raises NullReferenceException if n is null.

title: a nullable cast of a present value that does not fit raises OverflowException
rule: A present value v converts by T(v) under that conversion's own semantics, including its runtime checks (OverflowException on a non-fitting present value).

title: a nullable cast of a present value that fits converts by the underlying conversion
rule: A present value v converts by T(v) under that conversion's own semantics; the nullable cast form T?(x) is admitted exactly when the corresponding non-nullable conversion T(v) is admitted.

title: a nullable cast to an enum applies the declared-constant check to a present value
rule: A present value v converts by T(v) under that conversion's own semantics, including its runtime checks — for an enum target, §5.4's declared-constant check included.

title: a nullable cast whose non-nullable conversion is inadmissible is rejected
rule: For a target type T, the nullable cast form T?(x) is admitted exactly when the corresponding non-nullable conversion T(v) is admitted from the non-nullable form of x's type — and bool(n) remains an error in both the implicit and explicit forms (§5.2).

title: an in-range int converts to its enum constant
rule: An integer-to-enum cast E(n) is checked against the declared constants: it succeeds exactly when n equals the underlying value of some declared constant of E, and yields that value.

title: an integer-to-enum cast of a constant equal to no declared constant is a compile error
rule: When n is a compile-time constant equal to no declared constant, the cast is a compile error at the cast site — the same posture as §5.1's constant-narrowing range error.
check: compile error at the cast site

title: an int-to-enum cast of a non-constant undeclared value raises OverflowException
rule: When n is not a constant, a value equal to no declared constant raises OverflowException at runtime, the diagnostic naming the enum type and the value.
