title: FromUnderlyingOrNull returns null where the checked cast would fault
rule: Boundary code for which an undeclared value is an expected input branches instead of catching: every enum carries a compiler-provided static member E.FromUnderlyingOrNull(value: U): E?, which returns null where the cast would fault.

title: under duplicate constant values the declared-value set is the set of distinct values
rule: Under duplicate constant values (§10.2), the declared-value set is the set of distinct values: E(1) where Legacy := 1, Current := 1 yields that one value.

title: a widening cast from a byte-backed enum to int cannot fail
rule: int(p) is well-typed on every enum: for byte-backed Priority it is int(byte(p)) and cannot fail — the cast I(e) converts e to U and then applies §5.2's integer conversion I(u), so a widening never fails.

title: narrowing a long-backed enum value to int raises OverflowException out of range
rule: For long-backed HttpStatus, int(s) is int(long(s)) and raises OverflowException when a NON-CONSTANT value is outside int's range; a declared-constant operand outside it is a compile error at the cast site (v0.301). A local variable read is not a constant expression (§17.14).

title: An enum read from DateTime.DayOfWeek converts to int by explicit cast, also after a chained call
rule: Enums convert to their underlying integer types by explicit cast (spec 5.4); DayOfWeek.Friday is 5 and Saturday 6 (stdlib 2.5), and byte and long casts apply likewise.

title: integer addition whose mathematical result does not fit the result type raises OverflowException
rule: Operators +, -, *, /, mod, unary -, ++, and -- on integer types are checked for overflow. An operation whose mathematical result is not representable in the result type raises OverflowException.

title: integer division truncates toward zero
rule: Division / between two integers truncates toward zero. var q := -7 / 3; // -2.

title: mod follows the dividend's sign
rule: mod follows the dividend's sign. var r := -7 mod 3; // -1.

title: integer division by zero raises DivideByZeroException
rule: Division and mod raise DivideByZeroException when the right operand is zero.

title: integer mod by zero raises DivideByZeroException
rule: Division and mod raise DivideByZeroException when the right operand is zero.

title: a compile-time constant that overflows is rejected, never deferred to runtime
rule: An evaluation fault — integer or decimal overflow, division or mod by zero, a shift count outside the §6.5 domain — is a compile error at the constant expression, never a deferred runtime fault: const B := 2147483647 + 1;.
check: compile error at the constant expression

title: mod is not defined on float or double
rule: mod is not defined on float or double; an expression of the form x mod y where either operand has a binary floating-point type is a compile error.

title: mixed int/long arithmetic promotes the int operand and the result has the wider type
rule: When operands have different types, the smaller-range operand is implicitly promoted to the larger type. The result has the larger type.

title: arithmetic between double and decimal has no implicit conversion and is a compile error
rule: If no implicit conversion exists between the operand types (e.g. double and decimal), the operation is a compile error and an explicit cast is required.

title: a binary operator over literal operands yields the larger operand type, which selects the overload
rule: Literal operands select an overload. "An expression of integer type that is a compile-time constant implicitly converts to any integer type whose range contains its value" (§5.1); "The result has the larger type." (§6.2, v0.340). `1 + 2` is int, `1 + 2L` long, `1U + 2` uint (the constant 2 converts to uint), `1UL + 2` ulong and `1 + 2.0` double.

title: a constant operand converts to the other operand's uint type in either position, then widens to long
rule: A uint operand fixes the constant's type. "An expression of integer type that is a compile-time constant implicitly converts to any integer type whose range contains its value" (§5.1); "The result has the larger type." (§6.2, v0.340). With `u: uint`, `1 + u` and `u + 1` are uint (the int constant fits uint), and the uint result widens to a `long` parameter without wrapping.

title: floating-point overflow produces Infinity rather than raising
rule: float and double arithmetic follows IEEE 754. Overflow produces +/-Infinity. No exception is raised.

title: 0.0 / 0.0 produces NaN
rule: Operations involving NaN propagate NaN. Division by zero produces +/-Infinity or NaN. No exception is raised.

title: a nonzero double divided by zero produces Infinity rather than raising
rule: Division by zero produces +/-Infinity or NaN. No exception is raised.

title: decimal arithmetic that overflows raises OverflowException
rule: decimal arithmetic raises OverflowException on overflow and DivideByZeroException on division by zero ... There is no Infinity or NaN for decimal.

title: decimal division by zero raises DivideByZeroException
rule: decimal arithmetic raises OverflowException on overflow and DivideByZeroException on division by zero.

title: the bitwise AND operator is not valid on bool
rule: Operators &, |, ^, <<, >>, and unary ~ operate on the binary representation of integer values. They are not valid on bool, char, or floating-point types.

title: bitwise complement of a signed integer equals negation of the value plus one
rule: ~x is the bitwise complement; for signed types, ~x = -(x + 1).

title: bits shifted beyond the left operand's width are discarded silently and the result never faults
rule: Within the domain, bits shifted beyond the left operand's width are discarded silently — that is the operation, exactly as & discards bits — and the result never faults.

title: a compile-time-constant shift count outside the left operand's width domain is a compile error
rule: A count outside the domain — negative, or >= width — is a fault: a compile error when the count is a compile-time constant.

title: a non-constant shift count outside the domain raises OverflowException at runtime
rule: A count outside the domain ... raises OverflowException at runtime otherwise.

title: a compound assignment on a narrower integer target writes back through a checked narrowing
rule: When T is an integer type or char and R is an integer type, the result is converted back to T by the corresponding §5.2 checked narrowing: b += 10 on b: byte is b := byte(b + 10).

title: a compound assignment's narrow-integer write-back raises OverflowException out of range
rule: b += 10 on b: byte is b := byte(b + 10) — the addition runs in int per §6.2, and a result outside byte's range raises OverflowException — never a silent truncation.

title: a read-modify-write compound assignment on a nullable operand is a compile error
rule: A read-modify-write compound assignment is a compile error when the static type of its left-hand side, or of its right operand, is a nullable type — the desugared x op e has no meaning on a nullable operand.

title: ++ is not a user-overloadable operator token
rule: Unary operators have no compound forms; ++/-- are not overloadable (v0.289) — declare operator +, write c := c + 1;.

title: a compound assignment evaluates each constituent of its left-hand side exactly once
rule: Every constituent of the left-hand side's lvalue chain is evaluated exactly once, left to right — including every index expression in the chain.

title: a compound assignment evaluates chain, getter, right operand and setter in that order
rule: The order is: the LHS chain's constituent expressions, then the final segment's getter (where applicable), then e, then the operation, then the store; when the final segment is accessor-mediated, its getter and setter are each invoked exactly once.

title: the right operand of ??= is evaluated only when the assignment occurs
rule: ??= is not a read-modify-write: x ??= e assigns e only when x's current value is null. The LHS chain is evaluated once, the getter once; e is evaluated — and the setter invoked — only when the assignment actually occurs.

title: after ??= the target is narrowed non-null and admits the ordinary compound form
rule: ??= is unaffected — it is not a read-modify-write, and the absent case is its whole purpose; after x ??= e; the target is narrowed non-null (§7.4), so the ordinary compound form applies to it from the next statement on.

title: a double-typed result against a float target is a compile error
rule: In every other case the compound form is a compile error naming the explicit remedy — notably a binary-float or decimal result against a different LHS type (f += 2.5 where f: float promotes to double): write f := float(f + 2.5); when that loss is intended.

title: a float-typed result against a float target stores directly
rule: Let T be the left-hand side's type and R the type of x op e; if R is T, or R implicitly converts to T, the result is stored directly — write f += 2.5f; float promotion stays in-family.

title: a constant shift count outside the left operand's domain is rejected in <<=
rule: x <<= k and x >>= k inherit §6.5's count-domain rule through the desugaring: an out-of-domain count is the same fault — compile error for a constant count, OverflowException at runtime otherwise.

title: a non-constant shift count outside the domain raises OverflowException in <<=
rule: x <<= k and x >>= k inherit §6.5's count-domain rule through the desugaring: an out-of-domain count is the same fault — compile error for a constant count, OverflowException at runtime otherwise.

title: a nullable right operand to a read-modify-write compound assignment is rejected
rule: A read-modify-write compound assignment is a compile error when the static type of its left-hand side, or of its right operand, is a nullable type — either position, or both — static type read after §7.4's narrowing.

title: a nullable reference-typed target of += is rejected
rule: A read-modify-write compound assignment is a compile error when the static type of its left-hand side is a nullable type — a nullable reference-typed target included: the desugared x op e has no meaning on a nullable operand — static type read after §7.4's narrowing.

title: the narrow-integer write-back does not extend to a plain assignment
rule: The write-back is scoped to the compound form only: plain b := b + 10 remains the §6.2/§5.1 compile error it has always been, so the no-implicit-narrowing rule is undisturbed everywhere else.

title: a compound assignment selects a user operator whose parameter is a stdlib class
rule: For every operator above except `??=`, the statement `x op= e` is equivalent to `x := x op e` ([§6.6]). "For `a <op> b` on non-primitive operands, the candidate set is the union of the `operator <op>` overloads declared on the static types of both operands, including declarations inherited from their base classes" ([§25.2]): `v += r` is `v := v + r`, and it selects the `StringBuilder` overload.

title: a compound assignment selects a user operator whose parameter is Object
rule: For every operator above except `??=`, the statement `x op= e` is equivalent to `x := x op e` ([§6.6]). "reference types (classes including the heap arrays, interfaces, `string`, function types) directly" ([§5.1]): the `StringBuilder` operand converts to the `Object` parameter.

title: a compound assignment selects a user operator whose parameter is an interface
rule: For every operator above except `??=`, the statement `x op= e` is equivalent to `x := x op e` ([§6.6]). "records and enums by declaration" ([§5.1]): the record `Tag` conforms to `IA` by its declaration, so it converts to the `IA` parameter.

title: a compound assignment with no applicable user operator is rejected
rule: For every operator above except `??=`, the statement `x op= e` is equivalent to `x := x op e` ([§6.6]). "nor an overload from the candidate set above applies is a compile error at the expression" ([§25.2]): no overload accepts a `StringBuilder` for `IA`.

title: a non-nullable reference implicitly converts to its nullable form
rule: A non-nullable reference type implicitly converts to its nullable form.

title: a nullable reference does not implicitly convert to its non-nullable form
rule: The reverse (nullable to non-nullable) requires a null check or `!`.

title: a null literal is not passed to a non-nullable string parameter of a stdlib member
rule: Language spec §7.1 (v0.350): "A plain reference type is non-nullable; a `?` suffix produces its nullable form", and "The compiler enforces the distinction at every assignment, parameter pass, and return." The parameter is `s: string`, not `string?`, in stdlib §9.1's `public static pure method Parse(s: string): int;` (v0.350).

title: the same parse call with a non-null string argument is accepted and runs
rule: Language spec §7.1 (v0.350): "The compiler enforces the distinction at every assignment, parameter pass, and return." The parameter admits a string, and stdlib §9.1 (v0.350) declares `public static pure method Parse(s: string): int;`.

title: a nullable value type either holds a value or null
rule: A value type wrapped in `?` is an optional: it either holds a value or `null`.

title: assigning null to a non-nullable local is rejected
rule: Assigning `null` to a non-nullable target is a compile error.

title: assigning null to a nullable local is admitted
rule: Assigning `null` to a non-nullable target is a compile error (contrapositive: a nullable target admits it).

title: member access on an unnarrowed nullable value is rejected
rule: Member access, method calls, and indexing on a nullable value are compile errors unless the compiler has narrowed it to non-null.

title: a null test narrows the true branch for member access
rule: A null test — `x <> null` — narrows the true branch, admitting member access there.

title: an early exit on the null branch narrows the surviving path
rule: An early exit — after `if x = null then return; end;` — narrows the surviving path.

title: is not null narrows to the non-nullable form
rule: `x is not null` narrows to the non-nullable form.

title: a mutable field never narrows, even after a null check
rule: The compiler narrows local variables, parameters other than `ref` parameters, and `readonly` fields in the tracked shape below; these are the narrowing carriers. It never narrows mutable fields, properties, or `ref` parameters.

title: copying a mutable field to a local admits narrowing on the copy
rule: The standard pattern is to copy a nullable field to a local before narrowing; local-variable narrowing then applies to the copy.

title: reassignment from a nullable expression invalidates narrowing
rule: The narrowing of a variable is invalidated when, within the controlled block, the variable is reassigned from a nullable-typed expression.

title: passing a narrowed local as a ref argument invalidates narrowing
rule: The narrowing of a variable is invalidated when, within the controlled block, the variable is passed as a `ref` or `out` argument (the callee may reassign it).

title: a nullable readonly field narrows across an intervening call
rule: A nullable `readonly` field participates in flow narrowing, because outside its construction window it has no writer on any path, through any alias, so no call can invalidate a fact about its value.

title: a mutably-captured local loses its narrowing at an intervening call
rule: A variable that is mutably captured — assigned anywhere inside any lambda of the enclosing function body — loses its narrowing once the controlled block performs any operation that can transfer control to user code, such as a method call.

title: reassigning a narrowed local from a nullable expression inside a nested if invalidates it
rule: The narrowing of a variable is invalidated when, within the controlled block: the variable is reassigned from a nullable-typed expression; or   (v0.338 §7.4 lines 906, 908)

title: reassigning a narrowed local from a non-nullable expression leaves it narrowed
rule: after `x := expr;` where `expr`'s static type is non-nullable — or `expr` is itself narrowed non-null at that point — `x` is narrowed until invalidated (v0.338 §7.4 line 903; the invalidation list at lines 906-910 names only reassignment from a nullable-typed expression)

title: passing a narrowed local as a ref argument invalidates its narrowing
rule: the variable is passed as a `ref` **or `out`** argument (the callee may — for `out`, must (§22.3) — reassign it. ... (v0.338 §7.4 line 909)

title: passing a copy of a narrowed local as a ref argument leaves the original narrowed
rule: Local-variable narrowing applies to the copy, which no other thread can observe. (v0.338 §7.4 line 933) The invalidation at line 909 applies to the variable passed as a `ref` or `out` argument: here the argument is a different local, `c`, and `s` is not passed.

title: a mutably captured local loses its narrowing at an intervening invocation of a function value
rule: the variable is **mutably captured** — assigned, or passed as `ref`/`out`, anywhere inside any lambda of the enclosing function body (§27.5) — and the block performs *any* operation that can transfer control to user code: a method, constructor, accessor, or user-defined-operator call, an invocation of a function value, or an `await` (v0.338 §7.4 line 910)

title: a mutably captured local keeps its narrowing for a straight-line check-then-use
rule: Straight-line check-then-use of a captured local (`if x <> null then x.M(); end;` — no call *between* the test and the use) remains accepted. (v0.338 §7.4 line 910)

title: a narrowing is invalidated by a reassignment that reaches the loop head on the back-edge
rule: Narrowing is flow-sensitive: at each program point the compiler tracks, per local variable ... whether its value is known non-null. (v0.338 §7.4 line 898) The narrowing of a variable is invalidated when, within the controlled block: ... the variable is reassigned from a nullable-typed expression (v0.338 §7.4 lines 906, 908). title: a narrowing survives a loop back-edge when the loop reassigns from non-nullable

title: a declaration whose initializer is a non-null string narrows a nullable local for an argument
rule: from a declaration whose initializer is such an `expr` ([§7.4]), and "where `expr`'s static type is non-nullable": a string literal initializer narrows the local, so passing it where a non-nullable string is required is admitted.

title: a declaration whose initializer is a new class instance narrows a nullable local for an argument
rule: from a declaration whose initializer is such an `expr` ([§7.4]), and "where `expr`'s static type is non-nullable": the `new Dog()` initializer has a non-nullable static type, so the local is narrowed and passes to a non-nullable parameter.

title: a non-null int declaration initializer narrows a nullable local for a constructor argument

title: a null declaration initializer does not narrow the local for a non-nullable parameter
rule: The reverse requires a null check or `!`. ([§7.1]); a `null` initializer does not satisfy "where `expr`'s static type is non-nullable", so the declared `string?` local is not narrowed ([§7.4]).

title: a nullable call result as declaration initializer does not narrow the local for an argument
rule: The reverse requires a null check or `!`. ([§7.1]); the call's static type is `string?`, which fails "where `expr`'s static type is non-nullable", so the declared local is not narrowed ([§7.4]).

title: a copy of a nullable local that was never narrowed does not narrow, so passing the copy is rejected
rule: The reverse requires a null check or `!`. ([§7.1]); the initializer `t` has the nullable static type `string?`, which fails "where `expr`'s static type is non-nullable", so the copy is not narrowed ([§7.4]).

title: a catch arm that completes normally reads a nullable string after a call that may raise
rule: a fact holds at a point only when it holds on every path that reaches it ([§7.4]). "Any exception may propagate from any method call." ([§31.3]). The catch arm completes normally on the path where `s` was set to null before the call, so the read after the try sees a null `s`. "every statement of the block is a possible throw point for every `catch` arm and for the `finally`" ([§7.4]).

title: a catch arm that returns leaves only the non-null try path to the read
rule: a fact holds at a point only when it holds on every path that reaches it ([§7.4]). "`return` exits the nearest enclosing callable" ([§21.7]), so the catch arm reaches no point after the try; the only path to the read is the try block, which stores a non-null value last.

title: a finally that stores null makes the read after the try nullable
rule: `finally` runs whether the protected block completed normally, was exited by an exception (caught or uncaught), or was exited by `return` — or by a `break` or `continue` targeting an enclosing loop. ([§31.2]). "the variable is reassigned from a nullable-typed expression" ([§7.4]): the finally's null store is on the only path to the read.

title: a finally that stores a non-null string leaves the read after the try narrowed
rule: `finally` runs whether the protected block completed normally, was exited by an exception (caught or uncaught), or was exited by `return` — or by a `break` or `continue` targeting an enclosing loop. title: a catch arm reads a nullable string that the try stored null before a call that may raise
rule: a fact holds at a point only when it holds on every path that reaches it ([§7.4]). "Any exception may propagate from any method call." ([§31.3]). The arm is reached from the call that follows `s := null`, so `s` is null when the arm reads it. "every statement of the block is a possible throw point for every `catch` arm and for the `finally`" ([§7.4]).

title: a catch arm reads a string narrowed at entry to the try, past non-null stores in the block
rule: a fact holds at a point only when it holds on every path that reaches it ([§7.4]). "after `x := expr;` where `expr`'s static type is non-nullable" ([§7.4]) "`x` is narrowed until invalidated" ([§7.4]). "every statement of the block is a possible throw point for every `catch` arm and for the `finally`" ([§7.4]). "A `catch` arm and the `finally` block therefore begin with the facts that held at entry to the protected block, less every fact the block invalidates at any point (by the forms above), and no fact the block establishes reaches them" ([§7.4]). The two stores in the block, `s := "z"` and `s := "y"`, are non-nullable, so neither invalidates anything: the reassignment form invalidates only from a nullable-typed expression, and no `ref` or `out` argument or lambda capture is involved. No block-established fact reaches an arm, so the arm's read is narrowed only because the entry fact, the declaration narrowing of `var s: string? := "x"`, survives into the arm.

title: a break leaving a try runs the finally's null store before the read after the loop
rule: `finally` runs whether the protected block completed normally, was exited by an exception (caught or uncaught), or was exited by `return` — or by a `break` or `continue` targeting an enclosing loop. ([§31.2]). "the variable is reassigned from a nullable-typed expression" ([§7.4]): on the break path the finally's null store runs before the read after the loop.

title: a break leaving a try reads a narrowed string when the finally stores a non-null value
rule: `finally` runs whether the protected block completed normally, was exited by an exception (caught or uncaught), or was exited by `return` — or by a `break` or `continue` targeting an enclosing loop. ([§31.2]). "after `x := expr;` where `expr`'s static type is non-nullable" ([§7.4]) "`x` is narrowed until invalidated" ([§7.4]): every path to the read after the loop ends with a non-nullable finally store.

title: a read after a try with a catch arm is nullable when the arm exit carries the block's null store
rule: every statement of the block is a possible throw point for every `catch` arm and for the `finally` ([§7.4]). "The point after the statement is reached only through the block's normal completion or an arm's exit, each through the `finally`: it holds the facts common to those exits — the every-path rule" ([§7.4]). The block's normal completion ends with `s := "y"`, a non-nullable store, so `s` is non-null there. The arm's entry loses the declaration narrowing, because the block reassigns `s` "from a nullable-typed expression" ([§7.4]) (`s := null`). The arm's exit holds no narrowing of `s`, and the common facts omit it, so the read after the `try` is nullable.

title: a read after a try with a catch arm is narrowed by a non-null store that follows the try
rule: after `x := expr;` where `expr`'s static type is non-nullable ([§7.4]) "`x` is narrowed until invalidated" ([§7.4]). The store `s := "z"` after the statement is non-nullable, so the read is narrowed. The point after the statement is reached through the normal completion of the block or an arm's exit, and the store after the statement holds on every such path: the block does not throw, so the arm does not run and prints nothing.

title: a finally reads a string the block narrowed; its entry fact is null, so the read is nullable
rule: every statement of the block is a possible throw point for every `catch` arm and for the `finally` ([§7.4]). "A `catch` arm and the `finally` block therefore begin with the facts that held at entry to the protected block, less every fact the block invalidates at any point (by the forms above), and no fact the block establishes reaches them" ([§7.4]). The declaration `var s: string? := null` establishes no narrowing, since its initializer is not non-nullable ("from a declaration whose initializer is such an `expr`" ([§7.4])). The block's `s := "x"` establishes narrowing that does not reach the `finally`, so `s` is nullable there and the read is a compile error.
check: member access `.Length` on a nullable value requires narrowing

title: a finally narrows a nullable string inside its own null test and prints both lines
rule: A fact needed inside an arm or a `finally` is established inside it (`if s <> null then …`), and one needed after a `try` with arms is carried by every arm or re-established after the statement ([§7.4]). The test `s <> null` inside the `finally` narrows `s` for its body, so the read is legal and the `finally` prints its length, after the block has printed "a" through `Log`.

title: a finally reads a string its declaration narrowed, past a try that only forms a lambda
rule: The mutable-capture invalidation needs the block to perform an operation that can transfer control to user code: "a method, constructor, accessor, or user-defined-operator call, an invocation of a function value, or an `await`" ([§7.4]). The try block only forms a lambda that assigns `s`, which is "assigned, or passed as `ref`/`out`, anywhere inside any lambda of the enclosing function body" ([§7.4]), and it invokes nothing, so it invalidates nothing. The `finally` begins with the declaration narrowing "from a declaration whose initializer is such an `expr`" ([§7.4]), less "less every fact the block invalidates at any point" ([§7.4]), so `s.Length` reads 1.

title: a finally reads a nullable string after the try block stores null into it directly
rule: The try block stores the null literal into `s`, a nullable-typed expression, which is an invalidating form: "the variable is reassigned from a nullable-typed expression" ([§7.4]). The `finally` begins with "less every fact the block invalidates at any point" ([§7.4]), so `s` is not narrowed at the read, and "Member access, method calls, and indexing on a nullable value are compile errors unless the compiler has narrowed it to non-null" ([§7.4]) rejects `s.Length`.

title: a finally reads a string that a lambda invoked in the try block nulls
rule: The try block invokes the lambda, "an invocation of a function value" ([§7.4]), which is one of the operations that can transfer control to user code. The lambda assigns `s`: "assigned, or passed as `ref`/`out`, anywhere inside any lambda of the enclosing function body" ([§7.4]). So "the variable is mutably captured" ([§7.4]) holds in the block, and "less every fact the block invalidates at any point" ([§7.4]) removes the narrowing from the `finally`, which rejects `s.Length`.

title: a finally reads a string that a lambda nulls, after a method call in the try block
rule: The try block calls `P.Boom(false)`, "a method, constructor, accessor, or user-defined-operator call" ([§7.4]), which can transfer control to user code. The lambda formed later in the same block assigns `s`, and the rule is over "anywhere inside any lambda of the enclosing function body" ([§7.4]), so the position of the formation does not matter. "the variable is mutably captured" ([§7.4]) therefore holds in the block, and "less every fact the block invalidates at any point" ([§7.4]) leaves the `finally` unnarrowed, so `s.Length` is rejected.

title: a finally reads a narrowed string before it invokes a lambda that nulls it
rule: The lambda is formed before the `try` and invoked only in the `finally`, after the read. "A `catch` arm and the `finally` block therefore begin with the facts that held at entry to the protected block" ([§7.4]), and the protected block here is `var k := 1;`, which performs no operation that transfers control, so the entry fact survives. "Straight-line check-then-use of a captured local" ([§7.4]) is admitted, and the read comes before the call `f()`: "the `finally`'s own statements then establish and invalidate as any straight-line code does" ([§7.4]) puts the invalidation after the read. title: a finally calls a lambda that nulls a string, then reads the string
rule: The `finally` invokes the lambda, "an invocation of a function value" ([§7.4]), before the read, and the lambda assigns `s`, so "the variable is mutably captured" ([§7.4]). "the `finally`'s own statements then establish and invalidate as any straight-line code does" ([§7.4]): the invocation invalidates the narrowing before `s.Length` is read, and the read is rejected.

title: a finally reads a narrowed string past a try that only forms nested lambdas
rule: The try block forms one lambda inside another and invokes neither, so it performs no operation that can transfer control to user code. "A `catch` arm and the `finally` block therefore begin with the facts that held at entry to the protected block" ([§7.4]), and nothing in the block invalidates the narrowing: forming a lambda is not among the operations listed in "a method, constructor, accessor, or user-defined-operator call, an invocation of a function value, or an `await`" ([§7.4]). The `finally` reads `s.Length` as 1.

title: a finally reads a string after a try block passes it by ref to a method
rule: the variable is passed as a `ref` or `out` argument ([§7.4]): `P.Clear(ref s)` in the try block invalidates the narrowing, and so does the lambda formed in the block that assigns `s`, since "the variable is mutably captured" ([§7.4]) and the block performs a call. "(or `throw`, `break`, `continue` in that branch)" ([§7.4]) is an early exit, and "a fact rides its root (reassigning `v` drops it)" ([§7.4]).

rule: The compiler tracks, per local variable and per parameter other than a `ref` parameter, whether its value is known non-null and member access on a nullable value is a compile error "unless the compiler has narrowed it to non-null" (§7.4, v0.340); a `with` "result has the same static type as the source" (§9.5, v0.340), so the compiler "never narrows mutable fields, properties, or `ref` parameters" (§7.4, v0.340), so the early-exit test on `Item` does not make `Item with(...)` non-null.
check: the returned value is nullable but the target type is non-nullable

title: a with is not narrowed after a call when the local is mutably captured by a lambda
rule: The compiler tracks, per local variable and per parameter other than a `ref` parameter, whether its value is known non-null and member access on a nullable value is a compile error "unless the compiler has narrowed it to non-null" (§7.4, v0.340); a `with` "result has the same static type as the source" (§9.5, v0.340), so a mutably captured local loses its fact at the first operation that can transfer control to user code (§7.4, v0.340): the call `Id()` follows the test, and the lambda assigns `p`.

title: a with in the else branch of a <> null test is not narrowed
rule: The compiler tracks, per local variable and per parameter other than a `ref` parameter, whether its value is known non-null and member access on a nullable value is a compile error "unless the compiler has narrowed it to non-null" (§7.4, v0.340); a `with` "result has the same static type as the source" (§9.5, v0.340), so a test narrows only "the true branch" for `<>`; in the `else` branch the local is known null, never narrowed non-null.
check: the initializer for `r` is nullable but the target type is non-nullable

title: a with over a parameter narrowed by an is T test is the non-nullable record type
rule: The compiler tracks "per local variable and per parameter other than a `ref` parameter, whether its value is known non-null" (§7.4, v0.340), and when a test succeeds the carrier "is flow-narrowed to `T` within the controlled block" (§12.7, v0.340); a `with` "result has the same static type as the source" (§9.5, v0.340). So a `P?` parameter narrowed by an `is P` test has source type `P` in the block, and the `with` result is a `P`.

title: a with over a generic record narrowed by an is T test is the non-nullable generic record type
rule: The compiler tracks "per local variable and per parameter other than a `ref` parameter, whether its value is known non-null" (§7.4, v0.340), and when a test succeeds the carrier "is flow-narrowed to `T` within the controlled block" (§12.7, v0.340); a `with` "result has the same static type as the source" (§9.5, v0.340). The rule is independent of the record being generic: a `Box<int>?` narrowed by an `is Box<int>` test yields a `Box<int>` with.

title: a method call on an unnarrowed nullable local is rejected
rule: Member access, method calls, and indexing on a nullable value are compile errors unless the compiler has narrowed it to non-null.

title: a method call on an unnarrowed nullable parameter is rejected
rule: Member access, method calls, and indexing on a nullable value are compile errors unless the compiler has narrowed it to non-null. A parameter is a narrowing carrier — "the compiler narrows local variables, parameters other than `ref` parameters, and `readonly` fields" — but only once one of the narrowing forms has established the fact; a parameter that was never narrowed is read at its declared type.

title: a member access on a nullable property is rejected
rule: The compiler narrows local variables, parameters other than `ref` parameters, and `readonly` fields in the tracked shape below; these are the narrowing carriers. It never narrows mutable fields, properties, or `ref` parameters.

title: a member call on a nullable call result is rejected
rule: Member access, method calls, and indexing on a nullable value are compile errors unless the compiler has narrowed it to non-null. A call result is an expression, not a narrowing carrier, so it is read at its declared type.

title: a member call on a nullable index result is rejected
rule: Member access, method calls, and indexing on a nullable value are compile errors unless the compiler has narrowed it to non-null. An index expression is an expression, not a narrowing carrier, so it is read at its declared type.

title: a declaration whose initializer is a non-null literal narrows the local for a member call
rule: The knowledge is established by ... assignment: ... and from a declaration whose initializer is such an `expr` — `var x: T? := expr;` or `const x: T? := expr;` — which is the declaration's assignment.

title: a member call on an unnarrowed nullable readonly field is rejected
rule: Member access, method calls, and indexing on a nullable value are compile errors unless the compiler has narrowed it to non-null. A nullable `readonly` field participates in flow narrowing — it is a narrowing carrier — but only once a narrowing form has established the fact.

title: the false branch of an or composition sees the left operand's false-facts
rule: spec §7.4: "boolean composition of tests: in `A and B`, `B` (and the true branch) is checked under `A`'s true-facts; in `A or B`, `B` (and the false branch) sees `A`'s false-facts". On the false path of `r = null or false` the left operand's null test was false, so `r` is non-null there. The local itself is never narrowed — §7.4 narrows a declaration only from a non-nullable initializer, and this one is nullable-typed — so the composition is what narrows it.

title: a call result is not a binding the compiler tracks a narrowing for
rule: spec §7.4: "at each program point the compiler tracks, per local variable and per parameter other than a `ref` parameter ..., whether its value is known non-null", and the establishing forms it lists are a null test, a `case` arm, boolean composition, an early exit, an assignment, a declaration's initializer, and a `when true` postcondition. A call's result is none of them, so the nullable it returns stays nullable.

title: a type fact composes through an early exit
rule: spec §7.4: "an early exit: after `if x = null then return; end;` ... the surviving path is narrowed — and a type fact (§12.7) composes the same way: after `if x is not T then return; end;`, with the same exits and through `elif`/`else` branches that all exit, ... the surviving path is narrowed to `T`". After the `is not Dog` test the surviving path carries the Dog fact, so the `Animal?` parameter is a `Dog` there and is exact at the `Dog` parameter.

title: a narrowed int? passed as an int argument is its value, so IndexOf finds it
rule: After `if x is null then return; end;` "the surviving path is narrowed"; the stdlib's `Array<T>.IndexOf(item: T, startIndex: int := 0): int` returns "first occurrence at or after startIndex, or -1". The narrowed `n` is a non-nullable operand, and `n` is 1, at index 0 of `[1, 2]`.

title: a nullable local narrowed by an early return passes as its non-null int to a stdlib call
rule: Narrowing also applies after early return and "an early exit: after `if x is null then return; end;` … the surviving path is narrowed". On the surviving path `n: int?` is non-null, so `a.IndexOf(n)` takes it as an `int` argument, and `IndexOf` returns the zero-based index of the first match. (§7.4, v0.350; `IndexOf` is stdlib §4.4.)

title: A nullable passed to Math.Abs in the then-branch of `is null` stays nullable
rule: In the true branch of `e is null` the variable is known null, not non-null: "x = null or x is null (narrowing the *false* branch)" (§7.4, v0.350) narrows only the other branch, so `Math.Abs(e)` receives a `double?`, which `Abs(x: double)` refuses.

title: A nullable passed to Math.Max after a join point is not narrowed
rule: A fact "holds at a point only when it holds on every path that reaches it" (§7.4, v0.350). After `if e <> null then ... end;` the path where the test failed also reaches the join, so `e` is `double?` and Math.Max(e, 1.0) is refused.

title: A nullable passed to Math.Abs in the else branch of `<> null` stays nullable
rule: Only the true branch of `x <> null` is narrowed (§7.4, v0.350); in the else branch `e` is still `double?` and `Math.Abs(e)` is refused.

title: Reassigning a narrowed local from a nullable expression invalidates the narrowing
rule: The narrowing of a variable is invalidated when ... the variable is reassigned from a nullable-typed expression (§7.4, v0.350). After `d := null;` the `Math.Abs(d)` argument is `double?`.

title: A mutably captured local loses its narrowing after a call, so Math.Abs refuses it
rule: A variable assigned inside a lambda is mutably captured and "after the first such operation [a call] the narrowing is gone" (§7.4, v0.350). The call `h()` sits between the test and the use, so `Math.Abs(d)` receives a `double?`.

title: Math.Max of a mutably captured local is refused after an intervening call
rule: Same rule as the Abs form: "any operation that can transfer control to user code" invalidates a mutably captured local (§7.4, v0.350), and an invocation of a function value is one. Generic Max<T> then sees `double?`.

title: A non-readonly field is never narrowed, so Math.Abs of it is refused
rule: Narrowing applies to locals -- and `readonly` fields -- only (§7.4, v0.350). A mutable `double?` field tested with `<> null` stays `double?` at the use.

title: A nullable parameter is not narrowed without a null test, so Math.Abs is refused
rule: A parameter is narrowed only by the forms of §7.4 (v0.350); with no test, `x: double?` reaches `Math.Abs(x)` as `double?`, which `Abs(x: double)` refuses.

title: A nullable long reassigned null inside the test still reaches Convert.ToString as nullable
rule: Reassignment from a nullable-typed expression invalidates the narrowing (§7.4, v0.350). Convert.ToString(value: long) (stdlib §2.3) then receives `long?`.

title: Narrowed nullable passes to non-nullable parameter: a loop that reassigns a non-null value keeps the
rule: Narrowing is flow-sensitive: after `x := expr;` where expr's static type is non-nullable, x is narrowed until invalidated, and a `readonly` field narrows (spec 7.4, How narrowing is established). A narrowed nullable value converts to the non-nullable parameter type (spec 7.1). A loop body that only reassigns non-null values keeps the narrowing at the loop head.

title: Narrowed nullable passes to non-nullable parameter: a readonly field narrowed by a null test
rule: Narrowing is flow-sensitive: after `x := expr;` where expr's static type is non-nullable, x is narrowed until invalidated, and a `readonly` field narrows (spec 7.4, How narrowing is established). A narrowed nullable value converts to the non-nullable parameter type (spec 7.1). The readonly field `_n` narrows under `_n <> null`.

title: Narrowed nullable passes to non-nullable parameter: an early return on `x = null` narrows the surviv
rule: Narrowing is flow-sensitive: after `x := expr;` where expr's static type is non-nullable, x is narrowed until invalidated, and a `readonly` field narrows (spec 7.4, How narrowing is established). title: Narrowed nullable passes to non-nullable parameter: a conjunction of null tests narrows char and int

rule: Narrowing is flow-sensitive: after `x := expr;` where expr's static type is non-nullable, x is narrowed until invalidated, and a `readonly` field narrows (spec 7.4, How narrowing is established). A narrowed nullable value converts to the non-nullable parameter type (spec 7.1). `d := i * 1.5` has a non-nullable type, so d is narrowed at the use.

A narrowed nullable value converts to the non-nullable parameter type (spec 7.1). Char.ToLower, IsWhiteSpace, IsLetterOrDigit and IsPunctuation take a char (stdlib 9.5).

title: Narrowed nullable passes to non-nullable parameter: Double and Float statics over narrowed locals

A narrowed nullable value converts to the non-nullable parameter type (spec 7.1). Append has per-type overloads for the numeric primitives (stdlib 3.1); a decimal renders without trailing zeros (stdlib 9.3).

title: Nullable passed to non-nullable parameter is rejected: a loop whose body reassigns null invalidates

A fact holds at a join only when it holds on every path.

A call's static type is nullable and establishes no fact.

title: Nullable passed to non-nullable parameter is rejected: a ref argument invalidates the narrowing
rule: Narrowing is invalidated when the variable is reassigned from a nullable-typed expression, is passed as `ref`/`out`, or is mutably captured (spec 7.4, How narrowing is invalidated); an un-narrowed nullable argument for a non-nullable parameter is a compile error (spec 7.1). A `ref` argument may reassign the local, uniformly.

rule: Narrowing is invalidated when the variable is reassigned from a nullable-typed expression, is passed as `ref`/`out`, or is mutably captured (spec 7.4, How narrowing is invalidated); an un-narrowed nullable argument for a non-nullable parameter is a compile error (spec 7.1). StringBuilder declares no Append overload over a nullable value (stdlib 3.1).

title: null-conditional access performs the access when the receiver is non-null
rule: `x?.M` returns null if `x` is null; otherwise it performs the access. The result type is always nullable.

title: a null receiver skips the whole chain, including argument expressions
rule: If a null receiver is found, nothing to the right of it in the chain is evaluated — no member is read, no call is performed, and the argument expressions of the skipped suffixes are not evaluated: `user?.Log(Render(x))` calls neither `Log` nor `Render` when `user` is null.

title: a null segment anywhere in a chain makes the whole chain null
rule: If any segment of a chain is null, the remainder of the chain is skipped on the same terms and the whole chain's result is `null`.

title: a null-conditional Count on a non-null array is its count
rule: `x?.M` returns null if `x` is null; otherwise it performs the access. The result type is always nullable.

title: a null-conditional Count on a null array is null
rule: `x?.M` returns null if `x` is null; otherwise it performs the access. The null result is rendered as `null` in an interpolated hole (18.5).

title: a null-conditional Length on a non-null string is its length
rule: `x?.M` returns null if `x` is null; otherwise it performs the access. The result type is always nullable.

title: the result of a null-conditional Count is nullable and does not convert to int
rule: The result type is always nullable: `x?.M` has the nullable type of M's result, so a non-nullable int binding of `b?.Count` is a compile error.

title: the result of a null-conditional Count binds to a nullable int and holds the count
rule: The result type is always nullable: `x?.M` binds to a nullable int, and a non-null receiver yields the count.

title: a null-conditional Count call on a non-null array yields its count
rule: `x?.M` returns null if `x` is null; otherwise it performs the access. ([§7.5]). With a non-null receiver the access is the call `Count()`, which yields the element count, 2.

title: a null-conditional Count call on a null array falls back through ??
rule: `x?.M` returns null if `x` is null; otherwise it performs the access. ([§7.5]) and "`a ?? b` returns `a` if non-null, else `b`." ([§7.7]): a null receiver makes the `??` take its fallback, -1.

title: the result of a null-conditional Count call is nullable and does not convert to int
rule: The result type is always nullable ([§7.5]), so a non-nullable `int` binding of `a?.Count()` is a compile error.

title: the nullable result of a null-conditional Count call is well-typed with ?? to int
rule: The result type is always nullable ([§7.5]); "`a ?? b` returns `a` if non-null, else `b`." ([§7.7]): with the fallback `0` the `int` binding is well-typed and holds the count, 2.

title: a local named Count does not change a null-conditional Count call
rule: `x?.M` returns null if `x` is null; otherwise it performs the access. ([§7.5]) "`a ?? b` returns `a` if non-null, else `b`." ([§7.7]) A local named `Count` is a different binding from the member access `a?.Count()`, so `Count ?? -9` is the local's value, -9.

title: ?. on a nullable IGrouping with ?? defaults yields the group key and count
rule: `x?.M` returns null if `x` is null; otherwise it performs the access ([§7.5]), and "`a ?? b` returns `a` if non-null, else `b`" ([§7.7]). The groups of [1, 2, 2] have keys 1 and 2 with counts 1 and 2, and each iteration prints the key and then the count: 1, 1, 2, 2.

title: a null-conditional GroupBy then ToArray keeps the chain non-null and its Count is the group count
rule: `x?.M` returns null if `x` is null; otherwise it performs the access ([§7.5]). "public method GroupBy<TKey>(key: (T) -> TKey): IEnumerable<IGrouping<TKey, T>> where TKey: hashable;" (stdlib §5) puts 1 and 3 in one group and 2 and 4 in another for `x mod 2`, so the array has 2 groups and the count is 2.

title: a null-conditional access to an undeclared grouping member is refused
rule: `x?.M` returns null if `x` is null; otherwise it performs the access ([§7.5]). The grouping is not null here, so `g?.Foo` performs the access, and "readonly property Key: TKey;" ([stdlib §5]) is the only property "public interface IGrouping<TKey, T>: IEnumerable<T>" declares, so `Foo` names no member and the access is refused.

title: a null-conditional string member access short-circuits on a null receiver
rule: `x?.M` returns null if `x` is null; otherwise it performs the access. `?.` short-circuits: the receiver is evaluated first; if it is null the access does not occur and nothing to its right in the chain is evaluated. `Substring` and `IndexOf` are declared members of `String` (stdlib §9.6), so `s?.Substring(0)` and `t?.IndexOf('c')` are member accesses the rule admits. The second control line's value is fixed by stdlib §9.6's own contract — `IndexOf` returns the code-point index of the first occurrence, or -1 — and not by the compiler: `Substring` has no result contract in §9.6, so a control line that printed a `Substring` result would pin compiler behaviour rather than spec behaviour.

title: named arguments of a null-conditional call evaluate in written order, skipped on null
rule: `?.` short-circuits. The receiver is evaluated first; if it is null the access does not occur and nothing to its right in the chain is evaluated — no member is read, no call is performed, and the argument and index expressions of the skipped suffixes are not evaluated either. ... A call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order — left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs

title: a null-conditional call with named arguments in a lambda and a generic method evaluates in order
rule: `?.` short-circuits. The receiver is evaluated first; if it is null the access does not occur and nothing to its right in the chain is evaluated — no member is read, no call is performed, and the argument and index expressions of the skipped suffixes are not evaluated either. ... rule: `?.` short-circuits. title: a null-conditional read of Array.Count is the Count property: the count, or null for a null receiver
rule: `x?.M` returns null if `x` is null; otherwise it performs the access. The result type is always nullable

title: a null-conditional Array.LastIndexOf call yields its result on a non-null receiver, null otherwise
rule: returns null if `x` is null; otherwise it performs the access

title: a null-conditional call on a null function value is a no-op
rule: A function value of nullable function type may be invoked with `?(...)`; the invocation is a no-op when the function value is null.

title: argument expressions of a null-conditional call are not evaluated when null
rule: When the function-valued operand is null, the invocation does not occur and the argument expressions are not evaluated — `handler?(Next())` does not call `Next` when `handler` is null.

title: null-coalescing yields a non-nullable result when the right operand is non-nullable
rule: `a ?? b` returns `a` if non-null, else `b`; the result type is `T` when the right operand is non-nullable.

title: the right operand of ?? runs only when the left operand is null
rule: The left operand is evaluated exactly once, and the right operand is evaluated only when the left operand's value is `null` — when the left is non-null the right operand expression does not run at all.

title: mixing an owned arm and a borrowed arm of ?? is rejected
rule: When the operands are owned, `??` is a two-branch expression whose result ownership follows the meet rule of an if/else join: an owned arm mixed with a borrowed arm is rejected.

title: owned ?? owned is owned and the chosen value is discharged once
rule: When the operands are owned (or owned-nullable), `owned ?? owned` is owned — the chosen value is discharged once.

title: ??= evaluates its right-hand side and assigns only when the left is null
rule: The compound form `??=` evaluates its right-hand side, and invokes the setter, only when the assignment occurs.

title: a long constant that fits the int left type of ?? converts to it by value
rule: for a left operand of type `T?`, the right operand must be implicitly convertible ([§5.1]) "to `T` or to `T?`; the result type is `T` when the right operand is non-nullable and `T?` when it is nullable". "An expression of integer type that is a **compile-time constant**" "implicitly converts to any integer type whose range contains its value" ([§5.1]), and "the source may be a compile-time constant of **any** integer type — not only `int`".

title: a long constant outside the int range is rejected as the right operand of ?? on an int?
rule: for a left operand of type `T?`, the right operand must be implicitly convertible ([§5.1]) "to `T` or to `T?`; the result type is `T` when the right operand is non-nullable and `T?` when it is nullable". "A constant whose value does not fit the target's range is a **compile error** at the conversion site" ([§5.1]).

title: a double constant is not implicitly convertible to the int left type of ??
rule: for a left operand of type `T?`, the right operand must be implicitly convertible ([§5.1]) "to `T` or to `T?`". "A value of one type implicitly converts to another when no programmer-visible information is lost" ([§5.1]), and a `double` to `int` conversion loses information, so it is not implicit.

title: a non-nullable int right operand of ?? into a double? left operand has type double
rule: the result type is `T` when the right operand is non-nullable ([§7.7]), and the right operand is an `int` converted to `double`: "Implicit conversions to `float` from integers wider than 24 bits, and to `double` from integers wider than 53 bits, may lose precision but never overflow" ([§5.1]). "`R` and the **no-format `ToString()`** both produce the shortest string that parses back to the identical value" ([stdlib §2.18]).

title: a long? right operand of ?? into an int? left operand is not implicitly convertible
rule: for a left operand of type `T?`, the right operand must be implicitly convertible ([§5.1]) "to `T` or to `T?`". "A value of one type implicitly converts to another when no programmer-visible information is lost" ([§5.1]), and a `long` value does not implicitly convert to an `int`.

title: a double literal is not implicitly convertible to an unconstrained type parameter in ??
rule: for a left operand of type `T?`, the right operand must be implicitly convertible ([§5.1]) "to `T` or to `T?`". The implicit reference conversions name a type parameter only as the source, "a type parameter to an interface or class its constraints guarantee conformance to" ([§5.1]); a `double` value converts to an unconstrained `T` under no listed rule.

title: a chain of ?? over two string? operands ends at a non-nullable string and prints the terminal
rule: a right-associative chain stays nullable until a non-nullable operand terminates it ([§7.7]). Here the terminal operand is a non-nullable string literal, so the whole chain is non-nullable, and both null operands fall through to the literal.

title: a byte right operand of ?? into a short? left operand widens to short
rule: for a left operand of type `T?`, the right operand must be implicitly convertible ([§5.1]) "to `T` or to `T?`". "Widening from unsigned to a strictly larger signed type (e.g. `byte → short`, `ushort → int`) is permitted because no value is lost" ([§5.1]).

title: a negative constant is not implicitly convertible to the byte left type of ??
rule: for a left operand of type `T?`, the right operand must be implicitly convertible ([§5.1]) "to `T` or to `T?`". "A constant whose value does not fit the target's range is a **compile error** at the conversion site" ([§5.1]), and `-1` does not fit `byte`.

title: a byte right operand of ?? into an int? left operand is widened, not sign-extended
rule: for a left operand of type `T?`, the right operand must be implicitly convertible ([§5.1]) "to `T` or to `T?`; the result type is `T` when the right operand is non-nullable". "Widening from unsigned to a strictly larger signed type (e.g. `byte → short`, `ushort → int`) is permitted because no value is lost" ([§5.1]), so the `byte` value 200 is the `int` 200.

title: a ushort right operand of ?? into an int? left operand is widened, not sign-extended
rule: for a left operand of type `T?`, the right operand must be implicitly convertible ([§5.1]) "to `T` or to `T?`; the result type is `T` when the right operand is non-nullable". "Widening from unsigned to a strictly larger signed type (e.g. `byte → short`, `ushort → int`) is permitted because no value is lost" ([§5.1]), so the `ushort` value 60000 is the `int` 60000.

title: a uint right operand of ?? into a long? left operand widens to its full value
rule: for a left operand of type `T?`, the right operand must be implicitly convertible ([§7.7]). "Widening from unsigned to a strictly larger signed type" ([§5.1]) "is permitted because no value is lost" ([§5.1]): the `uint` 3000000000 widens to `long` as 3000000000.

title: a uint right operand of ?? into an int? left operand is not implicitly convertible
rule: for a left operand of type `T?`, the right operand must be implicitly convertible ([§7.7]). "The following are never implicit:" ([§5.1]) "Between signed and unsigned types of the same or narrower width" ([§5.1]): `uint` to `int` is that conversion, so the right operand does not convert to `int`.

title: a coalesce result of type int and of type byte is accepted at TimeOnly's named millisecond parameter
rule: the result type is `T` when the right operand is non-nullable and `T?` when it is nullable ... so a narrowed `d: Dog?` is exact at a `Dog` parameter and converts to an `Animal` or a `Dog?` one

title: null-forgiving on a non-null value yields the non-nullable form
rule: `x!` asserts non-nullness. The result is the non-nullable form of the expression.

title: null-forgiving on a null value raises NullReferenceException at runtime
rule: If `x` is null at runtime, `NullReferenceException` is raised.

title: a non-nullable field with no initializer and no constructor assignment is rejected
rule: Every non-nullable field must be either assigned a value in every constructor before the constructor returns, or given a field initializer at its declaration.

title: a non-nullable field assigned in the constructor is admitted
rule: Every non-nullable field must be assigned a value in every constructor before the constructor returns, or given a field initializer at its declaration.

title: a field initializer at declaration satisfies definite assignment
rule: Every non-nullable field must be given a field initializer at its declaration, as an alternative to constructor assignment.

title: reading a non-defaultable local before it is assigned is rejected
rule: Definite-assignment analysis applies the same rule to locals, keyed on the same property: a local of **non-defaultable** type must be assigned before it is read. A non-nullable class type is the common non-defaultable case.

title: a non-defaultable local assigned before its read is admitted
rule: A local of non-defaultable type must be assigned before it is read; once assigned, a read is admitted.

title: a nullable local declared without an initializer holds null
rule: A local of defaultable type can be declared without an initializer — it gets the type's default, `null` for a nullable local.

title: a defaultable field with no initializer satisfies the rule vacuously
rule: A field whose type is defaultable satisfies the must-initialize rule vacuously and is implicitly initialized to that default; an explicit initializer is permitted and overrides it.

title: a field of an enum type with no zero-valued constant needs an initializer
rule: A field whose type is not defaultable requires an explicit initializer: a field initializer, or assignment in every constructor. The compiler emits a definite-assignment error if neither path supplies a value. An enum type with no declared constant of underlying value 0 is not defaultable.

title: an enum field with a zero-valued constant is implicitly initialized to it
rule: A field whose type is defaultable satisfies the must-initialize rule vacuously and is implicitly initialized to that default; for an enum the default is the value with underlying integer 0.

title: a bare unconstrained type-parameter field must be explicitly initialized
rule: A field or local of bare type `T` under an unconstrained parameter follows the non-nullable-reference rules (must-initialize, no vacuous `null` default), since `T` may be instantiated non-nullable.

title: a bare unconstrained type-parameter field initialized from a constructor parameter is admitted
rule: A field or local of bare type `T` under an unconstrained parameter follows the non-nullable-reference rules (must-initialize); assignment in the constructor satisfies it.

title: a nullable value type does not satisfy where T: value
rule: `where T: value` restricts T to non-nullable value types. A nullable value type (e.g. `int?`) does not satisfy the constraint.

title: a non-nullable value type satisfies where T: value
rule: `where T: value` restricts T to non-nullable value types — primitives included.

title: a nullable reference type does not satisfy where T: class
rule: `where T: class` restricts T to non-nullable reference types — classes, interfaces, `string`, function types.

title: a non-nullable reference type satisfies where T: class
rule: `where T: class` restricts T to non-nullable reference types — classes, interfaces, `string`, function types.

title: a generic body's copy out of an as result is rejected at a move-only instantiation
rule: At a move-only substitution ... an operation the body writes as a copy of a `T`-typed value ... is **rejected at the instantiation** where its operand is held in the **borrowed** state: ... the result of `x as T` ... So over `class Hold<T>` with a field `_f: T?` and `method Take(v: T)` whose body binds `var r := v as T;` and stores `_f := r;`, `Hold<Slot>` is rejected at that store wherever it is named

title: storing the parameter itself moves it at a move-only instantiation and is admitted
rule: At a move-only substitution ... an operation the body writes as a copy of a `T`-typed value is a move where its operand is a named owned binding the body may consume — a plain or `owned` parameter ... So over `class Hold<T>` ... `Hold<Slot>` is rejected at that store wherever it is named, while `_f := v;` moves the parameter and is admitted.

title: arithmetic + does not lift over a nullable operand
rule: No operator lifts to a nullable type. An operand whose static type is a nullable value type is a compile error at every arithmetic operator.

title: coalescing a nullable operand to a value admits the arithmetic operator
rule: No operator lifts to a nullable type; the remedy is `??`, `!`, or a narrowing check before the operator applies.

title: the relational operator < does not lift over a nullable operand
rule: No operator lifts to a nullable type; `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` are rejected over a nullable operand because an ordering comparison over an absent participant has no defensible result.

title: null-forgiving before a relational operator admits it
rule: The rule reads the operand's static type, so an operand asserted non-null with `!` is a non-nullable operand and the ordinary operator applies to it unchanged.

title: string ordering requires non-nullable operands
rule: `s < t` performs ordinal lexicographic comparison; ordering requires non-nullable operands — an operand of static type `string?` is a compile error.

title: narrowing a nullable string first admits ordering
rule: `s < t` requires non-nullable operands; narrowing an operand to non-null admits the ordering operator on it (narrow first, §7.4).

title: there is no three-valued logic — a bool? operand at and is rejected
rule: There are no `bool?` logical operators. `and`, `or`, `not` operate only on `bool`; a `bool?` operand is a compile error.

title: and operates on a non-nullable bool operand
rule: `and`, `or`, `not` operate on `bool`; a non-nullable `bool` operand is admitted.

title: a relational pattern over a nullable scrutinee is rejected
rule: A nullable scrutinee — value or reference — is a compile error at a relational pattern: ordering admits no absent participant, and pattern position performs no narrowing of its own.

title: separating the null case first admits a relational pattern on the rest
rule: The absent case is separated first and the ordering interrogated on the bound value — `case n of null => …, var m: int when m > 70 => …, _ => … end`.

title: unary minus over an un-narrowed nullable int is rejected
rule: an operand whose static type is a nullable value type is a compile error at every arithmetic, bitwise, shift, and relational operator. The rejected operators. The binary +, -, *, /, mod, &, |, ^, <<, >>; the unary +, -, ~; and the relational <, <=, >, >=.

title: unary minus and complement apply to a nullable int once a null test narrows it
rule: The rule reads the operand's static type, so an operand that §7.4 has narrowed non-null is a non-nullable operand and the ordinary operator applies to it unchanged; no separate rule is needed for that case.

title: a user-declared unary operator is not applicable to an un-narrowed nullable record
rule: A user-declared `operator` on a record or class type (§25) is likewise not defined on a nullable operand: such an operand at a user-defined-operator position is the same compile error, naming the same remedies.

title: a user-declared unary operator applies to a nullable record once a null test narrows it
rule: The rule reads the operand's static type, so an operand that §7.4 has narrowed non-null is a non-nullable operand and the ordinary operator applies to it unchanged; no separate rule is needed for that case.

title: a user-defined binary operator rejects a nullable record right operand that is not narrowed
rule: A user-declared `operator` on a record or class type (§25) is likewise not defined on a nullable operand: such an operand at a user-defined-operator position is the same compile error, naming the same remedies.

title: a user-defined binary operator applies to a nullable record right operand narrowed non-null
rule: The rule reads the operand's static type, so an operand that §7.4 has narrowed non-null is a non-nullable operand and the ordinary operator applies to it unchanged; no separate rule is needed for that case.

title: user code cannot redeclare Object
rule: `Object` is a compiler intrinsic; method bodies are provided by the runtime. User code cannot redeclare or replace `Object`.

title: a class named MyObject is an ordinary declaration
rule: `Object` is a compiler intrinsic; user code cannot redeclare or replace `Object`. A type with any other name is unaffected.

title: GetType on a class instance answers a module-qualified Type.FullName
rule: `v.GetType()` returns the `Type` value for the runtime type of `v`; `Type.FullName` renders a named type qualified by its declaring module path.

title: GetType cannot be overridden
rule: `GetType` is non-virtual; runtime type identity is fixed at allocation and cannot be overridden.

title: overriding Equals without GetHashCode is rejected
rule: A type that overrides `Equals` must also override `GetHashCode`. The compiler enforces this.

title: overriding Equals together with GetHashCode is admitted
rule: A type that overrides `Equals` must also override `GetHashCode`. Declaring both together is admitted.

title: the default Equals for a class is reference equality
rule: The compiler generates a default `Equals` appropriate to each type kind; for a class the default is reference equality.

title: a record's plain own-typed Equals with no GetHashCode is rejected
rule: On a value kind, a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: an enum's plain own-typed Equals with no GetHashCode is rejected
rule: On a value kind, a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: a value-like choice's plain own-typed Equals with no GetHashCode is rejected
rule: On a value kind, a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: a generic record's plain own-typed Equals with no GetHashCode is rejected
rule: On a value kind, a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: a record nested in a class is held to the GetHashCode obligation
rule: On a value kind, a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: a plain GetHashCode discharges a record's plain own-typed Equals
rule: On a value kind, a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: a plain GetHashCode discharges an enum's plain own-typed Equals
rule: On a value kind, a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: an override own-typed Equals with a plain GetHashCode is accepted on a record
rule: On a value kind, a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: a plain Equals(Object?) on a record is rejected at the declaration
rule: On a record, an `Equals` at `Object?` is a compile error at its declaration, plain or `override`, and the diagnostic points at the own-typed spelling; the value kinds' Object slot is filled only by the own-typed `Equals` (v0.338, §9.2).

rule: A choice that no boxing reaches, one owning at every instantiation, has no slot to fill, so its declared `Equals` carries no such obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: a choice's plain Equals and plain GetHashCode run together
rule: On a value kind, a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

rule: On a value kind, a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

rule: On a value kind, a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: a plain GetHashCode discharges an enum's override own-typed Equals
rule: On a value kind, a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: a generic record's own-typed Equals with GetHashCode runs
rule: On a value kind, a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: a GetHashCode of the wrong signature does not discharge the obligation
rule: On a value kind, a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

rule: A choice that no boxing reaches, one owning at every instantiation, has no slot to fill, so its declared `Equals` carries no such obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: a choice owning only at some instantiations keeps the obligation
rule: A choice that no boxing reaches, one owning at every instantiation, has no slot to fill, so its declared `Equals` carries no such obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: a class-bounded choice with no owned payload obliges GetHashCode
rule: On a value kind, a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: an interface-bounded choice with no owned payload obliges GetHashCode
rule: On a value kind, a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: a second-parameter class-bounded choice with no owned payload obliges GetHashCode
rule: On a value kind, a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: an IComparable-bounded owned-payload choice is not owning at every instantiation
rule: A choice that no boxing reaches, one owning at every instantiation, has no slot to fill, so its declared `Equals` carries no such obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

rule: A choice that no boxing reaches, one owning at every instantiation, has no slot to fill, so its declared `Equals` carries no such obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

rule: A choice that no boxing reaches, one owning at every instantiation, has no slot to fill, so its declared `Equals` carries no such obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: an enum overriding Equals(Object?) needs GetHashCode even with an own-typed Equals

title: an owning choice overriding Equals(Object?) without GetHashCode is rejected
rule: A type that overrides `Equals` must also override `GetHashCode`. The compiler enforces this (v0.338, §8.3).

title: a generic choice without a parameter payload obliges GetHashCode

title: a value-constrained choice with a parameter payload obliges GetHashCode
rule: On a value kind, a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: a value-constrained choice without a parameter payload obliges GetHashCode
rule: On a value kind, a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation (v0.338, §8.3).

title: a plain Equals taking an interface type fills no Object slot, so a default on it is accepted
rule: A default value is permitted only on parameters with no modifier or `owned` ([§22.5]). The no-default restriction names the slot's parameter alone: "The slot's parameter declares no default value, on a class or a value kind" ([§8.3]). Here `Equals(other: I? := null)` takes the interface `I`, neither `Object?` nor the class's own type, and "Overriding `Equals` is filling the `Object` slot" only for those spellings ([§8.3]), so this member fills no slot and its default is legal.

title: a plain Equals at an unrelated class's parameter type fills no Object slot, so a default is accepted
rule: The slot's parameter declares no default value, on a class or a value kind ([§8.3]) names the slot's parameter only. On a class the slot is "`override Equals(other: Object?)` or the own-typed spelling" ([§8.3]). `Equals(other: B? := null)` on `C` takes the unrelated class `B`, so it fills no slot, and "A default value is permitted only on parameters with no modifier or `owned`" ([§22.5]) admits the default.

title: a class's own-typed Equals with a default value is rejected at its declaration
rule: The slot's parameter declares no default value, on a class or a value kind ([§8.3]). "A class's `Equals` taking the class's own type, `C` or `C?`, is the `Object` slot's second spelling, virtual, written with or without `override`" (the same sentence's section). So `Equals(other: C? := null)` on `C` fills the slot and may not declare the default; `C` declares `GetHashCode` beside it, so the default is the only violation.

title: null equals null under the null-safe equality wrapper
rule: `a = b` invokes `a.Equals(b)`, with a null-safe wrapper: `null = null` is `true`.

title: operator overloading of = is not permitted on classes
rule: Operator overloading of `=` and `<>` is not permitted on classes; classes customize equality by overriding `Equals`.

title: a class with no operator overload uses default Equals via =
rule: Operator overloading of `=` and `<>` is not permitted on classes; classes customize equality by overriding `Equals`.

title: = on a class invokes the overridden Equals
rule: For classes, `=` always invokes `Equals`.

title: = and <> in a generic body over a record type parameter and Object compare by value
rule: `a = b` invokes `a.Equals(b)`, with a null-safe wrapper: `null = null` is `true`; `null = nonNull` and `nonNull = null` are `false`. ([§8.4]). "`<>` is the negation." ([§8.4]). A positional record's default equality is "Field-by-field value equality" ([§8.3]), so a boxed `V(1)` equals a `V(1)` through the generic `=`, a `V(2)` does not, a null record equals only a null operand, and `<>` negates each result.
check: all:True False False True False\nFalse False

title: a present record or class compared with null is unequal on either side
rule: `a = b` invokes `a.Equals(b)`, with a null-safe wrapper: `null = null` is `true`; `null = nonNull` and `nonNull = null` are `false`. `<>` is the negation. (§8.4, v0.340) A present record value and a present class instance are both `nonNull`, so `= null` and `null =` are `false` and `<>` is `true`.

title: comparing a record with null does not dispatch to its overloaded equality operator
rule: `a = b` invokes `a.Equals(b)`, with a null-safe wrapper: `null = null` is `true`; `null = nonNull` and `nonNull = null` are `false`. `<>` is the negation. (§8.4, v0.340) The wrapper "belongs to the equality operators, not to `Equals`: ... only when both operands are present dispatch to the overloaded operator where one is declared" (§8.4). With `null` as one operand the operator body never runs, so none of its marker lines is printed before the four results.

title: a present value compared with null inside a generic body is unequal for every type argument
rule: `a = b` invokes `a.Equals(b)`, with a null-safe wrapper: `null = null` is `true`; `null = nonNull` and `nonNull = null` are `false`. `<>` is the negation. (§8.4, v0.340) Inside `G<T>`, `t = null` is the same null-safe wrapper for each instantiation, so a present record, class, overloaded-operator record or `int` is never equal to `null`.

title: the default ToString for a class renders the qualified type name
rule: The compiler-generated default `ToString` for classes returns the type's qualified name, the module-path-qualified rendering `Type.FullName` defines.

title: the default ToString for an enum renders the qualified type name, not the constant's name
rule: For enums, the compiler-generated default `ToString` returns the type's qualified name (the stdlib `FullName` rendering), not the constant's declared identifier. `NameOf` is the separate table that answers the constant's identifier (§10.4).

title: an enum that declares ToString to return NameOf renders the constant's name
rule: An enum may replace its default `ToString` by declaring a `ToString(): string` member; the replacement is used by every consumer, including interpolation. An enum whose rendering should be the constant's name declares `ToString` to return `E.NameOf(this)`.

title: an Object holding a StringBuilder renders its text until a closure reassigns the Object
rule: `ToString` is invoked via virtual dispatch for present values; a class instance held at an `Object` location renders through its own `ToString`. A captured `Object` variable assigned in a closure holds the new value afterwards.

title: An Object holding a StringBuilder renders its text, then the replacement on the next pass
rule: `ToString` is invoked via virtual dispatch for present values; a class instance held at an `Object` location renders through its own `ToString`, and after the location is reassigned it renders the new value.

title: An Object holding a StringBuilder renders in a hole and Append(Object), then the new value
