rule: Return types must match exactly under the interface's substitution, and own type parameters correspond by number and position, not by name. Interface P<T, U>(a: T): Array<(T) -> U> is matched by an implementation with the same names; the call through the interface reaches it.

title: a function-typed return with a concrete return type and a renamed own parameter matches
rule: Return types must match exactly under the interface's substitution, and own type parameters correspond by number and position, not by name. Interface P<T>(a: T): Array<(T) -> int> has a concrete return int in the function type; the renamed implementation P<A>(a: A): Array<(A) -> int> carries the same concrete return and matches.

title: a class type parameter substituted into a bare function-typed return matches
rule: Return types must match exactly under the interface's substitution, and own type parameters correspond by number and position, not by name. Under the substitution S := int, interface I<int>'s member is P(): (int) -> int, and the implementation's return (int) -> int is exactly that type.

title: a substituted bare function return of a different return type does not match
rule: Return types must match exactly under the interface's substitution, and own type parameters correspond by number and position, not by name. Under the substitution S := int, the interface's return is (int) -> int; the implementation's (int) -> string differs in the function's return type.

title: a renamed multi-parameter bare function-typed return matches
rule: Return types must match exactly under the interface's substitution, and own type parameters correspond by number and position, not by name. Interface P<T, U>(): (T, U) -> T is matched by P<A, B>(): (A, B) -> A: each own parameter corresponds by position.

title: a renamed curried bare function-typed return matches
rule: Return types must match exactly under the interface's substitution, and own type parameters correspond by number and position, not by name. Interface P<T, U>(): (T) -> (U) -> T is matched by P<A, B>(): (A) -> (B) -> A: the curried function type's parameters correspond by position.

title: a renamed nullable bare function-typed return matches
rule: Return types must match exactly under the interface's substitution, and own type parameters correspond by number and position, not by name. Interface P<T, U>(): ((T) -> U)? is matched by P<A, B>(): ((A) -> B)?: the nullable wrapper is the same and the function type's own parameters correspond by position.

title: a renamed Dictionary with a function-typed value in a bare return matches
rule: Return types must match exactly under the interface's substitution, and own type parameters correspond by number and position, not by name. Interface P<T, U>(): Dictionary<T, (U) -> T> is matched by P<A, B>(): Dictionary<A, (B) -> A>: the own parameters correspond by position inside the Dictionary's key and function-typed value.

title: an alias of a built-in type in an interface parameter matches the target spelled directly
rule: A type alias is a pure synonym (27.8); an implementer whose parameter is the alias target spelled directly matches the interface's declared parameter (11.2: the parameter types are exactly equal under the substitution, and an alias denotes its target).

title: an inline-array parameter with a renamed own type parameter matches by position
rule: A member matches an interface member when it is declared public, has the same name and arity, the same number of type parameters of its own, and parameter types that are exactly equal under the interface's substitution (and a return type exactly equal under it). A member's own type parameters take part in the match by number and position, not by name. The interface's substitution maps each of the interface's type parameters to the implementing type's argument, and each of the interface member's own type parameters to the candidate's type parameter at the same position; parameter types are compared after that mapping. So `[3]U` in the interface member and `[3]W` in the candidate match, with U and W corresponding by position.

title: an inline-array parameter whose own type parameters are swapped by position does not match
rule: A member matches an interface member when it is declared public, has the same name and arity, the same number of type parameters of its own, and parameter types that are exactly equal under the interface's substitution (and a return type exactly equal under it). A member's own type parameters take part in the match by number and position, not by name. The interface's substitution maps each of the interface's type parameters to the implementing type's argument, and each of the interface member's own type parameters to the candidate's type parameter at the same position; parameter types are compared after that mapping. Under the correspondence T to A and U to B, the interface's first parameter is [3]A and the implementation's is [3]B; the implementation swaps them.

title: an inline-array parameter whose own type parameters are in the same order by position matches
rule: A member matches an interface member when it is declared public, has the same name and arity, the same number of type parameters of its own, and parameter types that are exactly equal under the interface's substitution (and a return type exactly equal under it). A member's own type parameters take part in the match by number and position, not by name. The interface's substitution maps each of the interface's type parameters to the implementing type's argument, and each of the interface member's own type parameters to the candidate's type parameter at the same position; parameter types are compared after that mapping. This is the accepting twin of the swapped form: the same two inline-array parameters, in the interface's order under the position correspondence.

title: an inline-array parameter of a different concrete element type does not match
rule: A member matches an interface member when it is declared public, has the same name and arity, the same number of type parameters of its own, and parameter types that are exactly equal under the interface's substitution (and a return type exactly equal under it). Parameter types must be exactly equal; the interface's [3]int is not the implementation's [3]string.

title: a class type parameter substituted into an inline-array parameter matches
rule: A member matches an interface member when it is declared public, has the same name and arity, the same number of type parameters of its own, and parameter types that are exactly equal under the interface's substitution (and a return type exactly equal under it). The interface's substitution maps S to the implementing class's argument Z, so [3]S under I<int> is [3]int, which the implementation's [3]Z under K<int> matches.

title: an inline array nested in a generic argument matches its substituted concrete form
rule: A member matches an interface member when it is declared public, has the same name and arity, the same number of type parameters of its own, and parameter types that are exactly equal under the interface's substitution (and a return type exactly equal under it). The interface's substitution maps S to int, so Box<[3]S> under I<int> is Box<[3]int>, which the implementation's parameter Box<[3]int> is exactly equal to.

title: an inline array nested in a generic argument with the wrong substituted element does not match
rule: A member matches an interface member when it is declared public, has the same name and arity, the same number of type parameters of its own, and parameter types that are exactly equal under the interface's substitution (and a return type exactly equal under it). The interface's substitution maps S to int, so Box<[3]S> under I<int> is Box<[3]int>; the implementation's Box<[3]string> is not that type.

title: a function-typed parameter with a different parameter type does not match
rule: A member matches an interface member when it is declared public, has the same name and arity, the same number of type parameters of its own, and parameter types that are exactly equal under the interface's substitution (and a return type exactly equal under it). The interface's parameter is (int) -> int; the implementation's (string) -> int is not exactly equal to it.

title: a function-typed parameter substituted through a class type parameter matches
rule: A member matches an interface member when it is declared public, has the same name and arity, the same number of type parameters of its own, and parameter types that are exactly equal under the interface's substitution (and a return type exactly equal under it). The interface's substitution maps S to the implementing class's argument Z, so (S) -> int under I<int> is (int) -> int, which the implementation's (Z) -> int under K<int> matches.

title: a function-typed parameter substituted to a concrete type matches its interface form
rule: A member matches an interface member when it is declared public, has the same name and arity, the same number of type parameters of its own, and parameter types that are exactly equal under the interface's substitution (and a return type exactly equal under it). The interface's substitution maps S to int, so (S) -> int under I<int> is (int) -> int, which the implementation's P(f: (int) -> int) is exactly equal to.

title: an inline-array parameter of a different length does not match
rule: A member matches an interface member when it is declared public, has the same name and arity, the same number of type parameters of its own, and parameter types that are exactly equal under the interface's substitution (and a return type exactly equal under it). Parameter types must be exactly equal under the interface's substitution; [3]int and [2]int are not equal.

title: a candidate with more own type parameters than the interface member does not match
rule: A candidate declaring a different number of type parameters of its own does not match. The spec's example: Show<T, U>(x: T): string does not match an interface member Show<U>(x: U): string, since the candidate declares two own type parameters and the interface member one.

title: a non-generic candidate using the class type parameter does not match a generic member
rule: A candidate declaring a different number of type parameters of its own does not match. The spec's example: on a class C<T>, a non-generic Show(x: T): string whose T is the class's does not match a generic interface member Show<U>(x: U): string.

title: a candidate with the same number of own type parameters matches a generic interface member
rule: A candidate declaring a different number of type parameters of its own does not match. The accepting twin of s11_2_0108: the candidate declares one own type parameter at the same position, so it matches Show<U>(x: U): string.

title: an indexer's element type substituted to int matches the implementation's int indexer
rule: A read-write member satisfies a read-only interface member of the same name and type: if IReadOnlyList<T> declares `readonly property [i: int]: T` and IList<T> declares `property [i: int]: T`, a single read-write indexer satisfies both. The implementation's indexer must therefore have the same type as the interface's indexer, which under I<int> is the substituted element type. Under I<int> the element type T is int, so `readonly property [i: int]: T` and the implementation's `property [i: int]: int` match.

title: an indexer whose substituted element type is not matched by the implementation is rejected
rule: A read-write member satisfies a read-only interface member of the same name and type: if IReadOnlyList<T> declares `readonly property [i: int]: T` and IList<T> declares `property [i: int]: T`, a single read-write indexer satisfies both. The implementation's indexer must therefore have the same type as the interface's indexer, which under I<int> is the substituted element type. Under I<int> the element type is int; the implementation's indexer returns string, which is not exactly int.

title: a read-write property satisfies a read-only interface property of the same name and type
rule: `readonly property Value: int;` is the interface member; §11.2 states: "A read-write member satisfies a read-only interface member of the same name and type." The implementation declares `property Value: int := 5;`, which is read-write, and the match is on name and type.

title: a property whose substituted type is not matched by the implementation is rejected
rule: A read-write member satisfies a read-only interface member of the same name and type (§11.2). A member matches only when its type is exactly equal to the interface member's type under the interface's substitution. Under I<int> the property type is int; the implementation declares Value as string, which is not exactly int.

title: a property typed by the interface's parameter matches at the substituted type
rule: A member matches an interface member when it is declared public, has the same name and arity, the same number of type parameters of its own, and parameter types that are exactly equal under the interface's substitution (and a return type exactly equal under it). Under I<int> the property type T is int, and the implementation's property of type int is exactly equal to it.

title: a method's return type substituted to string matches the implementation's string return
rule: A member matches an interface member when it is declared public, has the same name and arity, the same number of type parameters of its own, and parameter types that are exactly equal under the interface's substitution (and a return type exactly equal under it). The return type is compared under the interface's substitution: under I<string> the return type T is string, which the implementation's return type string is exactly equal to.

title: a return type substituted to int does not match an implementation returning string
rule: A member matches an interface member when it is declared public, has the same name and arity, the same number of type parameters of its own, and parameter types that are exactly equal under the interface's substitution (and a return type exactly equal under it). Under I<int> the return type T is int; the implementation's return type string is not exactly equal to it.

title: a covariant string return does not match an Object return
rule: §11.2: "Return types must match exactly (no covariance in this version)." The interface returns Object and the implementation returns string, a subtype of Object.

title: an Object return on both sides matches: the accepting twin
rule: §11.2: "Return types must match exactly (no covariance in this version)." The exact match holds here: both sides declare Object. The string literal converts to Object by the §5.1 reference conversion, so the body is admitted.

title: a nullable return type does not match a non-nullable interface return
rule: §11.2: "Return types must match exactly (no covariance in this version)." The interface returns int and the implementation returns int?. The nullability widening in §11.2 is stated for parameters only.

title: the non-nullable return matches the interface's int return, the accepting twin of the nullable form
rule: §11.2: "Return types must match exactly (no covariance in this version)." Both sides declare int here.

title: a class inherits interface conformance from a base class two levels up
rule: §5.1 lists as implicit "a type to an interface it implements or conforms to: classes by declaration or inheritance (§11.2…)". Class D derives from B, which derives from A, and A declares the matching public member P, so D reaches I through inheritance.

title: an interface extending a generic interface carries the substitution of its argument
rule: §11.2: "An interface may extend other interfaces." §11.2's substitution rule: "The interface's substitution maps each of the interface's type parameters to the implementing type's argument." J<T> extends I<T>, so under K: J<int> the inherited member P returns int, and the implementation's int return matches.

title: an interface extending a generic interface: the inherited member's substituted return must match
rule: §11.2: "Return types must match exactly (no covariance in this version)." J<T> extends I<T>, so under K: J<int> the inherited member P returns int; the implementation returns string, which is not exactly int.

title: an interface extending a generic interface at a concrete argument is matched by the implementation
rule: §11.2: "An interface may extend other interfaces." Here J extends I<string> with a concrete argument, so its inherited P returns string. The implementation's return type string is exactly equal under that substitution.

title: a diamond of extended interfaces is satisfied by one implementation of the shared member
rule: §11.2: "Diamond resolution: a single implementation in the implementing class satisfies all interface methods with the same signature." J<T> extends H<T> and I<T>, and H<T> extends I<T>, so P is reached through two paths; both substitute to the same signature, and one P returning 6 satisfies both.

title: a read-write indexer of an extending interface satisfies the read-only indexer it inherits
rule: §11.2: "A read-write member satisfies a read-only interface member of the same name and type: … a single read-write indexer in the implementing class satisfies both." IRW<T> extends IRO<T>. The one read-write indexer of K satisfies the inherited readonly indexer as well; a value written through IRW is read back through IRO.

title: a dropped generic-method constraint does not match the interface
rule: §11.2: "and, for a generic method, a constraint set equivalent to the interface method's (§14.2)." The interface method constrains its own type parameter U with new(); the implementation's V carries no constraint, so the constraint sets differ.

title: a generic method keeping the constraint set matches: the accepting twin
rule: §11.2: "and, for a generic method, a constraint set equivalent to the interface method's (§14.2)." Both sides here carry where V: new() / U: new().

title: an extra class overload does not displace the interface member with the exact parameter type
rule: parameter types that are exactly equal under the interface's substitution (v0.338 §11.2)

title: an override's own method type parameter renamed by position is admitted
rule: **Generic members.** A member's own type parameters take part in the match by number and position, not by name.

title: an implementing class answers its own property and passes as the interface for its declared key
rule: Interface members are implicitly public, have no body, and end with `;` and "A class implements an interface implicitly: by declaring matching public members" ([§11.2]). `MyG` declares "readonly property Key: TKey;" ([stdlib §5]) as the interface requires and also a property `Extra` of its own. Through the class-typed local `Extra` reads 9; passed as the grouping parameter, the interface's `Key` has no body of its own, so it reads the class's `Key`, 1.

title: a value of an extending interface exposes the extended interface's member
rule: Language spec §11.2 (v0.345): "An interface may extend other interfaces … Multiple- interface inheritance is permitted" — and the inherited surface is the extending interface's own: "`Add`, `Clear`, `Remove`, and the rest of the mutating surface in the example above are inherited from `ICollection<T>`."

title: two fields with the same name clash
rule: A type may not declare two members that are not distinguishable from each other. Two members clash when they have the same name... two fields, properties, or nested types with the same name.

title: two distinctly-named fields do not clash
rule: A type may not declare two members that are not distinguishable from each other -- distinctly-named members are unaffected.

title: a field and a property with the same name clash
rule: A non-overloadable member -- a field, property, or nested type -- additionally clashes with any other member of the type that shares its name, regardless of kind.

title: two methods with an identical signature clash
rule: Two members clash when they have the same name... two methods... with the same name that are not distinguishable as overloads.

title: methods distinguished by parameter type are legal overloads, not a clash
rule: Legal overloads -- members of the same name that are distinguishable per §22.6 -- are unaffected; this rule rejects only the duplicates that overloading does not admit.

title: an owned/plain parameter pair over a where-T-class constraint clashes at the declaration (v0.338)
rule: **`owned` never distinguishes overloads (v0.338, proposal 0185).** Two same-name members that differ only by ordinary `owned` clash at the second declaration (§22.6, §11.3): `Append(item: Widget)` beside `Append(owned item: Widget)` is a compile error.

title: an owned/plain parameter pair over a where-T-IDisposable constraint is rejected (v0.338)
rule: **`owned` never distinguishes overloads (v0.338, proposal 0185).** An ordinary-`owned` / plain pair clashes at the second declaration (§11.3).

title: owned on an out parameter never distinguishes overloads
rule: owned on an out parameter and scoped never distinguish overloads; two methods differing only in the owned qualifier on an out parameter are a compile error (§22.6).

title: methods with different numbers of type parameters of their own never clash
rule: Two methods declaring different numbers of type parameters of their own never clash, whatever their parameters: `M<T>(x: T)` beside `M<T, U>(x: T)`.

title: a non-generic method and a one-parameter generic method with the same parameter types do not clash
rule: Two methods declaring different numbers of type parameters of their own never clash, whatever their parameters: `FromException<T>(owned exception: Exception)` beside the non-generic `FromException(owned exception: Exception)`.

title: methods with the same type-parameter count whose parameter types are permuted do not clash
rule: `M<T, U>(a: T, b: U)` and `M<T, U>(a: U, b: T)` do not clash: an explicit type-argument list naming two different types gives them different signatures, and a call that leaves them to inference is ambiguous. Two methods declaring the same number of type parameters compare their parameter types with those type parameters corresponding by position, not by name. The parameter types do not correspond positionally, so the pair is distinguishable.

title: the canonical modifier order is admitted on a static owned field
rule: visibility static (async|pure) (abstract|virtual|override|sealed override) (owned|scoped) readonly member-kind Name ... The combination static owned readonly is the canonical form for a static field that owns a long-lived resource.

title: readonly before owned is rejected
rule: The compiler rejects out-of-order modifiers. owned appears between the virtual-modifier slot and readonly.

title: owned before static is rejected
rule: visibility static (async|pure) (abstract|virtual|override|sealed override) (owned|scoped) readonly member-kind Name ... The compiler rejects out-of-order modifiers.

title: static before visibility is rejected
rule: visibility static (async|pure) (abstract|virtual|override|sealed override) (owned|scoped) readonly member-kind Name ... The compiler rejects out-of-order modifiers.

title: the canonical modifier order is admitted on an override
rule: visibility static (async|pure) (abstract|virtual|override|sealed override) (owned|scoped) readonly member-kind Name ...

title: visibility after override is rejected
rule: visibility static (async|pure) (abstract|virtual|override|sealed override) (owned|scoped) readonly member-kind Name ... The compiler rejects out-of-order modifiers.

title: virtual and override together are rejected as mutually exclusive
rule: abstract, virtual, override, and sealed override are mutually exclusive -- at most one may appear.

title: owned is rejected on a non-field member
rule: owned ... appears between the virtual-modifier slot and readonly. It applies only to fields; methods, properties, and other members do not carry owned.

title: a class body may declare nested types with required visibility
rule: A class body may declare nested classes, records, enums, and interfaces. Nested types may be public, internal, protected, or private, and the visibility keyword is required.

title: a nested type missing its visibility keyword is rejected
rule: A nested type is a class member, and §13.3's explicit-visibility rule applies with no exception for nested types -- omitting the keyword is a compile error, not a default.

title: a nested type's qualified name includes the enclosing path
rule: A nested type none of whose enclosing types is generic is referenced from outside as Outer.Nested, and the enclosing path is part of its qualified name wherever one is rendered.

title: a nested class may access the private members of an enclosing instance
rule: A nested class has access to all members (including `private`) of every class enclosing it, at any depth: an instance member through an instance of that class it holds

title: a type nested in a generic type is not named through its bare generic enclosing segment in new
rule: A bare enclosing segment fixes arity 0 ... In a type position, therefore, no name passes through a generic enclosing type: a type nested in a generic type, at any depth, is named only where §2.7's enclosing-type lookup reaches it (§11.6, v0.340). `new C.N()` names `N` through the bare generic `C`.

title: a nested type is not named through a bare generic enclosing segment in an annotation
rule: A bare enclosing segment fixes arity 0 ... In a type position, therefore, no name passes through a generic enclosing type: a type nested in a generic type, at any depth, is named only where §2.7's enclosing-type lookup reaches it (§11.6, v0.340). The annotation `C.N?` is a type position that passes through the generic `C`.

title: a chain head reaches a generic type's nested type through its static member and an unannotated local
rule: Elsewhere a chain head reaches its static members, and a local declared without a type annotation holds a value of it (`var n := tree.Root();`) (§11.6, v0.340). `C<int>.Make()` returns the nested `N` and `var n` holds it without naming `C.N`.

title: inside the generic enclosing type its nested type is named by its bare name
rule: a type nested in a generic type ... is named only where §2.7's enclosing-type lookup reaches it (§11.6, v0.340); inside `C<T>`'s own body the bare `N` is reached by that lookup.

title: a nested type of a generic type is not named at the right operand of `is`
rule: The bare-type-name row of §2.7's normative table: a name the grammar reads only as a `Type` — an ascription, `new`, a generic argument, a base or interface list, the right operand of `is`, `is not` or `as`, a `typeof` or `default` operand, a destructuring pattern's head, a `where` clause — reads a type position, and §11.6's "no name passes through a generic enclosing type" makes the bare generic segment in `C.N` an Appendix C.1 arity error (§2.7, §11.6, v0.340).

title: the same `is` operand names the nested type of a NON-generic enclosing type
rule: A nested type none of whose enclosing types is generic is referenced from outside as `Outer.Nested` (§11.6, v0.340) — with the enclosing class not generic, `C.N` is that spelling, and the same type position is legal.

title: a nested type of a generic type is not named at the right operand of `as`
rule: The bare-type-name row of §2.7's normative table: a name the grammar reads only as a `Type` — an ascription, `new`, a generic argument, a base or interface list, the right operand of `is`, `is not` or `as`, a `typeof` or `default` operand, a destructuring pattern's head, a `where` clause — reads a type position, and §11.6's "no name passes through a generic enclosing type" makes the bare generic segment in `C.N` an Appendix C.1 arity error (§2.7, §11.6, v0.340).

title: the same `as` operand names the nested type of a NON-generic enclosing type
rule: A nested type none of whose enclosing types is generic is referenced from outside as `Outer.Nested` (§11.6, v0.340) — with the enclosing class not generic, `C.N` is that spelling, and the same type position is legal.

title: a nested type of a generic type is not named as a generic type argument
rule: The bare-type-name row of §2.7's normative table: a name the grammar reads only as a `Type` — an ascription, `new`, a generic argument, a base or interface list, the right operand of `is`, `is not` or `as`, a `typeof` or `default` operand, a destructuring pattern's head, a `where` clause — reads a type position, and §11.6's "no name passes through a generic enclosing type" makes the bare generic segment in `C.N` an Appendix C.1 arity error (§2.7, §11.6, v0.340).

title: the same generic type argument names the nested type of a NON-generic enclosing type
rule: A nested type none of whose enclosing types is generic is referenced from outside as `Outer.Nested` (§11.6, v0.340) — with the enclosing class not generic, `C.N` is that spelling, and the same type position is legal.

title: a nested type of a generic type is not named in a `where` clause
rule: The bare-type-name row of §2.7's normative table: a name the grammar reads only as a `Type` — an ascription, `new`, a generic argument, a base or interface list, the right operand of `is`, `is not` or `as`, a `typeof` or `default` operand, a destructuring pattern's head, a `where` clause — reads a type position, and §11.6's "no name passes through a generic enclosing type" makes the bare generic segment in `C.N` an Appendix C.1 arity error (§2.7, §11.6, v0.340).

title: the same `where` clause names the nested type of a NON-generic enclosing type
rule: A nested type none of whose enclosing types is generic is referenced from outside as `Outer.Nested` (§11.6, v0.340) — with the enclosing class not generic, `C.N` is that spelling, and the same type position is legal.

title: inside a generic type a non-generic type enclosing a nested type below it is reached
rule: In a type position, therefore, no name passes through a generic enclosing type: a type nested in a generic type, at any depth, is named only where §2.7's enclosing-type lookup reaches it, or reaches a non-generic type enclosing it below the generic one (`Node<int>` in `Tree`'s own declaration or in the body of a type deriving from `Tree`; `Inner.Leaf` there for a `Leaf` nested in a non-generic `Inner`) (§11.6, v0.340).

title: inside a nested type a sibling nested type of the enclosing generic is reached by bare name
rule: Nested types of an enclosing type, generic or not, are reached by bare name, since a nested type is one type and needs no instantiation (§2.7's Through nesting, v0.340); inside `N`'s own body the enclosing lookup visits `N` and then `C`, and `C` has a nested type of the name `M2`.

title: a nested generic type under a non-generic enclosing type is named from outside
rule: A nested type none of whose enclosing types is generic is referenced from outside as `Outer.Nested` (§11.6, v0.340); the nested type here is itself generic, so A.5's `TypeNoNullable` takes its type arguments after the last segment: `E.G<int>`.

title: an enum nested in a generic type is reached through a chain head supplying the arguments
rule: A chain head that supplies the enclosing type's arguments (§2.7 rule 1, `Tree<int>.Node<int>.Create()`) reaches that one type whatever the arguments ... the rest of the chain resolves against that type's members, declared or inherited (a nested type, an enum constant, a static member — each segment in turn

title: a local declared without a type annotation holds a nested type's value from an instance method
rule: Elsewhere a chain head reaches its static members, and a local declared without a type annotation holds a value of it (`var n := tree.Root();`) (§11.6, v0.340) — the value's type is the nested type, and the local never names it.

title: a chain head supplying the enclosing type's arguments reaches a nested type's static member
rule: A chain head that supplies the enclosing type's arguments (§2.7 rule 1, `Tree<int>.Node<int> .Create()`) reaches that one type whatever the arguments, and its static members have one cell each (§22.12), not one per enclosing instantiation (§11.6, v0.340).

title: a static class may contain only static members
rule: A class declared static may contain only static members.

title: new on a static class is rejected
rule: A static class may not be instantiated: new on a static class is a compile error.

title: a static class may not declare an instance field
rule: A static class may not have instance fields, instance methods, instance properties, indexers, constructors (other than a static constructor), or destructors.

title: a static class may not be inherited from another class
rule: A static class may not be inherited from and does not implement interfaces.

title: sealed abstract is rejected, the diagnostic naming closed
rule: Combining `closed` with `abstract`, `sealed`, or `static` is a compile error; the modifier pair `sealed abstract` is rejected too, the diagnostic naming `closed`.

title: a closed class may declare abstract members and be subclassed within its own module
rule: A class declared with the closed modifier is a closed abstract class: a class that cannot be instantiated directly and cannot be inherited from outside the declaring module. A closed class may declare abstract members without carrying the abstract modifier.

title: closed combined with abstract is rejected
rule: Combining closed with abstract, sealed, or static is a compile error.

title: a static class may not declare an instance method
rule: A static class may not have instance fields, instance methods, instance properties, indexers, constructors (other than a static constructor), or destructors.

title: a static class may not declare an instance constructor
rule: A static class may not have instance fields, instance methods, instance properties, indexers, constructors (other than a static constructor), or destructors.

title: a static constructor is the one constructor a static class may declare
rule: A static class may not have constructors *other than a static constructor*; the static constructor runs after all static field initializers complete (§22.13).

title: a static owned readonly field on a static class is permitted
rule: Static `owned` fields are permitted: `static owned readonly` fields and `static readonly` owning-inline-array fields participate in §22.13's program-exit disposal exactly as on any other type — that mechanism is runtime-driven and independent of instance `Dispose()`.

title: a static class may not declare a destructor
rule: A static class may not have instance fields, instance methods, instance properties, indexers, constructors (other than a static constructor), or destructors.

title: a static class may not implement an interface
rule: A static class may not be inherited from and does not implement interfaces.

title: abstract and static are mutually exclusive
rule: The `abstract` and `static` modifiers are mutually exclusive, and `sealed` and `static` are mutually exclusive; combining either pair is a compile error.

title: sealed and static are mutually exclusive
rule: The `abstract` and `static` modifiers are mutually exclusive, and `sealed` and `static` are mutually exclusive; combining either pair is a compile error.

title: a closed class may not be instantiated directly
rule: A class declared with the `closed` modifier is a closed abstract class: a class that cannot be instantiated directly and cannot be inherited from outside the declaring module.

title: a closed class may not be subclassed from another module
rule: Classes derived from a `closed` base must be declared in the same module; the compiler rejects subclasses in other modules.

title: a static class's static method may be named GetType
rule: its static members may take any name of that surface, `Equals`, `GetHashCode`, `ToString` and `GetType` included ([§11.7]). S is a static class, so its static method GetType is not a hiding declaration of [§12.2], and the call S.GetType() returns the declared value 1.

title: a conforming type supplies static interface members with exact signatures
rule: An interface member may be declared static: a contract the conforming type -- not an instance -- must satisfy. A conforming type supplies the static members with exact signatures.

title: a static interface member may not declare a body
rule: Static interface members are abstract-only (no default bodies; the same diamond-avoidance posture as the declined default interface methods).

title: calling a static interface member through the interface name is rejected
rule: Static interface members contribute nothing to the instance surface... calling a static member on the interface name (INumber<int>.Zero()) is a compile error -- the interface declares no bodies to run.

title: an interface declaring static members may not mark a type parameter variant
rule: An interface that declares static members may not mark its type parameters variant (in/out) -- a compile error at the declaration.

title: T.Member(...) dispatches to the conforming type's static member
rule: In a generic body whose parameter T carries a static-interface constraint, T.Member(...) calls the conforming type's static member, and an operator applied to T-typed operands resolves through the constraint's static operators.

title: an override matching the base member exactly is admitted
rule: A method, property, or indexer is non-virtual unless marked virtual. To override a virtual member in a derived class, mark the matching member override.

title: an override with a mismatched parameter type is rejected
rule: Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly.

title: an override may widen a parameter from T to T?
rule: An override may declare a parameter as T? where the overridden member declares T -- the same contravariant nullability widening §11.2 grants interface implementations.

title: an override may not narrow a parameter from T? back to T
rule: The reverse direction (overridden T?, override T) is rejected, as in §11.2.

title: a virtual override runs through a base-typed reference
rule: A method, property, or indexer is non-virtual unless marked virtual. To override a virtual member in a derived class, mark the matching member override.

title: an extension member is resolved by the receiver's static type, not dispatched virtually
rule: A method, property, or indexer is non-virtual unless marked virtual -- an extension member has no override relationship at all, and §26.5 resolves it by the receiver's declared type.

title: an override may widen a built-in exception parameter to T?
rule: An override may declare a parameter as `T?` where the overridden member declares `T`; visibility, return type and parameter types otherwise match the base member exactly

title: an override may widen a built-in generic class parameter to T?
rule: An override may declare a parameter as `T?` where the overridden member declares `T`; visibility, return type and parameter types otherwise match the base member exactly (v0.338, §12.1).

title: widening to T? does not admit a different built-in class
rule: An override may declare a parameter as `T?` where the overridden member declares `T`; visibility, return type and parameter types otherwise match the base member exactly (v0.338, §12.1).
check: does not match the base member's parameter types

title: widening to T? does not admit a changed built-in generic argument
rule: An override may declare a parameter as `T?` where the overridden member declares `T`; visibility, return type and parameter types otherwise match the base member exactly (v0.338, §12.1).
check: does not match the base member's parameter types

title: an override in a generic derived class matches the substituted base parameter
rule: To override a virtual member in a derived class, mark the matching member `override`. Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly (v0.338, §12.1); the base clause `B<Box<U>>` instantiates `B<T>` with `T` = `Box<U>`, so the base member's parameter type is `Box<U>` (§14.1).

title: a three-level override chain matches each level's substituted parameter
rule: To override a virtual member in a derived class, mark the matching member `override`. Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly, and an override matches against the nearest overridden declaration (v0.338, §12.1); each base clause instantiates its generic base (§14.1).

title: two instantiations of one generic base dispatch to their own overrides
rule: To override a virtual member in a derived class, mark the matching member `override`. Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly (v0.338, §12.1); each base clause instantiates `B<T>` at its own argument (§14.1), so `B<int>` and `B<string>` have distinct members, and a class that does not override a member runs the base member.

title: a concrete subclass overrides an abstract generic member at the substituted type
rule: `abstract` on a member declares it without a body; every concrete subclass must override it (v0.338, §12.5), and the override must match the base member exactly after substitution (v0.338, §12.1; the base clause instantiates `B<T>` with `T` = `Box<int>`, §14.1).

title: an override of a nested generic parameter matches the substituted base member
rule: To override a virtual member in a derived class, mark the matching member `override`. Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly (v0.338, §12.1); the base clause `B<string>` instantiates `B<T>`, so the base parameter type `Box<T>` is `Box<string>` (§14.1).

title: an override may fix one base argument and keep a type parameter in another
rule: To override a virtual member in a derived class, mark the matching member `override`. Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly (v0.338, §12.1); the base clause `B<V, int>` instantiates `B<T, U>` with `T` = `V` and `U` = `int`, so the base member's parameters are `(x: V, y: int)` (§14.1).

title: an override of one generic-substituted overload leaves the sibling overload on its own slot
rule: To override a virtual member in a derived class, mark the matching member `override`. Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly (v0.338, §12.1); the base clause `B<Box<string>>` instantiates `B<T>` at `T` = `Box<string>`, which leaves two overloads of distinct parameter types (`Foo(x: Box<string>)` and `Foo(x: Item)`) in the base; overload selection among them is by exact applicability over the substituted signatures (v0.338, §22.6).

title: a generic-method override reached through a base-typed receiver runs the override
rule: A method, property, or indexer is non-virtual unless marked `virtual`. To override a virtual member in a derived class, mark the matching member `override`. Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly (v0.338, §12.1); a virtual member called through a base-typed reference is dispatched to the override.

title: a generic-method override in a class two generic levels down runs through a base-typed receiver
rule: To override a virtual member in a derived class, mark the matching member `override`. Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly (v0.338, §12.1), and a base clause instantiates a generic base at its own arguments (§14.1), so a class that does not override a member runs the nearest override above it.

title: a non-generic override matches the base parameter through an indirect generic base
rule: Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly (v0.338, §12.1). `E1` derives `D<int>`, which derives `B<T>`; the member `Show(a: T)` that `E1` inherits is `Show(a: int)` under the base-clause arguments (§14.1), so `override method Show(a: int)` matches it.

title: a non-generic override with a wrong parameter type through an indirect generic base is rejected
rule: Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly (v0.338, §12.1). `E2` derives `D<int>`, which derives `B<T>`; the base member it overrides is `Show(a: int)` under the base-clause arguments (§14.1), so `override method Show(a: string)` does not match it.

title: a property override through an indirect generic base dispatches through the base type
rule: A method, property, or indexer is non-virtual unless marked `virtual`. Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly (v0.338, §12.1). The property `V` that `E` inherits through `D<int>` is typed `int`, so `override property V: int` matches it.

title: a property override with the wrong type through an indirect generic base is rejected
rule: Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly (v0.338, §12.1), and the property `V` that `E` inherits through `D<int>` is typed `int`; an override declaring `property V: string` does not match it.

title: an indexer override through an indirect generic base dispatches through the base type
rule: A method, property, or indexer is non-virtual unless marked `virtual`. Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly (v0.338, §12.1). The indexer `[i: int]` that `E` inherits through `D<int>` has the key `int` and the element type `int`, so `override property [i: int]: int` matches it.

title: an indexer override with the wrong key type through an indirect generic base is rejected
rule: Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly (v0.338, §12.1). The indexer that `E` inherits through `D<int>` takes an `int` key; an override taking a `string` key does not match it.

title: an indexer override with a concrete element type dispatches through a generic base
rule: A method, property, or indexer is non-virtual unless marked `virtual`. To override a virtual member in a derived class, mark the matching member `override`. The indexer `[i: int]: T` of `B<string>` has element type `string`, so `override property [i: int]: string` matches it (v0.338, §12.1), and a call through `B<string>` reaches the override.

title: an override's own type parameter matches by position, not by name
rule: An override declares exactly as many type parameters of its own as the overridden member (none where that member declares none), the two lists corresponding by position, not by name (v0.338, §12.1): `public override method Echo<U>(x: U): string` overrides `public virtual method Echo<T>(x: T): string`. The base class's `U` is not in scope in `H`, so the override's `U` is its own.

title: an override declaring two type parameters where the base member declares one is rejected
rule: An override declares exactly as many type parameters of its own as the overridden member (none where that member declares none), the two lists corresponding by position (v0.338, §12.1); `Echo<T, U>(x: T): string` matches no virtual member of that name.

title: an override declaring a type parameter where the base member declares none is rejected
rule: An override declares exactly as many type parameters of its own as the overridden member (none where that member declares none), the two lists corresponding by position (v0.338, §12.1).

title: a generic-method override whose substituted parameter type differs from the base's is rejected
rule: Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly (v0.338, §12.1). The base member that `C` overrides through `B<int>` takes `t: int`, so an override declaring `t: string` does not match it.

title: a parameter widened to T? mid-chain cannot be narrowed back to T further down
rule: Widening is monotone down the chain: an override matches against the nearest overridden declaration, so once a parameter is `T?` a further override must keep it `T?` (v0.338, §12.1); narrowing back would let a `null` admitted through an intermediate static type reach a non-nullable parameter. `D` overrides `B.Q(t: int?)`, so `override method Q(t: int)` is rejected.

title: an override whose return type differs from the substituted base return type is rejected
rule: Return types must still match exactly (no covariance in this version) (v0.338, §12.1). `C` derives `B<int>`, whose virtual `Make()` returns `int`; an override returning `string` does not match it.

title: a swapped generic-base override dispatches to the matching override
rule: Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly (v0.338, §12.1). `D<X, Y>` derives `B<Y, X>`, so the base member it overrides takes `(e, x: Y, y: X)` for `D`'s own `X` and `Y`, and `override method M<U>(e: U, a: Y, b: X)` matches it; each base clause instantiates its generic base at its own arguments (§14.1).

title: an override taking a different class type parameter as its method parameter is rejected
rule: Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly, with one allowance: an override may declare a parameter as `T?` where the overridden member declares `T`
check: does not match the base member

title: an override taking a different class type parameter inside Array as its method parameter is rejected
rule: Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly, with one allowance: an override may declare a parameter as `T?` where the overridden member declares `T`
check: does not match the base member

title: an override returning a different class type parameter is rejected
rule: Return types must still match exactly (no covariance in this version).
check: does not match the base member

title: an override returning Array of a different class type parameter is rejected
rule: Return types must still match exactly (no covariance in this version).
check: does not match the base member

title: an indexer override with a different class type parameter as its key is rejected
rule: Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly, with one allowance: an override may declare a parameter as `T?` where the overridden member declares `T`
check: does not match the base member

title: an indexer override with Array of a different class type parameter as its key is rejected
rule: Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly, with one allowance: an override may declare a parameter as `T?` where the overridden member declares `T`
check: does not match the base member

title: an override with the same class type parameter as its method parameter is admitted
rule: Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly, with one allowance: an override may declare a parameter as `T?` where the overridden member declares `T`

title: an override whose parameter has a different name but the base's class type parameter is admitted
rule: Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly, with one allowance: an override may declare a parameter as `T?` where the overridden member declares `T`

title: an override of a substituted concrete parameter type is admitted
rule: Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly, with one allowance: an override may declare a parameter as `T?` where the overridden member declares `T`

title: an override whose parameter type differs from the alias-expanded base parameter is rejected
rule: Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly

title: a derived class may not redeclare a visible inherited member's name
rule: Declaring a member in a derived class with the same name as any inherited member visible at the derived class's declaration site is a compile error, unless the declaration is an override of a virtual member.

title: overriding a virtual base member is the sanctioned way to reuse its name
rule: Declaring a member in a derived class with the same name as any inherited member visible at the derived class's declaration site is a compile error, unless the declaration is an override of a virtual member with a matching signature.

title: an invisible private base member does not block the name in a derived class
rule: A private base member never blocks -- two same-named private fields in base and derived are distinct members and legal... When a base member was invisible at the derived declaration site, the derived declaration creates a distinct member.

title: a nested type named ToString hides the inherited Object.ToString and is rejected
rule: Declaring a member in a derived class with the same name as

title: a nested type named Equals hides the inherited Object.Equals and is rejected
rule: Declaring a member in a derived class with the same name as

title: a nested type named GetHashCode hides the inherited Object.GetHashCode and is rejected
rule: Declaring a member in a derived class with the same name as

title: base.Member bypasses virtual dispatch
rule: Inside a derived member, base.Name(...) calls the base class's implementation, bypassing virtual dispatch.

title: inheriting from a sealed class is rejected
rule: sealed on a class prevents inheritance from that class.

title: bare sealed on a member is rejected
rule: On a member, `sealed` appears only as the compound `sealed override`: a member declaration carrying `sealed` without `override` is a compile error, whatever the member's kind and whatever other dispatch modifier it carries.

title: virtual on a member of a sealed class is rejected
rule: A member of a `sealed` class may not be declared `virtual`: the class admits no subclass, so a new virtual slot on it can never be filled, and an inert modifier that reads as load-bearing misleads every reader of the declaration.

title: the same virtual member on a non-sealed class is admitted
rule: The rejection is keyed on the class being `sealed` — a class that admits subclasses may declare a new `virtual` slot, which is what §12.1's override-matching rule exists to fill.

title: a user class may not derive from Mutex, a compiler-known class its text does not open
rule: Every other compiler-known class is closed to inheritance exactly as a `sealed` class is, whether or not its listing writes `sealed`, and a base-type reference to one in a user declaration is a compile error naming this rule.

title: a user class may derive from Exception, a compiler-known class §31.4 opens
rule: A compiler-known class — a class of the standard library, or `Exception` and the built-in exception types (§31.4) — is a valid base class only where the text that declares it states that user code may derive from it: stdlib §1 (*Extensibility*) lists the library classes so opened, and §31.4 opens the exception family.

title: new on an abstract class is rejected
rule: new on an abstract or closed class is a compile error.

title: a class with an abstract member must itself be abstract or closed
rule: A class containing one or more abstract members must itself be abstract (or closed, §11.7).

title: async abstract is rejected
rule: async abstract is a compile error. An abstract method whose implementations are expected to be asynchronous declares a Task or Task<T> return type without async.

title: is T narrows the tested variable to T in the true branch
rule: is T tests whether a value is an instance of T and produces bool. When the test succeeds and the tested expression is one of §7.4's narrowing carriers — a local variable, a parameter other than a ref parameter, or a readonly field one field off an admitted root — the carrier is flow-narrowed to T within the controlled block.

title: a chain-extending store into a value-narrowed Object box is rejected
rule: A write whose store would land in the box is a compile error: an assignment, compound assignment, or ++/-- whose target is an lvalue chain extending the binding with a . or [...] hop.

title: a ref argument into a value-narrowed Object box is rejected
rule: A write whose store would land in the box is a compile error: such a chain passed as a ref or out argument, which §22.3's assignable-storage-location categories admit -- through which the callee's write reaches the payload.

title: a bare-binding compound assignment on a narrowed Object is not a box write
rule: What is not rejected is the bare-binding compound and ++/-- form: o += 1 and o++ are equivalent to o := o + 1, and that store targets the declared Object/interface location -- it boxes the result afresh.

title: an is test against a function type tests the value's formed type, not a retyped view
rule: A test whose target is a function type (§27.1) — `o is (Animal) -> ()`, `o as ((int) -> int)` — is decided by **identity of the function type**, not by §27.1.1's assignability ... over `f: (Animal) -> ()`, after `var g: (Dog) -> () := f; var o: Object := g;`, `o is (Animal) -> ()` is `true` and `o is (Dog) -> ()` is `false`.

title: an as conversion to a function type the value reaches only by variance yields null
rule: A test whose target is a function type (§27.1) — `o is (Animal) -> ()`, `o as ((int) -> int)` — is decided by **identity of the function type**, not by §27.1.1's assignability ... over `f: (Animal) -> ()`, after `var g: (Dog) -> () := f; var o: Object := g;`, `o is (Animal) -> ()` is `true` and `o is (Dog) -> ()` is `false`.

title: reassigning a type-narrowed carrier drops the narrowing whatever the right-hand side
rule: Reassignment within the controlled block invalidates the type narrowing, whatever the right-hand side's type (the assignment may still establish §7.4's non-null fact) (v0.338 §12.7 line 2114)

title: a type-narrowed carrier that is not reassigned keeps the narrowing
rule: When the test succeeds and the tested expression is one of §7.4's narrowing carriers, the carrier is **flow-narrowed** to `T` within the controlled block (v0.338 §12.7 line 2106)

title: an is not null test on an as-cast result, passed directly to Console.WriteLine, prints its value
rule: `as` returns the value cast to the target type, or `null` if the cast fails. Its result is always nullable. ([§12.7]). "`is not null` tests whether it is non-null and narrows to the non-nullable form." ([§12.7]). The first `as` casts a `StringBuilder` held in an `Object` local and succeeds, so `is not null` is true; the second casts a `Random` and yields null, so `is null` is true.

title: an is test on a StringBuilder and on a nullable StringBuilder answers for the value's instance
rule: `is T` tests whether a value is an instance of `T` and produces `bool` ([§12.7]). "`not (x is T)` is a different expression (a boolean negation of a relational test) with the same truth value" ([§17.4]). A null value is an instance of no type, so `n is StringBuilder` is false and `n is not StringBuilder` is true; a present `StringBuilder` is an instance of its own type.

title: an is test on an Object-typed local answers for the runtime type of a StringBuilder
rule: `is T` tests whether a value is an instance of `T` and produces `bool` ([§12.7]). A local typed `Object` that holds a `StringBuilder` is an instance of `StringBuilder`, and the local holding a `Random` is not, so the two tests are true, false.

title: an is not T test narrows the carrier to T in the else branch
rule: For an `is not T` test, "the variable is narrowed to `T` in the else branch" (§12.7, v0.340); a `with` "result has the same static type as the source" (§9.5, v0.340). So in the else branch of `c is not P` a `P?` carrier is narrowed to `P`, the `with` result is a `P`, and a `P` target accepts it.

title: a copy-out of an is-narrowed carrier reads the payload
rule: A narrowing converts nothing (§12.7, v0.340) — it changes the static type the carrier is seen at, not the value it holds. So a copy out of a `P?` carrier narrowed to `P` inside the controlled block copies the payload: the copied record's fields are the source's.

title: a narrowed nullable value type formats its payload, not the carrier
rule: `is null` tests whether the value is null. `is not null` tests whether it is non-null and narrows to the non-nullable form.

title: a type-test-narrowed nullable value type formats its payload, not the carrier
rule: When the test succeeds and the tested expression is one of [§7.4](#sec-narrowing-applies-to-locals-only)'s narrowing carriers, the carrier is **flow-narrowed** to `T` within the controlled block:

title: a narrowed nullable Guid renders its payload's D form, not the carrier
rule: `is null` tests whether the value is null. `is not null` tests whether it is non-null and narrows to the non-nullable form.

title: a base(...) chain argument may read the constructor's own parameters and constants
rule: The only reads a base(...)/this(...) argument may make are of the constructor's own parameters, constants, and statics.

title: a chain argument may not read a field of this
rule: it may not read a field or auto-property of the object under construction -- nothing of this is assigned yet.

title: a chain argument may not read a primary-constructor parameter
rule: nor, in a class with a primary constructor, a primary-constructor parameter (§22.10; the field half is §22.7's ground: nothing of this is assigned yet).

title: the implicit base() insertion requires a parameterless base constructor
rule: If neither base(...) nor this(...) is written, the compiler inserts an implicit base() call (which requires the base class to have a parameterless constructor; otherwise the chain must be explicit).

title: a covariant type parameter used only in output position is admitted
rule: out requires T to appear only in output positions (return types, read-only property types, out parameters).

title: a covariant type parameter used in input position is rejected
rule: out requires T to appear only in output positions... The compiler enforces position constraints.

title: a variance marker on a generic class is rejected
rule: Classes, records, and concrete generic types are always invariant -- and the variance markers are interface-only syntax: in/out on a generic parameter of a class... is a compile error.

title: a variant assignment whose source has a value-type type argument is rejected
rule: What is rejected is the variant assignment of IEnumerable<int> to IEnumerable<Object>, which would require per-element boxing at every access. For value-typed T, the only legal assignment of IEnumerable<T> is to IEnumerable<T> itself or to Object.

title: IEnumerable<Dog> is accepted as IEnumerable<Animal> under an explicit list
rule: Reference-typed T admits the full covariant chain — `IEnumerable<Dog>` is assignable to `IEnumerable<Animal>` and to `IEnumerable<Object>` because the underlying references compose without conversion.

title: a covariant type parameter under an invariant class wrapper is rejected
rule: Position is composed across nested type constructors. A type parameter inside another generic type inherits position from that wrapper's variance; classes, records, and concrete generic types are always invariant, so no marker survives one.

title: a covariant type parameter under a covariant interface wrapper is admitted
rule: Position is composed across nested type constructors. A type parameter inside another generic type inherits position from that wrapper's variance — `IEnumerable` is `out T`, so in a return type the composed position stays covariant.

title: a covariant type parameter in a function type's return, at a method parameter, is rejected
rule: Function types are themselves variant — covariant in return type, contravariant in parameter types — and the same composition rule applies, so T inside `() -> T` at a method parameter composes to contravariant.

title: the same declaration is admitted under a contravariant marker
rule: Function types are themselves variant — covariant in return type, contravariant in parameter types — and the same composition rule applies, so T inside `() -> T` at a method parameter composes to contravariant.

title: a contravariant type parameter in a covariant base's argument is rejected
rule: The extending interface instantiates the base's variant parameter with its own type parameter, holding the deriving interface's variance.

title: the same base instantiation is admitted under a covariant marker
rule: The extending interface instantiates the base's variant parameter with its own type parameter, holding the deriving interface's variance.

title: a covariant interface argument converts to the wider instantiation and not to string
rule: Reference-typed T admits the full covariant chain — `IEnumerable<Dog>` is assignable to `IEnumerable<Animal>` ([§12.9]). The same chain holds for an out-marked interface: DogBox implements IOBox<Dog>, which converts to IOBox<Animal> and not to IOBox<string>, so only the IOBox<Animal> overload is applicable.

title: an invariant interface parameter is applicable only at the instantiation the argument implements
rule: Type parameters without `out` or `in` are invariant. ([§12.9]). IBox has no variance marker, DogBox implements IBox<Dog> and not IBox<Animal>, so only the IBox<Dog> overload is applicable.

title: a contravariant interface argument converts to the narrower instantiation
rule: Generic interface type parameters may be marked `out` (covariant) or `in` (contravariant) ([§12.9]). ISink<in T> reverses the direction: AnimalSink implements ISink<Animal>, which converts to ISink<Dog>, so the ISink<Dog> overload is the only applicable one, and the assignment to ISink<Dog> prints the value the Animal sink returns.

title: a concrete generic class is invariant in its type argument
rule: Classes, records, and concrete generic types are always invariant ([§12.9]). Array<ArgumentException> does not convert to Array<Exception>, although ArgumentException derives from Exception.
check: not implicitly convertible to the target type

title: a nullable element view does not reverse to the non-nullable interface
rule: The relation a variant conversion asks of the two arguments is a reference conversion ([§12.9]), whose nullable forms are listed as "the nullable view of a reference type (`string` to `string?`)" ([§12.9]). The view runs from non-null to nullable only: IEnumerable<ArgumentException?> does not convert to IEnumerable<Exception>, because ArgumentException? to Exception is not a view of that kind.
check: not implicitly convertible to the target type

title: a class naming itself as its own base is a cycle
rule: The simplest case is a type naming itself (class C: C).

title: a two-class inheritance cycle is rejected
rule: the general case is a chain (class A: B, class B: C, class C: A) and the mixed class/interface chains the relation admits.

title: an interface extending itself is a cycle
rule: An inheritance cycle is a compile error. A type may not, directly or transitively, list itself among its base types — neither as the base class of a class, nor as an extended interface of an interface.

title: a two-interface extension cycle is rejected
rule: The relation followed is the union of base-class edges and extended-interface edges; a cycle is any sequence of types where each lists the next as a base type and the sequence returns to its start.

title: a three-class inheritance chain that returns to its start is rejected
rule: The general case is a chain (`class A: B`, `class B: C`, `class C: A`); the compiler detects the cycle and reports an error naming the participating types.

title: an acyclic chain over both edge kinds is accepted and dispatches
rule: An inheritance cycle is a compile error only where the sequence returns to its start; a chain over base-class edges and extended-interface edges that never returns to its start is admitted.

title: a private member is not visible outside the declaring class
rule: `private` — Visible to the declaring class only.

title: a private member is visible within its own declaring class
rule: `private` — Visible to the declaring class only.

title: an internal member is not visible from another module
rule: `internal` — Visible to code in the same module. A module is the set of source files declaring the same module name presented to the module's one compilation; a separately-compiled importing module is not that set.

title: an internal member is visible from another class in the same module
rule: `internal` — Visible to code in the same module. Unlike `private`, an internal member is reachable from any class compiled as part of the same module, not only the declaring class.

title: a protected member is reachable from a derived class in another module
rule: `protected` — Visible to the declaring class and all classes derived from it. §13.1: a derived class in a different module sees `protected` even though it does not see `internal` — that is the whole point of the level.

title: a protected member is not reachable from an unrelated class in the same module
rule: `protected` — Visible to the declaring class and all classes derived from it. §13.1: an unrelated class in the same module sees `internal` but not `protected` — module membership alone does not confer access; only the inheritance relationship does.

title: internal does not extend to a derived class in another module
rule: `internal` and `protected` are incomparable — a derived class in a different module sees `protected` but not `internal`. Inheriting from a class in another module confers no access to that class's internal members.

title: a top-level type declared protected is rejected
rule: Top-level types may be `public` or `internal`. They may not be `protected` (no enclosing class) or `private` (no file-scope concept).

title: internal is an admitted top-level visibility
rule: Top-level types may be `public` or `internal`.

title: a field with no visibility keyword is rejected
rule: Every class member must declare its visibility explicitly, except the four exempted kinds. On every other member, omitting the visibility keyword is a compile error.

title: a field with an explicit visibility keyword is admitted
rule: Every class member must declare its visibility explicitly, except the four exempted kinds.

title: a destructor given an explicit visibility keyword is rejected
rule: A `destructor` is a member kind user code can never invoke or name at a use site — for such a member no visibility choice exists to spell, and it carries no visibility keyword.

title: a destructor with no visibility keyword is admitted
rule: A `destructor` carries no visibility keyword — for such a member no visibility choice exists to spell.

title: files in Foo get no special access to files in Foo.Bar
rule: The dotted form is a single name; files in `Foo` get no special access to files in `Foo.Bar`.

title: a dotted module name is an ordinary whole name for internal access
rule: A module is the set of all source files declaring the same `module Name.Path;`; the dotted form is a single name, so files sharing the whole dotted name share internal access exactly as an undotted name would.

title: files in Foo.Bar get no special access to files in Foo
rule: The dotted form is a single name; `Foo` and `Foo.Bar` are unrelated modules in both directions — neither gets special access to the other's internal members.

title: two modules under a common dotted prefix are unrelated siblings
rule: The dotted form is a single name; it does not establish nesting (§2.1). `Foo.Bar` and `Foo.Baz` share a prefix but are unrelated modules — neither gets access to the other's internal members.

title: protected internal is not a valid combined visibility
rule: Bezel does not provide combined forms (no `protected internal`, no `private protected`).

title: protected alone is a valid single visibility
rule: Bezel does not provide combined forms (no `protected internal`, no `private protected`); a single level is unaffected.

title: an accessor visibility less restrictive than the property is rejected
rule: A property's `get` or `set` may carry its own visibility, which must not be less restrictive than the property's overall visibility.

title: a more restrictive accessor visibility is admitted
rule: A property's `get` or `set` may carry its own visibility, which must not be less restrictive than the property's overall visibility; a more restrictive accessor is the useful form.

title: an internal field typed at a private nested class is rejected
rule: Every type appearing in a member's signature must be at least as visible as the member — `internal _x: NestedPrivate;` is an error when `NestedPrivate` is `private`: the field's type is not as visible as the field.

title: a private field typed at a private nested class is admitted
rule: Every type appearing in a member's signature must be at least as visible as the member — `private _y: NestedPrivate;` is fine: also private, matches `NestedPrivate`'s visibility.

title: a protected member with an internal-typed parameter is rejected
rule: Every type appearing in a member's signature must be at least as visible as the member. The rule applies at every visibility level: a `protected` member's signature types must be at least `protected` — `internal` and `protected` are incomparable (§13.1), so an `internal` type does not satisfy it.

title: a protected member with a protected-typed parameter is admitted
rule: Every type appearing in a member's signature must be at least as visible as the member; equal visibility satisfies the rule.

title: an override declaring a different visibility than the base member is rejected
rule: An override must declare the same visibility as the base member.

title: an override matching the base member's visibility is admitted
rule: An override must declare the same visibility as the base member.

title: a generic class parameterizes its members over a type parameter
rule: Classes, interfaces, records, and methods may be generic; type parameters use angle brackets (§14.1).

title: a generic type named in receiver position is checked at the substitution there
rule: and a generic type named in **receiver position** of a static member access or at the head of a member chain (§22.12: `Reg<Pair>.Put(x)`, `Cache<string>.Default.Count`). ... Wherever a rule of this specification fires *at the instantiation site* — §3.6 rule 2's per-instantiation property evaluation, ... — it fires at every such site.

title: the same static access at a borrow-free argument is admitted
rule: and a generic type named in **receiver position** of a static member access or at the head of a member chain (§22.12: `Reg<Pair>.Put(x)`, `Cache<string>.Default.Count`). ... Wherever a rule of this specification fires *at the instantiation site* — §3.6 rule 2's per-instantiation property evaluation, ... — it fires at every such site.

title: a derived class calls its constructed generic base's members by bare name, also in a lambda
rule: An instantiation of a generic declaration is the constructed type or constructed member obtained by substituting type arguments for its type parameters (§14.1, v0.340). `Sub : Box<string>` inherits `Get(): T` and `Get(x: int): T` instantiated at `string`, so the bare call `Get().Length` and `Get(n).Length` type-check and run, including inside a lambda in `Sub`, and so does `base.Get()`.

title: a generic class method and a virtual method return a generic choice carrying their payload
rule: For a **generic** choice the type arguments are written at the construction (`Result<int, string>.Ok(value)`) (§35.3, v0.340); a generic member is evaluated at each instantiation after substituting the type arguments (§3.6 rule 2, §14.1), so the payload constructed in the generic body is the payload matched by the caller. `Box<int>.Get(7)` and the virtual `VGet(8)` return `Opt<int>.Some(x)`, and the caller's match reads 7 and 8.

title: generic methods returning a two-parameter generic choice keep case and payload at every placement
rule: For a **generic** choice the type arguments are written at the construction (`Result<int, string>.Ok(value)`) (§35.3, v0.340); a generic member is evaluated at each instantiation after substituting the type arguments (§3.6 rule 2, §14.1), so the payload constructed in the generic body is the payload matched by the caller. Each method builds `E<..>.L` or `E<..>.R` at its own instantiation; with `T = int` the results are `L1`, `R2`, `R40`, `L41`, `R5`, `RTrue` and `R7`, whichever of the two type parameters the generic argument stands for and whether the payload is `T`, a constant of another type, or `T` repeated.

title: generic methods returning a generic choice carry long, string and double payloads
rule: For a **generic** choice the type arguments are written at the construction (`Result<int, string>.Ok(value)`) (§35.3, v0.340); a generic member is evaluated at each instantiation after substituting the type arguments (§3.6 rule 2, §14.1), so the payload constructed in the generic body is the payload matched by the caller. The payloads are `long` 5000000000 (beyond `int`), the `long` 7 given as `T = int` 2, a `string`, and a `double` 2.5, in each of the two payload positions of `E<A, B>`.

title: an inherited generic indexer's argument is checked against the substituted type
rule: An instantiation of a generic declaration is the constructed type or constructed member obtained by substituting type arguments for its type parameters; its site is the program point at which the program forms one. The base clause `Root<Array<U>>` at `Mid<int>` forms the inherited indexer with its parameter type substituted to Array<int>, and a value of one type implicitly converts to another when no programmer-visible information is lost — no string to Array<int> conversion does.

title: the same inherited indexer accepts an argument of the substituted type
rule: An instantiation of a generic declaration is the constructed type or constructed member obtained by substituting type arguments for its type parameters; its site is the program point at which the program forms one. The base clause `Root<Array<U>>` at `Mid<int>` forms the inherited indexer with its parameter type substituted to Array<int>, and an Array<int> argument converts to it without loss, so the inherited member's body is the one that answers.

title: a generic method's instantiation reads the SUBSTITUTED element type
rule: §3.6 rule 2 - "Per-instantiation evaluation for generics. For a generic type or member, the property is evaluated at each instantiation, after substituting the type arguments." §14.1's instantiation site is where a generic method's type arguments are substituted, and stdlib §4.4 declares `Array<T>`'s element type to be `T` - so at the instantiation `F<Array<int>>` the index expression `x[0]` reads an `int` element, the substituted element type, and yields the array's first element. §23.4's indexer is the member the expression selects.

title: a class type satisfies where T: class
