rule: `where T: class` accepts non-nullable reference types only — classes, interfaces, string, function types (§14.2).

title: a record fails where T: class
rule: `where T: class` accepts non-nullable reference types only; a value type is excluded (§14.2).

title: a record satisfies where T: value
rule: `where T: value` accepts non-nullable value types — records, enums, choices, primitives, inline arrays, the unit type (§14.2).

title: a class fails where T: value
rule: `where T: value` admits only non-nullable value types; a reference type is excluded (§14.2).

title: a non-nullable class satisfies where T: notnull
rule: `where T: notnull` accepts non-nullable types only, value or reference (§14.2).

title: a nullable class type fails where T: notnull
rule: `where T: notnull` excludes a nullable type, value or reference — a nullable type is excluded (§14.2).

title: a class implementing the named interface satisfies where T: IFoo
rule: `where T: IFoo` admits non-nullable types conforming to `IFoo`: classes implementing it, directly or by inheritance (§14.2).

title: a class not implementing the named interface fails where T: IFoo
rule: `where T: IFoo` admits only types conforming to `IFoo` per the interface-conformance rule; a non-conforming class is excluded (§14.2).

title: a class with a public parameterless constructor satisfies where T: new()
rule: For `where T: new()`, a class substitution satisfies the constraint exactly when the class declares a parameterless constructor that is `public`; inside the generic body `new T()` produces an owned reference via that constructor (§14.2).

title: a class without a public parameterless constructor fails where T: new()
rule: A class substitution satisfies `where T: new()` exactly when the class declares a parameterless constructor that is `public` — not merely accessible from some scope — or declares no instance constructor at all, in which case §22.7's implicit parameterless constructor, which is `public`, satisfies it on the same terms. A class declaring only a parameterized constructor satisfies neither arm (§14.2).

title: a defaultable record satisfies where T: new() and new T() is default(T)
rule: A value-type substitution satisfies `where T: new()` exactly when it is defaultable; inside the generic body, `new T()` for a value substitution is equivalent to `default(T)` (§14.2).

title: an interface never satisfies where T: new()
rule: Interface substitutions never satisfy `new()` — no constructor exists (§14.2).

title: a choice never satisfies where T: new()
rule: Choices never satisfy the value-type arm of `where T: new()` — a consequence of the property: no choice is defaultable (§14.2, §17.11).

title: contradictory constraints are a compile error at the declaration
rule: Contradictory constraint combinations (e.g. `class, value`) are compile errors (§14.2).

title: int satisfies where T: sendable
rule: `where T: sendable` admits types whose sendable derived type property holds; all primitives are sendable (§14.2, §30.14).

title: an interface type fails where T: sendable
rule: `where T: sendable` is decided by the §30.14 computation; interface types are never sendable (§14.2, §30.14).

title: int satisfies where T: hashable
rule: Types whose **hashable** derived type property (§3.6) holds — consistent `Equals`/`GetHashCode`, usable as hash-container keys and elements — decided per instantiation by §3.6's computation.

title: a record with an explicit field and no user equality fails where T: hashable
rule: `hashable` excludes a record that is neither auto-hashable nor declares user equality; an explicit field declaration makes a body record not auto-hashable (§14.2, §3.6, §9.2).

title: a member where clause naming the enclosing type parameter is rejected
rule: A `where` clause on a member declaration may constrain only that member's own type parameters; a clause whose constrained parameter is a type parameter of the enclosing declaration is a compile error naming the conditionally-admitted-members subsection (§14.2 rule 1, v0.277).

title: a member where clause constraining its own type parameter, bound to an enclosing one, is admitted
rule: A clause constraining the member's own parameter is unaffected, including where its bound names an enclosing parameter (`method M<U>() where U: T` on `class C<T>`) — the ordinary constraint form of §14.2 (§14.2 rule 1, v0.277).

title: an interface implementation comparing its own unconstrained type parameter is rejected at its body
rule: Every body of a dispatched generic method ... is checked under its constraint set (above) as any generic body is, and a requirement of its own type parameter that the set does not establish is a **compile error at that body** ... The diagnostic names the requirement and the remedies: a constraint of this section on the **declaring** interface or base method, which every implementation then inherits (`where T: hashable` for an equality use ...).

title: the same equality implementation is admitted under where T hashable on the declaring interface
rule: The diagnostic names the requirement and the remedies: a constraint of this section on the **declaring** interface or base method, which every implementation then inherits (`where T: hashable` for an equality use ...).

title: a dispatched generic call at an owning inline array type argument is rejected at the call
rule: The type parameters of a dispatched generic method admit no move-only value type (§15.3) and no inline array of any form (§15.1) as a type argument. A call of one at such an argument ... is a **compile error at the call**

title: a call of the same interface generic method at a class type argument is admitted
rule: The type parameters of a dispatched generic method admit no move-only value type (§15.3) and no inline array of any form (§15.1) as a type argument.

title: a call on the conforming class of an inherited witness is excluded at an owning inline array
rule: The type parameters of a dispatched generic method admit no move-only value type (§15.3) and no inline array of any form (§15.1) as a type argument. ... a call on a receiver typed at a class for which the method is an inherited witness (*Constraints on overrides and interface implementations* above), or at a class deriving from it, is such a call

title: the same call on a receiver typed at the base class stays an ordinary generic call
rule: a call on a receiver typed at the base class that declares the witness as an ordinary, non-`virtual` generic method names no dispatched declaration and stays an ordinary generic call, checked per instantiation

title: a class type bound naming Object is rejected at the declaration
rule: A bound naming `Object` (§8.1) is a compile error at the declaration: write an unconstrained `T`, or `where T: notnull`.

title: a method type bound naming Object is rejected at the declaration
rule: A bound naming `Object` (§8.1) is a compile error at the declaration: write an unconstrained `T`, or `where T: notnull`.

title: where T notnull is the admitted spelling of what an Object bound meant
rule: A bound naming `Object` (§8.1) is a compile error at the declaration: write an unconstrained `T`, or `where T: notnull`.

title: where T hashable is not satisfied by a function type
rule: A function type is nonetheless not **hashable** (§3.6, clause (e)) ... a `Set<(int) -> int>`, a `Dictionary<(int) -> int, V>`, stdlib §5's hashable block and `where T: hashable` at a function type are rejected at the instantiation site

title: where T: U is not satisfied by boxing a primitive to Object
rule: a substitution S for `T` satisfies `where T: U` exactly when S is non-nullable and is a *subtype of* the substitution for `U` — identical to it, a class derived from a class substitution (§12), or a type conforming to an interface substitution ... — and by these three relations only: no other implicit conversion of §5.1 satisfies the bound, neither boxing to `Object`, numeric widening, nullable wrapping nor a variance-induced conversion

title: where T: U at U := Object does not admit string, which is not a class
rule: a substitution S for `T` satisfies `where T: U` exactly when S is non-nullable and is a *subtype of* the substitution for `U` — identical to it, a class derived from a class substitution (§12), or a type conforming to an interface substitution ... — and by these three relations only: no other implicit conversion of §5.1 satisfies the bound, neither boxing to `Object`, numeric widening, nullable wrapping nor a variance-induced conversion ... At `U := Object` the bound admits `Object` and every class type, and nothing else: `string`, interfaces and function types are not classes (§8.1)

title: where T: U is not satisfied by numeric widening
rule: a substitution S for `T` satisfies `where T: U` exactly when S is non-nullable and is a *subtype of* the substitution for `U` — identical to it, a class derived from a class substitution (§12), or a type conforming to an interface substitution ... — and by these three relations only: no other implicit conversion of §5.1 satisfies the bound, neither boxing to `Object`, numeric widening, nullable wrapping nor a variance-induced conversion

title: where T: U is not satisfied by nullable wrapping
rule: a substitution S for `T` satisfies `where T: U` exactly when S is non-nullable and is a *subtype of* the substitution for `U` — identical to it, a class derived from a class substitution (§12), or a type conforming to an interface substitution ... — and by these three relations only: no other implicit conversion of §5.1 satisfies the bound, neither boxing to `Object`, numeric widening, nullable wrapping nor a variance-induced conversion

title: where T: U is satisfied by a class type at U := Object
rule: a substitution S for `T` satisfies `where T: U` exactly when S is non-nullable and is a *subtype of* the substitution for `U` — identical to it, a class derived from a class substitution (§12), or a type conforming to an interface substitution ... — and by these three relations only: no other implicit conversion of §5.1 satisfies the bound, neither boxing to `Object`, numeric widening, nullable wrapping nor a variance-induced conversion ... At `U := Object` the bound admits `Object` and every class type, and nothing else: `string`, interfaces and function types are not classes (§8.1)

title: where T: U is satisfied by a value type conforming to an interface substitution
rule: a substitution S for `T` satisfies `where T: U` exactly when S is non-nullable and is a *subtype of* the substitution for `U` — identical to it, a class derived from a class substitution (§12), or a type conforming to an interface substitution ... — and by these three relations only: no other implicit conversion of §5.1 satisfies the bound, neither boxing to `Object`, numeric widening, nullable wrapping nor a variance-induced conversion

title: an interface extending a static-member interface satisfies its constraint at no instantiation
rule: An interface that declares or inherits **static** members (§11.8) is conformed to by no interface under this rule ... so `interface IThing: IZero<IThing>`, over an `IZero<T>` declared without §11.8's recurrence constraint, is a well-formed declaration that satisfies `where T: IZero<T>` at no instantiation site — `Gen.Make<IThing>()` is a compile error naming the constraint

title: a class conforming to a static-member interface satisfies its recurrence constraint
rule: An interface that declares or inherits **static** members (§11.8) is conformed to by no interface under this rule ... so `interface IThing: IZero<IThing>`, over an `IZero<T>` declared without §11.8's recurrence constraint, is a well-formed declaration that satisfies `where T: IZero<T>` at no instantiation site — `Gen.Make<IThing>()` is a compile error naming the constraint

title: a sealed class bound beside an interface the class does not implement is well-formed
rule: A combination empty only by declaration — a class bound naming a `sealed` class beside an interface that class does not implement — is not: it is well-formed, and no type argument satisfies it until the declarations it names change.

title: a class bound beside value admits no type by language rule and is rejected
rule: A constraint combination that admits no type — `class, value`; `value` with `IDisposable` or an interface extending it ... and every other combination whose admitted sets are disjoint as a matter of language rule — is a compile error at the declaration.

title: an inferred type argument at a dispatched generic call rejects an owning inline array
rule: The type parameters of a dispatched generic method admit no move-only value type (§15.3) and no inline array of any form (§15.1) as a type argument. This rule applies to INFERRED type arguments (§14.5) as well as explicit ones (§14.2) — the copy-for-dispatch problem exists regardless of how the type argument was supplied.

title: a class with a protected parameterless constructor does not satisfy where T: new()
rule: A class substitution satisfies `where T: new()` exactly when the class declares a parameterless constructor that is `public` — not merely accessible from some scope — (§14.2, v0.315). A class declaring only a `protected` parameterless constructor does not satisfy the constraint.

title: a class with an internal parameterless constructor does not satisfy where T: new()
rule: A class substitution satisfies `where T: new()` exactly when the class declares a parameterless constructor that is `public` — not merely accessible from some scope — (§14.2, v0.315). A class declaring only an `internal` parameterless constructor does not satisfy the constraint.

title: an ordinary interface does not guarantee a class requirement at the head of an extension
rule: an ordinary interface's conforming set is open, so an interface bound excludes only what a language rule excludes

title: where T: class meets OwningArray's class element requirement
rule: Non-nullable reference types only — classes (including Array<T>, OwningArray<T>, and other heap collection types), interfaces, string, function types.

title: a nested constraint on a class type parameter is rejected for an unconstrained parameter
rule: Where a constraint's satisfaction turns on a type parameter in scope, it is decided at the instantiation site that names the argument, by the constraints of the parameters it turns on. For class C<T> where T: new(), C<W> is admitted in class Box<W> where W: new() and rejected in an unconstrained class Box<W>.

title: the same nested constraint is admitted when the class type parameter carries it
rule: Where a constraint's satisfaction turns on a type parameter in scope, it is decided by the constraints of that parameter; a parameter carrying where W: new() satisfies the nested where T: new().

title: a one-argument OwningBuffer over an enum with no zero-valued constant is rejected
rule: The value presentation's one-argument constructor at a non-defaultable argument rejects the use: default(T) is a compile error for an enum type with no declared constant of underlying value 0 (17.11).

title: a one-argument OwningBuffer over an enum with a zero-valued constant runs
rule: The value presentation's one-argument constructor initializes every slot to default(T); default(T) is defined for an enum that declares a constant of underlying value 0 (17.11).

title: a one-argument OwningBuffer over a record with a non-defaultable enum field is rejected
rule: default(T) is a compile error for a record any of whose declared fields is not defaultable, including an enum with no zero-valued constant (17.11); the value presentation's one-argument constructor rejects the use.

title: a generic body's one-argument OwningBuffer<T> rejects an instantiation at a non-defaultable enum
rule: In a generic body, a use of a two-presentation type at a type argument that is a type parameter in scope is read at each instantiation; the value presentation's one-argument constructor at a non-defaultable argument rejects the instantiation, because default(T) is a compile error there (17.11).

title: a generic body's one-argument OwningBuffer<T> runs at an enum with a zero-valued constant
rule: In a generic body, the one-argument constructor is read at each instantiation; at an enum that declares a zero-valued constant, default(T) is defined (17.11), so the instantiation is admitted.

title: an override omitting the where clause inherits the base's constraint and is admitted
rule: An `override` of a generic method ... inherits the overridden declaration's constraints. Omitting the `where` clauses is the recommended spelling and means exactly the inherited set (v0.338, §14.2). `C` overrides `B<int>.Q<U>` under `where U: IComparable<U>`, and the call `b.Q<int>` satisfies it, since `int` implements `IComparable<int>`.

title: an override of a generic method that adds a where clause the inherited set lacks is rejected
rule: A differing clause — added, removed, narrowed, or widened relative to the inherited set — is a compile error naming the inherited constraints (v0.338, §14.2): dispatch flows through the base signature, so an added constraint on the override would go unenforced at every virtual call. `C`'s override adds `where V: IComparable<V>` to a base method that declares no constraint.

title: a base clause naming a generic class at an argument that fails its bound is rejected
rule: A generic type is instantiated by being named, including in a base clause; every such reference is an instantiation site, and this section's constraint checks fire at every such site (v0.338, §14.1, §14.2). `Derived` names `Box<Other>` in its base clause, and `Other` does not conform to `IFoo`, the bound of `Box`'s `T`.

title: a nullable reference type argument does not satisfy where T: class
rule: `where T: class` admits non-nullable reference types of any kind (§3.2, v0.340); "`where T: class` | Non-nullable reference types only" (§14.2 constraint table, v0.340). `D?` and `string?` are nullable, so each instantiation is rejected.

title: a member the constraint head does not declare is not found on the type parameter
rule: A generic body type-checks under the weakest assumption its constraints establish (§3.6 rule 2); inside the generic body, T's surface includes IFoo's members, regardless of which conformance category T belongs to — a name the head does not declare is on no surface the body may use.

title: a member a user interface inherits from a builtin owning interface is called at a constraint head
rule: Inside the generic body, T's surface includes IFoo's members, regardless of which conformance category T belongs to; the body cannot tell whether T was satisfied by a class, a record, an enum, an interface, a primitive, or another type parameter, and does not need to. The owning family's `Clear` disposes every element it holds (stdlib §4.2), so the call reaches that behaviour (§28.11).

title: a record implementing the named interface satisfies where T: IFoo
rule: Language spec §14.2 (v0.345), the interface conformance rule 2: "T is a record that lists I (or any interface extending I) in its inheritance clause and declares matching members" — and the rule's closing sentence: "`where T: IFoo` admits exactly the substitutions for which T conforms to `IFoo` per the rule above". A record listing a user interface therefore satisfies `where T: IFoo`.

title: a nullable type argument does not satisfy an interface bound, as Math.Max<int?> shows
rule: a class or interface bound admits only non-nullable substitutions, as `where T: class` does (§14.2, v0.350). `Math.Max<T>(a: T, b: T): T where T: IComparable<T>` (stdlib §2.2, v0.350) names an interface bound, so the reference `Math.Max<int?>` is rejected at its formation (§27.6, v0.350: a method reference formation is an instantiation site).

title: the non-nullable Math.Max<int> reference meets the interface bound and runs
rule: a class or interface bound admits only non-nullable substitutions, as `where T: class` does (§14.2, v0.350). The accepting twin of s14_2_0091: `int` is non-nullable, and `Math.Max<T>` declares `where T: IComparable<T>` (stdlib §2.2, v0.350), which `int` meets.

title: owned does not propagate through a generic type argument
rule: `owned` does not propagate through generic type arguments — so `Array<owned T>` is not a type (§14.4).

title: OwningArray<T> is the sanctioned replacement for Array<owned T>
rule: The owning forms are separate named types with their own declarations: `OwningArray<T>` beside `Array<T>` (§14.4).

title: a value type element is rejected on OwningArray<T>
rule: Most standard-library owning types restrict their element type T to class and interface types; value types are rejected at the instantiation site (§14.4).

title: a nullable class type element is admitted on OwningArray<T>
rule: The owning-type instantiation rule checks the underlying type, not the nullable wrapper; a nullable class type is admitted (§14.4).

title: a value type argument is rejected on OwningTask<T>
rule: `OwningTask<T>` is a compile error when T's underlying (nullability-stripped) type is neither a class nor an interface type (§14.4, Appendix C.6).

title: a nullable class type argument is admitted on OwningTask<T>
rule: Nullable class types are admitted for the owning task family: the underlying type is checked, and the nullability of the result is independent of the disposal obligation (§14.4).

title: an owning array of T? is admitted in a generic type whose constraints guarantee class
rule: So `OwningTask<T?>` or `OwningArray<T?>` formed in a generic body is admitted at the declaration exactly where `OwningArray<T>` is — under a constraint set that guarantees `class` (§14.2: `where T: class`, a class bound, a bound naming `IDisposable` or an interface extending it) — and decided at `T`'s substitutions as every instantiation-site rule is (§3.6 rule 2); under any other constraint set, an unconstrained `T` included, both are rejected at the declaration.

title: an owning array of T? under an unconstrained T is rejected at the declaration
rule: So `OwningTask<T?>` or `OwningArray<T?>` formed in a generic body is admitted at the declaration exactly where `OwningArray<T>` is — under a constraint set that guarantees `class` (§14.2: `where T: class`, a class bound, a bound naming `IDisposable` or an interface extending it) — and decided at `T`'s substitutions as every instantiation-site rule is (§3.6 rule 2); under any other constraint set, an unconstrained `T` included, both are rejected at the declaration.

title: an owning array of T? under a user interface bound is rejected at the declaration
rule: So `OwningTask<T?>` or `OwningArray<T?>` formed in a generic body is admitted at the declaration exactly where `OwningArray<T>` is — under a constraint set that guarantees `class` (§14.2: `where T: class`, a class bound, a bound naming `IDisposable` or an interface extending it) — and decided at `T`'s substitutions as every instantiation-site rule is (§3.6 rule 2); under any other constraint set, an unconstrained `T` included, both are rejected at the declaration.

title: the class-guaranteed owning array of T? is rejected at a string substitution
rule: So `OwningTask<T?>` or `OwningArray<T?>` formed in a generic body is admitted at the declaration exactly where `OwningArray<T>` is — under a constraint set that guarantees `class` (§14.2: `where T: class`, a class bound, a bound naming `IDisposable` or an interface extending it) — and decided at `T`'s substitutions as every instantiation-site rule is (§3.6 rule 2); under any other constraint set, an unconstrained `T` included, both are rejected at the declaration. ... the standard-library owning types are compiler-enforced to reject the runtime-managed reference types (`string`, function values)

title: a partial explicit type-argument list is rejected
rule: An explicit type-argument list binds the declared type parameters in declaration order and must supply exactly as many arguments as the method declares type parameters; a shorter or longer list is a compile error — there are no partial lists (§14.5).

title: a full explicit type-argument list binds every type parameter
rule: An explicit type-argument list binds the declared type parameters in declaration order; when a full explicit list is supplied, no inference runs (§14.5).

title: argument-driven unification infers a type parameter from a bare-parameter position
rule: A parameter type that is a bare type parameter X binds X to the argument's static type (§14.5, phase 1).

title: conflicting bindings for one type parameter fail inference
rule: All bindings a type parameter receives must be the same type; two different bindings are an inference failure — the compiler computes no common supertype and no widened join (§14.5, *Agreement*).

title: an explicit type argument resolves an agreement failure
rule: A conflicting-inference failure is remedied with explicit type arguments: with an explicit list, the parameter type is fixed and each argument converts at the ordinary argument-conversion site (§14.5, *Agreement*).

title: a record's type arguments are never inferred from constructor arguments
rule: Class-, record-, and interface-level type arguments are never inferred from constructor arguments: `new Pair(1, "x")` against `record Pair<TF, TS>(First: TF, Second: TS)` is a compile error directing to explicit arguments (§14.5).

title: explicit type arguments construct a generic record
rule: The remedy for uninferred record-level type arguments is explicit arguments: `new Pair<int, string>(1, "x")` (§14.5).

title: a type parameter appearing only in the return type is unbindable without a target
rule: A type parameter still unbound after arguments and lambdas is bound from the call's target type where one exists; a type parameter that remains unbound — appearing in no self-determined argument position and no target context — is a compile error naming the parameter (§14.5).

title: an explicit list longer than a single generic candidate declares is rejected
rule: A shorter or a longer list is a compile error; there are no partial lists. The error is reported only when no candidate declares that many type parameters.

title: an explicit type-argument list that matches no overload's argument types is rejected
rule: An explicit type-argument list binds the declared type parameters in declaration order; when a full explicit list is supplied, no inference runs. The bound parameter types then take part in overload applicability (22.6): when none of the candidates applies, the call is an error.

title: an explicit type argument that the argument does not convert to is rejected
rule: An explicit type-argument list binds the declared type parameters in declaration order and no inference runs; the argument must then convert to the parameter type the list binds.

title: an explicit list reaches only generic candidates while a plain call prefers the non-generic overload
rule: Where the name is overloaded, the list's length selects first: a non-generic candidate takes no list. Without a list, the non-generic candidate is preferred (22.6).

title: explicit constructed type arguments select between a value overload and an array overload
rule: An explicit type-argument list binds the declared type parameters in declaration order and no inference runs; the bound parameter types then rank the applicable overloads (22.6).

title: a valid explicit type-argument list runs and selects the generic overload
rule: When a full explicit list is supplied, no inference runs.

title: a generic overload is applicable through the unique instantiation an argument implements
rule: the unique instantiation of `G` that the argument's type implements or extends ([§14.5]). DogBox implements IBox<Dog> and no other IBox instantiation, so the generic F binds T to Dog and is applicable, while F(IBox<string>) is not; the generic candidate is the only applicable one.

title: a full explicit type-argument list binds T, so the generic body computes at the bound type
rule: An explicit type-argument list (obj.Method<int>(args), §22.12/A.7) binds the declared type parameters in declaration order and must supply exactly as many arguments as the method declares type parameters. When a full explicit list is supplied, no inference runs.

title: an int-typed constant and a byte argument give Math.Max's T two bindings and are rejected
rule: All bindings a type parameter receives — across arguments, lambda returns, and the target — must be the same type. Two different bindings are an inference failure: a compile error naming the type parameter and both types, remedied with explicit type arguments or an explicit cast. Constant expressions contribute their static types (Pick(b, 250) for b: byte is an error — 250 is an int).

title: a byte-typed constant and a byte argument agree, so Math.Max infers T as byte
rule: All bindings a type parameter receives — across arguments, lambda returns, and the target — must be the same type. Two different bindings are an inference failure: a compile error naming the type parameter and both types, remedied with explicit type arguments or an explicit cast. Constant expressions contribute their static types (Pick(b, 250) for b: byte is an error — 250 is an int).

title: under an explicit byte list an int literal beside a byte local constant-narrows at the argument site
rule: With an explicit list — Pick<byte>(b, 250) — the parameter type is byte and the literal constant-narrows at the argument conversion site as usual.

title: under an explicit byte list a non-constant int argument does not narrow even when its value fits
rule: With an explicit list — Pick<byte>(b, 250) — the parameter type is byte and the literal constant-narrows at the argument conversion site as usual. Between signed and unsigned types of the same or narrower width (e.g. int → uint, uint → int, short → ushort). ... This bullet governs non-constant expressions; an integer compile-time constant (§17.14) converts by value under constant narrowing (below), which may cross signedness

title: under an explicit byte list a constant int argument whose value fits narrows by value
rule: With an explicit list — Pick<byte>(b, 250) — the parameter type is byte and the literal constant-narrows at the argument conversion site as usual. An expression of integer type that is a compile-time constant (§17.14) implicitly converts to any integer type whose range contains its value.

title: an explicit long list admits a uint and an int argument that agree on no type of their own
rule: An explicit type-argument list (obj.Method<int>(args), §22.12/A.7) binds the declared type parameters in declaration order and must supply exactly as many arguments as the method declares type parameters. When a full explicit list is supplied, no inference runs.

title: an explicit double list types the call's result as double for two int arguments
rule: An explicit type-argument list (obj.Method<int>(args), §22.12/A.7) binds the declared type parameters in declaration order.

title: self-referential recursion at the same bare type parameter is legal
rule: Recursion at the same arguments stays legal: an edge substituting a type parameter of its target with a bare type parameter in scope at the source declaration is within the bounded-instantiation-closure rule (§14.6).

title: an in-SCC edge that nests a type parameter inside a larger argument is rejected
rule: Any substitution on an in-SCC edge other than a bare in-scope type parameter or a closed type is a compile error at the declaration holding the edge, with a diagnostic naming the cycle and the growing argument (§14.6).

title: an expanding cycle whose halves two sibling modules' implementations hold is rejected
rule: Cycles spanning modules are checked over the compilation closure §2.8.3 rule 1 supplies, and the graph is the **program's**: program assembly (§2.8) re-checks the per-edge condition over the union of every artifact's edges, so a cycle that no single compilation's closure holds — two implementations in sibling modules, each contributing one half of an expanding cycle between a third module's interface methods — is rejected at assembly

title: the same sibling implementations with a non-expanding edge form a legal cycle
rule: Cycles spanning modules are checked over the compilation closure §2.8.3 rule 1 supplies, and the graph is the **program's**: program assembly (§2.8) re-checks the per-edge condition over the union of every artifact's edges, so a cycle that no single compilation's closure holds — two implementations in sibling modules, each contributing one half of an expanding cycle between a third module's interface methods — is rejected at assembly

title: a private helper's edge closing a cross-module expanding cycle is carried to assembly
rule: For this check an artifact carries **every edge of the instantiation-request graph its compilation holds** — the requests of every declaration it compiles, generic or not, whatever its visibility: ... and of every internal declaration such an implementation's requests reach (a `private` helper `H<U>` called at `Box<T>` from an implementation, whose own body calls an imported interface method at `U` that a sibling module implements, holds the edge that closes that cycle)

title: an inline array with a defaultable element type default-initializes to zero
rule: When the element type T is defaultable, an inline array declaration without an explicit initializer is filled with that element default per slot (§15.1).

title: an inline array's explicit initializer fills its slots in order
rule: The initializer is a comma-separated list of N expressions in brackets (§15.1).

title: an inline array initializer with too few elements is a compile error
rule: The list must contain exactly N elements; mismatch is a compile error (§15.1).

title: a zero-size inline array is a compile error
rule: N must be greater than zero; `[0]T` is a compile error (§15.1).

title: inline arrays of different sizes are distinct types
rule: The size N is part of the type; `[3]int` and `[4]int` are distinct types that do not interconvert (§15.1).

title: multi-dimensional inline arrays are not admitted
rule: Inline arrays may not be elements of inline arrays in the form `[N][M]T` — multi-dimensional inline arrays are deferred to a future revision (§15.1).

title: a user generic storing T? named at an inline array is rejected at the instantiation site
rule: a type `T?` — a field, local, parameter or result, a payload or element type, a type argument, or a local the body declares — at a type parameter `T` substituted by an inline array is a compile error at the instantiation site (§3.6 rule 2), through any chain of user declarations

title: FirstOrNull on an Array of an inline array is rejected at the call
rule: a standard-library member whose **signature** forms `T?` at a type parameter of its receiver type ... the `*OrNull` tier (`FirstOrNull`) and the `Try*(out item: T?)` family (`TryPop`, `TryReceive`) among them, is a conditionally-admitted member where that type argument is an inline array (§14.2): a compile error at the use

title: an Array of an inline array is well-formed, indexed and iterated
rule: A standard-library declaration carries no requirement of this kind at its naming (§3.6 rule 2), so `Array<[3]float>` is a well-formed type, indexed and iterated as any other

title: the non-nullable Pop on a Stack of an inline array is admitted and runs
rule: a compile error at the use ... naming the member and the remedies, a count or index test, the non-nullable member, or an element type that wraps the array in a record

title: TryPop on a Stack of an inline array is rejected at the call
rule: a standard-library member whose **signature** forms `T?` at a type parameter of its receiver type ... the `*OrNull` tier (`FirstOrNull`) and the `Try*(out item: T?)` family (`TryPop`, `TryReceive`) among them, is a conditionally-admitted member where that type argument is an inline array (§14.2): a compile error at the use

title: move arr[i] on an owning inline array transfers ownership and requires restoration
rule: The `move arr[i]` form is admitted on `[N owned]T` slots; for non-nullable slots, restoration requires assigning a fresh owned T (§15.1.1).

title: the owned slot marker is rejected on a value-typed element
rule: `[N owned]T` requires T to be a class or interface type; value types are not admitted with the `owned` marker (§15.1.1).

title: string fails the class-or-interface restriction of an owning inline array at instantiation
rule: When T is a generic type parameter, the class-or-interface restriction on `[N owned]T?` is checked at instantiation, so instantiating with T = `string` is a compile error at the instantiation site (§15.1.1).

title: an owning inline array of nullable slots defaults to all null
rule: Nullable owned slots default to all null, with no initializer required at declaration (§15.1.1).

title: an owning inline array local disposes its slots in reverse slot order at scope end
rule: When an owning inline array's lifetime ends, the array's auto-dispose pass disposes each non-null slot **in reverse slot order**; for locals this happens at scope end via the standard owned-local discharge.

title: an owning-inline-array instance field disposes its slots in reverse slot order
rule: For **instance** fields of owning-inline-array type, the enclosing class's compiler-generated `Dispose()` disposes each non-null slot — in the same reverse slot order as every other ending of the value — and no user-written `destructor` is required.

title: whole-value reassignment disposes the displaced slots in reverse slot order
rule: A third ending is **whole-value reassignment**: overwriting an owning-inline-array local or instance field disposes each live slot of the displaced value before the store, in this section's reverse slot order — §15.3's per-slot drop-on-overwrite, the same pass run at the overwrite point.

title: a static owning-inline-array field disposes its slots in reverse slot order at program exit
rule: A fourth ending is **program exit**, for a static field of owning-inline-array type: the exit pass disposes each non-null slot of each such field, in this section's reverse slot order, taking the fields themselves in reverse order of static initialization.

title: an inline array's Length is a compile-time constant N
rule: Every inline array `[N]T` exposes `arr.Length: int` — a compile-time constant N (§15.1.2).

title: an inline array cannot be passed where IEnumerable<T> is expected
rule: Passing an inline array to a method expecting `IEnumerable<T>` is rejected: inline arrays are not class types and declare no interface conformances (§15.1.2).

title: an inline array of FFI-compatible scalars is admitted as an extern parameter
rule: Inline arrays of FFI-compatible scalar elements may appear as `extern` method parameters under the by-address rule (§15.1.3).

title: a heap array used at fixed size keeps its literal-constructed Count
rule: Users who want fixed-size discipline simply do not call resizing methods; the array's `Count` matches its construction-time capacity throughout its lifetime (§15.2).

title: an owning heap array constructed via literal owns its elements
rule: `OwningArray<T>` is a class type allocated with `new` and requiring disposal via `using var`; a collection literal transfers ownership of each element into it (§15.2).

title: reading a moved-from move-only local is a compile error
rule: A move-only value type is a value type whose instances cannot be duplicated; assignment transfers the value, leaving the source moved-from, and reading from a moved-from location is a compile error (§15.3).

title: a move-only value type may not be a field of a record
rule: A move-only value may not be a field of a record — records support only copy semantics, not move semantics (§15.3).

title: a move-only value carrying no borrows may be a field of a class
rule: A move-only value carrying no borrows may be a field of a class; the class's destructor disposes the field's owned slots (§15.3).

title: whole-value reassignment of an owning inline array disposes the displaced live slot
rule: Whole-value reassignment on a move-only local is drop-on-overwrite applied per slot: the RHS is evaluated first, then each live slot of the displaced value is disposed, then the new value is stored; the replacement is itself auto-disposed at scope end (§15.3, §15.1.1).

title: a wholly moved-from move-only local is readable again after reassignment
rule: After the move, `x` is in moved-from state and may not be read until reassigned; the standard restoration mechanism is to assign a fresh owned value (§15.3).

title: moving a move-only local while a closure capture of it is live is rejected
rule: The consume-site freeze applies regardless: moving a move-only local while a live borrow of it exists — e.g. a closure capture — is a compile error (§15.3, §28.9).

title: reassigning a move-only local is frozen while a borrow of a slot's object is live
rule: The reassignment is a consume of the displaced value — at a local, frozen while a live local borrow of the displaced value exists, a borrow of any slot's object included, since the pass disposes it (§15.3).

title: a non-nullable inline-array slot taken by a bare move arr[i] is rejected
rule: A slot taken by `move arr[i]` is exchanged, never emptied (§28.11; the replacing `move`, §28.8.1): a `[N owned]T?` slot holds `null` afterwards and a `[N owned]T` slot holds its replacement

title: assigning a fresh owned value restores a slot moved-from via move arr[i]
rule: The standard restoration mechanisms apply: assign a fresh owned value to the slot moved-from via `move arr[i]` before any exit edge (§15.3, §15.1.1).

title: a move-only argument is moved-from after the call and may not be read
rule: A parameter declared `(x: V)` for a move-only V is by value-move (transfer ownership); the caller's argument expression is in moved-from state after the call (§15.3).

title: owned on a move-only value parameter is admitted as a redundant marker
rule: A parameter declared `(owned x: V)` is identical to plain `(x: V)` for a move-only V; the modifier is admitted for documentation but is redundant (§15.3; §28.1's type requirement, clause 1).

title: equality over move-only values compares slot-wise by borrow and leaves both operands readable
rule: Move-only values support equality via borrowing comparison (reads each slot without moving), provided their element types support equality (§15.3; operator operands bind borrows, §25.2). An owning inline array's equality is element-by-element (§3.6's table), so two arrays whose slots compare equal are equal and two whose slots differ are not.

title: using var on an owning inline array locks out reassignment
rule: For a move-only inline-array local `using var` has no disposal effect, and its only observable consequence is preventing reassignment — the spelling for "fixed at construction and may not be rebound" (§15.3, §28.10).

title: a whole-value move out of a move-only local creates no restoration obligation
rule: A whole-value move — a plain binding, a plain argument, a return — creates no restoration obligation on a local: it leaves the local holding no value rather than a hole, so no pass walks it (§15.3).
