title: a local declared inside a do end block is out of scope after it ends
rule: Locals declared in a block are visible only until the matching `end`.

title: a method with a return type must return on every exit path
rule: A method or accessor with a return type must `return expression;` on every exit path.

title: a method with no return type uses return to exit early
rule: A method or accessor with no return type uses `return;` to exit early; falling off the end is implicit.

title: an exhaustive statement-case whose every arm exits grants totality
rule: A statement-position `case` counts as exiting on every path — so a callable may end with it, with no trailing `return` — when the match is proven statically exhaustive and every arm's body itself exits on every path.

title: return inside a finally block is a compile error
rule: `return` inside a `finally` block is a compile error.

title: a total record statement-case grants totality with no trailing return
rule: The statement-`case` totality grant is keyed to §19.6's closed-value-space registry, and that registry now carries the **record** bullet: a statement-`case` over a non-nullable record scrutinee whose unguarded arm is an all-slots-irrefutable destructure satisfies condition (i), so a callable may end with it and needs no trailing `return`.

title: throw expression as a statement raises and is caught
rule: `throw expression;` and the bare re-raise `throw;` are the statement spellings of the `throw` expression, equivalent to the expression form followed by `;`.

title: a bare re-raise outside a catch arm is a compile error
rule: The bare re-raise is valid only inside a catch arm body. Bare `throw` (either form) outside a catch arm body is a compile error.

title: a discarded non-unit expression statement result draws a warning
rule: An expression statement whose result is a non-`()` type is permitted but the compiler emits a warning: the result is silently discarded, which may indicate a bug.

title: the discard statement suppresses the unused-result warning
rule: To suppress the warning, use the discard form `_ := expression;`.

title: a bare Task-family statement result is a hard error, not a warning
rule: For `Task`, the warning is replaced by a hard error directing the caller to the discard `_ := expression;`, `using var _ := expression;`, an explicit `.Dispose()`, or `Task.FireAndForget` as appropriate.

title: a discarded string-returning call on a fluent receiver draws the unused-result warning
rule: An expression statement whose result is a non-`()` type is permitted but the compiler emits a warning: the result is silently discarded, which may indicate a bug.

title: the fluent-receiver discard draws no unused-result warning
rule: One exemption: the fluent-receiver discard. A discarded method-call result draws no warning when it is a §28.3 borrow whose source set lies within the statement's receiver chain and whose static type equals the receiver's static type — the `return this` fluent shape (`sb.Append(x);`).

title: a fluent method returning a base of the receiver's type stays warned
rule: A fluent method whose declared return is a *base* of the receiver's type stays warned — conservative by design; the exemption requires the result's static type to equal the receiver's static type.

title: a unit-returning call as a statement draws no unused-result warning
rule: Method calls returning `()` ... are the common cases; no warning is emitted for these.

title: awaiting a resultless Task as a statement draws no unused-result warning
rule: Method calls returning `()` and `await` expressions on `Task` (no result) are the common cases; no warning is emitted for these.

title: a bare-statement call returning a non-trivial-dispose class is a hard error
rule: For non-trivial-dispose class types ... the warning is replaced by a hard error directing the caller to the discard `_ := expression;` ... `OpenLog();` is rejected, and `_ := OpenLog();` is the remedy.

title: a local record is declared and used inside its enclosing body
rule: A `record` or `enum` may be declared as a statement, scoped to the enclosing body like a local variable. The local type is an ordinary nominal record.

title: a local record may not carry a visibility keyword
rule: The `Visibility?` slot must be empty — a local type has no access surface, so a visibility keyword is a compile error naming the rule.

title: a local record may not declare generic parameters
rule: The `GenericParams?` slot must be empty (v1) — a local type declares no type parameters of its own.

title: a local type must be declared before its first use
rule: The declaration must precede first use; local types are therefore order-significant.

title: a class may not be declared as a local type
rule: `class` and `interface` may not [be declared locally] — a class carries ownership, destructors, and the §28 disposal machinery, a body-scoped kernel surface for no recorded need.

title: an interface may not be declared as a local type
rule: `class` and `interface` may not [be declared locally] — … an interface is a contract for an outside a local has none of.

title: a choice may not be declared as a local type
rule: `choice` may **not** be declared locally (its payload-derived three-way classification, owning-match consume obligations, and coverage machinery are a heavier admission deserving its own study).

title: a local type may not appear in a member signature
rule: The name may not appear in any member signature of an ENCLOSING or SIBLING declaration — parameter, return, field/property/indexer, generic-constraint, or base/interface positions — which is a compile error naming that rule ("a method-local type may not appear in a member signature"), v0.301.

title: a local type may not reference an enclosing generic parameter
rule: A local type may not reference an enclosing generic parameter (an enclosing method's or class's `T`) — a compile error naming the rule.

title: a local type may not shadow a type visible at its declaration point
rule: The declared name may not shadow any type name visible at the declaration point (a local `NameAge` silently shadowing a module-level `NameAge` is a trap, not a convenience — the collision is an error).

title: a local type's name leaves scope at the end of its enclosing block
rule: A local type's name is in scope from its declaration statement to the end of the innermost enclosing statement block — exactly a local variable's scope.

title: a local enum is a §10 enum wholesale, prefix omission included
rule: A local `enum` is a §10 enum wholesale: constants, explicit values, underlying types, methods, interface conformances, and `case` matching with prefix omission (§10.6) and enum-scrutinee exhaustiveness (§19.6) inside the scope.

title: a local record gets §9.2 auto-equality like any other record
rule: The local type is an ordinary nominal record — every §9 rule applies unchanged; auto-equality (§9.2) is computed by its existing rules from the declaration.

title: a local record declared inside a record method body is usable within that body
rule: A `record` or `enum` may be declared as a **statement**, scoped to the enclosing body like a local variable

title: the spec's Render example builds its rows from a local record and renders them
rule: The form lets a shape used once — a projection's result record, a small closed constant set scoped to one algorithm — live next to its single use

title: a local record is not visible outside the body that declares it
rule: A `record` or `enum` may be declared as a **statement**, scoped to the enclosing body like a local variable

title: a local enum declared as a statement compares its members like an enum at namespace scope
rule: The local type is an **ordinary nominal record or enum** — every §9 (records) and §10 (enums) rule applies unchanged

title: a local record supports with-expressions and this with inside its own method
rule: are all computed by their existing rules from the declaration.

title: a local record overrides ToString and compares by value like a module-level record
rule: are all computed by their existing rules from the declaration.

title: a local record names an earlier local record inside its own method body
rule: Within its scope the name is an ordinary type reference in

title: a local record method returns its own local record type and folds an array argument
rule: except that a local type's scope also covers its own body (below).

title: two same-named local records in different methods are distinct types
rule: two same-shaped local records in different methods are distinct types

title: a local record that implements an interface is returned boxed through that interface
rule: that implements an interface may be "such a box is genuinely self-contained"

title: a local record declared in a constructor body is usable there
rule: `LocalTypeDecl` is admitted wherever a `Statement` is: method, constructor, destructor, and accessor bodies

title: two sibling do blocks may each declare a local record with the same name
rule: A local type's name is in scope from its declaration statement to the end of the

title: a local record in a generic method declares its own generic method and calls it at two types
rule: The local type is an ordinary nominal record or enum — every §9 (records) and §10 (enums) rule applies unchanged. The GenericParams? slot must be empty (v1) — a local type declares no type parameters of its own.

title: a method body inside a local record may not name the enclosing method's type parameter
rule: A local type may not reference an enclosing generic parameter (an enclosing method's or class's `T`) — a compile error naming the rule.

title: a local record that names an interface but omits one of its members is rejected
rule: The local type is an ordinary nominal record or enum — every §9 (records) and §10 (enums) rule applies unchanged; interface implementation (§9.6), and the derived type properties ... are all computed by their existing rules from the declaration.

title: a local record declared in a lambda do-body implements an interface and is used there
rule: `LocalTypeDecl` is admitted wherever a `Statement` is: method, constructor, destructor, and accessor bodies, lambda `do`-bodies, `do … end` blocks, loop bodies, and statement-position arm bodies.

title: a method declares a return type after the colon
rule: A method has a return type after `:`, or no `:` clause for a procedure (return type `()`).

title: a procedure omits the colon return-type clause entirely
rule: A method has a return type after `:`, or no `:` clause for a procedure (return type `()`).

title: an expression body replaces the block when the body is one expression
rule: When the body is a single expression, `=> expression` replaces the block.

title: a method with no declared return type may use an assignment as its arrow body
rule: A method with **no declared return type** may also use a single *assignment* as its arrow body, the same shape the accessor form `set => _x := value;` has always had.

title: the assignment arrow body is an error under a declared return type
rule: On a method with a declared return type the assignment form is an error (an assignment produces no value).

title: an expression body under a declared choice return type target-types a bare case
rule: An expression body under a declared return type is a declared-result position: a bare choice-case construction in it target-types against the declared type, exactly as a `return` operand does.

title: a ref local argument is a true alias, visible through the caller's location
rule: `ref` local and field targets alias: callee writes are visible through the caller's location immediately (the `Swap(ref a, ref b)` semantics presupposes this).

title: the caller must write ref at the call site
rule: `ref` — pass by reference. The caller writes `ref` at the call site.

title: the callee assigns every out parameter on every normal-completion path
rule: The callee must assign every `out` parameter on every normal-completion (return) path.

title: an out parameter left unassigned on some normal-completion path is rejected
rule: The callee must assign every `out` parameter on every normal-completion (return) path; failing to do so is a compile error.

title: omitting the move marker on a named owned binding argument is rejected
rule: Omitting the marker on a named owned binding is a compile error naming the fix ("this call consumes `x`; write `M(move x)`").

title: a named owned binding fed with the move marker reaches the owned parameter
rule: **Call-site marker:** when the argument is a named owned binding, the caller writes the transfer marker at the call site: `M(move x)`.

title: writing move on a fresh producer is rejected as redundant
rule: Writing [the move marker] on a borrow, a fresh producer, or a non-`owned` parameter position is likewise an error. A fresh producer — a `new` expression ... — stays unmarked: no live binding is invalidated, so there is nothing to announce.

title: a fresh producer stays unmarked at an owned parameter
rule: A fresh producer — a `new` expression, a call returning `owned T`, an operator result, or a `move obj._field` — stays unmarked: no live binding is invalidated, so there is nothing to announce.

title: writing move at a non-owned parameter position is rejected
rule: Writing [the move marker] ... on a non-`owned` parameter position is likewise an error (at a non-`owned` position the diagnostic names the borrow default — an owned expression may not feed a borrow slot).

title: a ref argument's static type must exactly match the referent type
rule: **Exact referent type.** The argument's static type must be **exactly** the parameter's referent type. Because the parameter aliases the caller's location, no implicit conversion is admitted — not even a widening one that an ordinary by-value argument would take.

title: a ref argument may not name a location of owned state
rule: A `ref` or `out` argument must be an assignable storage location, subject to two recorded v1 bounds (liftable): no location of owned state — an owned local or `owned` parameter, an `owned` field, an owning-collection or owning-inline-array slot.

title: out owned is the only modifier compound; others are mutually exclusive
rule: The combination `out owned` is the only modifier compound; the others are mutually exclusive.

title: a lambda's written ref parameter of an owning choice is a compile error
rule: A ref parameter whose declared type is a move-only value type (§15.3; an owning choice's nullable wrapper C? among them, §35.9), a function type's ref slot included, is a compile error at the declaration

title: a function type's ref slot of an owning choice is rejected at each written position
rule: A ref parameter whose declared type is a move-only value type (§15.3; an owning choice's nullable wrapper C? among them, §35.9), a function type's ref slot included, is a compile error at the declaration

title: a function type's ref slot is admitted for a nullable copyable choice and a nullable owning class
rule: A ref parameter whose declared type is a move-only value type (§15.3; an owning choice's nullable wrapper C? among them, §35.9), a function type's ref slot included, is a compile error at the declaration

title: a ref parameter of an owning inline array is a compile error at the declaration
rule: A `ref` parameter whose declared type is a move-only value type (15.3; an owning inline array [N owned]T among them) is a compile error at the declaration: no argument can bind it.

title: a ref parameter of a copyable inline array of the same class is admitted
rule: Move-only membership follows from structure: an inline array is move-only exactly when its slots carry the owned marker (15.3); without it the parameter is an ordinary ref parameter.

title: a ref parameter of a nullable owning inline array is a compile error at the declaration
rule: A `ref` parameter whose declared type is a move-only value type (15.3; the owning inline array [N owned]T? included) is a compile error at the declaration.

title: a ref parameter whose type is a bare type parameter is not rejected at its declaration
rule: A `ref` parameter whose declared type is or contains a type parameter is not rejected at its declaration; at a substitution that makes that type a move-only value type, no argument binds it.

title: a Set<int> produced by a call reaches an owned parameter with its elements intact
rule: A fresh producer — a `new` expression, a call returning `owned T`, an operator result, or a `move obj._field` — stays unmarked: no live binding is invalidated, so there is nothing to announce.

title: a named Set<int> binding fed with the move marker reaches an owned parameter
rule: the caller writes the transfer marker at the call site: `M(move x)`.

title: a SortedSet<int> produced by a call reaches an owned parameter with its elements intact
rule: A fresh producer — a `new` expression, a call returning `owned T`, an operator result, or a `move obj._field` — stays unmarked: no live binding is invalidated, so there is nothing to announce.

title: a fresh producer is admitted at an owned parameter reached through a constraint head
rule: A **fresh producer** — a `new` expression, a call returning `owned T`, an operator result, or a `move obj._field` — stays unmarked: no live binding is invalidated, so there is nothing to announce. Inside the generic body, T's surface includes IFoo's members, regardless of which conformance category T belongs to (§14.2), so the call is an ordinary call whose argument forms are read at the head's own signature (stdlib §4.2 declares `Add(owned item: T)`).

title: the move call-site marker is rejected at a function-value invoke
rule: Writing [the move marker] ... on a non-`owned` parameter position is likewise an error (at a non-`owned` position the diagnostic names the borrow default — an owned expression may not feed a borrow slot) (§22.3, v0.343). The marker is a property of the argument position, not of the spelling used to make the call — so a function-value invoke rejects it as the direct call does.
check: only valid on an argument to an `owned` parameter

title: out var name declares a new variable inline, typed from the parameter
rule: `out var name` declares a new variable inline. Its type is inferred from the method's `out` parameter declaration.

title: out var underscore is a compile error
rule: `out var _` is a compile error — it would declare nothing; write `out _`, which already means exactly this.

title: out underscore is the admitted discard spelling
rule: `out var _` is a compile error — it would declare nothing; write `out _`, which already means exactly this.

title: out using var is accepted against an out owned parameter
rule: For disposal-aware inline declarations against an `out owned` parameter, use `out using var`.

title: out using var against a plain out parameter is rejected
rule: A caller cannot write `out using var` against a plain `out` parameter (the result would have no owned source).

title: an explicit type annotation on the inline out form is not permitted
rule: An explicit type annotation is not permitted in the inline `out` form; the type is inferred from the method's `out` parameter declaration.

title: a short-circuited and-guard definitely assigns the inline out variable
rule: The analysis is required to honor the standard short-circuit facts (`A and Call(out var x)` assigns `x` when the whole expression is `true`) ... so the idiomatic guarded read stays accepted.

title: reading a non-nullable-reference out variable off the guarded path is rejected
rule: On a path where the call may not have run, a read of a **non-nullable-reference-typed** out variable is a compile error, exactly as for any other unassigned non-nullable local — an inline `out` variable counts as assigned only on paths where the introducing call was actually evaluated.

title: a pre-declared uninitialized local adopts owned against out owned
rule: A pre-declared local passed as plain `out x` is admitted against `out owned` exactly when it is in one of the two adoptable states — uninitialized or polymorphic-null — and adopts owned on every normal-return path of the call.

title: named arguments may appear in any order
rule: Named arguments may appear in any order after positional arguments.

title: a positional argument after a named argument is rejected
rule: Named arguments may appear in any order after positional arguments.

title: a ref or out argument has no named spelling
rule: A `ref`/`out`/`scoped` argument is positional-only: those modifiers inhabit the `ArgModifiers` alternative of `Argument`, which has no named form — `M(out var result := n)` has no reading and does not parse, the `:=` of the binding form and the `:=` of the named form being the same token.

title: a default value may be a literal or constant expression
rule: A default-value expression must be type-compatible with the parameter's declared type ... [it] may be a literal, constant, or `default(T)`.

title: a default value may not reference instance state
rule: A default-value expression may not reference instance state (`this`, instance fields, instance properties) — the default belongs to the method's signature, not to a particular receiver's frame.

title: a default value may read an earlier parameter, never a later one
rule: A default-value expression may "read other parameters appearing **earlier** in the same parameter list (e.g. `M(a: int, b: int := a + 1)` is permitted; later-parameter forward references are not)."

title: supplied arguments evaluate in call-site textual order regardless of naming
rule: A call's **supplied** argument expressions are evaluated in **call-site textual order** — left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike (`M(b := Next(), a := Next())` evaluates the `b` expression first).

title: an owned primary-constructor parameter with a literal default owns it for the object lifetime
rule: A default value is permitted only on parameters with no modifier or `owned` (an `owned` default is the owned-allocation form this section already blesses ...) ... the parameter then receives ownership per §22.3/§28.8 and the callee discharges it (§22.5 *Defaults and modifiers*, v0.340). So `owned xs: Array<T> := [..]` filled from its default is an array the object owns and reads correctly after the constructing expression: ints (3), strings (2 + len("bb") = 4) and records (1 + 1 = 2), and the supplied-argument form (`[9, 9]` -> 2; `["q", "rr"]` -> 4) behaves the same. The plain-parameter twin is not pinned here: a literal given to a stored plain parameter faults when read later (#7045).

title: an owned default that mentions an earlier parameter sees that parameter's value
rule: A default value is permitted only on parameters with no modifier or `owned` (an `owned` default is the owned-allocation form this section already blesses ...) ... the parameter then receives ownership per §22.3/§28.8 and the callee discharges it (§22.5 *Defaults and modifiers*, v0.340). The default `[x, x]` of `owned ys` is evaluated at the construction with `x` bound: `new A(5)` gives two 5s (`2 * 100 + 5 + 5` = 210), and a supplied `[1, 2, 3]` replaces it (`300 + 1 + 2` = 303).

title: an owned generic primary-constructor default builds the literal at the instantiation
rule: A default value is permitted only on parameters with no modifier or `owned` (an `owned` default is the owned-allocation form this section already blesses ...) ... the parameter then receives ownership per §22.3/§28.8 and the callee discharges it (§22.5 *Defaults and modifiers*, v0.340). For `A<T>(owned xs: Array<T> := [])` the default is the empty literal at `T = int` and `T = string` (0, 0); for `B<T>(x: T, owned xs := [x, x, x])` it holds three elements (3, 3).

title: owned defaults of a base primary constructor are filled with and without arguments
rule: A default value is permitted only on parameters with no modifier or `owned` (an `owned` default is the owned-allocation form this section already blesses ...) ... the parameter then receives ownership per §22.3/§28.8 and the callee discharges it (§22.5 *Defaults and modifiers*, v0.340). The base `Base(owned bs := [1, 2, 3], owned c := ["q"])` is reached through `D(): Base` (defaults: 3 * 10 + 1 = 31), `D2(k): Base([7])` (one supplied, one default: 10 + 1 = 11) and an explicit `base()` call (31).

title: a call through a constraint head that supplies two arguments for one parameter is rejected
rule: Each supplied argument binds **exactly one** parameter and each parameter is bound by **at most one** supplied argument: naming a parameter already bound positionally ... or naming the same parameter twice, is a compile error at the call naming that parameter.

title: a call through a constraint head that leaves a required parameter unbound is rejected
rule: **Every parameter that declares no default must be bound**, positionally or by name; leaving one unbound is the opposite disposition from binding one twice — it makes the candidate **inapplicable**, so at an overloaded name an applicable sibling still resolves and the error is reported only where no candidate survives.

title: the same arity check applies at a user interface's inherited member
rule: Each supplied argument binds **exactly one** parameter and each parameter is bound by **at most one** supplied argument: naming a parameter already bound positionally ... or naming the same parameter twice, is a compile error at the call naming that parameter. Inside the generic body, T's surface includes IFoo's members, regardless of which conformance category T belongs to (§14.2).

title: a call to a string member that declares a required parameter and supplies no argument is rejected
rule: **Every parameter that declares no default must be bound**, positionally or by name; leaving one unbound is the opposite disposition from binding one twice — it makes the candidate **inapplicable**, so at an overloaded name an applicable sibling still resolves and the error is reported only where no candidate survives. stdlib §9.6 declares `Equals(other: string): bool` and `Equals(other: string?, ignoreCase: bool): bool` — neither declares a default — so a call supplying no argument binds no parameter of either candidate, neither candidate survives, and the call is a compile error.

title: a call's argument expression runs before the callee's range check raises
rule: Evaluation order. A call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order - left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs. The order is observable through side-effecting arguments and non-constant defaults (DateTime.Now, factory calls) and is normative. The argument is evaluated before the call begins - §28.3 reads the same boundary as "not yet transferred because the call to Combine never began" - so the argument's side effect runs before the callee's own range check, and stdlib §9.6's contract for the member is what raises: totalWidth < 0 raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException.

title: a reordered named argument on a built-in member binds to the parameter it names
rule: §22.5, binding: each supplied argument binds exactly one parameter, and naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs - so a reordered named argument on a built-in member selects the parameter it names. stdlib §2.2 declares `Pow(x: double, y: double)`, `Fmod(x: double, y: double)`, `Clamp(value: T, low: T, high: T)`, `Min<T>(a: T, b: T)` and `Max<T>(a: T, b: T)`, and stdlib §2.3 declares `ToString(value: int, toBase: int)`; each reordered spelling therefore computes the same value as the positional one.

title: named arguments after a positional one bind to the parameter they name
rule: §22.5, mixed spellings: a call that mixes positional and named arguments binds its positional arguments to the leading parameters and each named one to the parameter it names - named arguments may appear in any order after positional arguments, and each supplied argument binds exactly one parameter. So `Clamp(100, high := 10, low := 0)` is `Clamp(value: 100, low: 0, high: 10)` (stdlib §2.2) and returns 10; `Pow(3, y := 2)` is `Pow(x: 3, y: 2)`; and `ToString(255, toBase := 16)` is `ToString(value: 255, toBase: 16)` (stdlib §2.3).

title: a named argument on a string member binds to the parameter it names
rule: stdlib §9.6 declares `Remove(startIndex: int, length: int): string` and `Repeat(c: char, count: int): string`. §22.5: named arguments may appear in any order after positional arguments, and each supplied argument binds exactly one parameter - so `Remove(length := 2, startIndex := 1)` removes two characters starting at index 1, and `Repeat(count := 3, c := 'x')` repeats "x" three times.

title: a string member's supplied arguments run once each, in call-site textual order
rule: stdlib §9.6 declares `Remove(startIndex: int, length: int): string`. §22.5, Evaluation order: a call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order - left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs. The `length` expression is written first, so it runs first, and it runs once - the call reads "len" once and "start" once.

title: naming a parameter already bound positionally is a compile error at the call
rule: naming a parameter already bound positionally (`Log(Failed", message := "Retry")` against `Log(message: string, level: string := "INFO")`), or naming the same parameter twice, is a compile error at the call naming that parameter"

title: a named argument binds the parameter it names after a positional one
rule: Each supplied argument binds **exactly one** parameter and each parameter is bound by **at most one** supplied argument. Here the positional "a" binds text and width := 2 binds width, so both bindings are unique.

title: Named arguments of a stdlib constructor evaluate in written order (Semaphore, OwningBuffer)
rule: A call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order, left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs. Binding by name covers `Semaphore(initialCount, maxCount)` and `OwningBuffer<T>(length, init)` in any written order.

title: a Semaphore constructed with reordered named arguments holds initialCount permits
rule: A call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order, left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs. Naming binds `initialCount: 2` and `maxCount: 5`, so exactly two permits are available and a third acquisition cannot succeed.

title: Array size and fill named arguments in reverse order evaluate in written order
rule: A call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order, left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs. `Array<int>(size, fill)` called as `(fill := e1, size := e2)` runs `e1` first.

title: JsonDeserializer named options and input evaluate in written order
rule: A call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order, left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs. `JsonDeserializer(input, options)` called as `(options := e1, input := e2)` runs `e1` first.

title: ArraySpan named Length, Start and Source evaluate in written order
rule: A call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order, left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs. The positional record `ArraySpan<T>(Source, Start, Length)` called as `(Length := e1, Start := e2, Source := e3)` runs `e1` first.

title: Span records and BinaryDeserializer bind positional, named and reordered arguments alike
rule: A call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order, left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs. Each of the spellings below binds the same parameters, so every one reads the same elements (20, 30) or the same integer (42).

title: BinaryDeserializer with only ignoreUnknownFields named leaves input unbound
rule: Each supplied argument binds exactly one parameter and each parameter is bound by at most one supplied argument; every parameter that declares no default must be bound (spec 22.5). `BinaryDeserializer(input, ignoreUnknownFields := false)` declares no default for `input`.

title: BinaryDeserializer() with no arguments leaves input unbound
rule: Each supplied argument binds exactly one parameter and each parameter is bound by at most one supplied argument; every parameter that declares no default must be bound (spec 22.5). `BinaryDeserializer(input, ignoreUnknownFields := false)` declares no default for `input`.

title: BinaryDeserializer with input bound positionally and by name is rejected
rule: Each supplied argument binds exactly one parameter and each parameter is bound by at most one supplied argument; every parameter that declares no default must be bound (spec 22.5). Naming a parameter already bound positionally is a compile error (spec 22.5).

title: Semaphore with only maxCount named leaves initialCount unbound
rule: Each supplied argument binds exactly one parameter and each parameter is bound by at most one supplied argument; every parameter that declares no default must be bound (spec 22.5). `Semaphore(initialCount, maxCount)` declares no default for `initialCount`.

title: Semaphore naming initialCount twice is rejected
rule: Each supplied argument binds exactly one parameter and each parameter is bound by at most one supplied argument; every parameter that declares no default must be bound (spec 22.5). Naming the same parameter twice is a compile error (spec 22.5).

title: An exception from a reordered named constructor argument propagates; no object is built
rule: A call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order, left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs. An argument expression that throws ends the call before it begins: no object is constructed and the exception is the call's outcome, reordered or not, generic enclosing method or not.

title: ArgumentException and TimeoutException accept their constructor arguments by name in either order
rule: Each supplied argument binds exactly one parameter by name (spec 22.5). `ArgumentException` declares `(message, paramName)` (spec 31.4) and `TimeoutException` declares `(message, inner)` (stdlib 6.1), so the written order of the names does not change which value lands where.

title: nested named-argument calls evaluate their supplied arguments in textual order
rule: A call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order, left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs.

title: nested string.Join with reversed named arguments evaluates in textual order
rule: Supplied argument expressions are evaluated left to right as written, for named arguments too; naming an argument never changes when it runs.

title: reordered named arguments to a generic-context call evaluate in textual order repeatedly
rule: Supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order, for named arguments alike, on every evaluation of the call, including inside a generic method instantiated at several type arguments.

title: a named-argument call that throws on a later argument has still run the earlier ones
rule: Supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order; an earlier argument has run when a later one throws (named arguments included).

title: a null-conditional call evaluates its named arguments only when the receiver is non-null
rule: Supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order; a null-conditional call short-circuits (the argument expressions of the skipped suffix are not evaluated, spec 7.5), so its arguments do not run on a null receiver.

title: named arguments after a null-forgiving receiver: textual order, and a null receiver faults ...
rule: A call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order, left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs (spec 22.5 Evaluation order, v0.350, example M(b := Next(), a := Next())). The receiver is an operand written before the arguments and is evaluated first.

title: named arguments around an await are evaluated in textual order
rule: A call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order, left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs (spec 22.5 Evaluation order, v0.350, example M(b := Next(), a := Next())). The receiver is an operand written before the arguments and is evaluated first.

title: positional and named arguments of a call evaluate in written order, whatever the parameter order
rule: A call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order, left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs (spec 22.5 Evaluation order, v0.350, example M(b := Next(), a := Next())). The receiver is an operand written before the arguments and is evaluated first.

title: named-argument order holds when a local shadows a built-in static class name
rule: A call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order, left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs (spec 22.5 Evaluation order, v0.350, example M(b := Next(), a := Next())). The receiver is an operand written before the arguments and is evaluated first.

title: named-argument order holds inside lambda bodies
rule: A call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order, left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs (spec 22.5 Evaluation order, v0.350, example M(b := Next(), a := Next())). The receiver is an operand written before the arguments and is evaluated first.

title: named-argument order holds in a generator body across iterations
rule: A call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order, left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs (spec 22.5 Evaluation order, v0.350, example M(b := Next(), a := Next())). The receiver is an operand written before the arguments and is evaluated first.

title: named-argument order holds after a field-chain receiver
rule: A call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order, left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs (spec 22.5 Evaluation order, v0.350, example M(b := Next(), a := Next())). The receiver is an operand written before the arguments and is evaluated first.

title: named-argument order holds for built-in String methods (Substring, ...
rule: A call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order, left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs (spec 22.5 Evaluation order, v0.350, example M(b := Next(), a := Next())). The receiver is an operand written before the arguments and is evaluated first.

The receiver is an operand written before the arguments and is evaluated first.

title: naming PadLeft's totalWidth twice by name is rejected

rule: Every parameter that declares no default must be bound

title: Array<int>.LastIndexOf with 2 argument(s) is rejected: it declares one parameter

title: Array<int>.LastIndexOf with 3 argument(s) is rejected: it declares one parameter

title: Path.Combine("x", "y", c := "z") is rejected: c names no parameter of Combine

title: Path.Combine(b := "y") is rejected: required a is left unbound

title: two overloads indistinguishable by arity, types, modifiers clash
rule: A type may not declare two members indistinguishable under §22.6's rules — the clash rejected at the second declaration.

title: overloads distinguished by arity are admitted
rule: Overload resolution considers number, types, the `ref`/`out` modifiers, and the presence of `owned` on an ordinary parameter — overloads differing in any of these are distinguishable.

title: overloads distinguished by the ref modifier are admitted
rule: Overload resolution considers number, types, the `ref`/`out` modifiers ... — overloads differing in any of these are distinguishable.

title: example 1 -- exact match preferred over a widening conversion
rule: For a single argument position, one candidate is better than another when the better candidate requires no implicit conversion ... and the other requires an implicit conversion.

title: example 2 -- two equally-ranked conversions are ambiguous
rule: Two candidates that both require an implicit conversion at the same position are equally ranked there, regardless of which conversion each uses.

title: example 3 -- exact on one argument, conversion on the other, is unambiguous
rule: A candidate is unambiguously better than another when it is better-or-equal on every argument position and strictly better on at least one.

title: example 4 -- each candidate exact on a different argument is ambiguous
rule: If no candidate is unambiguously better — because each of two candidates is exact on a different argument ... the call is ambiguous and is a compile error.

title: example 5 -- no reachable candidate cites no candidates
rule: If no candidate is applicable at all ... the call is a compile error with no candidates cited, because no overload was reachable.

title: example 6 -- applicability filtering removes an inapplicable candidate
rule: byte→sbyte is NOT implicit ... ⇒ Process(sbyte) is not applicable. byte→ushort IS implicit ... ⇒ Process(ushort) is the only applicable candidate.

title: the defaulted-arity tie-break prefers the candidate that fills no default
rule: A candidate applicable **without filling any default** is preferred over a candidate that fills one or more ... `M(5)` against `M(n: int)` and `M(n: int, m: int := 0)` resolves to `M(int)`.

title: a non-generic candidate is preferred over a generic one on a tie
rule: When a non-generic candidate and a generic candidate are both applicable, and neither the ranking ... nor the defaulted-arity tie-break separates them, the non-generic candidate is selected ... `Show(x: int)` and `Show<T>(x: T)` on `Show(5)` resolve to the non-generic.

title: the defaulted-arity tie-break applies before the non-generic preference
rule: the defaulted-arity tie-break applies first: `M(n: int, m: int := 0)` and `M<T>(x: T)` on the call `M(5)` resolve to the *generic* candidate — it fills no default.

title: an unmarked borrow read of a same-type owned/ordinary pair is rejected at the declaration (v0.338)
rule: **`owned` never distinguishes overloads (v0.338, proposal 0185).** `Append(item: Widget)` beside `Append(owned item: Widget)` clash at the second declaration (§22.6, §11.3); a borrow read is no longer selected.

title: a move-marked production of a same-type owned/ordinary pair is rejected at the declaration (v0.338)
rule: **`owned` never distinguishes overloads (v0.338, proposal 0185).** `Append(item: Widget)` beside `Append(owned item: Widget)` clash at the second declaration (§22.6, §11.3); the owned production is not selected.

title: owned on an out parameter never distinguishes overloads
rule: **`owned` never distinguishes overloads.** Two same-name members that differ only by `owned` on a parameter — an ordinary parameter or an `out` parameter — are indistinguishable and clash at the second declaration (§11.3) ... as is `TryGet(name: string, out c: Conn?)` beside `TryGet(name: string, out owned c: Conn?)`

title: scoped never distinguishes overloads
rule: `scoped` does not participate in overload resolution: two overloads differing only in `scoped` on a parameter ... are a compile error.

title: an owned/ordinary pair over a where-T-class constraint clashes at the declaration (v0.338)
rule: **`owned` never distinguishes overloads (v0.338, proposal 0185).** Two same-name members that differ only by ordinary `owned` clash at the second declaration (§22.6, §11.3): `Append(item: Widget)` beside `Append(owned item: Widget)` is a compile error.

title: an owned/ordinary pair over a where-T-IDisposable constraint is rejected at the declaration (v0.338)
rule: **`owned` never distinguishes overloads (v0.338, proposal 0185).** An ordinary-`owned` / plain pair clashes at the second declaration; no constraint lifts it (§22.6, §11.3).

title: a record primary and a body constructor that both convert at every position are ambiguous
rule: If no candidate is unambiguously better — because each of two candidates is exact on a different argument, or because the remaining candidates all rely on implicit conversions that this rule treats as equally ranked — the call is **ambiguous** and is a compile error. The compiler reports the error and cites the candidate overloads; it never silently selects one.

title: a record primary constructor is a candidate at new and wins on an exact match
rule: Methods and constructors may be overloaded by parameter list. ... A candidate is **unambiguously better** than another when it is better-or-equal on every argument position and strictly better (an exact match where the other converts) on at least one. The call resolves to a candidate that is unambiguously better than every other applicable candidate.

title: a user-class operand is ambiguous between an Animal and an Object operator overload
rule: A call on an `Animal` argument's dog-typed operand versus `Object` is ambiguous when neither candidate is exact (v0.338, §22.6).

title: a built-in exception operand is ambiguous between an Exception and an Object operator overload
rule: A call on an `Animal` argument's dog-typed operand versus `Object` is ambiguous when neither candidate is exact (v0.338, §22.6).

title: an exact operator overload beats an Object overload on a class operand
rule: An exact match is the only relation that distinguishes one applicable candidate from another at an argument position (v0.338, §22.6).

title: two interfaces with same-name overloads bind each member to its exact-typed witness
rule: parameter types that are exactly equal under the interface's substitution; An exact match is the only relation that distinguishes one applicable candidate from another at an argument position (v0.338 §11.2, §22.6)

title: an interface member binds the inherited override with the exact parameter type
rule: parameter types that are exactly equal under the interface's substitution; An exact match is the only relation that distinguishes one applicable candidate from another at an argument position (v0.338 §11.2, §22.6)

title: an interface call with an explicit list binds each overload to its exact-typed witness
rule: A call through an interface selects among the interface's overloads by the explicit list and the argument types, and runs the witness that implements the selected overload (11.2).

title: a direct call with an explicit list picks the only applicable overload of a generic class
rule: Overload ranking considers only applicable candidates (22.6); with the explicit list binding V := int, the Array<Array<V>> overload is the only one an Array<Array<int>> argument matches.

title: an interface call with an explicit list ranks a function-typed parameter by its slot
rule: Overload ranking considers only applicable candidates (22.6). With the explicit list binding U := int, a lambda of type (int) -> int is applicable only to the overload whose function slot returns int.

title: explicit type arguments that name an enclosing method's type parameter select the nested overload
rule: Explicit type arguments may name a type parameter in scope; the list binds the declared parameter and the overload is then ranked by applicability (22.6).

title: an int argument is not applicable to Array<V> under an explicit list, beside a string overload
rule: Applicability over the (substituted) signatures: parameter types under the implicit conversions (§5.1) and the `ref`/`out` modifiers — this section.

title: an int argument is not applicable to Array<V> under an explicit list, with no other overload
rule: Applicability over the (substituted) signatures: parameter types under the implicit conversions (§5.1) and the `ref`/`out` modifiers — this section.

title: a string argument is not applicable to IEnumerable<int> under an explicit list
rule: Applicability over the (substituted) signatures: parameter types under the implicit conversions (§5.1) and the `ref`/`out` modifiers — this section.

title: an int argument is not applicable to Span<V> under an explicit list
rule: Applicability over the (substituted) signatures: parameter types under the implicit conversions (§5.1) and the `ref`/`out` modifiers — this section.

title: a call whose argument fits no overload candidate is rejected with no applicable overload
rule: If no candidate is applicable at all
check: no overload of `F` is applicable to these arguments

title: a negative literal that does not fit ulong selects the long constructor overload
rule: literal formation is range-checked

title: a narrowed nullable argument selects the overload taking the non-nullable parameter
rule: `F(x: T)` beside `F(x: T?)` on a narrowed `T?` argument selects `F(T)` ([§22.6]). "The argument's static type is its type at the call" ([§22.6]): the unnarrowed call selects the nullable overload.

title: an exact argument type beats a covariant conversion in overload ranking
rule: the better candidate requires *no* implicit conversion (the argument's static type matches the parameter type exactly) and the other requires an implicit conversion ([§22.6]). The argument is an IEnumerable<Dog>, exact for the IEnumerable<Dog> overload and a covariant conversion for the IEnumerable<Animal> overload, so the Dog overload wins.

title: two covariant interface conversions at one position are equally ranked and ambiguous
rule: two candidates that both require an implicit conversion at the same position are **equally ranked** there, regardless of which conversion each uses ([§22.6]). Array<Dog> converts to IEnumerable<Animal> and to IEnumerable<Dog>, neither is exact, so the call S.F(v) is ambiguous and a compile error.

title: no applicable candidate for an invariant interface argument is a compile error
rule: with no applicable candidate at all, the no-candidate error ([§22.6]). DogBox implements only IBox<Dog>, which is neither IBox<Animal> nor IBox<string> under the invariant marker of IBox, so no overload is applicable.

title: no candidate is applicable when the generic overload's closed parameter does not match the argument
rule: with no applicable candidate at all, the no-candidate error ([§22.6]). The generic F<T> needs its second parameter to be IBox<string>, and IntBox implements only IBox<int>; the non-generic overload needs a string first argument, and the literal 5 is an int. Neither candidate is applicable.

title: a string argument to RawBytes.From, whose parameter is Array<byte>, has no applicable candidate
rule: If no candidate is applicable at all — no candidate is reachable: a conversion §5.1 does not admit as implicit, ... — the call is a compile error with no candidates cited, because no overload was reachable.

title: an Array<int> argument to Encoding.GetString matches none of its byte-buffer overloads
rule: If no candidate is applicable at all — no candidate is reachable: a conversion §5.1 does not admit as implicit, ... — the call is a compile error with no candidates cited, because no overload was reachable.

title: a null literal operand reaches only the Pt? operator overload; two Pt operands take the exact one
rule: A null literal has no static type of its own (§14.5: it binds no type parameter, and a candidate it leaves unbound is inapplicable): it is applicable at every nullable parameter and at no non-nullable one.

title: a null literal operand is not applicable at an operator whose formals are non-nullable
rule: A null literal has no static type of its own (§14.5: it binds no type parameter, and a candidate it leaves unbound is inapplicable): it is applicable at every nullable parameter and at no non-nullable one.

title: a null literal reaching two nullable operator overloads separates neither and the call is ambiguous
rule: A null literal has no static type of its own (§14.5: it binds no type parameter, and a candidate it leaves unbound is inapplicable): it is applicable at every nullable parameter and at no non-nullable one, and is graded alike at every candidate it reaches, so it separates none.

title: a byte argument converts to every Math.Abs overload and the call is ambiguous
rule: two candidates that both require an implicit conversion at the same position are **equally ranked** there, regardless of which conversion each uses (§22.6, v0.340); the stdlib declares `Math.Abs` for exactly `int`, `long`, `double` and `decimal` (stdlib §2.2). A `byte` converts to all four (§5.1), none is exact, so the call is ambiguous.

title: a uint argument is ambiguous among the long, double and decimal Math.Abs overloads
rule: two candidates that both require an implicit conversion at the same position are **equally ranked** there, regardless of which conversion each uses (§22.6, v0.340); the stdlib declares `Math.Abs` for exactly `int`, `long`, `double` and `decimal` (stdlib §2.2). A `uint` converts to `long`, `double` and `decimal` but not `int` (§5.1); the three remaining candidates all convert and none is exact. The call is therefore ambiguous.

title: a ulong argument is ambiguous between the double and decimal Math.Abs overloads
rule: two candidates that both require an implicit conversion at the same position are **equally ranked** there, regardless of which conversion each uses (§22.6, v0.340); the stdlib declares `Math.Abs` for exactly `int`, `long`, `double` and `decimal` (stdlib §2.2). A `ulong` converts to `double` and `decimal` only (§5.1); both convert and neither is exact. The call is therefore ambiguous.

title: an exact Math.Abs overload is chosen and a float argument has a single applicable candidate
rule: the one that is exact is better (§22.6, v0.340): `Math.Abs` on an `int`, `long`, `double` or `decimal` argument selects the identity overload. A `float` converts only to `double` among the four (§5.1), so that is the sole applicable candidate and no ambiguity arises.

title: a compile-time integer constant is read at its own static type
rule: spec §22.6: "A **compile-time integer constant** (§17.14) is read at its own static type too — `int` for an unsuffixed literal that fits `int` (§4.2), a `const`'s declared type". The `const` is declared `long`, so it is exact at the `long` parameter and converts at the `int` one: the `long` candidate is the only exact match and is selected.

title: a constant the narrowing reaches at two candidates is ambiguous
rule: spec §22.6: "§5.1's constant narrowing enters resolution as an *applicability* rule only: a candidate the narrowing reaches *converts* at that position, never exact, and ranks co-equal with every other conversion. So ... `M(3)` against `M(byte)` beside `M(short)` is ambiguous — both candidates convert — remedied as every ambiguity is, by a cast".

title: bool.Parse of an int argument reaches no candidate
rule: stdlib §9.4 declares `public static pure method Parse(s: string): bool;` — a `string` parameter and no other. Language spec §22.6: "If no candidate is applicable at all — no candidate is reachable: a conversion §5.1 does not admit as implicit ... the call is a compile error with no candidates cited, because no overload was reachable." An `int` argument reaches no candidate, so the call is a compile error.

title: bool.ParseOrNull of an int argument reaches no candidate
rule: stdlib §9.4 declares `public static pure method ParseOrNull(s: string): bool?;` — a `string` parameter and no other. Language spec §22.6: "If no candidate is applicable at all — no candidate is reachable: a conversion §5.1 does not admit as implicit ... the call is a compile error with no candidates cited, because no overload was reachable." An `int` argument reaches no candidate, so the call is a compile error.

title: char.Parse of an int argument reaches no candidate
rule: stdlib §9.5 declares `public static pure method Parse(s: string): char;` — a `string` parameter and no other. Language spec §22.6: "If no candidate is applicable at all — no candidate is reachable: a conversion §5.1 does not admit as implicit ... the call is a compile error with no candidates cited, because no overload was reachable." An `int` argument reaches no candidate, so the call is a compile error.

title: a Convert call whose operand matches no parameter type is a compile error with no candidates cited
rule: If no candidate is applicable at all — no candidate is reachable: a conversion §5.1 does not admit as implicit, a parameter-count difference at a function-typed slot, a method-reference formation that fails, or an inference that finds no binding — the call is a compile error with no candidates cited, because no overload was reachable.

title: a Convert call whose operand matches a parameter type selects that overload
rule: If no candidate is applicable at all — no candidate is reachable: a conversion §5.1 does not admit as implicit, a parameter-count difference at a function-typed slot, a method-reference formation that fails, or an inference that finds no binding — the call is a compile error with no candidates cited, because no overload was reachable.

title: a Parse call whose operand matches no parameter type is a compile error with no candidates cited
rule: If no candidate is applicable at all — no candidate is reachable: a conversion §5.1 does not admit as implicit, a parameter-count difference at a function-typed slot, a method-reference formation that fails, or an inference that finds no binding — the call is a compile error with no candidates cited, because no overload was reachable.

title: a Convert.TryToDouble call whose operand matches no parameter type is a compile error
rule: If no candidate is applicable at all — no candidate is reachable: a conversion §5.1 does not admit as implicit, a parameter-count difference at a function-typed slot, a method-reference formation that fails, or an inference that finds no binding — the call is a compile error with no candidates cited, because no overload was reachable.

title: a Convert.TryToDouble call whose operand matches a parameter type selects that overload
rule: If no candidate is applicable at all — no candidate is reachable: a conversion §5.1 does not admit as implicit, a parameter-count difference at a function-typed slot, a method-reference formation that fails, or an inference that finds no binding — the call is a compile error with no candidates cited, because no overload was reachable.

title: int.TryParse of an int argument reaches no candidate
rule: Language spec §22.6 (v0.345): "If no candidate is applicable at all — no candidate is reachable: a conversion §5.1 does not admit as implicit … the call is a compile error with no candidates cited, because no overload was reachable."

title: Guid.TryParse of an int argument reaches no candidate
rule: Language spec §22.6 (v0.345): "If no candidate is applicable at all — no candidate is reachable: a conversion §5.1 does not admit as implicit … the call is a compile error with no candidates cited, because no overload was reachable."

title: the null literal bound by name to DateOnly's non-nullable day parameter is rejected
rule: it is applicable at every nullable parameter and at no non-nullable one

title: the null literal bound by name to DateTime's non-nullable hour parameter is rejected
rule: it is applicable at every nullable parameter and at no non-nullable one

title: a narrowed byte? is read as byte and widens to int at named and positional constructor parameters
rule: so a narrowed `d: Dog?` is exact at a `Dog` parameter and converts to an `Animal` or a `Dog?` one ... | `byte` | `short`, `ushort`, `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` |

title: a user class overloading LastIndexOf by parameter count selects each overload by the call arity
rule: Methods and constructors may be overloaded by parameter list

title: a constructor may chain to another constructor of the same class with this
rule: Multiple constructors are permitted; chaining uses `this(...)` or `base(...)` in the chaining position before the body.

title: a derived constructor may chain to a base constructor with base
rule: Multiple constructors are permitted; chaining uses `this(...)` or `base(...)` in the chaining position before the body.

title: a this-chain argument may not read a field of the not-yet-constructed instance
rule: A `this(...)` argument may read neither a primary-constructor parameter nor any field of `this` — in the chaining position no field of the declaring type is yet assigned (§22.8's step-1-before-step-2 sequence, restated at §22.7's chaining-position clause).

title: a this-chain argument may read the delegating constructor's own parameter
rule: The only reads a chaining argument may make are of the constructor's own parameters, constants, and statics (§22.10); and "for a `this(...)` chain, the chained-to constructor runs to completion (its own steps of this sequence) before control returns here" (§22.8 step 1).

title: an instance method call on this in the chaining position is rejected
rule: A synchronous observation of `this` — an instance method ... invocation with receiver `this` ... is admitted only at points where every field ... is definitely assigned on every reaching path. In the chaining position ... any observation of `this` there is a compile error.

title: a virtual call on this from a non-sealed class's constructor body is rejected
rule: No virtual dispatch from constructor bodies of non-sealed classes. A call from a constructor body to a `virtual`, `override`, or `abstract` member with receiver `this` ... is a compile error unless the declaring class is `sealed` and not `abstract`.

title: a caught exception inside a static constructor does not fail the type
rule: An exception caught inside the static constructor's body does not transition the type to the failed state — the constructor completes normally and static initialization is considered successful.

title: a dispatching call on this from a sealed non-abstract constructor body is admitted
rule: A call from a constructor body to a `virtual`, `override`, or `abstract` member with receiver `this` — any dispatching call not through `base.` — is a compile error unless the declaring class is `sealed` and not `abstract`. In a sealed, non-abstract class the dispatch target is statically bounded and the call is admitted under rule 1's gate.

title: a class declaring no instance constructor has an implicit public parameterless one
rule: A class that declares **no instance constructor** and no primary-constructor parameter list has an implicit parameterless constructor: `public`, no parameters, an empty body, chaining implicitly per §12.8 — and it satisfies `where T: new()` on the same terms a declared public parameterless one does (§14.2), which is what `new T()` reaches at such a substitution.

title: a primary-constructor parameter list suppresses the implicit parameterless constructor
rule: Declaring **any** instance constructor suppresses the implicit parameterless constructor, a primary-constructor parameter list included.

title: a static constructor does not suppress the implicit parameterless constructor
rule: A `static constructor` does not suppress the implicit parameterless constructor (it is never a chaining or `new` target); it runs once before the type's first use.

title: a standard-library builtin gets no implicit parameterless constructor
rule: A **standard-library builtin** type is excepted from the implicit parameterless constructor: its constructor surface is closed by §17.7, and `Subscription` declares none, so `new Subscription(...)` is a compile error at any argument list.

title: new C() reaches the implicit parameterless constructor directly
rule: A class that declares **no instance constructor** and no primary-constructor parameter list has an implicit parameterless constructor: `public`, no parameters, an empty body. It is what `new C()` reaches on such a class.

title: a derived construction is a first use of the base, whose static constructor runs first
rule: A static constructor runs once before the type's **first use**: the first time any code of the type runs or any of its static state is read — ... a run of an instance constructor (the base's too, when a derived class's construction chains to it, §12.8)

title: constructing a class derived from a permanently failed type raises TypeInitializationException
rule: Every subsequent use of the type — an access to a static member (field read, field write, method call, property read or write, indexer), an instance construction of the type or of a class derived from it, and a call of an instance member — raises `TypeInitializationException`

title: an imported base's static constructor runs before its constructor body at a derived construction
rule: A static constructor runs once before the type's **first use**: ... a run of an instance constructor (the base's too, when a derived class's construction chains to it, §12.8), or a call of an instance member — whatever module declares the type

title: a field declared in a class may include an initializer
rule: A field declared in a class or record may include an initializer.

title: a readonly field assigned in an ordinary method is rejected
rule: A field declared `readonly` may be assigned only in a field initializer or in a constructor body; assignment anywhere else is a compile error.

title: a readonly field assigned once in the constructor body is admitted
rule: A field declared `readonly` may be assigned ... in a constructor body; the field is also assigned at most once.

title: a readonly field with an initializer assigned again in the constructor body is rejected
rule: A field initializer and a constructor-body assignment are therefore **two** assignments wherever both run, which is wherever the constructor's chaining position holds `base(...)` or the implicit `base()`.

title: a readonly field assigned in mutually exclusive branches is admitted
rule: Assignments in mutually exclusive branches are one assignment per path and are admitted.

title: a readonly assignment inside a loop body is rejected unconditionally
rule: An assignment lexically inside a loop body within the assignment window is rejected unconditionally: a loop could assign on more than one iteration.

title: a field initializer may not reference this or an instance member
rule: Field initializers may **not** reference: `this`, instance members, `base`, virtual methods, or any expression that would observe `this` indirectly.

title: a constructor may not assign another instance's readonly storage
rule: The context is per-instance, not per-type — an instance `readonly` field is assignable only through an lvalue chain rooted at `this`, so a constructor of the declaring type may not write another value's `readonly` storage held in a parameter, local, or field.

title: a static readonly field assigned in an instance constructor is rejected
rule: a `static readonly` field is assignable only in its own static field initializer or in the declaring type's **static** constructor body, spelled as the bare name or `TypeName.F` ... and an instance constructor of the declaring type is not an assignment site for it, so no `new C()` writes `C._s`.

title: a static readonly field assigned in the static constructor is admitted
rule: a `static readonly` field is assignable only in its own static field initializer or in the declaring type's **static** constructor body, spelled as the bare name or `TypeName.F`

title: a readonly field assigned inside a lambda written in a constructor body is rejected
rule: **The window is lexical and does not include a nested function body**: the body of a lambda (§27.3) written inside a constructor body, a field initializer, a static constructor or a static field initializer is outside every assignment window ... so an assignment to a `readonly` field inside a lambda ... is a compile error wherever the lambda stands

title: a static readonly field assigned inside a lambda written in the static constructor is rejected
rule: **The window is lexical and does not include a nested function body**: the body of a lambda (§27.3) written inside a constructor body, a field initializer, a static constructor or a static field initializer is outside every assignment window ... so an assignment to a `readonly` field inside a lambda ... is a compile error wherever the lambda stands

title: a lambda in a constructor body may read a readonly field the constructor assigned
rule: so an assignment to a `readonly` field inside a lambda ... is a compile error wherever the lambda stands ... assign the field in the constructor and let the lambda read it.

title: a constructor may not write an element of a readonly inline array in another instance's field
rule: The context is per-instance, not per-type: an *instance* `readonly` field is assignable only through an lvalue chain rooted at `this` ... so a constructor of the declaring type may **not** write another value's `readonly` storage held in a parameter, local, or field.

title: a constructor may not increment an element of a readonly inline array in another instance's field
rule: The context is per-instance, not per-type: an *instance* `readonly` field is assignable only through an lvalue chain rooted at `this` ... so a constructor of the declaring type may **not** write another value's `readonly` storage held in a parameter, local, or field.

title: a constructor may not compound-assign an element of a readonly array in another instance's field
rule: The context is per-instance, not per-type: an *instance* `readonly` field is assignable only through an lvalue chain rooted at `this` ... so a constructor of the declaring type may **not** write another value's `readonly` storage held in a parameter, local, or field.

title: a constructor may not write a readonly inline-array element through a local of another instance
rule: The context is per-instance, not per-type: an *instance* `readonly` field is assignable only through an lvalue chain rooted at `this` ... so a constructor of the declaring type may **not** write another value's `readonly` storage held in a parameter, local, or field.

title: a constructor may write an element of its own readonly inline array field
rule: The context is per-instance, not per-type: an *instance* `readonly` field is assignable only through an lvalue chain rooted at `this` ... so a constructor of the declaring type may **not** write another value's `readonly` storage held in a parameter, local, or field.

title: a constructor may copy a readonly inline array into a local, write the copy, and store it
rule: A value type is copied on assignment; each variable holds an independent value.

title: a constructor may not pass an element of another instance's readonly array as a ref argument
rule: an *instance* `readonly` field is assignable only through an lvalue chain rooted at `this` ... so a constructor of the declaring type may **not** write another value's `readonly` storage held in a parameter, local, or field (§22.8, v0.340); a `ref` or `out` argument is a write location and admits "no `readonly` field outside its per-instance assignable context" (§22.3). The argument `o.A[0]` lands in the `readonly` array of `o`, not of `this`.

title: a constructor may not pass an element of another instance's readonly array as an out argument
rule: an *instance* `readonly` field is assignable only through an lvalue chain rooted at `this` ... so a constructor of the declaring type may **not** write another value's `readonly` storage held in a parameter, local, or field (§22.8, v0.340); a `ref` or `out` argument is a write location and admits "no `readonly` field outside its per-instance assignable context" (§22.3). The argument `o.A[1]` lands in the `readonly` array of `o`, not of `this`.

title: a constructor may not pass a readonly array element reached through a local alias as a ref argument
rule: an *instance* `readonly` field is assignable only through an lvalue chain rooted at `this` ... so a constructor of the declaring type may **not** write another value's `readonly` storage held in a parameter, local, or field (§22.8, v0.340); a `ref` or `out` argument is a write location and admits "no `readonly` field outside its per-instance assignable context" (§22.3). The local `n` holds another instance; the chain is not rooted at `this`.

title: a constructor may not pass a readonly array element of an owned field's instance as a ref argument
rule: an *instance* `readonly` field is assignable only through an lvalue chain rooted at `this` ... so a constructor of the declaring type may **not** write another value's `readonly` storage held in a parameter, local, or field (§22.8, v0.340); a `ref` or `out` argument is a write location and admits "no `readonly` field outside its per-instance assignable context" (§22.3). `this.Next` is another instance of `H`, so the chain `this.Next.A[0]` passes through a field of `this` but lands in the `readonly` storage of `Next`.

title: a lambda in a constructor may not bind its own readonly array element to a ref parameter
rule: The window is lexical and does not include a nested function body ... an assignment to a `readonly` field inside a lambda ... is a compile error wherever the lambda stands, and so is binding the field to a `ref` or `out` parameter there (§22.8, v0.340). The twin `Util.Bump(ref this.A[0])` directly in the constructor body is the accepting case s22_8_0025.

title: a constructor may bind its own readonly array elements to ref and out parameters
rule: an *instance* `readonly` field is assignable only through an lvalue chain rooted at `this` — an explicit `this.F := e` or the bare in-scope spelling that resolves to `this`'s storage (§22.8, v0.340); `ref this.A[0]`, `out this.A[1]` and the bare `ref A[1]` are chains rooted at `this`, so each binding is admitted in the constructor body.

title: a constructor-body throw disposes the step-2 owned field, not the class's own destructor
rule: An exception in the constructor body (step 3) triggers disposal of every owned field assigned during initialization (step 2) and the base subobject. ... the throwing class's `destructor` body is **never** executed on these edges.

title: an exception in a field initializer disposes earlier-completed owned fields in reverse order
rule: An exception during a **field initializer** (step 2) triggers disposal of any earlier derived owned fields whose initializers completed, in reverse declaration order, followed by the base subobject's `Dispose()`.

title: an exception during the base constructor call leaves no derived state to clean up
rule: An exception during the **base or chained constructor call** (step 1) leaves no derived state to clean up ... The exception propagates to the derived ctor's caller; the derived instance is never observable.

title: a this-chaining body throw after the chain completes runs the normal dispose
rule: If the chaining constructor's **body** throws, the chained-to construction completed and the instance is at that point fully initialized: the runtime disposes it through the normal generated-`Dispose()` path ... before the exception propagates.

title: primary constructor parameters are in scope inside field initializers
rule: Primary-constructor parameters are in scope inside field initializers.

title: primary constructor parameters are in scope in the inheritance clause's base call
rule: Primary-constructor parameters are in scope inside the inheritance clause's base call; this replaces an explicit `base(...)` call.

title: a primary constructor parameter referenced in a body position is captured and readable from methods
rule: The parameters are in scope inside the body of any method, property, constructor, or destructor of the class. The compiler captures them as private fields automatically.

title: a convenience constructor's this(...) chaining position may not read a primary-constructor parameter
rule: Primary-constructor parameters are not in scope in a convenience constructor's chaining position: the arguments of a `this(...)` call run before the chained-to primary's capture step, so reading a primary-constructor parameter there is a compile error.

title: a convenience constructor's this(...) chaining position may read its own parameters
rule: The only reads a chaining argument may make are of the constructor's own parameters, constants, and statics.

title: ref is rejected on a primary constructor parameter
rule: A primary-constructor parameter list admits plain and `owned` parameters only; `ref` and `out` are rejected semantically.

title: out is rejected on a primary constructor parameter
rule: A primary-constructor parameter list admits plain and `owned` parameters only; `ref` and `out` are rejected semantically.

title: an owned primary-constructor parameter referenced only in an initializer is not captured
rule: Referenced only in field initializers (or the base call): not captured — the initializer consumes it.

title: an owned primary-constructor parameter referenced in a body position is captured as an owned field
rule: Referenced in a body position: captured as a compiler-generated owned private field, disposed by the generated `Dispose()` exactly like a declared owned field.

title: an owned primary parameter used in an initializer and a body position is rejected
rule: Referenced both in an owned-consuming initializer and in a body position: compile error — the body reference is a read of a moved-from value.

title: a class-typed scoped primary-constructor parameter is admitted and captured as a non-owned field
rule: A class- or interface-typed `scoped` primary-constructor parameter follows the same capture rule: referenced in a body position, it is captured as a compiler-generated non-owned private field — exactly the direct non-owned field of the bounding object that §28.14's callee side admits, the constructed object being the bounding object.
