At the call site the argument carries the marker — `new Box(scoped src)` — and is admitted under §28.14's bounding-object forms exactly as at a declared constructor: the holder is a `using var` local or `this`, the source is declared before the holder.

title: primary constructor parameters are not automatically promoted to public properties
rule: Primary-constructor parameters are not automatically promoted to public properties. To expose one, declare a property explicitly.

title: only the primary constructor may chain to base(...)
rule: A class with a primary constructor may declare additional convenience constructors. Each must chain to another constructor via `this(...)`; only the primary may chain to `base(...)`.

title: a convenience constructor chains to the primary via this(...)
rule: A class with a primary constructor may declare additional convenience constructors. Each must chain to another constructor via `this(...)`; only the primary may chain to `base(...)`.

title: a primary constructor's inheritance-clause base call replaces an explicit base(...)
rule: When a class with a primary constructor has a base class, the base call appears in the inheritance clause. This replaces an explicit `base(...)` call.

title: a fresh producer at a scoped primary-constructor argument is rejected
rule: At the call site the argument carries the marker and is admitted under §28.14's bounding-object forms exactly as at a declared constructor: a fresh producer is rejected — the unbound owned temporary dies at the end of the full expression (§9.7's no-temporary-source rule); bind the source first.

title: scoped on a value-typed primary-constructor parameter is rejected
rule: A primary-constructor parameter list admits plain, `owned`, and class- or interface-typed `scoped` parameters. `scoped` is valid on function-typed parameters and on class/interface-typed parameters; other parameter types are rejected semantically (Appendix A.4).

title: an unreferenced scoped primary parameter captures no field and its call site is still admitted
rule: The freeze is keyed on the signature, not on the capture: a `scoped` parameter referenced in no body and no initializer captures no field, and the call site freezes its source all the same, harmlessly.

title: the holder of a scoped primary-constructor borrow is disposed before its source
rule: At the call site the argument is admitted under §28.14's bounding-object forms exactly as at a declared constructor: the holder is a `using var` local, the source is declared before the holder, and the source is frozen until the holder's scope exits. With declared-before admission, the freeze, and reverse-declaration-order disposal (§21.6, §28.10), the source provably outlives the bounding object including its destructor.

title: inheritance-clause base call forwards the paramName to a built-in argument exception
rule: When a class with a primary constructor has a base class, the base call appears in the inheritance clause ([§22.10]). The base call is the clause's argument list, so R's paramName reaches `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`'s `(message, paramName)` form; "public readonly property ParamName: string?;" ([§31.4]) is the property that form supplies, and the `ArgumentException` arm reads it back.

title: a primary-constructor root's positional field survives an explicit-constructor middle class
rule: Parameters used only in field initializers or in the inheritance clause's base call are *not* captured: their values flow directly into the field they initialize or the base argument they supply ([§22.10]). `D`'s `m` reaches `C`'s base call and `D`'s own initializer; `C`'s explicit constructor passes the logged string on to `A`, whose positional `m` the field `Msg` stores, so each construction reads `r1!` in `Msg`.
check:
all:LOG r1
r1! r1!a r1d
LOG r2
r2! r2!a r2d
LOG r3
r3! r3!a r3d
N=3

title: an explicit-constructor middle class with a this-hop constructor stores the root's positional field
rule: Each must chain to another constructor via `this(...)`; only the primary may chain to `base(...)` ([§22.10]). `E2`'s argument selects `B2`'s convenience constructor, which chains to the explicit constructor that makes the base call; the root `A`'s positional `m` is then stored in `Msg`, so the counter reads 1 after `D2` and 2 after `E2`.

title: an owned OwningArray primary-constructor parameter given a literal keeps its elements
rule: a primary-constructor parameter may be declared `owned`, and the same ownership-transfer rules as regular constructor parameters apply (§22.10, v0.340): `owned xs: OwningArray<R>` given the literal `[new R("a"), new R("b")]` makes the object the owner of both elements, so `Live()` reads 2 after the literal expression ends, even with another array allocated meanwhile.

title: a collection literal in the base clause of a primary constructor reaches an owned base parameter
rule: Parameters used only in field initializers or in the inheritance clause's base call are not captured: their values flow directly into the field they initialize or the base argument they supply (§22.10, v0.340); an `owned` parameter of the base primary constructor receives the literal by transfer (§22.3, §28.8). The derived classes `DOI(): OBI([1, 2, 3])`, `DOS()` and `DOR()` pass ints, strings and records; each base object owns its array, so `N()` reads 3, 4 and 2.

title: a collection literal in an explicit base call reaches an owned base primary-constructor parameter
rule: Parameters used only in field initializers or in the inheritance clause's base call are not captured: their values flow directly into the field they initialize or the base argument they supply (§22.10, v0.340); an `owned` parameter of the base primary constructor receives the literal by transfer (§22.3, §28.8). The explicit constructors `EOI: OBI public constructor() base([1, 2, 3]);` pass the literal by transfer to the base's owned parameter; `N()` reads 3, 4 and 2.

title: a generic derived class passes a literal in its base clause to an owned base parameter
rule: Parameters used only in field initializers or in the inheritance clause's base call are not captured: their values flow directly into the field they initialize or the base argument they supply (§22.10, v0.340); an `owned` parameter of the base primary constructor receives the literal by transfer (§22.3, §28.8). `D<T>(d: T): GB<T>([d, d])` gives the base an owned two-element array at `T = int` and `T = string`: `2 4 2 zz`.

title: a collection literal chained through this() reaches an owned primary-constructor parameter
rule: the arguments of a `this(...)` call run before the chained-to primary's capture step and may read only the constructor's own parameters, constants and statics (§22.10, v0.340); the literal `[5, 6, 7]` is a fresh producer passed by transfer to `owned c`, so `CL()` reads `3 + 100` = 103.

title: a with expression over a class-typed source is rejected
rule: The object-initializer block does not exist: a `with` expression requires a record-typed source, and a class-typed source is a compile error.

title: with on a freshly-constructed record is unaffected by the retirement
rule: Record `with` on a freshly-constructed record (`new Point(1, 2) with(Y := 9)`) is unaffected.

title: named and optional constructor arguments replace the retired object-initializer block
rule: In its place, use named/optional constructor arguments — which run the constructor and respect its invariants.

title: binding the instance to a local and assigning members replaces the retired form
rule: In its place, ... bind the instance to a local and assign its members as ordinary statements, whose exception-path disposal is §28.3's general discharge of an owned local.

title: static methods, properties, fields, and constructors are declared with static
rule: Static methods, properties, fields, and constructors are declared with `static`.

title: a class-level const is implicitly static
rule: A class-level `const` is implicitly static; writing `static const` is redundant but permitted for clarity — both forms declare the same constant.

title: static const is the redundant-but-permitted spelling of a class-level const
rule: A class-level `const` is implicitly static; writing `static const` is redundant but permitted for clarity — both forms declare the same constant.

title: const requires a primitive value type or string
rule: `const` declarations require a compile-time-constant expression and a primitive value type or `string`.

title: const requires a compile-time-constant expression
rule: `const` declarations require a compile-time-constant expression and a primitive value type or `string`.

title: static readonly of immutable content is unrestricted
rule: `static readonly` of immutable content — value types of sendable-value category, `string`, enums — and `const` are unrestricted (shared-immutable).

title: a mutable static field of an ordinary class type is rejected
rule: any other class type — `owned` or not — takes: mutable: error † — a mutable static admitted by none of (i)-(iv) is a compile error naming this rule.

title: a mutable static field of a primitive value type warns
rule: A mutable static whose declared type is a primitive value type or an enum type ... warns (iii): the obligation is to confine every use of the storage to one domain, or take the synchronized spelling.

title: a static readonly field of a synchronized handle type is admitted warning-free
rule: declares synchronized, not displacement-unbounded — the form-(i) set — `static readonly`: ok — in the set.

title: a static readonly field of a class outside the warning-suppression set warns
rule: A `static readonly` (including `owned`) field or auto-property of class type is admitted with a declaration-site warning unless the class is in this rule's warning-suppression set.

title: a static readonly Channel field deliberately still warns
rule: A `static readonly Channel<T>` deliberately still warns (`Channel<T>` declares no facts) — the reminder that the channel is the single-consumer receiving end and must stay confined to one consuming domain.

title: a mutable static field of bare generic parameter type is rejected at the declaration
rule: A mutable static field or auto-property whose declared type is a bare generic parameter, or its nullable form, is admitted by no form above and is a compile error at the declaration site, whatever the parameter's constraints or eventual substitutions.

title: a Task-typed lazy cache static field is admitted
rule: Lazy task cache: a static whose declared type is `Task?` or `Task<T>?` — the admission is keyed to the declared type alone.

title: an OwningTask-typed static field is not admitted as a lazy task cache
rule: `OwningTask<T>?` — mutable: error — not (ii), †.

title: each distinct instantiation of a generic class has its own static state
rule: A static member of a generic class is accessed by supplying the type arguments on the type name in receiver position. Each distinct instantiation has its own static state.

title: a static owned readonly SharedEventSource field is the admitted warning-free publication point
rule: A process-global publication point is an ordinary static field of type `SharedEventSource<T>` — a form-(i) member, admitted warning-free in the recommended shape `private static owned readonly _e: SharedEventSource<T> := new();`.

title: a capturing handler passed to SharedEventSource.Subscribe is rejected
rule: Every call resolving to a subscribe position declared on `ISharedEvent<T>`/`SharedEventSource<T>` admits only capture-free handlers: a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference.

title: a static owned readonly Mutex is in the warning-suppression set and is silent
rule: A `static readonly` (including `owned`) field of class type is admitted with a declaration-site warning **unless the class is in this rule's warning-suppression set** — every type declaring the **synchronized** or the **immutable** fact, `Mutex` among them.

title: the same static owned readonly field at a class outside the set warns
rule: A `static readonly` (including `owned`) field or auto-property of **class type** is admitted with a **declaration-site warning** unless the class is in this rule's warning-suppression set: confining its use to one domain is the programmer's obligation.

title: a static owned readonly CancellationTokenSource is silent under 4(a)
rule: The four members outside rule 2's form (i) — `Locked<T>`/`RwLocked<T>`, `FrozenArray<T>`, and `CancellationTokenSource`, the process-global shutdown source — are in the warning-suppression set; `owned` enrols the field in §22.13's program-exit disposal.

title: a static owned readonly FrozenArray is silent by its immutable fact
rule: The warning-suppression set is derived, not curated: every type declaring the **synchronized** or the **immutable** fact — `FrozenArray<T>` among them — so a `static owned readonly` of it is admitted warning-free.

title: static readonly is the warning-free spelling of a process-global primitive
rule: `static readonly` of **immutable content** — value types of sendable-value category, `string`, enums — is unrestricted (shared-immutable); it is the warning-free spelling where the value never changes after initialization.

title: dropping readonly from the same primitive static draws form (iii)'s warning
rule: **(iii) Warned value static:** a mutable static whose declared type is a primitive value type ... the obligation it names is to confine every read and write of the field to one domain, or to move to a synchronized spelling.

title: a static owned readonly Locked registry is the canonical warning-free process-global
rule: The four members outside rule 2's form (i) — the data-owning locks `Locked<T>`/`RwLocked<T>` (`static owned readonly` being the canonical process-global registry idiom) ... — are in rule 4's warning-suppression set, so the declaration is admitted warning-free.

title: a slot store through a static readonly owning inline array is rejected
rule: Its slots are fixed at initialization: a slot store or a `move arr[j]` through it is a compile error naming K9.4 — static owned storage is disposed only by the exit pass, and no per-method window can cover it.

title: a static readonly owning inline array is admitted and its slots may be read
rule: An owning-inline-array-typed `static readonly` field takes the default warning and *is* disposed at exit by §22.13's owning-inline-array clause; it is the one admitted static of owning-inline-array type (a mutable one is rule 2's closing error).

title: a static owned readonly OwningTask field is a compile error at the declaration
rule: A `static readonly` field or auto-property of type `OwningTask<T>` or `OwningTask<T>?` — `owned` or not — is a **compile error at the declaration site** naming this rule, as its mutable form already is.

title: the same static owned readonly field at Task of a class is admitted with rule 4's warning
rule: A `static readonly` (including `owned`) field or auto-property of **class type** is admitted with a **declaration-site warning** unless the class is in this rule's **warning-suppression set** — `OwningTask<T>` excepted, a compile error under (j)

title: a static readonly bare-parameter field named at an OwningTask instantiation is rejected there
rule: a class-type substitution takes this rule's warning unless the substituted class is in the warning-suppression set, an `OwningTask<X>` substitution excepted, rejected on (j)'s single-award ground ... The diagnostic lands **at the instantiation site** and names the offending type argument

title: the same bare-parameter static named at Task of a class is admitted
rule: A `static readonly` field or auto-property whose declared type is a **bare generic parameter**, or its nullable form (`T`, `T?`), is admitted at the declaration and classified **per instantiation, after substitution**: ... a class-type substitution takes this rule's warning unless the substituted class is in the warning-suppression set

title: static fields of a single type are initialized in textual declaration order
rule: Within a single type, static fields are initialized in textual declaration order.

title: a static readonly field may not read a static readonly field of the same type declared after it
rule: If the initializer expression for a `static readonly` field F reads a `static readonly` field G of the same type declared after F in the source — directly — the reference is rejected at compile time.

title: a forward read routed through a statically-resolvable call is rejected
rule: ...directly, or transitively through the bodies of statically-resolvable calls (static methods and static property getters reached by direct name within the compilation unit) — the reference is rejected at compile time.

title: a static constructor body may freely reference fields in any order
rule: A static constructor body may freely reference any of the type's static fields in any order; the constructor body runs after all field initializers have completed, so no forward-reference question arises there.

title: forward references between const declarations are not subject to the ordering rule
rule: Forward references between `const` declarations are not subject to this rule: a `const` initializer must be a compile-time-constant expression, so forward references between consts are either resolved at compile time or are themselves a compile error for non-constant operands.

title: a cyclic static-initialization dependency between two types is a compile error
rule: The compiler builds a static-initialization dependency graph over distinct types ... A cycle in this graph is a compile error naming the participating types.

title: TypeInitializationException carries the original exception as InnerException
rule: A touch of a type whose static initialization is in progress raises TypeInitializationException; more generally, every subsequent access to a static member of a permanently-failed type raises TypeInitializationException whose InnerException is the original exception.

title: every access to a permanently-failed type observes the same cached TypeInitializationException
rule: The instance constructed on first failure is the one cached and rethrown; the triggering access and every subsequent access see the same cached TypeInitializationException instance.

title: eager startup assignment of a Task cache avoids the check-then-store race
rule: Eager startup assignment of the task cache — assign the `Task<T>?` cache before any spawn or other first use; the check-then-store race never arises and the work runs exactly once.

title: await is rejected in a static field initializer
rule: `await` may not appear in static field initializers or static constructor bodies.

title: await is rejected in a static constructor body
rule: `await` may not appear in static field initializers or static constructor bodies.

title: static owned fields of one type are disposed at program exit in reverse declaration order
rule: Within a single type, multiple static `owned` fields are disposed in reverse declaration order, mirroring the instance-field disposal rule.

title: a static readonly class-typed field without owned is exempt from the ownership-discharge requirement
rule: A `static readonly` field of class type or interface type that is not marked `owned` is exempt from the ownership-discharge requirement: assigning a fresh owned value into such a field discharges the producer. The value lives for the duration of the program.

title: a static readonly field of a non-trivial-dispose class declared without owned warns
rule: The compiler warns (not errors) when a `static readonly` field of a class type whose `Dispose()` is non-trivial — a class with a user-defined destructor ... — is declared without `owned`.

title: a mutable static owning-inline-array field is a compile error at the declaration
rule: **owning inline array** `[N owned]T?` / `[N owned]T` **field** | error (iii)-closed ... the tables' **error (iii)-closed** cells are compile errors under this rule's closing sentence

title: a variadic-style signature uses Array<T> with a collection literal at the call site
rule: There is no `params` keyword. A variadic-style signature uses `Array<T>` with a collection literal at the call site.

title: a pure method may call another pure member
rule: The compiler rejects, inside a pure body, any call whose statically resolved declaration is not pure — a call to a pure member is therefore admitted.

title: a pure body may not call a non-pure member
rule: The compiler rejects, inside a pure body, any call whose statically resolved declaration is not pure.

title: a pure member declares no ref parameter
rule: A pure member declares no `ref`, `out`, `out owned`, `owned`, or `scoped` parameters: `ref` is a writable alias of caller storage.

title: a pure member declares no out parameter
rule: A pure member declares no `ref`, `out`, `out owned`, `owned`, or `scoped` parameters: `out` obliges a caller-visible assignment channel.

title: a pure member declares no owned parameter
rule: A pure member declares no `ref`, `out`, `out owned`, `owned`, or `scoped` parameters: `owned` brings a disposal obligation into the frame whose discharge runs `Dispose` — user code at disposal time.

title: a pure member rejects a move-only value parameter
rule: A move-only value parameter — an owning-choice instantiation, or an owning inline array — is likewise rejected: the plain spelling is identical to the `owned` spelling for such a type.

title: an owned class-typed return is rejected on a pure member
rule: The return type is unrestricted except: an `owned` class-typed return is rejected.

title: a move-only value return is rejected on a pure member
rule: So is a move-only value return — an owning-choice instantiation, or an owning inline array — no pure body can produce an owned class instance or a value that carries one.

title: pure is rejected on an async member
rule: `pure` is rejected on async members and async lambdas: an `async` body interleaves with the domain's continuation queue and traffics in tasks; `pure` implies non-`async`.

title: pure is rejected on an iterator method
rule: `pure` is rejected on iterator methods (`yield`) — a pure-iterator form is deliberately left open, not designed.

title: pure is rejected on a destructor
rule: `pure` is rejected on destructors — disposal is the effect context purity fences off.

title: pure is rejected on an auto-property as redundant
rule: Fields and auto-properties as declarations: the auto-accessor classification is implicit; writing `pure` on an auto-property is rejected as redundant.

title: pure is rejected on a static constructor
rule: `pure` is rejected on static constructors — no call site exists to consume the fact.

title: a pure body may not store to an instance field outside a pure constructor's birth store
rule: Prohibited, as the closed list's contrapositive: any store whose target root is an instance field ... (stores to `this`'s fields outside pure constructors' birth stores included).

title: a pure body may not store to a static field
rule: Prohibited, as the closed list's contrapositive: any store whose target root is an instance field, a static field, an indexer slot of a class instance, or whose access path dereferences a class-typed reference.

title: a pure body may mutate a record-typed parameter's fields as frame-private state
rule: Locals and frame-local mutation: assignment ... where the target's root is a local variable or by-value parameter of this body and the access path from that root traverses only value-typed storage (record fields, inline-array slots).

title: a pure body may not construct a class instance outside the throw carve-out
rule: Prohibited: class construction — `new C(…)` ... except the throw operand below (constructors and destructors run arbitrary user code, and an owned instance drags in the discharge machinery).

title: the throw carve-out admits a pure-constructed trivial-dispose exception operand
rule: Inside a pure body, `new E(args)` is admitted only as the immediate operand of a `throw` statement or `throw` expression, and only when the invoked constructor of E is pure-declared and E is a trivial-dispose class.

title: the throw carve-out is rejected when the exception class is not trivial-dispose
rule: `new E(args)` is admitted [in a throw operand] only when ... E is a trivial-dispose class.

title: a pure body may not invoke a function-typed value
rule: Prohibited: invoking function-typed values (the value's type carries no effect information).

title: a pure body's for loop over a concrete Array<T> source is the normative elision
rule: A source whose static type at this body's own check site is concretely `Array<T>`, `OwningArray<T>`, class-typed `OwningBuffer<T>`, or `string` — the admitted protocol elision is likewise the normative semantics inside a pure body.

title: a pure body's for loop over an interface-typed source is rejected
rule: A source whose static type is an interface (`IEnumerable<T>` included) or a generic type parameter remains rejected: the remedy is declaring the source at a concrete sequence type.

title: an override of a pure member must itself be declared pure
rule: Purity is never dropped. An override of a pure member must itself be declared `pure`, and a class member implementing a pure interface member must be declared `pure`; omission is a compile error at the override or implementation.

title: an override may strengthen purity where the base member is not pure
rule: Purity may be strengthened. An override or implementation may declare `pure` where the overridden or interface member is not.

title: purity is monotone down an override chain once a member becomes pure
rule: Monotone down the chain. An override matches against the nearest overridden declaration: once a chain member is pure, every further override is pure.

title: a pure constructor's birth-store rule admits assignment to this's fields
rule: A constructor may be declared `pure`. Its body is checked under the pure-body rules with one addition, the birth-store rule: assignments whose target root is a field of `this` are permitted — the instance under construction is unreachable from any other holder until the constructor returns.

title: pure is rejected on a set accessor
rule: Purity attaches to the getter; `pure` on `set` is always rejected.

title: a violated requires clause raises ContractViolationException in every build mode
rule: A `requires` clause is evaluated on every invocation, after argument binding and before any execution of the member; a clause evaluating `false` raises `ContractViolationException`, in every build mode.

title: a satisfied requires clause lets the member run normally
rule: A `requires` clause is evaluated on every invocation ...; a clause evaluating `false` raises `ContractViolationException`. (A clause evaluating `true` on every invocation lets the member proceed.)

title: a contract clause's expression must be of type bool
rule: The expression must be of type `bool` (§4.1 — no truthiness).

title: a contract clause may call only pure members
rule: Each clause's expression is of type `bool`, is admitted under the pure-body discipline of §22.15.

title: await is rejected in a contract clause, even on an async member
rule: `await` is rejected, on every member including `async` ones (a clause is not part of an async body's statement sequence and has no suspension semantics).

title: throw is rejected in a contract clause
rule: Three clause-specific amendments: `throw` is rejected (a clause states a proposition; the mechanism, message, and blame of a violation belong to this section's machinery).

title: result denotes the returned value in an ensures clause, read as a borrow
rule: Within an `ensures` clause of a member with a declared return type, `result` denotes the value being returned, typed as the declared return type, in a read-only borrow position.

title: result is a compile error in a unit-typed member's clauses
rule: `result` is a compile error in a unit-typed member's clauses, in a constructor's clauses, and in any `requires` or `invariant` clause.

title: result is a compile error in a requires clause
rule: `result` is a compile error ... in any `requires` or `invariant` clause.

title: result is a compile error in a constructor's clauses
rule: `result` is a compile error in a unit-typed member's clauses, in a constructor's clauses, and in any `requires` or `invariant` clause.

title: old is a compile error in a requires clause
rule: `old` is a compile error in `requires` clauses, in `invariant` members, in constructor clauses, and outside clauses entirely.

title: old is a compile error in an invariant member
rule: `old` is a compile error in `requires` clauses, in `invariant` members, in constructor clauses, and outside clauses entirely.

title: old is a compile error in a constructor's clauses
rule: `old` is a compile error in `requires` clauses, in `invariant` members, in constructor clauses, and outside clauses entirely (fields sit at §22.7's null watermark — no prestate exists).

title: old(old(E)) is a compile error
rule: `old(old(E))` is a compile error.

title: a move-only value operand is a compile error at old
rule: A move-only value operand is a compile error at the contract clause: a copy is the operation move-only-ness forbids, and the literal desugaring would not copy but consume.

title: an override may not declare requires clauses
rule: An override or implementation may not declare `requires` clauses. Strengthening a precondition breaks every caller dispatching through the base contract.

title: an override may add ensures clauses, conjoined with the inherited ones
rule: An override or implementation may add `ensures` clauses, conjoined with the inherited ones at its return edges — strengthening the postcondition, always sound for callers.

title: an undischargeable call to a static requires member is a compile error at the call
rule: The `static` clause qualifier demands the proven tier: a `static` clause the implementation cannot discharge statically is a compile error.

title: a static requires clause may mention only state its call sites can see
rule: A `static requires` clause may mention only state its call sites can see (the member's parameters, and members visible to every caller); a `static requires` over non-public state is a compile error at the declaration.

title: a static clause that is a constant expression folding to true is proven
rule: The current prover floor: exactly two things inhabit the proven tier: a clause whose expression (after call-site substitution, for `requires`) is a constant expression folding to `true`.

title: an invariant member given a visibility keyword is rejected
rule: `invariant(E);` declares no visibility choice to spell; it carries no visibility keyword (§13.3's principle).

title: an invariant member with no visibility keyword is admitted
rule: `invariant(E);` carries no visibility keyword — for such a member no visibility choice exists to spell.

title: an invariant in a static class is a compile error
rule: Out of scope in this revision, each recorded: ... static-class and static-state invariants (an `invariant` in a static class is a compile error — no instance boundary exists).

title: a constructor's requires clause may not observe this
rule: A constructor's `requires` may not observe `this` in any of §22.7's senses (no field of the declaring type is assigned at clause time) — it reads parameters and statics only.

title: requires clauses evaluate in declaration order and stop at the first false
rule: In declaration order, stopping at the first clause producing `false` — clause granularity is semantic: the clause is the unit of ... evaluation order (stop at first failure).

title: clauses never distinguish overloads; two members differing only in clauses clash
rule: Clauses never distinguish overloads and are not part of §22.6 resolution; two members differing only in clauses are the same signature and clash.

title: old over a borrow-bearing inline array is captured by copy
rule: An operand of a value type that holds borrows (§3.6's holds-borrows property: a borrow-bearing record or inline array, or a choice that holds borrows — §9.7, §15.1.2, §35.4) is admitted with its carried borrows under §9.7's ordinary rules — an inline array's under the one source set §15.1.2 gives the array value.

title: old over a borrow-bearing record is captured by copy
rule: An operand of a value type that holds borrows (§3.6's holds-borrows property: a borrow-bearing record or inline array, or a choice that holds borrows — §9.7, §15.1.2, §35.4) is admitted with its carried borrows under §9.7's ordinary rules — an inline array's under the one source set §15.1.2 gives the array value.

title: old over a choice that holds borrows is captured by copy
rule: An operand of a value type that holds borrows (§3.6's holds-borrows property: a borrow-bearing record or inline array, or a choice that holds borrows — §9.7, §15.1.2, §35.4) is admitted with its carried borrows under §9.7's ordinary rules — an inline array's under the one source set §15.1.2 gives the array value.

title: a generic method with an ensures clause returns a generic choice by expression and block body
rule: Contract clauses sit between a signature and its body (§22.16, v0.340) and add nothing to the value a body returns; "For a **generic** choice the type arguments are written at the construction (`Result<int, string>.Ok(value)`)" (§35.3, v0.340); a generic member is evaluated at each instantiation after substituting the type arguments (§3.6 rule 2, §14.1), so the payload constructed in the generic body is the payload matched by the caller. Contract clauses: the contract clause `ensures(n >= 0)` (§22.16, v0.340) holds for `n = 1`, and adds nothing to the result: `Wrap<int>(5, 1)` (expression body) and `WrapB<int>(6, 1)` (block body) return `Some(5)` and `Some(6)`.

title: the four auto-property forms are admitted
rule: An auto-property is read-write, read-write with a restricted setter (`private set`), read-only (`readonly`), or read-only with an initializer; the compiler generates the backing field.

title: a readonly auto-property may not be assigned from an ordinary method
rule: A `readonly` auto-property may be assigned only in a field initializer or in a constructor, under §22.8's per-instance assignable context.

title: a constructor may not write another instance's readonly auto-property
rule: The assignment is admitted only through `this` for an instance auto-property — the assignable context is per-instance, so a constructor may not write another value's readonly storage.

title: readonly on an expression-bodied property is rejected
rule: On every body-bearing form read-onlyness is already expressed by the shape, and writing `readonly` there is a compile error.

title: an expression-bodied property without readonly is admitted
rule: An expression-bodied property's body is checked against the declared type; the shape expresses read-onlyness, so no `readonly` is written.

title: readonly on a get-only block-form property is rejected
rule: A get-only block form expresses read-onlyness by its shape; `readonly` there is a compile error.

title: readonly on a block form declaring a setter is rejected
rule: On a block form declaring a setter `readonly` is contradictory and is likewise an error.

title: a block-form property names its setter parameter value implicitly
rule: The implicit setter parameter is `value`. Each accessor uses `=> expression` or `=> do ... end`.

title: a block-form setter body runs on assignment through the property
rule: A property's accessors are member bodies: a store through the property invokes the setter, and a read invokes the getter.

title: an expression-bodied indexer is admitted
rule: An indexer is a property whose name is replaced by a parameter list in square brackets.

title: a block-form indexer closes with a bare end
rule: A block-form indexer's `end` clause has no name to reference; it is plain `end;`.

title: a block-form indexer closed with an identifier label is rejected
rule: An `end`-label that is supplied must match the construct it closes; an indexer has no name to reference, so a supplied identifier is a mismatch.

title: an indexer may take several parameters
rule: An indexer is a property whose name is replaced by `[parameters]`; the list may hold more than one parameter.

title: indexers overload by parameter type list
rule: Indexers may be overloaded by parameter type list.

title: an enum may not declare an indexer
rule: Enums may not declare indexers.

title: a static indexer is rejected
rule: Static indexers are not supported.

title: a ref parameter in an indexer parameter list is rejected
rule: `ref` and `out` parameters are not allowed in indexer parameter lists.
check: indexer parameter may not be declared with

title: a named argument at an index position is rejected
rule: Index arguments are positional-only; the named-argument form (`Identifier :=`) is not admitted at an index position — a compile error naming this rule.

title: an enum may overload an operator
rule: Records, enums, choices, and classes may overload operators; an enum body admits operator overloads among the members it may declare (§10.4), and public static is the required spelling.

title: unary and binary operator overloads are admitted on a record
rule: Records, enums, choices and classes may overload operators; operators are declared as `public static` methods using the `operator` keyword. The unary set is `+`, `-`, `~` and the binary set includes `+`, `-`, `*`.

title: not is not user-overloadable
rule: `not` is not user-overloadable. It is the boolean-negation operator and applies only to `bool`; a domain-specific inversion is a named method.

title: the null-coalescing operator is not overloadable
rule: The null-forgiving `!`, the null-coalescing `??`, and the type-test operators have null-aware or type-system semantics fixed by the language; user types do not customize them.

title: an operator overload declared without public is rejected
rule: `public` is required: an operator invoked through `a + b` syntax has no call-site spelling that could name a restricted member, so any other visibility is a compile error.

title: an operator overload declared without static is rejected
rule: Operators are declared as `public static` methods using the `operator` keyword.

title: equality may not be overloaded on a class
rule: `=` and `<>` may not be overloaded on classes or on inline arrays. For classes, `=` always invokes `Equals`.

title: a homogeneous equality overload with Equals and GetHashCode beside it
rule: A record, enum or choice that overloads `=`/`<>` with both operands of the declaring type must also declare `Equals(T)` and `GetHashCode`.

title: a homogeneous equality overload without Equals and GetHashCode is rejected
rule: The co-declaration rule is compiler-enforced: the three surfaces (`=`, `Equals`, hashing) can otherwise silently diverge exactly where it hurts — `a = b` true while a `Set<T>` treats them as distinct.

title: a lone relational overload is rejected as an incomplete group
rule: Comparison operators must be overloaded as a complete group: `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` together; `=` and `<>` together.

title: the four relational operators declared together are admitted
rule: Comparison operators must be overloaded as a complete group: `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` together.

title: a ref modifier on an operator parameter is rejected
rule: Operator parameters admit no parameter modifiers: `ref`, `out`, `owned` and `scoped` on an operator's parameter list are rejected semantically.

title: an owned modifier on an operator parameter is rejected
rule: Operands are received as plain borrows (or value copies) under their type kinds; the return slot's optional `owned` is the sole ownership annotation on operators.

title: an operator whose parameters never mention the declaring type is rejected
rule: At least one parameter of an operator overload must be the declaring type; an operator whose parameters never mention it would be unreachable by the resolution rule.

title: a binary overload may carry the declaring type in either position
rule: A binary overload may pair the declaring type with any other type in either position.

title: operands are matched in order, with no automatic commutation
rule: Parameters match operands in order — there is no automatic commutation (`4 - v` is not matched against `operator -(v: V, n: int)`).

title: the co-declaration rule is satisfied on a record by a plain own-typed Equals and a plain GetHashCode
rule: A record, enum, or choice that overloads `=`/`<>` with both operands of the declaring type must also declare `Equals(T)` and `GetHashCode` — on a record, an enum, or a choice alike (`override` or plain on each

title: a compound over ArgumentException selects the exact overload when Exception is declared first
rule: For a single argument position, one candidate is better than another when the better candidate requires no implicit conversion

title: a non-null Exception operand selects the non-nullable overload
rule: For a single argument position, one candidate is better than another when the better candidate requires no implicit conversion

title: a nullable Exception operand selects the Exception? overload
rule: For a single argument position, one candidate is better than another when the better candidate requires no implicit conversion

title: a nullable ArgumentException operand takes the nullable base overload
rule: A derived-typed operand satisfies a base-typed parameter by the ordinary argument rules.

title: a binary operator's interface parameter accepts an array of the matching element type
rule: For `a <op> b` on non-primitive operands, the candidate set is the union of the `operator <op>` overloads declared on the static types of both operands, including declarations inherited from their base classes ([§25.2]). "classes by declaration or inheritance" ([§5.1]): `Array<int>` converts to `IEnumerable<int>`.

title: a binary operator's interface parameter rejects an array of a non-matching element type
rule: nor an overload from the candidate set above applies is a compile error at the expression ([§25.2]). An `Array<string>` operand does not convert to `IEnumerable<int>`.

title: a derived-typed right operand satisfies an interface-typed operator parameter
rule: classes by declaration or inheritance ([§5.1]): `Dog` inherits from `Animal`, which implements `IA`, so a `Dog` operand converts to the `IA` parameter.

title: a binary operator rejects a right operand that does not implement the parameter's interface
rule: nor an overload from the candidate set above applies is a compile error at the expression ([§25.2]). A `StringBuilder` operand does not implement `IA`, so it does not convert to the parameter.

title: a left operand converts to the first, interface-typed operator parameter
rule: Parameters match operands in order ([§25.2]). "classes by declaration or inheritance" ([§5.1]): the `Array<int>` left operand converts to the first parameter, `IEnumerable<int>`.

title: a left operand that does not implement the first parameter's interface is rejected
rule: Parameters match operands in order ([§25.2]). "nor an overload from the candidate set above applies is a compile error at the expression" ([§25.2]): a `StringBuilder` left operand converts to no first parameter.

title: a relational operator with an interface parameter applies to an array operand
rule: For `a <op> b` on non-primitive operands, the candidate set is the union of the `operator <op>` overloads declared on the static types of both operands, including declarations inherited from their base classes ([§25.2]). "classes by declaration or inheritance" ([§5.1]): the `Array<int>` operand converts to the `IEnumerable<int>` parameter of `<`.

title: a relational operator rejects an operand that matches none of its overloads
rule: nor an overload from the candidate set above applies is a compile error at the expression ([§25.2]). A `StringBuilder` operand converts to no relational overload parameter.

title: a null literal operand binds the nullable operator formal at its own position, left or right
rule: Parameters match operands in order — there is no automatic commutation (4 - v is not matched against operator -(v: V, n: int)).

title: a block-bodied operator closes with end operator and its token
rule: When an operator overload is block-bodied, the optional name in the closing `end` is written as `end operator OpToken;`.

title: a block-bodied operator closed with the wrong token is rejected
rule: An `end`-label that is supplied must match the construct it closes; for a keyword-labelled construct the operator token is part of the label.

title: an overloaded operator is invoked by the operator syntax
rule: For `a <op> b` on non-primitive operands the candidate set is drawn from the operator overloads declared on the static types of both operands.

title: there is no user-defined conversion between record types
rule: User-defined types cannot declare implicit or explicit conversion operators; the explicit-cast expression `T(value)` applies only to the built-in conversions enumerated in §5.

title: a named factory method is the sanctioned conversion between user types
rule: To express a conversion between user types, define a named factory or instance method.

title: an extension block adds a method and a computed property
rule: An extension block is declared at module level and adds methods and computed read-only properties to a type; inside the block `this` refers to the receiver.

title: an extension block may close with end extension
rule: The block ends with `end;` or `end extension;`.

title: a primitive type may be extended
rule: Classes, interfaces, records, enums and built-in primitive types may be extended.

title: a nullable type may not be extended directly
rule: Nullable types may not be extended directly (`extension int?`); extend the non-nullable form and let callers handle nullability at the call site.

title: a choice may not be extended
rule: The extendable list is closed against the choice kind: choices cannot be extended.

title: an extension block may not declare a field
rule: An extension block declares only methods and computed read-only properties: no fields, auto-properties, constructors, destructors, or `owned` fields.

title: an extension property must be expression-bodied
rule: An extension property is expression-bodied only; the block-accessor form is not admitted — multi-statement logic goes in a method.

title: an extension block may not declare an operator overload
rule: An extension block declares no operator overloads.

title: an extension block may not declare an indexer
rule: An extension block declares no indexers.

title: a static member inside an extension block is rejected
rule: An extension block adds receiver-directed members only: a `static` modifier inside an extension block is a compile error.

title: an extension member may not be private
rule: Extension members must be declared `public` or `internal`; `protected` and `private` are compile errors — an extension block has no declaring class and no inheritance, so §13.1's definitions for those levels do not apply.

title: an extension member may not be virtual
rule: An extension block declares no `virtual`, `override`, `abstract` or `sealed` members — extensions are statically dispatched.

title: an extension property on a StringBuilder receiver is found and its receiver runs once
rule: An extension property is **expression-bodied only** (`property Name: Type => expr;`) ... Inside the block, methods and computed properties are written as if they were instance members. `this` refers to the receiver.

title: a bare identifier in the extended type's argument position binds a parameter
rule: In the extended type's argument positions, each bare single-segment non-nullable identifier introduces a fresh block-level type parameter.

title: a nullable-marked identifier in an argument position is rejected
rule: A nullable-marked identifier in an argument position (`extension Array<T?>`) binds nothing and is a compile error naming this rule — only the bare non-nullable identifier introduces a parameter.

title: a concrete instantiation is a legal extension head
rule: A concrete instantiation is written with keyword/primitive types, qualified names, or generic instantiations — none of which are bare single-segment identifiers, so none binds a parameter.

title: a generic extension member boxing its block parameter is rejected at a borrow-bearing receiver
rule: Each member of a generic extension block is read, for §3.6 rule 2, §14.1 and §14.2, as a **generic method that declares the block's parameters before its own** — bound by the receiver at a call or a property read ... a requirement a member body carries on a block parameter is checked at each such call, read or formation as §3.6 rule 2 checks a method's own parameter

title: the same extension member called at a borrow-free element type is admitted
rule: Each member of a generic extension block is read, for §3.6 rule 2, §14.1 and §14.2, as a **generic method that declares the block's parameters before its own** — bound by the receiver at a call or a property read ... a requirement a member body carries on a block parameter is checked at each such call, read or formation as §3.6 rule 2 checks a method's own parameter

title: a block-level T local swaps elements of an Array<double> receiver
rule: The block-level type parameter is in scope throughout the block. ... Each member of a generic extension block is read ... as a generic method that declares the block's parameters before its own — bound by the receiver at a call or a property read (§26.5 step 2)

title: a block-level T local swaps elements of an Array<long> receiver
rule: The block-level type parameter is in scope throughout the block. ... Each member of a generic extension block is read ... as a generic method that declares the block's parameters before its own — bound by the receiver at a call or a property read (§26.5 step 2)

title: a block-level T local swaps elements of an Array<record> receiver
rule: The block-level type parameter is in scope throughout the block. ... Each member of a generic extension block is read ... as a generic method that declares the block's parameters before its own — bound by the receiver at a call or a property read (§26.5 step 2)

title: a block-level T local swaps elements of an Array<choice> receiver
rule: The block-level type parameter is in scope throughout the block. ... Each member of a generic extension block is read ... as a generic method that declares the block's parameters before its own — bound by the receiver at a call or a property read (§26.5 step 2)

title: a block-level T local swaps elements of an Array<int?> receiver
rule: The block-level type parameter is in scope throughout the block. ... Each member of a generic extension block is read ... as a generic method that declares the block's parameters before its own — bound by the receiver at a call or a property read (§26.5 step 2)

title: a block-level T local swaps elements of an Array<string> receiver (T-free swap)
rule: The block-level type parameter is in scope throughout the block. ... Each member of a generic extension block is read ... as a generic method that declares the block's parameters before its own — bound by the receiver at a call or a property read (§26.5 step 2)

title: an extension on a user generic class Box<T> binds T per receiver instantiation
rule: The block-level type parameter is in scope throughout the block. ... Each member of a generic extension block is read ... as a generic method that declares the block's parameters before its own — bound by the receiver at a call or a property read (§26.5 step 2)

title: an extension with where T: class and a nested Array<Array<T>> head both bind T per receiver
rule: The block-level type parameter is in scope throughout the block. ... Each member of a generic extension block is read ... as a generic method that declares the block's parameters before its own — bound by the receiver at a call or a property read (§26.5 step 2)

title: mutually recursive extension methods keep T bound while swapping, in lambdas too
rule: The block-level type parameter is in scope throughout the block. ... Each member of a generic extension block is read ... as a generic method that declares the block's parameters before its own — bound by the receiver at a call or a property read (§26.5 step 2)

title: an extension on a two-parameter generic class binds A and B independently
rule: The block-level type parameter is in scope throughout the block. ... Each member of a generic extension block is read ... as a generic method that declares the block's parameters before its own — bound by the receiver at a call or a property read (§26.5 step 2)

title: block-level T stays bound per receiver when an outer generic method or class has its own T
rule: The block-level type parameter is in scope throughout the block. ... Each member of a generic extension block is read ... as a generic method that declares the block's parameters before its own — bound by the receiver at a call or a property read (§26.5 step 2)

title: an instance member wins over a same-named extension member
rule: Instance members win — by name. If the receiver's declared type declares any instance member of that name, instance resolution is committed and extension blocks are never consulted for that name on that receiver.

title: a failed instance lookup does not fall back to an extension
rule: If the committed instance lookup fails — no applicable overload — the call is a compile error citing the instance members; it does not fall back to an extension.

title: an extension member is reached when the type declares no such name
rule: If the receiver's type declares no instance member of that name, the compiler searches the current module and all imported modules for extension blocks on the receiver's type, base types, or implemented interfaces.

title: an extension block declared in an imported module reaches the receiver
rule: If the receiver's type declares no instance member of that name, the compiler searches the current module and all imported modules for extension blocks on the receiver's type. `Doubled` is declared in `Lib`, not in `App`, and is reached because `App` imports `Lib`.

title: an extension's own module must be imported even when its type is only used
rule: Extension members are the one exception to use-without-import: they are candidates only from the current module and imported modules (§2.8.3 rule 2). `Widget` reaches `App` transitively through `Factory` with no import needed to *use* it, but `Doubled` lives in `Lib`, which `App` never imports, so it is not a candidate.

title: importing an extension's own module makes it reachable
rule: Extension members are candidates only from the current module and imported modules. Once `App` also imports `Lib`, `Doubled` is a candidate for the `Widget` receiver.

title: a default-internal extension block is invisible from an importing module
rule: The compiler considers only extension members visible at the call site (§26.3's effective-visibility rule); an extension block is `public` or `internal`, default `internal` (§26.1). `Lib`'s block carries no `public` keyword, so it is internal to `Lib` and not a candidate for `App`'s call, even though `App` imports `Lib`.

title: a public extension block is visible from an importing module
rule: The compiler considers only extension members visible at the call site. Marking the block `public` makes its member a candidate for any importing module.

title: two equally-specific extensions from different imported modules are ambiguous
rule: If two equally-specific extensions match, the call is a compile error (rule 4). Nothing in the same module can conflict this way (§26.6 merges same-module blocks and rejects duplicate *signatures*); the ambiguity here comes from two distinct imported modules each declaring the same substituted head and name.

title: narrowing the import to one candidate module resolves the ambiguity
rule: The remedies for extension ambiguity are the mechanisms that exist: remove or narrow a conflicting import. Importing only `ExtA` leaves one candidate, so the call resolves.

title: specificity ordering picks the more specific extension across two imported modules
rule: Extensions on the most specific type are preferred (rule 3, §26.5.1). `ExtCircle`'s block on `Circle` is more specific than `ExtShape`'s block on `Shape`, and the ordering holds even though the two candidates come from two different imported modules, neither importing the other.

title: instance members win over a same-named extension imported from another module
rule: Instance members win — by name. If the receiver's declared type declares any instance member of that name, instance resolution is committed and extension blocks are never consulted — regardless of which module declares the conflicting extension.

title: a failed instance lookup does not fall back to an extension from another module
rule: If the committed instance lookup fails — no applicable overload — the call is a compile error citing the instance members; it does not fall back to an extension, even one visible from an imported module.

title: the current module's own extension conflicts with an imported one

title: multiple extension blocks on the same type are merged
rule: Multiple `extension` blocks targeting the same type may appear across files in the same module. The compiler merges them.

title: duplicate signatures across merged blocks are a compile error
rule: Multiple `extension` blocks targeting the same type may appear; the compiler merges them. Duplicate signatures are a compile error.

title: merged blocks may contribute distinct overloads of the same name
rule: Multiple `extension` blocks targeting the same type are merged; duplicate *signatures* are a compile error, but two blocks contributing different overloads of one name are not duplicates.

title: an extension cannot return this as owned
rule: The receiver is always a borrow; extensions cannot store `this`, return it as `owned`, or dispose it.

title: an extension may return this as an ordinary receiver-sourced borrow
rule: The receiver is always a borrow; extensions cannot return it as `owned` — but an ordinary (non-owned) borrow return of the receiver remains legal, the same receiver-sourced borrow return every instance or extension method may make.

title: extensions may return owned values
rule: Extensions may return `owned` values.

title: a value-kind extension body cannot store into the receiver's own storage
rule: For a value-kind receiver, §9.4's value-receiver rule applies in the extension body exactly as in a declared member body: a store landing in the receiver's own storage is a compile error.

title: a value-kind extension body may read the receiver's own storage
rule: For a value-kind receiver, §9.4's value-receiver rule applies in the extension body exactly as in a declared member body — only a *store* landing in the receiver's own storage is rejected; a bare read of the same storage is ordinary member access and is legal.

title: other parameters may be owned in an extension, following normal method rules
rule: Other parameters may be `owned`, following normal method rules.

title: a two-parameter function type mirrors a two-parameter method declaration
rule: A function type is written `(params) -> returnType`; `method Foo(x: int, y: int): int` parallels `(int, int) -> int`.

title: a method with no return type has function type returning the unit type
rule: A method without a return type has function type returning `()`; `method Foo()` parallels `() -> ()`.

title: an owned-parameter function type is distinct from the unmarked form
rule: Function types may include the parameter modifier `owned`; `method Foo(owned t: T)` parallels `(owned T) -> ()`, and the modifier is part of the type.

title: the out-owned modifier compound forms its own function type
rule: Function types may include the modifier combination `out owned`; `method Foo(out owned r: T)` parallels `(out owned T) -> ()`.

title: named parameters in a function type are documentation, calls are positional
rule: Function types may include parameter names; names are documentation only and do not affect type identity — `(int, int, int) -> bool` and the named form are the same type, and calls are positional.

title: a named-argument call through a function-typed value is rejected
rule: A call through a function-typed value admits no named argument (v0.295): the named form at an invocation whose callee is a function-typed value is a compile error naming this rule.

title: a call through a function-typed value takes positional arguments
rule: A call through a function-typed value admits no named argument (v0.295); calls through a function-typed value are positional.

title: a wider-parameter function value is usable where a narrower one is expected
rule: Parameter slots of class or interface type, nullable or not, are contravariant: the target's parameter type must reach the value's by a reference conversion (§5.1), its nullable lift or the nullable view of a reference type, never the view's reverse ... a `(Animal) -> ()` value is usable where `(Dog) -> ()` is expected

title: a narrower-parameter function value is not usable where a wider one is expected
rule: Parameter slots of class or interface type, nullable or not, are contravariant: the target's parameter type must reach the value's by a reference conversion (§5.1), its nullable lift or the nullable view of a reference type, never the view's reverse

title: a narrower-return function value is usable where a wider return is expected
rule: The return slot, when of class or interface type, nullable or not, is covariant: the value's return type must reach the target's by a reference conversion, its nullable lift or the nullable view of a reference type, never the view's reverse ... a `() -> Dog` value is usable as `() -> Animal`

title: a wider-return function value is not usable where a narrower return is expected
rule: The return slot, when of class or interface type, nullable or not, is covariant: the value's return type must reach the target's by a reference conversion, its nullable lift or the nullable view of a reference type, never the view's reverse

title: a function value is never usable at a function type with a different parameter count
rule: Every rule of function-type assignability is slot-wise over equal parameter counts — a value is never usable at a function type with a different number of parameter slots, whatever the slots' types (v0.296).

title: modifier slots must match exactly between two function-typed values
rule: Modifier slots (`owned`/`ref`/`out`/`out owned`/`scoped`) must match exactly (§27.1); there is no conversion between a modified and an unmodified parameter slot.

title: a lambda's written wider parameter type is admitted at a narrower target slot
rule: the admission of a lambda literal at a target-typed non-call position (§27.3) is the one other site-typed bridge — the literal, like a formed reference, is typed at the site: its body's inferred return type converts to the target's return slot under §5.1, while a written parameter type or return ascription is judged as a value's slot under this subsection ... a `(Animal) -> ()` value is usable where `(Dog) -> ()` is expected

title: a lambda's written narrower parameter type is not bridged at a wider target slot
rule: the admission of a lambda literal at a target-typed non-call position (§27.3) is the one other site-typed bridge — the literal, like a formed reference, is typed at the site: its body's inferred return type converts to the target's return slot under §5.1, while a written parameter type or return ascription is judged as a value's slot under this subsection ... Parameter slots of class or interface type, nullable or not, are contravariant: the target's parameter type must reach the value's by a reference conversion (§5.1), its nullable lift or the nullable view of a reference type, never the view's reverse

title: parentheses around a function type are required before a trailing question mark
rule: The parentheses around the function type are required before `?`; `((int) -> bool)?` is a nullable function returning bool, callable with the null-conditional call form.

title: a null-conditional call on a null function value is a no-op yielding null
rule: `((int) -> bool)?` is a nullable function returning bool; the null-conditional call result is nullable, and a null hole renders the four characters `null` (§18.5).

title: a non-null function returning a nullable value is a distinct type from a nullable function
rule: Without the parentheses, the `?` attaches to the return type — `(int) -> bool?` is a non-null function returning a nullable bool, a different type from `((int) -> bool)?`, and modifier/nullability slots follow the standard §7 rules under assignability (§27.1.1).

title: a lambda's parameter types are inferred from the target type
rule: When the lambda's target type is known from context, parameter type annotations may be omitted; the compiler infers them from the target.

title: a zero-parameter lambda spells the empty parameter list, never omits it
rule: A lambda expression's parenthesized parameter list is the empty pair for zero parameters; there is no paren-free form.

title: a return-type ascription is a written integer target for a target-typed constant
rule: The return-type ascription behaves exactly as a method's declared return type; it is a written integer target for §4.2's target-typed integer constant — `lambda(): long => 3_000_000_000` is admitted by §5.1's constant narrowing.

title: a block-bodied lambda where one path returns a value and another does not is rejected
rule: A body where one path returns a value and another exits without one is a compile error, the same totality rule as for methods.

title: a value-returning lambda does not convert to a procedure function type
rule: A target type, when present, is checked against the procedure-lambda classification — a procedure-bodied lambda does not convert to a value-returning function type, nor the reverse.

title: a lambda literal at a target-typed non-call position admits an implicit widening body
rule: A lambda literal at a position that supplies a function-typed target other than a call argument is admitted under the argument-position rule (v0.292); its inferred return type must equal the target's return slot or implicitly convert to it — `var f: (int) -> long := lambda(x) => x * 2;` is admitted, the `int` body widening to `long`.

title: an ascription narrows what a target-typed non-call position admits
rule: An ascribed lambda's ascription must agree with the target, judged as a value's return type under §27.1.1 — so an ascription narrows what the position admits: `var g: (int) -> long := lambda(x): int => x * 2;` is rejected where the unascribed form is admitted.

title: several ignore parameters may coexist in one lambda's parameter list
rule: A parameter slot may be the ignore `_`; because nothing is named, several ignores may coexist — `lambda(_, _) => 0` is legal.

title: no parameter modifier composes with the bare ignore
rule: No parameter modifier and no type annotation compose with the bare ignore — `FuncParamMods` with `_` is rejected, because a `ref` parameter reads and writes through its operand, which an ignore cannot supply.

title: a lambda's written wider parameter type is admitted at a narrower target slot
rule: an **explicitly written** parameter type is judged as a value's parameter slot under §27.1.1: the target's parameter type must be identical to it or reach it as §27.1.1's parameter bullet states at a class, interface or `string` slot, so `var f: (Dog) -> () := lambda(a: Animal) => a.Speak();` is admitted and `lambda(d: Dog)` at an `(Animal) -> ()` target is rejected

title: a lambda's written narrower parameter type is rejected at a wider target slot
rule: an **explicitly written** parameter type is judged as a value's parameter slot under §27.1.1: the target's parameter type must be identical to it or reach it as §27.1.1's parameter bullet states at a class, interface or `string` slot, so `var f: (Dog) -> () := lambda(a: Animal) => a.Speak();` is admitted and `lambda(d: Dog)` at an `(Animal) -> ()` target is rejected

title: a do-end block lambda with no value return is a procedure lambda at () -> ()
rule: A block-bodied lambda is a **procedure lambda** — its type is `(…) -> ()` — exactly when no path through its body executes a value-carrying `return e;` (v0.338 §27.3)

title: a bare return is a procedure exit; the block lambda is a procedure lambda at () -> ()
rule: its exits are bare `return;` and falling off the end (v0.338 §27.3)

title: a procedure lambda does not convert to a value-returning function type
rule: a procedure-bodied lambda does not convert to a value-returning function type, nor the reverse (v0.338 §27.3)

title: a block lambda whose every exit path returns a value is a value lambda at () -> int
rule: Inside a value-returning block-bodied lambda, `return` is required on every exit path. (v0.338 §27.3)

title: a block lambda whose only exit is a bare return is a procedure lambda and is rejected at () -> int
rule: A block-bodied lambda is a **procedure lambda** — its type is `(…) -> ()` — exactly when no path through its body executes a value-carrying `return e;`: its exits are bare `return;` and falling off the end. […] A target type, when present, is checked against this classification — a procedure-bodied lambda does not convert to a value-returning function type, nor the reverse. (v0.338 §27.3)

title: a block lambda that breaks out of a loop and falls off the end is rejected at () -> int
rule: A block-bodied lambda is a **procedure lambda** — its type is `(…) -> ()` — exactly when no path through its body executes a value-carrying `return e;`: its exits are bare `return;` and falling off the end. […] A target type, when present, is checked against this classification — a procedure-bodied lambda does not convert to a value-returning function type, nor the reverse. (v0.338 §27.3)

title: a block lambda with a value return and a throw is a value lambda at () -> int
rule: A block-bodied lambda is a **procedure lambda** — its type is `(…) -> ()` — exactly when no path through its body executes a value-carrying `return e;`: its exits are bare `return;` and falling off the end. (v0.338 §27.3)

title: a block lambda whose exits are a bare return and a throw is rejected at () -> int
rule: A block-bodied lambda is a **procedure lambda** — its type is `(…) -> ()` — exactly when no path through its body executes a value-carrying `return e;`: its exits are bare `return;` and falling off the end. […] A target type, when present, is checked against this classification — a procedure-bodied lambda does not convert to a value-returning function type, nor the reverse. (v0.338 §27.3)

title: an expression-bodied lambda whose body is a lambda yields the inner lambda as its value
rule: Expression-bodied lambdas need no inference rule: the body expression's type is the return type. (v0.338 §27.3)

title: a block lambda whose only return is a lambda takes that lambda's function type as its return type
rule: A value-returning block-bodied lambda's return type is inferred only when every `return e;` expression in the body has the same type. (v0.338 §27.3, Return-type inference without a target)

title: a procedure-bodied lambda is rejected for the sole constructor value-returning function parameter
rule: a procedure-bodied lambda does not convert to a value-returning function type, nor the reverse ([§27.3]); the constructor's only overload takes `() -> int`, so the procedure lambda has no admissible slot.

title: a procedure-bodied lambda is rejected for the sole static method value-returning function parameter
rule: a procedure-bodied lambda does not convert to a value-returning function type, nor the reverse ([§27.3]); the method's only overload takes `() -> int`, so the procedure lambda has no admissible slot.

title: a procedure-bodied lambda is rejected beside a same-name overload of a different arity
rule: a procedure-bodied lambda does not convert to a value-returning function type, nor the reverse ([§27.3]); the only overload applicable by arity takes `() -> int`, so the procedure lambda has no admissible slot.

title: a procedure-bodied lambda is rejected when every same-name overload takes a value-returning function
rule: a procedure-bodied lambda does not convert to a value-returning function type, nor the reverse ([§27.3]); both same-name overloads take a value-returning function, so no slot admits the procedure lambda.

title: a procedure lambda selects the () -> () constructor and an expression lambda the () -> int one
rule: between overloads taking `() -> int` and `() -> ()` only the procedure slot is applicable ([§27.3]); the expression-bodied lambda `lambda() => 3` is value-returning and takes the `() -> int` slot.

title: a procedure lambda with a console body selects the () -> () extension overload
rule: between overloads taking `() -> int` and `() -> ()` only the procedure slot is applicable ([§27.3]); the lambda's body writes to the console and returns no value, so an extension method's same-name overloads select the procedure slot.

title: a procedure lambda with a console body selects the () -> () interface method overload
rule: between overloads taking `() -> int` and `() -> ()` only the procedure slot is applicable ([§27.3]); the lambda's body writes to the console and returns no value, so the interface call's same-name overloads select the procedure slot.

title: a procedure lambda with a console body selects the () -> () class method overload
rule: between overloads taking `() -> int` and `() -> ()` only the procedure slot is applicable ([§27.3]); the lambda's body writes to the console and returns no value, so the class method's same-name overloads select the procedure slot.

title: a throw-only procedure lambda selects the () -> () extension overload, not the () -> int one
rule: A body none of whose paths returns at all, every path throwing or looping forever, executes no value-carrying `return` and is a procedure lambda too ([§27.3]), and "between overloads taking `() -> int` and `() -> ()` only the procedure slot is applicable" ([§27.3]).

title: a throw-only procedure lambda selects the () -> () interface method overload, not the () -> int one
rule: A body none of whose paths returns at all, every path throwing or looping forever, executes no value-carrying `return` and is a procedure lambda too ([§27.3]), and "between overloads taking `() -> int` and `() -> ()` only the procedure slot is applicable" ([§27.3]).

title: a top-level lambda with no target type must specify parameter types
rule: In top-level contexts with no target type (`var f := lambda(x) => x * 2;`), parameter types must be specified.

title: an explicit parameter type admits a top-level lambda with no target type
rule: In top-level contexts with no target type, parameter types must be specified; an explicitly typed parameter satisfies the requirement.

title: a positional-record destructuring parameter binds each field by desugaring
rule: A lambda parameter may be a positional record destructuring; `lambda(Entry(k, v)) => ...` behaves as a lambda over the record type with each slot bound to the corresponding positional field.

title: a destructuring parameter slot may be the discard
rule: Each slot of a lambda-parameter destructuring is a naked identifier binding, a discard `_`, or a nested destructuring meeting the same rules.

title: a destructuring parameter's head must exactly name the target's parameter type
rule: The head of a lambda-parameter destructuring must name a positional record type, and it must be exactly the parameter's type: when a target type supplies the parameter type, a head naming any other type is a compile error.

title: a constant is a refutable element and is rejected inside a destructuring parameter
rule: Constants, ranges, relationals, type tests, `var`-form bindings, and alternatives are compile errors in destructuring parameter position — they are refutable, and a parameter list is not a `case`.

title: a captured local is shared, not copied, between a closure and its enclosing scope
rule: A lambda may reference variables from its enclosing scope; captured variables are heap-allocated in a closure object, and modifications to a captured variable inside the lambda are visible outside, and vice versa.

title: each for-loop iteration produces a fresh binding a captured lambda sees
rule: For `for` loop variables, each iteration produces a fresh binding; a lambda captured inside the body sees that iteration's value.

title: a closure may not assign to a captured owned binding
rule: For a captured owned binding the sharing is read-only in the ownership sense — the lambda may not assign to it, transfer from it, or dispose it (§28.3).

title: a closure may not move a captured owned binding
rule: `move` is an error inside a closure over a captured owned binding — captured owned bindings are uniformly in borrow state, so a closure cannot consume, reassign, or dispose one (§28.3).

title: a closure may not discard a captured owned binding
rule: For a captured owned binding, an explicit `Dispose()` or discard of it is a compile error — a closure cannot consume, reassign, or dispose a captured owned binding (§28.3).

title: a closure may not be stored in a field while it captures a borrow
rule: A closure is a borrow-carrying value whose source set is the union of its captures' sources; while it captures anything, it may not be stored in a field or a collection (§28.3, v0.298).

title: a closure may not be returned from the method while it captures a borrow
rule: While a closure captures anything, it may not be returned from the method — a function type announces no source set, so no caller could bound it (§28.3, v0.298).

title: a closure that captures a borrow may be passed to a plain function-typed parameter
rule: A capture-bearing closure may be passed as an argument to a function-typed parameter — a plain parameter is call-bounded, and the callee's use is bounded by the call (§28.3, v0.298).

title: reassigning a plain function-typed local from a capturing closure is legal
rule: Reassigning a plain function-typed local is fine — each assignment is checked on its own (§28.3, v0.298).

title: using var on a function-typed local forbids reassignment
rule: A closure value may be bound to a local, plain `var` or `using var` alike, whose scope does not strictly enclose any source's scope, `using var` adding only non-reassignability (§28.3, v0.298).

title: a local captured two lambda levels down is shared with the enclosing scope
rule: A lambda may reference variables from its enclosing scope. Captured variables are heap-allocated in a closure object. Modifications to a captured variable inside the lambda are visible outside, and vice versa. (v0.338 §27.5)

title: a nested lambda keeps reading its enclosing lambda's parameter after that lambda has returned
