rule: A lambda may reference variables from its enclosing scope. Captured variables are heap-allocated in a closure object, so the closure outlives the call that formed it. (v0.338 §27.5)

title: a write after a two-level nested lambda was formed is seen when that lambda is called
rule: Modifications to a captured variable inside the lambda are visible outside, and vice versa. (v0.338 §27.5)

title: each for-loop iteration gives a nested lambda its own binding
rule: For `for` loop variables, each iteration produces a fresh binding; a lambda captured inside the body sees that iteration's value. (v0.338 §27.5)

title: several nested closures built from one enclosing parameter share a single outer local
rule: Captured variables are heap-allocated in a closure object. Modifications to a captured variable inside the lambda are visible outside, and vice versa. (v0.338 §27.5)

title: a static method reference is usable directly as a function value
rule: When a lambda's body is just a call to an existing method, the method reference may be used directly; method references work for static methods.

title: a property reference produces the getter, typed (Receiver) -> PropertyType
rule: Method references work for properties; a property reference produces the getter, and its type is `(Receiver) -> PropertyType` for instance properties.

title: a bound instance method reference captures the receiver at formation
rule: Method references work for instance methods — the instance is captured at formation, by reference for class-typed receivers.

title: a reference to an overloaded method with no target type is ambiguous
rule: When no target type is available (e.g. `var f := Math.Abs;` with no annotation), the reference is ambiguous and the compiler reports an error pointing to the candidate overloads.

title: a type annotation disambiguates a reference to an overloaded method
rule: The user disambiguates an ambiguous method reference by adding a type annotation: `var f: (int) -> int := Math.Abs;`.

title: an exact-match overload is preferred over a converting one when forming a reference
rule: Among unifying candidates, one whose parameter types and return type match the target's exactly is preferred; candidates that unify only through conversion are co-equal and lose to the exact candidate.

title: a method reference to Sort at an unordered element type is rejected at the formation
rule: A method reference, bound or unbound, or a property reference formed over a **conditionally-admitted member** (§14.2 ...) is a use of the member: at a receiver instantiation that does not satisfy the member's condition, the formation is rejected **at the formation site** with the condition's diagnostic and remedy, exactly as the call would be ... So `var s: () -> () := xs.Sort;` at `xs: Array<Widget>`, for a `Widget` conforming to no `IComparable<Widget>`, is rejected naming the comparer-taking overload

title: the same reference against a comparer-taking target selects the unconditioned overload
rule: The overload is selected against the target first; the condition is read on the overload selected and takes no part in the selection ... the comparer-taking overload, which the same reference against a comparer-taking target selects and no condition reaches

title: a method reference over a generic method with no type-argument list is rejected
rule: A method reference over a **generic method** — one declaring type parameters of its own — names its type arguments on the member name (`Util.Keep<Pair>`, `s.Put<[2 owned]Item>`, `xs.Select(Util.Id<int>)`), under §14.5's all-or-nothing rule for explicit lists; a reference to a generic method with no list is a compile error naming the type parameters to supply, and no inference binds them from the target.

title: the same reference written with its type-argument list is formed and invoked
rule: A method reference over a **generic method** — one declaring type parameters of its own — names its type arguments on the member name (`Util.Keep<Pair>`, `s.Put<[2 owned]Item>`, `xs.Select(Util.Id<int>)`), under §14.5's all-or-nothing rule for explicit lists; a reference to a generic method with no list is a compile error naming the type parameters to supply, and no inference binds them from the target.

title: a generic method reference is checked against its constraints at the formation
rule: The formation is an **instantiation site** (§14.1): §3.6 rule 2's requirements, §14.2's constraints, its dispatched-method exclusion (§14.2) and §28.3's two per-instantiation exclusions ... are read at the formation exactly as at a call with that list, and never at an invocation through the formed value, which reads the function type alone.

title: a generic method reference at an argument meeting its constraints is formed and invoked
rule: The formation is an **instantiation site** (§14.1): §3.6 rule 2's requirements, §14.2's constraints, its dispatched-method exclusion (§14.2) and §28.3's two per-instantiation exclusions ... are read at the formation exactly as at a call with that list, and never at an invocation through the formed value, which reads the function type alone.

title: a reference to Math.Max without its type-argument list is rejected
rule: Overload selection follows §14.5's list rule: with a list, only candidates declaring that many type parameters of their own take part; without one, only candidates declaring none take part, and the error above is reported where every candidate is generic (`var f: (int) -> int := Math.Abs;` selects among `Abs`'s non-generic overloads; `Math.Max` must be written `Math.Max<int>`).

title: a reference to Math.Max with its list, and to the non-generic Math.Abs, are formed
rule: Overload selection follows §14.5's list rule: with a list, only candidates declaring that many type parameters of their own take part; without one, only candidates declaring none take part, and the error above is reported where every candidate is generic (`var f: (int) -> int := Math.Abs;` selects among `Abs`'s non-generic overloads; `Math.Max` must be written `Math.Max<int>`).

title: a generic method reference passed as an argument without its list is rejected
rule: When a lambda's body is just a call to an existing method, the method reference may be used directly. A reference to a generic method with no list is a compile error naming the type parameters to supply, and no inference binds them from the target.

title: a non-generic Math.Abs reference written with a type-argument list is rejected
rule: Overload selection follows the list rule: with a list, only candidates declaring that many type parameters of their own take part; without one, only candidates declaring none take part.

title: a Math.Max reference with two type arguments for one type parameter is rejected
rule: An explicit type-argument list is all-or-nothing: it must supply exactly as many arguments as the method declares type parameters. A shorter or a longer list is a compile error.

title: a generic reference whose type argument fails the callee's constraint is rejected at formation
rule: The formation is an instantiation site: its constraints are read at the formation exactly as at a call with that list (the constraint of Math.Min is where T: IComparable<T>).

title: the same reference at a type argument that conforms to IComparable is formed and invoked
rule: The formation is an instantiation site: its constraints are read at the formation exactly as at a call with that list; string conforms to IComparable<string>.

title: a generic Math.Max reference with its list, passed as an argument, is formed at the parameter's type
rule: A method reference over a generic method names its type arguments on the member name; the reference is formed against the target slot it is passed to.

title: a method reference to a class-only member is accepted on the class-typed receiver
rule: If `x`'s declared type (or any base type) *declares* any instance member named `Foo` ... instance resolution is committed (§26.5 rule 1, v0.340); a bound method reference `obj.Method` (§27.6) over the class-typed `m` reaches `MyList.Extra`, a member the class declares beyond the interface.

title: a bare reference to a class-only member is rejected on an IList-typed receiver
rule: the member resolved on the value exactly as the call `v.Scaled()` is (§27.6, v0.340): the call `il.Extra()` over `il: IList<int>` is rejected, since `IList<T>` declares no `Extra` (stdlib §4.1) and no extension applies (§26.5), so the bare reference `il.Extra` is rejected the same way even though the class behind the value declares it.

title: a bare reference to an undeclared member of an unannotated IList-typed local is rejected
rule: the member resolved on the value exactly as the call `v.Scaled()` is (§27.6, v0.340): `Nope` is not a member of `IList<T>` (stdlib §4.1: Count, IsReadOnly, Add, Clear, Contains, Remove, Insert, the indexer, and the inherited `GetEnumerator`), and no extension applies (§26.5), so `il.Nope` is rejected as `il.Nope()` is; the declared member `Count` on the same local is read without error.

title: a receiver-qualified reference to a user extension on IList<int> is formed and invoked
rule: Receiver-qualified — `v.Scaled` over `extension Vec`, the member resolved on the value exactly as the call `v.Scaled()` is (§26.5) — the reference is a bound reference ... the resulting function has the method's own parameters only (§27.6, v0.340). The extension on `IList<int>` applies to the `IList<int>`-typed `il`, so `il.Twice` and `il.Tag` form `() -> int` references, and `il.Tag()` is the same call.

title: an extension on IEnumerable<int> is reached by a bare reference via three receiver types
rule: the compiler searches ... for extension blocks on `x`'s type, base types, or implemented interfaces (§26.5 rule 2, v0.340). `IList<T>` and `IReadOnlyList<T>` extend `IEnumerable<T>` (stdlib §4.1), so the receiver- qualified reference of §27.6 `r.Tag` resolves to `extension IEnumerable<int>` at all three static types.

title: an extension on IReadOnlyList<int> is reached by a bare reference through an IList<int> receiver
rule: the compiler searches ... for extension blocks on `x`'s type, base types, or implemented interfaces (§26.5 rule 2, v0.340). `IList<T>` is declared `IList<T>: IReadOnlyList<T>, ICollection<T>` (stdlib §4.1), so the reference `il.OnlyRO` of §27.6 resolves to `extension IReadOnlyList<int>`.

title: an extension on IReadOnlyList<int> is not reached by a bare reference via IEnumerable<int>
rule: the compiler searches ... for extension blocks on `x`'s type, base types, or implemented interfaces (§26.5 rule 2, v0.340). `IEnumerable<T>` neither is nor extends `IReadOnlyList<T>` (stdlib §4.1, §4.12), so no extension applies to `e.OnlyRO`, and `IEnumerable<T>` declares no such member: the reference is rejected as `e.OnlyRO()` is.

title: a bare GetEnumerator reference on an IOwningEnumerable-typed receiver is rejected
rule: the member resolved on the value exactly as the call `v.Scaled()` is (§27.6, v0.340). `IOwningEnumerable<T>` declares `GetOwningEnumerator` and inherits `Dispose` (stdlib §4.13); it has no `GetEnumerator`, which belongs to `IEnumerable<T>` (stdlib §4.12), so `r.GetEnumerator` names no member at the static type `IOwningEnumerable<Item>`.

title: a method reference to ICollection's Contains is formed over an ICollection-typed receiver
rule: Method references work for static methods, instance methods (the instance is captured at formation — by reference for class- or interface-typed receivers, **by copy** for value-shaped receivers ...) (§27.6, v0.340). `ICollection<T>` declares `method Contains(item: T): bool` (stdlib §4.1), and §26.5 rule 1 commits instance resolution to the head's declared member, so `h.Contains` names that member and forms a bound `(int) -> bool` reference over the `ICollection<int>`-typed `h`. KNOWN DIVERGENCE (#4704): the compiler rejects the formation in codegen with the #853 fence (".Contains` through a polymorphic collection interface ... is not yet supported in codegen"), so the reference never forms; no spec sentence rejects it.

title: a method reference to IOwningCollection's Contains is formed over an owning receiver
rule: Method references work for static methods, instance methods (the instance is captured at formation — by reference for class- or interface-typed receivers, **by copy** for value-shaped receivers ...) (§27.6, v0.340). `IOwningCollection<T>` declares `method Contains(item: T): bool` (stdlib §4.2), and §26.5 rule 1 commits instance resolution to the head's declared member, so `h.Contains` names that member and forms a bound `(Item) -> bool` reference over the `IOwningCollection<Item>`-typed `h`. KNOWN DIVERGENCE (#4704): the compiler rejects the formation in codegen with the #853 fence (".Contains` through a polymorphic collection interface ... is not yet supported in codegen"), so the reference never forms; no spec sentence rejects it.

title: a bound reference over an interface-typed receiver captures the instance by reference
rule: Method references work for static methods, instance methods (the instance is captured at formation — by reference for class- or interface-typed receivers, **by copy** for value-shaped receivers ...) (§27.6, v0.340). The receiver `t` is interface-typed, so the formation captures the instance by reference: the two calls through `f` act on the same `Thing`, whose counter answers 1 and then 2. This row pins that the formation binds the receiver INSTANCE. It does not by itself discriminate by-reference from by-copy capture: the receiver is class-backed, and a copy of a class-typed value is a copy of the reference, so a by-copy capture would answer 1 and then 2 as well. The observable that discriminates the two captures is function-value equality (§27.7.1): the interface-typed head's two evaluations are equal (`s27_7_1_0008`), while a value-shaped head's are unequal (`s27_7_1_0009`).

title: a bare Clear reference on an IReadOnlyCollection-typed receiver is rejected
rule: the member resolved on the value exactly as the call `v.Scaled()` is (§27.6, v0.340). `IReadOnlyCollection<out T>` declares only `pure readonly property Count: int` (stdlib §4.1); `Clear` is declared by `ICollection<T>`, the interface that *extends* `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`, and a receiver's declared type and its base types are the ones §26.5 rule 1 consults, so `ro.Clear` names no member at the static type `IReadOnlyCollection<int>` and is rejected as `ro.Clear()` is.

title: a method reference over an interface-typed head holding a record forms and is called through
rule: Method references work for static methods, instance methods (the instance is captured at formation — by reference for class- or interface-typed receivers, by copy for value-shaped receivers) (§27.6, v0.340). The head `t` is interface-typed, so the formation captures the instance by reference; the record's member answers its constant, so the two calls through `f` answer 7 twice. The by-copy capture rule is discriminated by the function-value equality case `s27_7_1_0009`, which is the observable that tells the two captures apart.

title: a method reference to a concrete Array's Contains member is admitted
rule: Method references work for static methods, instance methods (the instance is captured at formation — by reference for class- or interface-typed receivers, by copy for value-shaped receivers) (§27.6, v0.340). The head `a` is a concrete `Array<int>` — a class type, so the capture is by reference and the formation is admitted. KNOWN DIVERGENCE (#7093): the compiler rejects the formation in codegen with the #2470/#2492 fence ("a bare reference to `Contains` is not yet supported on `Array<T>`"), while the same reference over the interface head is admitted; the two receivers disagree and no spec sentence rejects the formation.

title: a runtime const local takes an ordinary method reference
rule: Method references work for static methods, instance methods (the instance is captured at formation — by reference for class- or interface-typed receivers, by copy for value-shaped receivers) (§27.6, v0.340), and §21.1 makes a `const` local that fails the compile-time-const conditions a **runtime const** rather than an error — a binding, not an error, so the method reference over it forms and calls through.

title: a bare reference to the generic Math.Sign is rejected even with a target type
rule: a reference to a generic method with no list is a compile error naming the type parameters to supply, and no inference binds them from the target (§27.6, v0.350). `Math.Sign` is `public static method Sign<T>(x: T): int where T: INumber<T>` (stdlib §2.2, v0.350), and its only overload is generic, so the target `(int) -> int` binds nothing.

title: a reference to Math.Sign written with its type-argument list is formed and invoked
rule: a method reference over a generic method … names its type arguments on the member name … under §14.5's all-or-nothing rule for explicit lists (§27.6, v0.350). The accepting twin of s27_6_0036: `Math.Sign<int>` supplies the list, and `int` satisfies `where T: INumber<T>` (stdlib §2.2, v0.350). Sign yields -1, 0 or 1 (stdlib §2.2).

title: a function-typed value is called with ordinary call syntax
rule: A function-typed value is called with ordinary call syntax: `var sum := add(2, 3);`.

title: a null-conditional call on a null function value is a no-op
rule: `maybeHandler?(42);` is a null-conditional call — a no-op when the function value is null.

title: the result of a null-conditional call through a present function value is nullable
rule: The null-conditional call result is nullable.

title: a function-typed property is called with call syntax on its receiver
rule: Calling function values (§27.7, v0.350): a value of function type is invoked with ordinary call syntax, `add(2, 3)`. A property whose declared type is a function type is such a value, so `u.F(4)` invokes the lambda the property holds with the argument 4 and yields 5.

title: two separately-constructed lambdas with identical source text are not equal
rule: A lambda (closure) value equals only itself — reference equality on the closure instance. Two separately-constructed lambdas with identical source text are not equal, even if they capture the same variables.

title: repeated evaluations of a method reference on the same receiver are guaranteed equal
rule: A method reference equals another method reference iff both denote the same method and, for instance references, are bound to the same receiver — repeated evaluations of `obj.Method` on the same class-typed `obj` are therefore guaranteed equal.

title: a lambda never equals a method reference
rule: A lambda never equals a method reference.

title: a collection of callbacks is an Array whose Contains compares by function-value equality
rule: a `Set<(int) -> int>`, a `Dictionary<(int) -> int, V>`, stdlib §5's hashable block and `where T: hashable` at a function type are rejected at the instantiation site, and a collection of callbacks is an `Array<(int) -> int>`, whose `Contains` and `Remove` compare by this equality

title: a Set of Object holds two evaluations of one static method reference as one element
rule: A function value's `GetHashCode` **agrees with this equality** ... The hash ... holds at `Object`, where a capture-free function value is admitted ... and is an ordinary key: a `Set<Object>` holds two evaluations of one static method's reference as one element

title: equal method references hash alike through Object under where T hashable
rule: a method reference's hash is derived from the method it denotes and, where the equality compares a receiver, from that receiver's identity hash, so any two references the equality makes equal hash alike ... and `where T: hashable` at `Object` promises nothing a function value breaks

title: two type-qualified references to one extension method are equal and differ from another method's
rule: A reference that captures no receiver — a static method reference to `M`, or the extension-method reference to `M` that §27.6 forms type-qualified, the receiver being the function's first parameter — equals every other such reference to `M`

title: two method references over an interface-typed receiver are equal
rule: A method reference equals another method reference iff both denote the same method and, for instance references, are bound to the same receiver — receiver sameness being reference identity for class-typed receivers (§27.7.1, v0.340). The head `t` is interface-typed and holds one class instance, so the two evaluations of `t.Bump` denote the same method and bind the same receiver: the two function values are equal.

title: two method references over a value-shaped receiver are unequal
rule: A method reference equals another method reference iff both denote the same method and, for instance references, are bound to the same receiver (§27.7.1, v0.340), and a value-shaped receiver — a record, an enum, a copyable choice, a non-owning inline array, a primitive, the unit value, a `string`, a function value — has no receiver identity: each evaluation captures its own copy, so the two references are unequal even when the head is the same binding.

title: a type alias is a pure synonym interchangeable with the aliased type
rule: A type alias is a pure synonym — it does not create a new type; `UserId` and `int` are interchangeable.

title: a generic type alias may not reference itself
rule: An alias may not reference itself, directly or through other aliases, in its aliased type or in its `where` clause.

title: an indexer override whose index parameter is spelled through a type alias overrides the base indexer
rule: A type alias is not a separate kind of type; identity, equality and method dispatch all see through the alias. An override whose index parameter is spelled EA (an alias of Exception) overrides the base indexer declared over Exception, so a read through a base-typed receiver dispatches the override.

title: an alias spelled on the override index parameter still overrides the base indexer
rule: A type alias is not a separate kind of type; identity, equality and method dispatch all see through the alias, so the override's index parameter and the base's index parameter denote the same type and the override dispatches. Here the base spells [e: Exception] and the override spells [e: EA].

title: an alias of an alias on the base index parameter still overrides the indexer
rule: A type alias is not a separate kind of type; identity, equality and method dispatch all see through the alias, so the override's index parameter and the base's index parameter denote the same type and the override dispatches. Here the base spells [e: EB] and the override spells [e: Exception].

title: an alias to a generic instance spelled on the base index parameter still overrides the indexer
rule: A type alias is a pure synonym, so an index parameter declared AI (type AI := Array<int>) and one declared Array<int> denote the same type, and the override dispatches through a base-typed receiver.

title: with no alias anywhere an indexer override dispatches through a base-typed receiver
rule: A type alias is not a separate kind of type; the control here has no alias, so it shows the override dispatches through a base-typed receiver when both index parameters are spelled Exception. The alias rows are read against this control.

title: an alias of an alias on a base return type is overridden by a derived return
rule: Type aliases — generic or not — see through to the aliased type for identity, equality, method dispatch, and overload resolution.

title: an override whose parameter is spelled through a generic alias dispatches through a base receiver
rule: Type aliases — generic or not — see through to the aliased type for identity, equality, method dispatch, and overload resolution.

title: a generic alias index parameter on the base is overridden by an indexer seen through a base receiver
rule: Type aliases — generic or not — see through to the aliased type for identity, equality, method dispatch, and overload resolution.

title: a nested generic alias argument on the base parameter is overridden through a base receiver
rule: Type aliases — generic or not — see through to the aliased type for identity, equality, method dispatch, and overload resolution.

title: an override and its base both spelled through an alias of an alias dispatch through a base receiver
rule: Type aliases — generic or not — see through to the aliased type for identity, equality, method dispatch, and overload resolution.

title: an alias-typed nullable carrier narrowed by an is T test takes a with
rule: A type alias is a pure synonym — it does not create a new type (§27.8, v0.340); a `with` "result has the same static type as the source" (§9.5, v0.340); and when a test succeeds the carrier "is flow-narrowed to `T` within the controlled block" (§12.7, v0.340). So an alias-typed `P?` carrier narrowed by an `is P` test has source type `P` in the block, and the `with` result is a `P`.

title: an alias of an alias used as a parameter type is the aliased record's type
rule: A type alias is a pure synonym — it does not create a new type (§27.8, v0.340), and an alias of an alias is still that synonym; when a test succeeds the carrier "is flow-narrowed to `T` within the controlled block" (§12.7, v0.340) and a `with` "result has the same static type as the source" (§9.5, v0.340). So a parameter spelled through an alias of an alias is narrowed and copied like the record itself.

title: an interface-typed value may be discarded and is disposed by dispatch at end of statement
rule: The discard form `_ := expr;` disposes the value at the end of the discard statement for any class or interface type; at an interface-typed location the discard is permitted and disposes via runtime dispatch, so a future non-trivial implementation poses no cross-module hazard (§28's summary of disposal obligations by type kind).

title: a record local carries no disposal obligation and draws no discharge diagnostic
rule: Records, enums, and primitives need no disposal — their memory is reclaimed when their containing scope exits; the chapter's summary table records "Disposal required? No" for each, with no mechanism to announce (§28).

title: owned on a method parameter of class type is admitted
rule: The `owned` modifier is admissible on method parameter declarations: `method M(owned p: T)` takes ownership of the value at the call site.

title: owned on a method parameter of primitive type is rejected
rule: The declared type of an `owned` parameter, nullability stripped, must be a class type, an interface type, or a bare type parameter; a primitive is a compile error.

title: owned on a return type of class type is admitted
rule: The `owned` modifier is admissible on return type declarations: `method Acquire(): owned Connection` transfers responsibility for disposal to the caller.

title: owned on a return type of enum type is rejected
rule: **Any other type** — a primitive, `string`, `Type`, a function type, an ordinary record, a value-like or borrow-bearing choice (§35.4), an enum, a non-owning inline array, or the unit type: `owned` is a **compile error**. Such values carry no disposal obligation to transfer

title: owned on an out parameter of class type is admitted
rule: The `owned` modifier is admissible on `out` parameter declarations: `out owned p: T` produces an owned reference for the caller to take.

title: owned on a function-type parameter slot is admitted and consumes at the call
rule: The parameter slot of a function type may carry `owned`: `(owned T) -> ()` — the modifier is part of the function type's identity, and an invocation through the slot consumes the argument.

title: owned choice payload field is admitted
rule: The `owned` modifier is admissible on choice payload fields: `Fetched(owned response: Response)` takes ownership at construction.

title: owned inline-array slot marker is admitted
rule: The `owned` keyword placed between the size and the closing bracket (`[N owned]T?`) marks the inline array's slots as owned.

title: owned on a bare unconstrained type parameter is admitted
rule: `owned` requires the declared type, nullability stripped, to be a class type, an interface type, or a bare type parameter; at a bare type parameter the generic body type-checks under the class-or-interface assumption.

title: owned on a bare type parameter constrained to value is rejected at the declaration
rule: A declaration whose constraints exclude class and interface substitutions outright (`where T: value`) rejects the `owned` marker at the declaration — it could never be more than redundant.

title: Dispose is idempotent at run time: a second explicit call performs no second disposal
rule: `Dispose()` on any class instance is idempotent: the first call performs the disposal; subsequent calls are no-ops. That no-op carve-out states the **runtime** contract of a repeated call and suppresses no diagnostic — a second `Dispose()` on the same binding is a use of it and draws §28.2's use-after-dispose warning.

title: Dispose through a record receiver has no such member
rule: `Dispose()` is not on `Object`; it is class-only — a member of class types and of the interfaces that are or extend `IDisposable` or declare it (below), and of nothing else

title: a straight-line read after an explicit Dispose raises the use-after-dispose warning
rule: The compiler must emit a warning when a local variable is used after an explicit `Dispose()` call on the same variable that dominates the use site on every path.

title: a straight-line read after a discard raises the same mandatory warning
rule: The compiler must emit a warning when a local variable is used after a discard of the binding that dominates the use site on every path.

title: a conditional dispose joins to maybe-consumed and a later read is rejected
rule: A conditional kill of the variable: at a join of an explicitly-disposed path with a still-owned path the variable is maybe-consumed and a later use is a compile error.

title: every class implicitly implements IDisposable via a generated Dispose
rule: Every class implicitly implements `IDisposable` via a compiler-generated `Dispose()`; user code declares no `Dispose` member, and the generated one is callable on an instance the caller owns.

title: a class member named Dispose is rejected at a non-empty parameter list
rule: Declaring a member named `Dispose` on a class or a record is a compile error at that declaration, whatever its parameter list; the rule is keyed on the name, and at an optional-parameter declaration `Dispose(mode: int := 0)` it is additionally ambiguous against the compiler-generated `Dispose()` at every zero-argument call.

title: a record member named Dispose is rejected
rule: Declaring a member named `Dispose` on a class or a **record** is a compile error at that declaration, whatever its parameter list; on a record the name promises a disposal contract the kind does not have (§9.7 — records do not implement `IDisposable`).

title: the same member under any other name is admitted, optional parameter included
rule: The rule is keyed on the **name** `Dispose`, not on the shape of the declaration: a class member with the identical parameter list under any other name collides with no compiler-generated member and is admitted, callable at zero arguments through §22.5's optional parameter.

title: an interface may declare a member named Dispose
rule: Interfaces are unaffected by the class-and-record rejection of a member named `Dispose` — `IDisposable` declares `method Dispose();` and interfaces extend it.

title: the default build is checked: a read through a surviving borrow after Dispose faults
rule: Checked mode — any instance member access on a logically-disposed instance — an instance method call, a property or indexer accessor invocation, or a field access through the reference — raises `DisposedAccessException`. This is the default: a build that selects neither mode is a checked build.

title: the same program under the explicitly selected unchecked relaxation is accepted only
rule: Unchecked (release) mode — use of a disposed instance is undefined behavior; a build selects it explicitly. A program that would raise `DisposedAccessException` in checked mode has undefined behavior in unchecked mode: unchecked mode is the release-build relaxation of the default checked semantics, not a different language.

title: a closure that captures a disposed local warns at the call that reads it
rule: The compiler additionally must emit a compile-time warning when a local variable is used (read, borrowed from, or consumed) after an explicit `Dispose()` (§28.2, v0.340). The closure captures a borrow of `d`, and the capture is read at invoke time — the call after the explicit `Dispose()` reads a disposed value, so the warning is required.

title: a record nested in a class that declares a member named Dispose is rejected
rule: Declaring a member named `Dispose` on a **class** or a **record** is a **compile error** at that declaration, whatever its parameter list; the rule is keyed on the name, and the nesting of the record does not change it.

title: a record nested in a class with an ordinary method name is accepted
rule: The rule of §28.2 is keyed on the name `Dispose`: "a member named `Dispose`" is the compile error, so a member of the same record with another name is an ordinary method. This is the accepting twin of s28_2_0014.

title: a class nested in a class that declares Dispose with an optional parameter is rejected
rule: Declaring a member named `Dispose` on a **class** or a **record** is a **compile error** at that declaration, whatever its parameter list; at an optional-parameter declaration `Dispose(mode: int := 0)` it is additionally ambiguous at every zero-argument call.

title: a nested class with an optional-parameter method of another name is accepted
rule: The rule of §28.2 is keyed on the name `Dispose`; a method `Release(mode: int := 0)` with the same nesting and parameter list is an ordinary member. This is the accepting twin of s28_2_0016.

title: a class nested in a class that declares a parameterless Dispose is rejected
rule: Declaring a member named `Dispose` on a **class** or a **record** is a **compile error** at that declaration, whatever its parameter list; the nesting of the class does not change it.

title: a generic class nested in a class that declares Dispose is rejected
rule: Declaring a member named `Dispose` on a **class** or a **record** is a **compile error** at that declaration, whatever its parameter list; a generic class is a class, so its `Dispose` is rejected at the declaration.

title: a class nested in a generic class that declares Dispose is rejected
rule: Declaring a member named `Dispose` on a **class** or a **record** is a **compile error** at that declaration, whatever its parameter list; the class is rejected whatever the type parameters of its enclosing class.

title: a Dispose declared at three nesting levels draws the rule at each declaration
rule: Declaring a member named `Dispose` on a **class** or a **record** is a **compile error** at that declaration, whatever its parameter list; each class and record declaring it is its own compile error, at its own declaration, so no level is exempt for being nested inside another.

title: an interface nested in a class may declare Dispose
rule: Declaring a member named `Dispose` on a **class** or a **record** is a **compile error**; "Interfaces are unaffected: the rule reaches classes and records only, and an interface may declare `Dispose()` itself." This is the accepting twin of s28_2_0018 for an interface nested in a class.

title: a nested class implementing IDisposable without declaring Dispose is accepted
rule: The compiler generates `IDisposable` on every non-static class. The class satisfies IDisposable through the compiler-generated `Dispose()`, so a nested class that names IDisposable and declares no `Dispose` member is an ordinary class. This is the accepting companion to the rejected declarations of s28_2_0018 to s28_2_0021.

title: a static method returning a plain class type is rejected at the declaration
rule: A static method whose declared return type (nullability stripped) is a class or interface type must announce its classification in the signature — `owned`, a mint-announcing type, or a bare type parameter with a non-empty source set. Any other such signature is a compile error at the declaration.

title: an undischarged plain-var owned local raises the must-use warning
rule: The compiler emits a warning at the implicit-drop site of a plain-`var` owned local, to surface a drop that may have been unintended; the exception edge does not carry it.

title: an unmarked read of an owned binding is always a borrow
rule: The no-silent-consume rule: an unmarked read of a class-typed binding never consumes; `var b := a;` is always a borrow of `a`.

title: an owned argument fed without move is rejected
rule: Omitting `move` is a compile error when a named owned binding feeds an `owned` argument: write `M(move x)`.

title: an owned argument fed with move is admitted
rule: `move x` is the required spelling for a named owned binding feeding an `owned` argument.

title: assigning a borrow into an owned-state local is rejected
rule: State match on reassignment: an owned-state LHS requires an owned RHS; assigning a borrow to an owned-state LHS is rejected.

title: assigning a marked transfer into an owned-state local is admitted
rule: An owned-state LHS accepts a named owned binding under the explicit transfer marker: `x := move y;`, disposing the displaced value.

title: an if-expression merging an owned arm with an unmarked owned-binding arm is rejected
rule: owned meets borrowed at an if-expression merge is rejected; an unmarked read of a named owned binding is a borrow arm.

title: marking the if-expression arm transfer equalizes the merge
rule: The marked arm transfer `move x` as an if-expression branch is an owned producer, equalizing a merge with another owned arm.

title: move on a return operand under an owned return is rejected as redundant
rule: The transfer marker is rejected as redundant at a marker-free position: `return x;` under an owned return, never `return move x;`.

title: a return operand under an owned return carries no marker
rule: `return` under an `owned` return type is marker-free: the declared return type already announces the transfer.

title: move on a throw operand is rejected as redundant
rule: The transfer marker is rejected as redundant on a `throw` operand: `throw x;`, never `throw move x;`.

title: a throw operand carries no marker
rule: The `throw` keyword itself announces the consume; no marker is written at the operand.

title: move on a discard right-hand side is rejected as redundant
rule: The transfer marker is rejected as redundant on a discard right-hand side: `_ := x;`, never `_ := move x;`.

title: a discard right-hand side carries no marker
rule: The discard itself is the announcement; a named owned binding discards unmarked.

title: move on a store into an owned field is rejected as redundant
rule: The transfer marker is rejected as redundant on a store into an `owned` field: `sink._f := x;`, never `sink._f := move x;`.

title: a store into an owned field carries no marker
rule: The declared `owned` field already announces the transfer; the store is marker-free.

title: move on an owning iterator's yield return is rejected as redundant
rule: The transfer marker is rejected as redundant on an owning iterator's `yield return`: the declared owning interface already announces.

title: an owning iterator's yield return carries no marker
rule: The owning iterator's declared return type is the announcement; `yield return x;` is marker-free.

title: move on a borrow is rejected
rule: `move` is also an error on a borrow: the marker asserts a transfer, and a plain parameter carries no obligation to transfer.

title: using var y := move x is the adoption spelling
rule: `using var y := move x;` is the standard way to turn an owned local's obligation into scope-bound disposal: the value is disposed at the end of the adopting block.

title: using var over a borrowing alias is a borrow-pin that assumes no obligation
rule: An unmarked `using var y := a;` where `a` is a borrow-state named binding (here a borrowing alias `var a := w;`) does not assume a disposal obligation: the owner `w` keeps it and stays readable, and the pin extends the source's required liveness to the block's end (§28.10 v0.350, "`using var` initialized from a borrow": an unmarked read of a **borrow-state** named binding — a plain parameter, a borrowing alias or loop variable, a captured owned binding inside a closure). The unmarked `using var pin := w;` directly over the owned `w` is a compile error since v0.350 (§28.10 *Adopting a named owned binding*; case s28_10_0015), so the pin is taken through the alias.

title: a using var local is not reassignable
rule: `using var` is a scope pin: non-reassignable.

title: a using var local can never be moved out of
rule: `using var` is never movable out of: `using var fresh := new Buffer(); return fresh;` is a compile error; a factory uses plain `var`.

title: a borrow assigned to a local whose scope strictly encloses its source is rejected at the assignment
rule: A borrow may not be assigned to a local whose scope strictly encloses its source's scope; rejected at the assignment, not at the later use.

title: the back-reference idiom admits a parameter-sourced borrow stored in a field
rule: A borrow whose source outlives the object is admissible: the back-reference idiom binds a constructor parameter into a non-owned class-typed field.

title: a borrow of a scope-bound local stored in a field is rejected
rule: A borrowed scope-bound local never satisfies the field-store rule: it is disposed at the end of its scope, which a field of the object outlives.

title: a borrow of an owned parameter stored in a field is rejected
rule: An `owned` parameter is scope-bound: the method disposes its undischarged value at its own end, so a borrow of it is rejected in a field store exactly as a borrow of a scope-bound local is.

title: a fresh owned value returned through a plain class-typed return is rejected
rule: An instance method whose declared return type is a plain concrete class type may return only a receiver-sourced borrow; a fresh owned value is rejected — declare `owned`.

title: returning a receiver-sourced borrow is admitted
rule: A receiver-sourced borrow from an instance method — a bare field read — is an admissible borrow return.

title: a merge of an owned branch with a borrowed branch is rejected
rule: At a control-flow merge, owned meets borrowed is rejected: the program must equalize the branches before the merge; the compiler never equalizes for it.

title: equalizing both branches to owned admits the merge
rule: Producing an owned value on both branches equalizes the merge to owned.

title: reading a variable that is owned on one path and moved-from on another is rejected
rule: owned meets moved-from is maybe-consumed at the join; a later use is a compile error.

title: consuming an owned binding while a live local borrow of it exists is rejected
rule: The consume-site freeze: consuming an owned binding while a live local borrow of its current value exists is a compile error.

title: transfer first, then re-borrow from the new owner, is the freeze's mechanical rewrite
rule: The mechanical rewrite for the frozen case is transfer first, then re-borrow from the new owner.

title: an explicit Dispose while a borrow is live is not frozen
rule: Site-announced kills are unfrozen: an explicit `Dispose()` is permitted while a live local borrow of the value exists — a borrow is live when some path from the consume site reaches a later use of it.

title: a discard while a borrow is live is not frozen
rule: Site-announced kills are unfrozen: the discard `_ := x;` is permitted while borrows of the value live.

title: a static method returning owned T announces its classification and is admitted
rule: Every admissible static signature is type-announced: `owned` on the declared return type admits a fresh or owned value.

title: an instance method that creates a fresh value through a non-owned return is rejected
rule: An instance method that produces a fresh value must declare `owned`; a freshly-produced owned value returned through a non-owned return is rejected.

title: declaring owned on the return admits the freshly-produced value
rule: An instance method that creates something must say `owned`; the declared `owned` return admits the fresh value.

title: a property getter returning a fresh owned value is rejected
rule: A property or indexer getter may never return a fresh owned value; getters lend only.

title: a property getter returning a receiver-sourced borrow is admitted
rule: A getter may lend a receiver-sourced borrow; expose a factory as a method returning `owned T` instead for a fresh value.

title: an unbound owned temporary is disposed at the end of the full expression
rule: An unbound owned temporary is disposed at the end of the full expression in which it is produced, after every borrowing use within that expression.

title: a binding atom disposes its owned temporary at the atom's completion
rule: A binding atom's clause whose initializer is an owned production is a named unbound owned temporary bounded by the atom, disposed at the atom's completion if undischarged.

title: a borrow of a binding atom's own owned binding may not escape the atom
rule: A borrow sourced by an atom binding may not escape the atom, not in the body's value; it is rejected, never lifetime-extended.

title: a case scrutinee's unbound owned temporary survives the selected arm
rule: A `case` scrutinee extends the disposal boundary to the whole `case` construct, so pattern bindings survive the selected arm.

title: an uninitialized local adopts the ownership state of its first assignment
rule: A local holding no classified value adopts the classification of the first assignment reaching it on each path; two owned-producing branches adopt owned on both.

title: an owned local live across an exception edge is disposed during unwinding
rule: Edge parity: owned locals live when an exception propagates out of their enclosing block are disposed implicitly during stack unwinding, exactly as on the normal edge.

title: a do end block disposes a using var early, before the outer scope continues
rule: A `using var` local is owned and additionally subject to scope-based disposal at the end of the enclosing block; a `do … end` block is such a block, so the value is disposed at its end, not at the method's.

title: an undischarged plain-var owned local in a library method draws the must-use warning
rule: At the implicit-drop site of a plain-`var` owned local or an undischarged `owned` parameter that is not trivial-dispose under §28.9's ceremony exemption ... the compiler emits a **warning** (not an error): a plain `var` that is implicitly dropped is indistinguishable in *effect* from a `using var`, so the drop may have been unintended

title: using var suppresses the must-use warning on an owned local
rule: The warning is **suppressed** by exactly these conditions ... the local is declared `using var` (the scope-bound intent is then explicit)

title: an explicit Dispose suppresses the must-use warning on an owned local
rule: The warning is **suppressed** by exactly these conditions ... it is explicitly disposed or discarded

title: a discard suppresses the must-use warning on an owned local
rule: dispose it explicitly with `.Dispose()` or discard it with `_ := …` (§17.13) ... The warning is **suppressed** by exactly these conditions ... it is explicitly disposed or discarded

title: a move into an owned argument suppresses the must-use warning
rule: The warning is **suppressed** by exactly these conditions ... it is moved or returned (no implicit drop occurs)

title: returning an owned local under an owned return suppresses the must-use warning
rule: The warning is **suppressed** by exactly these conditions ... it is moved or returned (no implicit drop occurs)

title: the null-conditional dispose spelling suppresses the must-use warning
rule: The warning is **suppressed** by exactly these conditions ... it is explicitly disposed or discarded — including through the null-conditional and null-forgiving spellings `x?.Dispose()` / `x!.Dispose()`, required for nullable owned locals

title: the null-forgiving dispose spelling suppresses the must-use warning
rule: The warning is **suppressed** by exactly these conditions ... it is explicitly disposed or discarded — including through the null-conditional and null-forgiving spellings `x?.Dispose()` / `x!.Dispose()`, required for nullable owned locals

title: an undischarged owned parameter draws the must-use warning at its declaration
rule: At the implicit-drop site of a plain-`var` owned local or an undischarged `owned` parameter that is not trivial-dispose under §28.9's ceremony exemption ... the compiler emits a **warning** (not an error)

title: the using var move adoption suppresses the owned-parameter must-use warning
rule: The adoption idiom `using var r := move reader;` suppresses the must-use warning on an `owned` parameter exactly as `using var` suppresses the local form.

title: under the report mode, a plain constructor parameter stored into a non-owned field reports
rule: In that mode, at every site where the compiler makes an admission that rests on a K4.3-recorded trust clause, it **emits a warning** ... the **field-held** clause (the borrowed-field store rule above, wherever restated) ... **The warning** names the rule and its clause, the borrow and its source, the holder ... The site is the admitting site — the store, the call, the abandon or the `await` the clause admits

title: under the trust-admission report mode, a scoped construction reports nothing
rule: A class- or interface-typed `scoped` parameter upgrades the residual-trust back-reference admission to a static bound on the source, with no K4.3-recorded trust clause (spec §28.14); the trust-admission report mode reports only admissions that rest on such a clause.

title: under the trust-admission report mode, a keys-based store reports nothing
rule: A compilation unit that emits no report under the trust-admission report mode carries no recorded trust clause: a SlotHandle stored in a field or a collection is a value, not a borrow, and no K4.3 clause attaches to it.

title: under the report mode, a parameter borrow added to a borrowing collection field reports
rule: In that mode, at every site where the compiler makes an admission that rests on a K4.3-recorded trust clause, it **emits a warning** ... the **collection-held** clause (§28.11's store rule, a store whose receiver the structural check leaves unclassified included) ... **The warning** names the rule and its clause ... The trust-admission report (§28.3) names a parameter-, receiver- or field-path-sourced element at its store

title: outside the trust-admission report mode, an admitted collection-held borrow draws no diagnostic
rule: The trust-admission report is informative: it changes no verdict and no generated code, and outside the mode it is not emitted.

title: under the trust-admission report mode, abandoning a task minted over a borrowed receiver reports
rule: In that mode, at every site where the compiler makes an admission that rests on a K4.3-recorded trust clause, it **emits a warning** ... the **frame-held** clause (§30.1, §30.5) ... **The warning** names the rule and its clause ... The site is the admitting site — the store, the call, the abandon or the `await` the clause admits

title: under the trust-admission report mode, awaiting the task in its sources' scope reports nothing
rule: The settlement obligation of a frame holding a borrowed receiver is discharged by awaiting the task before any source's scope exits (spec §30.1); the trust-admission report mode reports only admissions that rest on a K4.3-recorded trust clause, and an awaited frame carries none.

title: a call-bounded callback stored to a bare auto-property identifier is rejected
rule: A property or indexer assignment of a function-typed value with a non-empty source set is rejected at the site (spec §28.3, v0.314). A bare auto-property identifier resolves to PropertySymbol, not FieldSymbol, and was previously missed by the sink check.

title: a call-bounded callback stored through a local indexer is rejected
rule: A property or indexer assignment of a function-typed value with a non-empty source set is rejected at the site (spec §28.3, v0.314). A local indexer store (items[i] := cb where items is a local variable) was previously missed because the existing IndexExpr arm only checked collection reachability, not whether the indexer's set accessor itself is a capturing sink.

title: a bare-T result lent from a lambda's capture may not be stored past the captured local
rule: What each operand contributes: ... a function-typed argument bound to a source parameter whose declared type, nullability stripped, is a function type that mentions the returned parameter in its return slot or in a `ref` or `out` parameter slot, other than a slot declared `owned` (`f: () -> T`, `f: (T) -> T`, `f: () -> () -> T`, `f: (out T) -> bool`), and the function value of a function-value invocation, their source sets ... `static method Apply<T>(f: () -> T): T => f();` lends, at `T = Item`, from what its argument captures ... The result is usable only where every contributing source is still live

title: a bare-T result lent from a lambda capturing a plain parameter may be stored in a field
rule: What each operand contributes: ... a function-typed argument bound to a source parameter whose declared type, nullability stripped, is a function type that mentions the returned parameter in its return slot or in a `ref` or `out` parameter slot, other than a slot declared `owned` (`f: () -> T`, `f: (T) -> T`, `f: () -> () -> T`, `f: (out T) -> bool`), and the function value of a function-value invocation, their source sets ... `static method Apply<T>(f: () -> T): T => f();` lends, at `T = Item`, from what its argument captures ... The result is usable only where every contributing source is still live

title: a bare-T function-value invocation over a type-parameter argument is rejected at Map<int, Item>
rule: `static method Map<A, B>(a: A, f: (A) -> B): B => f(a);` is rejected at every instantiation whose `B` this check reaches, `Map<int, Item>` as well as `Map<Item, Item>`: `a` is no source parameter, and an argument typed by a type parameter counts under the weakest assumption its constraints establish; `Map` is admitted where `B` is a value type that carries no borrow

title: the same Map body is admitted where the returned parameter is a value type
rule: `static method Map<A, B>(a: A, f: (A) -> B): B => f(a);` is rejected at every instantiation whose `B` this check reaches, `Map<int, Item>` as well as `Map<Item, Item>`: `a` is no source parameter, and an argument typed by a type parameter counts under the weakest assumption its constraints establish; `Map` is admitted where `B` is a value type that carries no borrow

title: a concretely typed argument to the invoked source parameter is admitted at a class B
rule: every return path must supply `null` or a borrow whose sources outlive the call: ... a plain source parameter — directly, a borrow reached through it, or the result of invoking a function-typed source parameter, itself classified by this rule, so that each plain argument of the invocation is a source of the result and must be admissible here in turn

title: a bare-T result at a borrow-bearing record substitution may not be returned past its source
rule: At one that is a value type that holds borrows (§3.6's holds-borrows property), the borrows the result carries take clause 1's union, clause 2's temporary bound included, and §9.7's rules read them: over `static method Id<T>(a: T): T => a;` and `record Pair(Item: Item)`, `return Id<Pair>(new Pair(x));` with `x` scope-bound is rejected at the return.

title: a bare-T result at a borrow-bearing record substitution may be bound and used in its source's scope
rule: At one that is a value type that holds borrows (§3.6's holds-borrows property), the borrows the result carries take clause 1's union, clause 2's temporary bound included, and §9.7's rules read them: over `static method Id<T>(a: T): T => a;` and `record Pair(Item: Item)`, `return Id<Pair>(new Pair(x));` with `x` scope-bound is rejected at the return.

title: a scoped parameter's value may not be stored into an out location
rule: A borrow sourced at a `scoped` parameter is not a plain-parameter source and is rejected there: its own value, which §28.14 admits only into the bounding object's fields, a borrow reached through it, and the result of invoking it.

title: a plain parameter's value may be stored into an out location
rule: A `ref` or plain `out` argument location whose type, after substitution, can carry a borrow ... is caller storage: the callee may store into it a borrow sourced at its receiver, a plain parameter, or static storage

title: a frame built in a generic body over its own T-typed local may not be returned
rule: A returned frame carrying a borrow of anything else — a scope-bound local, a `using var`, a temporary — is rejected at the return site, since the frame would outlive the source ... In a generic body an argument whose type is a type parameter, or whose borrow-bearing or holds-borrows classification turns on one, therefore counts what it contributes at every substitution its constraints admit.

title: a frame built in a generic body over a forwarded T parameter may be returned
rule: A non-iterator method may therefore compose and return such a frame ... provided every borrow the returned frame carries is sourced from the method's own parameters or receiver

title: a function value read from a property carries the empty set and may be stored in a field
rule: A function value **read from a field, a collection, a property or an indexer**, or **narrowed from `Object`**, or from a value whose type is a bare type parameter, by an `as` or a typed-pattern binding (§17.4, §19.3), carries the empty set: those holders, every position declared `Object`, and every position a generic body declares at a type parameter (*Set-erasing positions* below), admit only capture-free function values

title: an indexer getter may not return a capture-bearing function value
rule: A function-typed holder is a field (a `scoped` field excepted), ... or the enclosing method's return or `yield return` slot (a property or indexer getter's included), whose declared type ... is a function type ... At every function-typed holder the closure bullet's sink rule holds: a store of a function value admits a capture-free value and rejects one whose source set is non-empty

title: invoking a lambda-built (Item) -> Pair over a local yields a value that may not be returned
rule: Over `record Pair(Item: Item)`, `var g: (Item) -> Pair := lambda(i) => new Pair(i);` is admitted and `return g(x);` with `x` scope-bound is rejected at the return.

title: a lambda at a borrow-bearing return slot may return a value carrying its parameter's borrow
rule: Over `record Pair(Item: Item)`, `var g: (Item) -> Pair := lambda(i) => new Pair(i);` is admitted and `return g(x);` with `x` scope-bound is rejected at the return.

title: an out location filled by an unbound constructor call may not outlive the full expression
rule: The caller therefore treats each such location as receiving any borrow the call carries: the sources the receiver and every plain (non-`owned`, non-`scoped`) argument contribute ... (the receiver as an argument of its type: at a constructor call, the object or value constructed, read as the binding or field its result initializes or, for an unbound result, as an unbound owned temporary bounded to the full expression

title: an out location filled by a constructor call bound to a using var lives with that binding
rule: The caller therefore treats each such location as receiving any borrow the call carries: the sources the receiver and every plain (non-`owned`, non-`scoped`) argument contribute ... (the receiver as an argument of its type: at a constructor call, the object or value constructed, read as the binding or field its result initializes or, for an unbound result, as an unbound owned temporary bounded to the full expression

title: a capture-bearing lambda stored into a bare-T field at a function-type instantiation is rejected
rule: A **set-erasing position** is ... a field (instance or static; not a `scoped` field ...), parameter, return slot, ... whose declared, pre-substitution type ... is a bare type parameter, at an instantiation substituting a function type or `Object`, nullable or not, for it — ... `b.V := f` at `b: Box<Object>` or `b: Box<() -> int>` over `class Box<T> public V: T; end Box;` (the same store in a class deriving from either included) ... At every set-erasing position **a function value with a non-empty source set is rejected, and a capture-free one is admitted**

title: a static method reference stored into a bare-T field at a function-type instantiation is admitted
rule: A **set-erasing position** is ... a field (instance or static; not a `scoped` field ...), parameter, return slot, ... whose declared, pre-substitution type ... is a bare type parameter, at an instantiation substituting a function type or `Object`, nullable or not, for it — ... `b.V := f` at `b: Box<Object>` or `b: Box<() -> int>` over `class Box<T> public V: T; end Box;` (the same store in a class deriving from either included) ... At every set-erasing position **a function value with a non-empty source set is rejected, and a capture-free one is admitted**

title: a capture-bearing function value as the receiver of an extension on Object is rejected
rule: as the receiver of an extension call whose head is `Object` — which §26.5 rule 2 reaches from a function-typed receiver (§3.1) — it is, the twin of §9.7's clause for the receiver of such a call ... At every set-erasing position **a function value with a non-empty source set is rejected, and a capture-free one is admitted**

title: a capture-free function value as the receiver of an extension on Object is admitted
rule: as the receiver of an extension call whose head is `Object` — which §26.5 rule 2 reaches from a function-typed receiver (§3.1) — it is, the twin of §9.7's clause for the receiver of such a call ... At every set-erasing position **a function value with a non-empty source set is rejected, and a capture-free one is admitted**

title: a function-typed out location carries the empty set after the call and may be a field
rule: except at a location whose type, after substitution, is a function type: the callee can store there only a capture-free function value ..., so the call's borrows need no admissibility check against it, and on the call's normal return an `out` location carries the empty set and a `ref` location the set it carried before the call

title: a borrow passed as an earlier argument freezes the binding a later argument moves
rule: A borrow of the consumed binding passed as an argument or operand evaluated **before** a consuming argument of the same call (§22.5's textual order) is such a borrow, its use being the call itself ... `Sink(x, move x)` and `Sink(x.Child(), move x)` are rejected at the `move`

title: a receiver-sourced borrow of the binding as an earlier argument freezes the later move
rule: A borrow of the consumed binding passed as an argument or operand evaluated **before** a consuming argument of the same call (§22.5's textual order) is such a borrow, its use being the call itself ... `Sink(x, move x)` and `Sink(x.Child(), move x)` are rejected at the `move`

title: a value-typed argument read from the binding before its move is no borrow and is admitted
rule: A borrow of the consumed binding passed as an argument or operand evaluated **before** a consuming argument of the same call ... is such a borrow, its use being the call itself (a value-typed argument read from it, `Add(x.Id, move x)`, is no borrow and is unaffected)

title: a maybe-consumed owned local is reassignable and displaces only on the paths that own it
rule: A **maybe-consumed** LHS (K1 state 4) is an owned-state LHS whose displaced value exists on exactly the paths that did not consume it: the store requires an owned RHS, disposes the displaced value on the paths that still own it ... and displaces nothing on the moved-from ones ... and leaves the binding owned and readable.

title: reassigning a local disposed on one path frees that value without disposing it again
rule: An **explicitly-disposed** LHS requires an owned RHS too and displaces a **logically disposed** value: the store is that value's release point — §28.2's compiler-inserted free, the `Dispose()` a no-op on the set flag and then the reclamation of the block ... A **maybe-consumed** LHS ... disposes the displaced value on the paths that still own it, frees the logically disposed value on the explicitly-disposed paths

title: undischarged owned parameters of a method are disposed in reverse declaration order on every edge
rule: Undischarged `owned` parameters' implicit disposals are established at entry to the body, in declaration order — so, undischarged, they are disposed in reverse declaration order, for a method, a constructor, a lambda and an uncaptured primary-constructor parameter alike

title: a returned owned value is disposed by the callee's unwind when a return-edge disposer raises
rule: The slot's value transfers to the caller only when every cleanup on the return edge has completed normally; if one raises — a `finally` that throws, a `using var`'s or an auto-dropped local's disposer that throws (§28.4) — the return is abandoned and no caller-side holder ever exists ... and the slot's value is disposed by the unwind

title: the return slot's value is disposed at the raise, before a callee handler's arm runs
rule: the slot's value is disposed by the unwind as an owned local established at that point would be: **at the raise**, before every cleanup still pending on the edge that was established before the `return` statement and before any handler's arm in the callee, whichever scope the raising cleanup belongs to ... so a handler that catches the exception finds no returned value left to dispose.

title: a throwing finally on the return edge leaves the returned value to the callee's unwind
rule: if one raises — a `finally` that throws, a `using var`'s or an auto-dropped local's disposer that throws (§28.4) — the return is abandoned and no caller-side holder ever exists — the call completes by the exception unless a handler in the callee catches it — and the slot's value is disposed by the unwind

title: in an async body a raising return-edge cleanup faults the task and disposes the result once
rule: In an `async` body the slot is the frame's: the task records its result at the body's normal completion only (§30.1), and a raise from a cleanup on the return edge faults the task and disposes the slot's value in the frame's unwind — a faulted task has no owned result (§30.5).

title: a later argument reading a binding an earlier argument moved is a moved-from read
rule: **moved-from** — the obligation has transferred out; the binding is unreadable until reassigned, and discharge machinery skips it

title: a closure stored before its captured binding is assigned a using var is rejected at the store
rule: A captured binding — a local or parameter, in any state, that a lambda in the body captures — holds, for this count and wherever else its source set is read ... every value it is ever assigned ... Over `var b: Item? := null; var f := lambda() => b; _f := f; using var it := new Item(); b := it;`, `f`'s set is `{it}`, so `_f := f;` is rejected where it stands

title: invoking a closure whose captured binding is later assigned a using var cannot be returned
rule: A captured binding — a local or parameter, in any state, that a lambda in the body captures — holds, for this count and wherever else its source set is read ... every value it is ever assigned ... and a `return f();` or `return b;` after `b := it;` is rejected too

title: a captured function-typed local later assigned a capturing lambda taints the closure that calls it
rule: A lambda literal contributes the sources of the borrows it captures ... a captured function value its own set, transitively ... its set is the union, over its initializer and every assignment to it in any body ... whatever the assignment's position relative to the capture or to the read

title: an assignment made inside a lambda body counts toward the captured binding's set at its own return
rule: A captured binding — a local or parameter, in any state, that a lambda in the body captures — holds, for this count and wherever else its source set is read ... every value it is ever assigned ... its set is the union, over its initializer and every assignment to it in any body ... over `var g := lambda() => do s := zs.AsSpan(); end; g(); return s;`, `s` carries `zs` at the return

title: a slot store into a captured inline array after the closure is stored is counted in its set
rule: A captured binding — a local or parameter, in any state, that a lambda in the body captures — holds, for this count and wherever else its source set is read ... every value it is ever assigned ... a store through a member or index chain that lands in the binding's own storage (a slot of a captured inline array, §15.1.2; a settable member of a captured record, §9.4's own storage), which adds the stored value's sources as a slot store does

title: a member store into a captured record after the closure is stored is counted in its set
rule: A captured binding — a local or parameter, in any state, that a lambda in the body captures — holds, for this count and wherever else its source set is read ... every value it is ever assigned ... a store through a member or index chain that lands in the binding's own storage (a slot of a captured inline array, §15.1.2; a settable member of a captured record, §9.4's own storage), which adds the stored value's sources as a slot store does

title: two captured function-typed locals calling each other carry the sources their assignments bring in
rule: Where these sets depend on one another through captures — a lambda assigned to a binding it captures (§27.5's recursive closure), or two captured function-typed locals each assigned a lambda that calls the other — they are the least sets that satisfy this clause: a cycle adds nothing beyond the sources its assignments carry in from outside it

title: a captured counter and a captured binding assigned a parameter stay usable in scope
rule: a captured value that carries no borrow — a value type that holds none, a null-source value, a `string` — contributes nothing, and lives in its heap capture cell ... A captured binding — a local or parameter, in any state, that a lambda in the body captures — holds ... every value it is ever assigned

title: a plain parameter stored into a mutable static Mutex field is rejected
rule: A borrow of any other source — a plain or `scoped` parameter, `this`, a field, getter or indexer reached through the receiver, a capture, a local in any state, an `owned` parameter, a temporary, or the result of invoking a function value — is a compile error at the store ... `_m := m;` with `m` a plain parameter is rejected

title: a plain Task parameter stored into a lazy task cache static is rejected
rule: A store into a non-`owned` static field — a mutable static §22.12 rule 2 admits ... of a class- or interface-typed borrow admits it only when it is static-storage-sourced ... A borrow of any other source — a plain or `scoped` parameter, `this`, a field, getter or indexer reached through the receiver, a capture, a local in any state, an `owned` parameter, a temporary, or the result of invoking a function value — is a compile error at the store

title: a receiver-sourced borrow assigned to a settable static property is rejected
rule: A store into a non-`owned` static field ... or into a static property not through `set(owned)` (the preceding bullet) of a class- or interface-typed borrow admits it only when it is static-storage-sourced ... A borrow of any other source — a plain or `scoped` parameter, `this`, a field, getter or indexer reached through the receiver, a capture, a local in any state, an `owned` parameter, a temporary, or the result of invoking a function value — is a compile error at the store

title: a method result reached through a static's referent is not static storage
rule: A borrow reached through such a read — a field, getter, indexer or method result of the referent (`T.f.g`, `T.P.Peek()`) — is not static storage: its source is the referent's own state, which a store or drop-on-overwrite (§28.7) can replace

title: a fresh value, a transfer and a static-storage read may each be stored into a mutable static
rule: the remedies are a fresh value (`_m := new Mutex();`), a transfer from an owned binding (`_m := move m;` — the owner gives the object up and it becomes process-lived), or static storage (`_m := Other._shared;`)

title: transferring the source of a live lazy-query local is rejected
rule: A live local holding an iterator or enumerator frame or a lazy query ... counts as a live local borrow of every source the frame carries ... `sink.Take(move xs);` while `it` or `q` has a later use is rejected

title: a lazy query enumerated through an unbound call before the transfer is admitted
rule: The remedies: transfer first, then re-derive the frame from the new owner; enumerate the frame through an unbound call (`for var x in Each(xs.AsSpan()) do … end;`, whose hidden `__source` is disposed at the loop's exit) or dispose it (`it.Dispose();`) before the transfer

title: transferring the source inside a for body over an iterator frame of it is rejected
rule: A live local holding an iterator or enumerator frame or a lazy query — `var it := Each(xs.AsSpan());`, `var q := xs.Where(f);`, the `for` desugaring's hidden `__source` (§29.2) — counts as a live local borrow of every source the frame carries

title: a bound iterator frame explicitly disposed before the transfer frees its source
rule: The frame's own disposal is such a use — an explicit `Dispose()`, a `using var`'s scope end, or K3.14's auto-drop ... so a bound frame keeps its sources frozen until it is disposed or moved ... or dispose it (`it.Dispose();`) before the transfer

title: a using var iterator frame keeps its source frozen to its scope end
rule: The frame's own disposal is such a use — an explicit `Dispose()`, a `using var`'s scope end, or K3.14's auto-drop — because a partially-consumed frame's disposal runs its pending cleanup, `finally` blocks included, which may read the carried sources

title: a plain parameter may be assigned a borrow of a top-level using var
rule: A parameter's scope is the body's outermost block for this comparison: it does not strictly enclose a local declared at the body's top level, so a whole-value assignment `p := it` to a plain parameter ... are admitted for such a source and rejected for a source declared in a nested block

title: a plain parameter may not be assigned a borrow of a nested-block using var
rule: A parameter's scope is the body's outermost block for this comparison: it does not strictly enclose a local declared at the body's top level, so a whole-value assignment `p := it` to a plain parameter ... are admitted for such a source and rejected for a source declared in a nested block

title: a parameter assigned a local borrow carries that source to a later field store
rule: A parameter's scope is the body's outermost block for this comparison: it does not strictly enclose a local declared at the body's top level, so a whole-value assignment `p := it` to a plain parameter ... are admitted for such a source and rejected for a source declared in a nested block; the parameter's later escapes — a return, a field store, a capture — are read off its source set, which carries the assigned source

title: under the report mode, transferring a local held in a local collection reports
rule: The site is the admitting site — the store, the call, the abandon or the `await` the clause admits — except for a collection element sourced in the body (a borrow of an owned local or `owned` parameter, a value that holds one, or an iterator, enumerator or lazy-query frame carrying one, or a borrow of such a frame, transitively), which is reported at the transfer of that binding by an obligation-moving kill that sets no flag the K4.1 backstop can schedule (the consume table's rows K3.1–K3.4, K3.6, K3.7 and K3.12)

title: outside the report mode, transferring a local held in a local collection is silent
rule: The report is informative: it changes no verdict and no generated code, and outside the mode it is not emitted

title: under the report mode, moving a collection-held local into an owning array reports
rule: The site is the admitting site — the store, the call, the abandon or the `await` the clause admits — except for a collection element sourced in the body (a borrow of an owned local or `owned` parameter, a value that holds one, or an iterator, enumerator or lazy-query frame carrying one, or a borrow of such a frame, transitively), which is reported at the transfer of that binding by an obligation-moving kill that sets no flag the K4.1 backstop can schedule (the consume table's rows K3.1–K3.4, K3.6, K3.7 and K3.12)

title: under the report mode, moving a collection-held local into another local reports
rule: The site is the admitting site — the store, the call, the abandon or the `await` the clause admits — except for a collection element sourced in the body (a borrow of an owned local or `owned` parameter, a value that holds one, or an iterator, enumerator or lazy-query frame carrying one, or a borrow of such a frame, transitively), which is reported at the transfer of that binding by an obligation-moving kill that sets no flag the K4.1 backstop can schedule (the consume table's rows K3.1–K3.4, K3.6, K3.7 and K3.12)

title: under the report mode, disposing a collection-held local is not reported
rule: The claim reaches exactly the recorded clauses — not the flag-backstopped kills (the site-announced kills, K4.2, and a reassignment's drop-on-overwrite, K3.11, each runtime-checked under §28.2)

title: under the report mode, overwriting a collection-held local is not reported

rule: Unbound owned temporaries are disposed at their full expression's end, after their uses, in reverse production order
