title: the generated Dispose runs the destructor body, then owned fields, then the base chain
rule: The compiler generates a public, idempotent `Dispose()` that (1) runs the destructor body, (2) disposes all owned-bearing fields in reverse declaration order, (3) chains to the base class's `Dispose()`.

title: destructors run in subclass-to-base order across three levels
rule: Destructors run in subclass-to-base order.

title: Dispose cannot be overridden
rule: `Dispose()` cannot be overridden; the customization point is `destructor`.

title: an owning-inline-array field disposes only its non-null slots
rule: Disposing all owned-bearing fields covers fields of owning-inline-array type (`[N owned]T?`): each non-null slot's `Dispose()` is called, and a null slot disposes nothing.

title: the destructor body runs exactly once, the first time Dispose is called
rule: A class may declare at most one destructor. Its body runs exactly once, the first time `Dispose()` is called.

title: a class may declare at most one destructor
rule: A class may declare at most one destructor.

title: a throwing disposer does not skip the remaining disposals in the same cleanup pass
rule: In a multi-value cleanup pass, a throwing disposer does not skip the remaining values: every remaining disposal still runs, and the exception then propagates from the disposal point.

title: the destructor body runs on disposal, never on construction unwind
rule: A constructor that throws unwinds instead: owned fields assigned before the throwing statement are disposed, and the throwing class's own destructor body is not run.

title: an owned field of class type is admitted and auto-disposed with its container
rule: Owned fields are restricted to class- or interface-typed fields; a class holding one needs no destructor, the field being disposed with its container.

title: owned on a string field is rejected
rule: The declared type of an `owned` slot, nullability stripped, must be a class type, an interface type, or a bare type parameter. On `string` — a runtime-managed type — `owned` is a compile error.

title: an owned field of interface type is admitted and disposes via dynamic dispatch
rule: Only fields whose type is a **class type or an interface type** take the `owned` field modifier as a marking of their own. ... Interface-typed owned fields are admitted because runtime dispatch resolves disposal to the underlying class's `Dispose()`

title: owned on a function-typed field is rejected
rule: Function-typed fields may not be `owned`. Function values are runtime-managed.

title: owned on a class-typed field is admitted (function-typed field twin)
rule: Only fields whose type is a class type or an interface type may be `owned`; a class type is admitted where a function type is not.

title: owned on an inline-array field without the owned slot marker is rejected
rule: Inline-array fields (`[N]T`, `[N]T?`) without the `owned` slot marker may not be `owned`. The array's slots hold borrows; there is no per-slot ownership to manage.

title: an inline-array field without the owned slot marker is admitted unmarked
rule: Inline-array fields (`[N]T`, `[N]T?`) without the `owned` slot marker may not be `owned`; declared without the field modifier, the field is ordinary borrow-holding storage.

title: an owning-inline-array field needs no owned field modifier
rule: Inline-array fields with the `owned` slot marker (`[N owned]T`, `[N owned]T?`) are admissible as class fields without a separate `owned` modifier on the field; the inline array's own slot marker already signals that the class's generated `Dispose()` disposes each non-null slot (§28.4 step 2), and no user-written destructor is required.

title: double-marking an owning-inline-array field owned is rejected
rule: Writing `private owned slots: [16 owned]Connection?;` is rejected as a double-marking error — the field modifier is omitted because the type-level marker already conveys the obligation.

title: an owned field on a record is rejected
rule: Records may not have `owned` fields (records support only copy semantics, not move semantics).

title: a plain (non-owned) class-typed field on a record is admitted
rule: Records may not have `owned` fields; a plain reference-typed field (a borrow) is ordinary record storage — reference-typed fields in records are always borrows.

title: an owning-inline-array field on a record is rejected
rule: Records also cannot have inline-array fields whose slots carry the `owned` marker (`[N owned]T?` or `[N owned]T`); such fields are move-only value types, and records support only copy semantics.

title: a plain inline-array field (no owned slot marker) on a record is admitted
rule: Records cannot have inline-array fields whose slots carry the `owned` marker; an inline-array field without that marker holds per-slot borrows or value-typed copies, which a record may hold.

title: a generic owned field instantiated at a runtime-managed type is rejected
rule: When a generic class declares `private owned _slot: T` (where T is a type parameter), the restrictions above are checked at each instantiation, reading the substituted type as they read a declared one ... every other substitution — `string`, `Type`, a function type, a copyable value type, and an owning inline array ... — is a compile error at the instantiation site

title: a generic owned field instantiated at a class type is admitted
rule: A generic class's `owned` field is checked per instantiation; a class-typed instantiation of `where T: class` is admissible.

title: owned fields are disposed in reverse declaration order
rule: The `owned` modifier auto-disposes the field when the containing object is disposed, in reverse declaration order.

title: owned fields are disposed after the destructor body runs
rule: The `owned` modifier auto-disposes the field when the containing object is disposed, after the destructor body runs.

title: a null owned field disposes nothing
rule: A nullable owned field is null-checked before disposal, and a null field disposes nothing.

title: owned on an owning-choice field is admitted but redundant, and the cascade disposes the payload once
rule: On a field of **owning-choice** type (§35.4 rule 1, a move-only value type) the modifier is **admitted-but-redundant**, as §28.1's type requirement reads a move-only value type at every marked position: the field is owned-bearing with or without it

title: owned on a field of a value-classified choice is rejected
rule: Only fields whose type is a **class type or an interface type** take the `owned` field modifier as a marking of their own. On a field of **owning-choice** type ... the modifier is **admitted-but-redundant**

title: a generic owned field instantiated at an owning choice is admitted and disposes the payload once
rule: When a generic class declares `private owned _slot: T` (where T is a type parameter), the restrictions above are checked at each instantiation, reading the substituted type as they read a declared one ... an owning-choice substitution ... is admitted-but-redundant, exactly as the first bullet reads the direct field

title: a generic owned field instantiated at an owning inline array is rejected
rule: every other substitution — `string`, `Type`, a function type, a copyable value type, and an owning inline array, whose declared form `owned [N owned]T` is the double-marking error above — is a compile error at the instantiation site, with a message naming the rejected type

title: a bare read of an owned field returns as a receiver-sourced borrow
rule: A bare read of an owned field lends and may be returned through a non-`owned` return type as a borrow of the field — its source is the receiver.

title: a freshly-produced owned value stored into a non-owned field is rejected
rule: A freshly-produced owned value — a `new` expression, a call returning `owned T`, a `move` expression, or an owned operator result — stored into a non-`owned` (borrow) field is an error.

title: a freshly-produced owned value stored into an owned field is admitted
rule: A freshly-produced owned value stored into a non-`owned` field is an error; declaring the field `owned` gives the containing object a place to hold and dispose it.

title: a property getter returning a fresh owned value is rejected
rule: A property or indexer getter may not return a freshly-produced owned value. A getter is a borrow-producing position, and a fresh owned value returned through it would escape with no owner and leak.

title: a factory method returning owned is the remedy for a minting getter
rule: A property or indexer getter may not return a freshly-produced owned value; expose the factory as a method returning `owned T` instead, which can hand the caller ownership.

title: an unmarked mint-announcing method may not lend a stored frame field
rule: A mint-announcing-typed field is not returnable through an unmarked mint-announcing method return, that return type being container-ownership-transferring; a stored frame is instead re-exposed through a property, field, or collection slot.

title: a stored mint-announcing view is re-exposed through a property
rule: A mint-announcing-typed field is not returnable through an unmarked mint-announcing method return; a stored frame is instead re-exposed through a property, field, or collection slot.

title: a moved owned field is returned through an owned return via take-restore-return
rule: Transferring an owned field's value out to the caller is only admissible through an `owned` return type, in the take-restore-return shape: build the replacement, take the field, restore it, then return the taken value.

title: Dispose through a borrowed parameter is rejected
rule: `Dispose()` through a borrow is a compile error. The borrow receivers include a borrowed local or parameter.

title: Dispose through an owned parameter is admitted
rule: Explicit disposal requires a receiver the disposer owns: an owned local or `owned` parameter, among the admitted receivers.

title: an object may not dispose itself through this
rule: The borrow receivers include a borrowed local or parameter — including `this`: an object may not dispose itself out from under its owner.

title: disposing an owned field from within its declaring class is admitted
rule: Explicit disposal requires an owned receiver; an `owned` field read by code of the owning object's declaring type is such a receiver — unlike `this`, which an object may never dispose out from under its owner.

title: disposing an owned field read from outside its declaring class is rejected
rule: The borrow receivers for `Dispose()` include an owned-field read outside the declaring class — that read is a borrow, and disposing through it is rejected with no exception.

title: disposing another instance's owned field is admitted from the same declaring class
rule: The field admission is by declaring type, matching §13.1's levels: code of class C may dispose an owned field of any C instance it can reach — the same access symmetry as any private-member touch.

title: disposing a caught exception binding is rejected
rule: The borrow receivers for `Dispose()` include a `catch`-arm binding.

title: reading a caught exception binding without disposing it is admitted
rule: A `catch`-arm binding is a borrow; reading it (without disposing it) is ordinary borrow use.

title: disposing a case pattern binding is rejected
rule: The borrow receivers for `Dispose()` include a pattern binding.

title: using a case pattern binding without disposing it is admitted
rule: A pattern binding is a borrow of the scrutinee; ordinary borrow use (without disposal) is admitted.

title: disposing a captured owned binding inside a closure is rejected
rule: The borrow receivers for `Dispose()` include a captured owned binding inside a closure.

title: reading a captured owned binding inside a closure is admitted
rule: Inside a closure a captured owned binding is uniformly in borrow state: reads borrow, while assignment, a marked transfer, an explicit `Dispose()` or a discard of it are compile errors.

title: disposing a default-iteration element borrow is rejected
rule: No element-borrow disposal. An element borrow obtained from a borrowing-family collection — a default-iteration variable — is a borrow like any other: disposing it is a compile error, with no exception.

title: reading default-iteration elements without disposing them is admitted
rule: A default-iteration variable over a borrowing-family collection is a borrow of the slot; ordinary borrow use (without disposal) is admitted.

title: disposing a borrowed owning collection's container is rejected
rule: A borrow of an owning collection may not be disposed: the borrower does not own the container, and the actual owner disposes the container and cascades to its elements at scope/destructor end.

title: adding to a borrowed owning collection (pass-and-fill) is admitted
rule: Every operation but `Dispose` remains available on a borrowed owning collection — the idiomatic pass-and-fill pattern `method Fill(a: OwningArray<T>) a.Add(...)` takes a borrowed `OwningArray<T>` and adds to it.

title: a method returning this under an owned return type is rejected
rule: A method that returns `this` returns a borrow of the receiver. The returned borrow may not be assigned to an `owned` field or returned as `owned` — it is the receiver under a different name.

title: a method returning this without owned is admitted
rule: A method that returns `this` returns a borrow of the receiver — the return type is the class type, not `owned`. This enables method chaining.

title: an owned field passed as a plain argument may be stored as a back-reference borrow
rule: Passing an owned field as a plain argument is permitted; the callee receives a parameter-sourced borrow and may store the borrow into a non-owned class-typed field only where the borrowed-field store rule admits it (the back-reference idiom).

title: a freshly-produced owning value through a non-owned return escapes
rule: A `move`d owned field returned through a non-`owned` return is an **error** ... and a freshly-produced owning value (`return new OwningArray<T>(...)`) returned through a non-`owned` return is likewise an error

title: the same fresh owning value through an owned return transfers to the caller
rule: Handing a freshly-produced owning value to the caller is admissible through an `owned` return type — the caller assumes responsibility for its disposal — which is the remedy the non-`owned`-return rejection names.

title: a direct DisposeAsync() through a borrowed parameter is rejected
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter.

title: base.DisposeAsync() directly in a DisposeAsync override is admitted as the chain
rule: In the body of a `DisposeAsync` override itself, not in a lambda nested in it, `base.DisposeAsync()` is §28.12 step 2's chain, not a disposal of `this`, and is admitted.

title: this.DisposeAsync() in a CloseAsync-style method is rejected
rule: The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter — including `this`: an object may not dispose itself out from under its owner ... no other `this`-rooted disposal call is, in that body or elsewhere.

title: disposing a static owned field from its declaring type is rejected
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: ... a `static owned` field read (a borrow of K2's always-live source, which only §22.13's exit pass disposes — K9.4)

title: an early-disposed instance owned field is disposed once and the cascade is the no-op
rule: The call is an **early release point**, not a discharge of the slot's obligation: the slot keeps its reference and its K9 obligation, and the containing object's teardown still runs the cascade over it (§28.4 step 2) ... where the second call is §28.2's no-op and the block is then reclaimed

title: under the unchecked relaxation the cascade over an early-disposed field still runs once
rule: The call is an **early release point**, not a discharge of the slot's obligation: the slot keeps its reference and its K9 obligation, and the containing object's teardown still runs the cascade over it (§28.4 step 2) ... where the second call is §28.2's no-op and the block is then reclaimed — the explicit call performed logical disposal only, and the compiler's single free stays at the holder's release point

title: a this-returning chain over a new root is a borrow of a temporary, not an owned value
rule: When a chain originates from a `new` expression or another owned producer ... the root is an **unbound owned temporary** (§28.3) and every `this`-returning call on it is a borrow of that temporary ... bound to a `var`, stored, returned, or passed to an `owned` parameter it is rejected as a borrow of a temporary (K8.4) — `Keep(new Pool().First())` lends `Pool`'s inner object from a temporary `Pool` and is a compile error at the argument.

title: the same chain used within its full expression runs and disposes the root at statement end
rule: The chain is usable within its full expression only: as an expression statement it runs and the root is disposed at the statement's end

title: a slot of a local owning inline array is disposed explicitly and the scope end disposes it once
rule: requires a receiver the disposer owns ... or a slot of an owning inline array held by an owned local or `owned` parameter of the body

title: an alias of a using-var owner cannot dispose it
rule: Dispose() or a direct DisposeAsync() call through a borrow is a compile error. The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter (§28.6, v0.340). `il` is an unmarked alias of the `using var` owner `a`, so it is a borrow of `a`, and `il.Dispose()` is disposal through a borrow — a compile error. The program also draws the spurious "`using var` `a` is vacuous" warning, because the ownership pass does not see that a collection literal is an owned production (§28.3's producers table). That warning is a separate defect, carried by the row `s28_10_0016` (issue #7092); this row asserts the §28.6 rejection only.

title: the owner of an owned local may dispose it
rule: Explicit disposal — `x.Dispose()` ... — requires a receiver the disposer owns: an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary, a `move` result, or an `owned` field (§28.6, v0.340). `a` is the owner of the collection literal it was bound to (§28.3's producers table), so `a.Dispose()` is a disposal by the owner and is admitted; the scope-end pass finds the binding already disposed and disposes nothing a second time (§28.2's idempotence), so the program ends normally.

title: a two-step alias chain cannot dispose the owner either
rule: Dispose() or a direct DisposeAsync() call through a borrow is a compile error. The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter (§28.6, v0.340). `b` is an unmarked alias of the owned `a`, so it is a borrow of `a`; `il` is an unmarked alias of `b`, so it is a borrow of a borrow — still a borrow, and `il.Dispose()` is disposal through a borrow, which is a compile error. The rule is structural: it reads the receiver expression's ownership classification, which §28.3 computes at every call site.

title: an alias of an owner that was assigned a collection literal cannot dispose it
rule: Dispose() or a direct DisposeAsync() call through a borrow is a compile error. The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter (§28.6, v0.340), and "A collection literal (`[1, 2, 3]`) targeting a reference type is **Owned**" (§28.3's producers table). The assignment `a := [1, 2, 3];` makes `a` the owner of that literal, so `il` — an unmarked alias of `a` — is a borrow of it, and `il.Dispose()` is disposal through a borrow: a compile error.

title: an unmarked alias of an owned local cannot dispose it
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter (§28.6, v0.343), and "An **unmarked read of a class-typed binding never consumes**: `var b := a;` is always a borrow for class-typed `a`" (§28.3 rule 13, v0.343). `a` owns the collection literal it was bound to (§28.3's producers table), so `il` — an unmarked alias of `a` — is a borrow of `a` and takes no ownership of its own; `il.Dispose()` is disposal through a borrow: a compile error.

title: the owner of an owned local may dispose it while a two-step alias chain is live
rule: Explicit disposal — `x.Dispose()` ... — requires a receiver the disposer owns: an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary, a `move` result, or an `owned` field (§28.6, v0.343). `a` owns the collection literal it was bound to (§28.3's producers table), so `a.Dispose()` is a disposal by the owner and is admitted. The two aliases `b` and `il` are borrows of `a` (§28.3 rule 13) and neither changes the owner's status, so the scope-end pass finds the binding already disposed and disposes nothing a second time (§28.2's idempotence) — the program ends normally.

title: a three-step alias chain cannot dispose the owner either
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter (§28.6, v0.343), and "An **unmarked read of a class-typed binding never consumes**: `var b := a;` is always a borrow for class-typed `a`" (§28.3 rule 13, v0.343). `b` is a borrow of the owned `a`, `c` is a borrow of `b`, and `il` is a borrow of `c` — three hops of aliasing, every one of them a borrow, so `il.Dispose()` is disposal through a borrow: a compile error. The rule is structural: it reads the receiver expression's ownership classification, which §28.3 computes at every call site, so the depth of the chain does not change the verdict.

title: an alias of a move result cannot dispose it
rule: Explicit disposal — `x.Dispose()` ... — requires a receiver the disposer owns: an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary, a `move` result, or an `owned` field (§28.6, v0.343). The `move` expression is the only owned read (§28.8.1), so `var b: Array<int> := move a;` makes `b` an owner and `a` moved-from; `b` is therefore a receiver the disposer owns and may be disposed. `il`, however, is an unmarked alias of `b` — "an unmarked read of a class-typed binding never consumes: `var b := a;` is always a borrow for class-typed `a`" (§28.3 rule 13, v0.343) — so `il.Dispose()` is disposal through a borrow: a compile error.

title: a two-step alias chain over a reassigned owner cannot dispose it
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter (§28.6, v0.343), and "An **unmarked read of a class-typed binding never consumes**: `var b := a;` is always a borrow for class-typed `a`" (§28.3 rule 13, v0.343). `b` is an unmarked alias of the owned `a`, and `il` is an unmarked alias of `b` — a borrow of a borrow, still a borrow. The reassignment `a := [1, 2, 3];` makes `a` the owner of the literal it stores (§28.3's producers table) without making `b` or `il` owners, so `il.Dispose()` is still disposal through a borrow: a compile error.

title: an alias of a borrowed parameter cannot dispose it
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter (§28.6, v0.343), and "An **unmarked read of a class-typed binding never consumes**: `var b := a;` is always a borrow for class-typed `a`" (§28.3 rule 13, v0.343). The parameter `p` is a borrowed parameter — the caller's argument is still the owner's — so `il`, an unmarked alias of `p`, is a borrow of a borrow, still a borrow; `il.Dispose()` is disposal through a borrow: a compile error.

title: an alias of an owned field read from outside its declaring class cannot dispose it
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: ... an owned-field read outside the declaring class (§28.6, v0.343), and "An **unmarked read of a class-typed binding never consumes**: `var b := a;` is always a borrow for class-typed `a`" (§28.3 rule 13, v0.343). `h.V` is an owned-field read made from outside `Holder`, so it is a borrow of the field; `b`, an unmarked alias of that read, is a borrow of a borrow, still a borrow; `b.Dispose()` is disposal through a borrow: a compile error.

title: a non-owned field read cannot be disposed through
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: ... a non-`owned` field read (§28.6, v0.343). `V` is a non-`owned` field, so `h.V` is a borrow of the field's value and not an owned receiver; the field's actual owner disposes it. `h.V.Dispose()` is therefore disposal through a borrow: a compile error.

title: an interface-typed alias hop cannot dispose the owner
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter (§28.6, v0.343), and "An **unmarked read of a class-typed binding never consumes**: `var b := a;` is always a borrow for class-typed `a`" (§28.3 rule 13, v0.343). The aliasing is not undone by the declared type of the alias: `il` is an unmarked alias of the owned `a` and is a borrow of it, and `il2`, an unmarked alias of `il`, is a borrow of a borrow — an interface-typed hop is still a borrow, so `il2.Dispose()` is disposal through a borrow: a compile error.

title: an alias of a non-owned field read cannot dispose it
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: ... a non-`owned` field read (§28.6, v0.343), and "An **unmarked read of a class-typed binding never consumes**: `var b := a;` is always a borrow for class-typed `a`" (§28.3 rule 13, v0.343). `h.V` is a non-`owned` field read, so it is a borrow of the field's value; `b`, an unmarked alias of that read, is a borrow of a borrow, still a borrow; `b.Dispose()` is disposal through a borrow: a compile error. KNOWN DIVERGENCE (#7097): the compiler admits the program — no diagnostic at all — and it double-frees at run time.

title: a using var alias of a non-owned field read cannot dispose it
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: ... a non-`owned` field read (§28.6, v0.343), and "An **unmarked read of a class-typed binding never consumes**: `var b := a;` is always a borrow for class-typed `a`" (§28.3 rule 13, v0.343). `h.V` is a non-`owned` field read, so it is a borrow of the field's value, and a `using var` binding adopts a borrow as a borrow (§28.10) and takes no disposal obligation of its own; `b.Dispose()` is disposal through a borrow: a compile error. KNOWN DIVERGENCE (#7097): the compiler admits the program, drawing only the §28.9 "vacuous" warning, and it double-frees at run time.

title: an alias of a non-owned field read inside the declaring class cannot dispose it
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: ... a non-`owned` field read (§28.6, v0.343), and "An **unmarked read of a class-typed binding never consumes**: `var b := a;` is always a borrow for class-typed `a`" (§28.3 rule 13, v0.343). The declaring class is not the exemption the `owned`-field rule gives (§28.6's owned-field read outside the declaring class is a borrow, and its inside-the-class counterpart is the only owned receiver): `V` is a non-`owned` field, so the read `V` inside `Holder` is a borrow all the same; `b`, an unmarked alias of that read, is a borrow of a borrow, still a borrow; `b.Dispose()` is disposal through a borrow: a compile error. KNOWN DIVERGENCE (#7097): the compiler admits the program — no diagnostic at all — and it double-frees at run time.

title: a const alias of an owner cannot dispose it
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter (§28.6, v0.343), and "An **unmarked read of a class-typed binding never consumes**: `var b := a;` is always a borrow for class-typed `a`" (§28.3 rule 13, v0.343). The `const` binding reads `b` without a marker, so `c` is a borrow of `b` — and `b` is itself a borrow of the owned `a` — whatever the binding's constness: `c.Dispose()` is disposal through a borrow: a compile error.

title: a using var bound over an alias cannot dispose it
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter (§28.6, v0.343). The right-hand side of the `using var` is a borrow rather than an owned value, so the binding does not assume a disposal obligation: at scope end no `Dispose()` is called, because the value is not owned by this scope (§28.10, v0.343). `c` is therefore a borrow of `b`, which is itself a borrow of the owned `a`, and `c.Dispose()` is disposal through a borrow: a compile error.

title: an alias of two mutually aliased locals cannot dispose it
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter (§28.6, v0.343), and "An **unmarked read of a class-typed binding never consumes**: `var b := a;` is always a borrow for class-typed `a`" (§28.3 rule 13, v0.343). Each of the two assignments is such an unmarked read, so neither binding becomes an owner by the other's; `z` is a borrow of a borrow, still a borrow, and `z.Dispose()` is disposal through a borrow: a compile error. The check is structural and decidable — it reads the receiver expression's ownership classification, which §28.3 computes at every call site (§28.6, v0.343).

title: an alias of a conditionally assigned owner cannot dispose it
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter (§28.6, v0.343), and "An **unmarked read of a class-typed binding never consumes**: `var b := a;` is always a borrow for class-typed `a`" (§28.3 rule 13, v0.343). Whichever arm of the `if` runs, `a` is a named binding, so the unmarked assignment `il := a` is a borrow of `a` — the alias never becomes an owner, and the conditional does not change that: `il.Dispose()` is disposal through a borrow: a compile error.

title: a method group over `this.Dispose` is rejected at the formation
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter — including `this`: an object may not dispose itself out from under its owner, ... (§28.6, v0.343). Every receiver-side rule of the call the formation resolves as is read at the formation (§27.6, v0.343) — so forming `this.Dispose` is rejected as the call `this.Dispose()` would be.

title: a method group over a borrowed parameter's Dispose is rejected
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter ... (§28.6, v0.343). Every receiver-side rule of the call the formation resolves as is read at the formation (§27.6, v0.343) — so forming `d.Dispose` over a non-`owned` parameter is rejected as the call `d.Dispose()` would be.

title: a method group over a non-owned field read's Dispose is rejected
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: ... a non-`owned` field read (§28.6, v0.343). Every receiver-side rule of the call the formation resolves as is read at the formation (§27.6, v0.343) — so forming `this._d.Dispose` is rejected as the call `this._d.Dispose()` would be.
check: cannot call `Dispose()` through a field read

title: a method group over an owned field read outside its declaring class is rejected
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: ... an owned-field read outside the declaring class (§28.6, v0.343). Every receiver-side rule of the call the formation resolves as is read at the formation (§27.6, v0.343) — so forming `h.d.Dispose` from outside the declaring class is rejected as the call `h.d.Dispose()` would be.
check: cannot call `Dispose()` through a field read

title: a method group over an interface-typed parameter's Dispose is rejected
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter ... (§28.6, v0.343). Every receiver-side rule of the call the formation resolves as is read at the formation (§27.6, v0.343) — so forming `d.Dispose` over an interface-typed parameter is rejected as the call `d.Dispose()` would be.

title: a method group over an alias of a borrowed parameter's Dispose is rejected
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter ... (§28.6, v0.343). Every receiver-side rule of the call the formation resolves as is read at the formation (§27.6, v0.343) — and an unmarked read of a class-typed binding is always a borrow (§28.3, v0.343) — so forming `b.Dispose` over an alias of a borrowed parameter is rejected as the call `b.Dispose()` would be.

title: a method group over an alias of an owned local's Dispose is rejected
rule: `Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter ... (§28.6, v0.343). Every receiver-side rule of the call the formation resolves as is read at the formation (§27.6, v0.343) — and an unmarked read of a class-typed binding is always a borrow (§28.3, v0.343) — so forming `b.Dispose` over an alias of an owned local is rejected as the call `b.Dispose()` would be.

title: a method group over an owned parameter's Dispose is admitted
rule: Explicit disposal ... requires a receiver the disposer **owns** ...: an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary, a `move` result, or an `owned` field (§28.6, v0.343). Every receiver-side rule of the call the formation resolves as is read at the formation (§27.6, v0.343) — so forming `d.Dispose` over an `owned` parameter is admitted as the call `d.Dispose()` would be.

title: a method group over a using var owner's Dispose is admitted
rule: Explicit disposal ... requires a receiver the disposer **owns** ...: an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary, a `move` result, or an `owned` field (§28.6, v0.343). Every receiver-side rule of the call the formation resolves as is read at the formation (§27.6, v0.343) — so forming `d.Dispose` over a `using var` owner is admitted as the call `d.Dispose()` would be.

title: a method group over an owned field read inside its declaring class is admitted
rule: Explicit disposal ... requires a receiver the disposer **owns** ...: ... or an `owned` field ... read by code of the owning object's declaring type (§28.6, v0.343). Every receiver-side rule of the call the formation resolves as is read at the formation (§27.6, v0.343) — so forming `d.Dispose` over an owned field read inside the declaring class is admitted as the call `d.Dispose()` would be.

title: a this-returning extension method chains on a fresh StringBuilder temporary 100 times
rule: The chain is usable within its full expression only: as an expression statement it runs and the root is disposed at the statement's end ... A method that returns `this` returns a borrow of the receiver

title: reassigning an owned field evaluates the RHS before disposing the displaced value
rule: Assignment to an owned field disposes the displaced value; the right-hand side is evaluated first, then the previous live value is disposed, then the new value is stored.

title: reassigning a plain-var owned local disposes the displaced value
rule: Assignment to an owned field or owned local disposes the displaced value; the scope of this rule covers `owned` fields and plain-`var` owned locals alike.

title: reassigning a moved-from field stores without disposal
rule: The disposal is null-guarded and dynamically dispatched; a moved-from or null location therefore stores without disposal, which is how the move-then-reassign idiom stays single-disposal.

title: an explicit Dispose before reassignment composes with drop-on-overwrite as a no-op
rule: An explicit `field.Dispose();` before the assignment remains legal and behavior-preserving — Dispose is idempotent, so the implicit disposal of an already-disposed value is a no-op.

title: reassigning an owned field while a live borrow of the displaced value exists is admitted
rule: Reassigning an owned field or collection slot is not statically frozen — a borrow of the displaced value is invalidated at the overwrite, caught as DisposedAccessException in checked disposal mode and undefined unchecked, not rejected at compile time.

title: reassigning an owned local while a live local borrow of it exists is rejected
rule: Reassigning a plain-var owned local while a live local borrow of its current value exists is rejected by the consume-site freeze — the implicit disposal would silently invalidate the borrow.

title: whole-value reassignment of an owning inline array disposes live slots in reverse order
rule: An owning inline array takes drop-on-overwrite per live slot, in reverse slot order (v0.260) — the RHS is evaluated first, then each live slot of the displaced value is disposed, then the new value is stored.

title: a throwing RHS leaves the field untouched and still owned
rule: A throwing RHS leaves the field/local untouched and still-owned — the implicit path has no exception-unsafe window.

title: reassigning a Set<int> local leaves the new set holding only the new elements
rule: Assignment to an owned field or owned local disposes the displaced value.

title: reassigning an owned Set<int> field leaves the field holding only the new elements
rule: Assignment to an owned field or owned local disposes the displaced value.

title: reassigning an owned SortedSet<int> field leaves the field holding only the new elements
rule: Assignment to an owned field or owned local disposes the displaced value.

title: reassigning an Object-typed owned local while a live local borrow of it exists is rejected
rule: Reassigning a plain-var owned local while a live local borrow of its current value exists is rejected by the consume-site freeze (§28.3.9) - the implicit disposal would silently invalidate the borrow. The rule names a LOCAL, not a class-typed local: the reader's static type does not decide whether a use-after-free is diagnosed.

title: an owned parameter transfers ownership and may be stored into an owned field directly
rule: When a parameter is `owned`, the caller relinquishes ownership; the owned-field assignment drop-on-overwrites the displaced value, so a replacement method needs no explicit dispose-first step.

title: implicit boxing produces no disposal obligation and draws no discharge diagnostic
rule: Implicit boxing is not subject to the discharge rule of this section — when a value type is boxed to be used where `Object` is expected, the boxed wrapper is a runtime-managed value, not an owned `new`-result; the boxing itself is not a `new` expression and produces no disposal obligation.

title: the caller may not use an argument it transferred to an owned parameter
rule: When a parameter is `owned`, the caller relinquishes ownership and may not use the argument after the call (§28.8, K3.3).

title: the take-restore-return idiom hands an owned field's contents to the caller
rule: Moving an owned field's contents out uses the `move` expression form: the field is left moved-from and must be reassigned on every path to the method's exit, so the pattern for "atomically take this field's contents and return them as owned" builds the replacement first, takes, restores, then returns the taken value (§28.8, §28.8.1).

title: move on a field takes it out and a restoring assignment on every exit path satisfies the rule
rule: The field-restoration rule: every control-flow path from the move site to the method's exit must execute a restoring assignment `x.f := value;` between the move and the exit.

title: a terminal bare move of a non-nullable field is rejected even under an owned return
rule: Where the location's declared type is nullable ... the `with` clause may be omitted: `move x.f` stores `null`. Where it is not, the clause is required; its absence is a compile error naming the two remedies — `move x.f with fresh`, or a nullable declaration

title: a field moved on one branch and not reassigned on the other is rejected
rule: The rule applies to every reachable exit; the compiler rejects a move whose restoring assignment is missing on some path to the method's exit.

title: scoping the move to the branch where reassignment is mandatory satisfies the rule
rule: The fix is to scope the move to the branch where reassignment is reachable, so every path that performs the move also restores the field before the method's exit.

title: a throwable construction between the move and the restoration is an unrestored exception edge
rule: A throwable expression between the move and the reassignment introduces an exit path on which the reassignment has not run — the exception edge is an unrestored exit.

title: building the replacement before the move leaves no throwable edge between move and restoration
rule: Build before take — perform any throwable construction before the move, leaving only non-throwable assignments and the return between the move and the exits.

title: a loop that may execute zero times does not satisfy the field-restoration rule
rule: Loops that may execute zero times do not satisfy the rule — the analysis reuses the definite-assignment dominance machinery, so a restoration reachable only through a conditionally-taken loop body does not dominate the exit.

title: restructuring so the reassignment dominates the exits satisfies the loop case
rule: The fix is the same as the conditional case — restructure so the reassignment dominates the exits, moving the move after the loop.

title: moving a field before its first constructor assignment is a definite-assignment violation
rule: Inside a constructor body, the field has no value to move until it has been assigned; a `move x.f` before the field's first assignment is a definite-assignment violation, the same rule as for any other read of an unassigned non-nullable slot.

title: move on a field is permitted after its first constructor assignment
rule: After the first assignment, `move` is permitted, with the same field-restoration rule applying to constructor exit paths.

title: a destructor body takes its own non-nullable field bare and discharges it like any other owned value
rule: Inside a destructor body, a field of the object being torn down is read for final disposal, and may be taken bare whatever its nullability ... The taken value must still be discharged through one of the standard mechanisms — assigned to a local with `using var`, passed as `owned` to a helper, or explicitly disposed.

title: using var u := move x.f is the canonical take-and-consume pattern
rule: `using var u := move x.f;` is the canonical pattern for 'take the field's value out and consume it scope-bound.' The using var discharges the moved value at scope end; the field-restoration rule still applies at the surrounding method's exits.

title: detaching via a nullable field moves the contents out and leaves the field null
rule: A nullable location a bare take leaves holding `null` is an ordinary null field: its holder's cascade disposes nothing through it, and a later read reads `null`.

title: an argument-position move whose restoration follows a throwable call is rejected
rule: A method call is throwable, so an argument-position move whose restoration follows the call is rejected on the call's exception edge.

title: restoring the field before the call that may throw fixes the argument-position hazard
rule: The fix is to construct the replacement and reassign before the call — the same "build then take then restore" discipline, with the call moved to after the restore.

title: a new expression's argument expressions classify on their own between the move and the restoration
rule: The exclusion covers the construction only — a `new` expression's argument expressions classify on their own, so `_r := new Res(Fetch());` still puts Fetch()'s exception edge between the move and the restoration.

title: move with on a non-nullable field yields the old value and the field holds the replacement at once
rule: `move loc with e` — `loc` an owned field `x.f` or an owning slot `coll[i]`, `e` an expression — evaluates `loc`'s receiver and index, then `e`, and then, in one step with no intermediate state, stores `e`'s value into the location and yields the location's previous value, owned.

title: a bare take of a nullable owned field stores null and needs no later store
rule: Where the location's declared type is nullable — read as declared: `T?`, a nullable slot type, and not a bare type parameter `T`, whatever its substitution — the `with` clause may be omitted: `move x.f` stores `null`.

title: the replacing move through a borrowed parameter receiver is admitted
rule: The receiver `x` in `move x.f` is any object expression ... whose field `f` is `owned` and accessible at the site ... a borrowed parameter included, as v0.332 ruled for the take

title: a named owned binding is the replacement written unmarked
rule: The replacement `e` is an owned value for the location's declared type: a fresh producer, a `move` result, a named owned binding — the position is marker-free, as every store into an owned location is

title: a borrow as the replacement of a replacing move is rejected
rule: a borrow is rejected, as it is at any store into an owned location

title: a using var as the replacement of a replacing move is rejected
rule: a borrow is rejected, as it is at any store into an owned location ... and so is a `using var`

title: a with clause on the move of a local binding is rejected
rule: The "with" Expression clause is the REPLACING move of §28.8.1, admitted at (a) and (b) only ... At (c) a `with` clause is a compile error.

title: with followed by a parenthesized assignment list after a move operand is the record update
rule: A `with` followed by `(` and `Identifier :=` is the record-update suffix and binds to the operand: `move r with(X := 1)` is `move (r with(X := 1))`, a `move` of a record value, rejected by this section's operand rule, the diagnostic naming the replacing form with its replacement parenthesized, `move loc with (e)`.

title: a parenthesized replacement that is not an assignment list is the replacing move's clause
rule: One tie-break decides every spelling: `with` followed by `(` and `Identifier :=` is the record-update suffix binding to the expression before it ... any other `with` opens the cancellation clause in an `await for` header and the replacement clause after a `move` operand

title: a replacement that throws leaves the field unchanged and the cascade disposes it once
rule: An exception raised while evaluating the receiver, the index or the replacement, or by one of those checks ... leaves the location unchanged

title: a destructor body's bare take of a non-nullable field is rejected as in any other body
rule: Inside a destructor body, the fields of the object being torn down are owned locations like any other: `move x.f with e` exchanges, `move x.f` at a nullable field stores `null`, and a non-nullable field is not taken bare — the compile error names, beside the two remedies above, the field's explicit `Dispose()` where the destructor's class declares the field.

title: a destructor's bare take of a non-nullable owning slot is rejected
rule: A field of another object, and an owning slot, take the same rules in a destructor body as elsewhere.

title: a replacing move of a static readonly owning inline array's slot is rejected
rule: Static fields are not eligible ... static owned storage — a `static owned` field, and the slots of a `static readonly` owning inline array ... — admits no `move`, no slot store and no explicit disposal: it is the always-live source ... so it is neither taken nor replaced

title: the bounds check of a slot exchange runs after the replacement is evaluated
rule: The checks that read the location's current state — an owning indexer's bounds and key checks, and `!`'s null test ... — run when `e` has been evaluated, immediately before the exchange, so nothing `e` does (a call that resizes the collection or empties the field, a suspension at an `await`) can invalidate them.

title: a getter returning a freshly-computed string needs no owned announcement
rule: Runtime-managed types are exempt from the ceremony this chapter states for class-typed values; a getter body whose result is a fresh runtime-managed production (an interpolation, a concatenation) remains admissible with no `owned` announcement.

title: a closure that would outlive its captured local borrow's source is rejected
rule: Runtime management relaxes nothing about the values a closure captures — a captured borrowed class reference is subject to §28.3's borrow-escape rules, so a function value that outlives the captured borrow's source is rejected.

title: a function value carrying no captured borrow may be returned from its method
rule: Runtime management governs the function value itself, and the compiler tracks captured borrows separately from the function value's own lifetime — a function value that captures no borrow has an empty source set, so nothing it carries can be outlived and it is admitted at the escaping sinks a capture-bearing one is not.

title: a closure may not dispose an owned local it captures
rule: Capturing an owned class-typed local does not transfer ownership into the closure — the closure may not assign to, transfer from, or dispose the captured binding.

title: a closure may read a captured owned local while the original binding retains the obligation
rule: The capture is a borrow whose source is the local's enclosing scope, borrow-state throughout, and the original `using var` (or other owned location) retains the disposal obligation.

title: move through a closure's captured borrow of a move-only local is rejected
rule: Capturing a move-only local follows the same rule — the closure captures a borrow whose source is the local's enclosing scope; reads of slots through the captured borrow are admitted, `move arr[i]` through it is not, because the closure does not own the array.

title: reading a slot through a closure's captured borrow of a move-only local is admitted
rule: Reads of slots through the captured borrow are admitted — the closure captures a borrow whose source is the local's enclosing scope.

title: using var on a function-typed local still forbids reassignment, though disposal there is a no-op
rule: A `using var` local of function type is nonetheless permitted (disposal at scope end is a no-op) and serves only the non-reassignability role — a plain `var` of function type scopes its captures identically.

title: an undischarged plain-var local of a trivial-dispose class draws no must-use warning
rule: No must-use / auto-drop diagnostic attaches to a trivial-dispose value: the §28.3 must-use warning is not emitted at the implicit-drop site of a plain-`var` owned local whose type is trivial-dispose — a class with no destructor and no `owned` fields of non-trivial-dispose type (§28.9).

title: adding a destructor makes the same undischarged local draw the must-use warning
rule: The ceremony exemption's boundary is exactly the runs-no-user-code line: a class that declares a destructor is not trivial-dispose, so the §28.3 must-use warning is emitted at the implicit-drop site of its plain-`var` owned local (§28.9, §28.3).

title: a trivial-dispose declared type over a destructor-bearing production is not exempt
rule: The exemption's classification is read from the produced type where the drop site's value has a statically-known producer: a trivial-dispose declared type standing over a destructor-bearing production — `var b: Base := new Derived();` at a trivial-dispose `Base` — is not exempt (§28.9).

title: an owned field of trivial-dispose type leaves the holder trivial-dispose
rule: The trivial-dispose check is recursive: an `owned` field whose declared type is itself trivial-dispose does not disqualify the holder — the synthesized disposal cascade over such fields frees memory and runs no user code, so the holder keeps the ceremony exemption (§28.9).

title: an owning collection is not trivial-dispose at any instantiation
rule: The owned-element variants of the standard collection types are not trivial-dispose at any instantiation: they own their elements, disposal cascades through to them, and their storage primitive declares a destructor — so the ordinary discharge obligations apply and the ceremony exemption does not (§28.9).

title: a borrowing collection is trivial-dispose even at a non-trivial element type
rule: The rule does not require the type arguments to be themselves trivial-dispose: `Array<MyClass>` is trivial-dispose even if `MyClass` is not — the elements are owned elsewhere and the array's free does not dispose them — so its undischarged local draws no must-use warning (§28.9).

title: owned over the Type token is inadmissible
rule: `Type` is runtime-managed: no `Type` expression is an owned production, none lends a borrow, and no holder carries an obligation for one — `owned` over `Type` is inadmissible (§28.9, v0.300; §28.1's type requirement names a class type other than `Type`).

title: an interface-typed owned binding is never exempt from the must-use warning
rule: An interface-typed binding is never exempt from the must-use warning, its conformance set being open across modules (§28.9's possibly-non-trivial-dispose reading), whatever the concrete class behind it does (§28.9, §28.3).

title: an undischarged owned parameter of trivial-dispose type draws no must-use warning
rule: The exemption covers **every holder form the warning attaches to**: the must-use warning is not emitted at the implicit-drop site of an undischarged `owned` parameter — a method's, an iterator's, or an async method's — whose type is trivial-dispose; the auto-drop itself is unconditional at every one of them.

title: a Type value is runtime-managed and its holder carries no obligation
rule: `Type` is runtime-managed: the runtime holds exactly one instance per type for the life of the process and user code never allocates one, so no `Type` expression is an owned production, none lends a borrow, and no holder carries an obligation for one — the compiler neither warns about an undisposed one nor requires it to appear in a `using var`.

title: a class with an owning-choice field is not trivial-dispose and its undischarged local warns
rule: A class whose disposal **provably runs no user code and releases only memory** — it has no destructor, no `owned` fields of non-trivial-dispose type, no fields of move-only value type (§15.3 — an owning inline array, ... or an owning choice, nullable or not, §35.4 ...) ... — is a **trivial-dispose class**

title: the same class with a plain value field is trivial-dispose and its local is silent
rule: User-defined classes with no destructor, no owned fields of non-trivial-dispose type, and no fields of move-only value type (owning-inline-array or owning-choice) are automatically trivial-dispose.

title: a using var declared inside a loop body is disposed on a break exit
rule: Disposal happens on every exit path — normal completion, break, return, or exception.

title: a using var established inside a try's protected block is disposed before the try's own finally
rule: A try statement's own finally is established at entry to the protected block; an owned local or using var declared inside the protected block, established later, is disposed before the finally runs, in reverse establishment order.

title: using var admits an if expression whose two arms are both owned producers
rule: An expression whose arm-meet is owned — an if expression over fresh producers — is an owned producer for using var's admission.

title: the anonymous using var _ adopts a moved named owned binding exactly as the named form would
rule: Adoption composes — `using var _ := move x;` consumes `x` into the anonymous binding exactly as the named form would.

title: a using var initialized from a borrow does not assume a disposal obligation
rule: When the right-hand side of a using var declaration is a borrow rather than an owned value — a method call without an owned return, an indexer access, a field read, or an unmarked read of a borrow-state named binding — the using var does not assume a disposal obligation: at scope end no Dispose() is called, because the value is not owned by this scope. An unmarked read of a class- or interface-typed named owned binding is rejected, and an unmarked read of a move-only value binding moves instead and is an owned right-hand side.

title: an explicit Dispose of a borrow-pin's source is a site-announced kill the pin leaves unfrozen
rule: The using var still pins the borrow's source for the duration of the scope ... the site-announced kills stay unfrozen under their flag backstop ... an explicit `Dispose()` of the source is permitted; a read through the pinned binding that the disposal dominates is §28.2's compile error, and one the disposal reaches on only some paths raises `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode.

title: using var accepts a runtime-managed right-hand side, where disposal at scope end is a no-op
rule: using var accepts a value-type or runtime-managed right-hand side; for ordinary value types and runtime-managed types the disposal at scope end is a no-op, and the only effect is the reassignability restriction.

title: reassigning a using var of runtime-managed type is still a compile error
rule: using var is a scope pin — it is implicitly non-reassignable, whatever the right-hand side's type kind; reassigning a using var variable is a compile error.

title: moving a borrow-pin's source is a frozen kill the pin still rejects
rule: The using var still pins the borrow's source for the duration of the scope — the borrow stays live until the using-var's scope ends, and the consume-site freeze then governs every consume of the source in that range: the frozen kills — a move, a transfer, a reassignment of the binding — are compile errors.

title: an unmarked using var over a move-only local adopts rather than pins
rule: Where `x` is a local of **move-only value type**, the unmarked `using var y := x;` **adopts**: a move-only binding has no borrow reading to disambiguate, so the plain read moves, `y` carries the value's owned slots to the end of *its* block, and `x` is left moved-from.

title: the source of an unmarked using var adoption is left moved-from
rule: Under the unmarked move-only adoption, `x` is left **moved-from** — the plain read moved the value — and reading from a moved-from location is a compile error (§15.3). The whole-value move leaves the local holding no value rather than a hole, so it owes no restoration.

title: a read through a borrow-pin after the source's explicit Dispose faults in checked mode
rule: The site-announced kills stay unfrozen under their flag backstop: an explicit `Dispose()` of a borrow-pin's source is permitted, and a read through the pinned binding afterwards raises `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode.

title: using var over an if arm-meet of two unmarked owned locals is rejected
rule: When **every** arm of the meet — `null`-literal and `throw` arms set aside — is an unmarked read of a class- or interface-typed named owned binding, and at least one arm is, the `using var` is **rejected** on that paragraph's ground: `using var y := (if c then a else b);` and `using var y := a ?? b;` over two owned locals say neither that `y` adopts the selected binding nor that it views it, and the compiler does not choose.

title: the marked-arm remedy (if c then move a else move b) adopts and is admitted
rule: The remedies are the marked arms where the arm position admits the marker — `(if c then move a else move b)`, an expression-`case` likewise — except at an arm naming a `using var` source or the `case` scrutinee's own binding.

title: an unmarked using var over a named owned binding is a compile error
rule: An unmarked `using var y := x;` is a compile error when its right-hand side is a named owned binding whose declared type, nullability stripped, is a class or interface type (§28.10, v0.340) — the covered spelling does not say whether `y` adopts `x` or views it, and the compiler does not choose. `a` is a local whose ownership state is owned (the collection literal is an owned production, §28.3's producers table) and whose declared type `Array<int>` is a class type, so `using var b := a;` is rejected. KNOWN DIVERGENCE (#5582): the compiler admits the program and draws a spurious "`using var` `b` is vacuous" warning.

title: a using var over a collection literal is owned and draws no vacuity warning
rule: `using var x := expr;` where `expr` is an owned producer ... is owned, additionally subject to scope-based disposal at the end of the enclosing block (§28.10, v0.340), and "A collection literal (`[1, 2, 3]`) targeting a reference type is **Owned**" (§28.3's producers table). The literal is an owned production, so `a` is owned and its scope-end disposal is a real obligation: the "`using var` is vacuous" warning has no premise here and must not fire. KNOWN DIVERGENCE (#7092): the ownership pass does not see the producers row for a literal, so it reports the binding as having no disposal obligation.

title: a using var of the protected block is disposed before that try's finally on the loop-exit edge
rule: A `try` statement's own `finally` is established at entry to the protected block — before any establishment the block itself performs. Consequently, on every exit edge, an owned local or `using var` declared inside the protected block (established later) is disposed before the `finally` runs ...; cleanups established before the `try` run after the `finally`, as before (§28.10, v0.340). So a `using var` declared inside the protected block is still alive after a `break` out of a nested `try` — the `break` leaves only that inner `try` — and it is disposed before the enclosing `finally` runs.

title: using var over a value-type right-hand side disposes nothing at scope end
rule: `using var` accepts a value-type or runtime-managed right-hand side. For ordinary value types and runtime-managed types, the disposal at scope end is a no-op (these types do not require disposal per [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)), and the only effect is the reassignability restriction.

title: Unmarked using var over an owned local of interface type is rejected
rule: An unmarked `using var y := x;` is a compile error when its right-hand side is a named owned binding whose declared type, nullability stripped, is a class or interface type: it says neither that y adopts x nor that it views it (spec 28.10, Adopting a named owned binding); `move x` adopts, a `var` or `const` binding views. A local of interface type holding a fresh `new Thing()` is a named owned binding of an interface type, so the unmarked read is covered.

title: Unmarked using var over a `using var` source (never movable out) is rejected
rule: An unmarked `using var y := x;` is a compile error when its right-hand side is a named owned binding whose declared type, nullability stripped, is a class or interface type: it says neither that y adopts x nor that it views it (spec 28.10, Adopting a named owned binding); `move x` adopts, a `var` or `const` binding views. A `using var` local is a named owned binding too; its remedy is a view, since a `using var` source is never movable out (axiom A5).

title: Unmarked using var over `await using var` over an owned local is rejected
rule: An unmarked `using var y := x;` is a compile error when its right-hand side is a named owned binding whose declared type, nullability stripped, is a class or interface type: it says neither that y adopts x nor that it views it (spec 28.10, Adopting a named owned binding); `move x` adopts, a `var` or `const` binding views. `await using var y := x;` is covered exactly as the plain form (spec 28.10, 28.12).

title: Unmarked using var over a `??` whose arms are two owned locals is rejected
rule: An unmarked `using var y := x;` is a compile error when its right-hand side is a named owned binding whose declared type, nullability stripped, is a class or interface type: it says neither that y adopts x nor that it views it (spec 28.10, Adopting a named owned binding); `move x` adopts, a `var` or `const` binding views. A `??` meet whose every arm is an unmarked read of a class-typed named owned binding is rejected on the same ground (nullability stripped).

title: Unmarked using var over an owned local re-owned by assignment after a move is rejected
rule: An unmarked `using var y := x;` is a compile error when its right-hand side is a named owned binding whose declared type, nullability stripped, is a class or interface type: it says neither that y adopts x nor that it views it (spec 28.10, Adopting a named owned binding); `move x` adopts, a `var` or `const` binding views. A local that adopted the owned state by assignment is a named owned binding at the declaration.

title: Unmarked using var over an expression `case` whose every arm is an unmarked owned read is rejected
rule: An unmarked `using var y := x;` is a compile error when its right-hand side is a named owned binding whose declared type, nullability stripped, is a class or interface type: it says neither that y adopts x nor that it views it (spec 28.10, Adopting a named owned binding); `move x` adopts, a `var` or `const` binding views. An expression-position `case` meet whose every arm is an unmarked read of a named owned binding is rejected on the same ground.

title: Unmarked using var over an `owned` parameter of bare type-parameter type is rejected
rule: An unmarked `using var y := x;` is a compile error when its right-hand side is a named owned binding whose declared type, nullability stripped, is a class or interface type: it says neither that y adopts x nor that it views it (spec 28.10, Adopting a named owned binding); `move x` adopts, a `var` or `const` binding views. A bare type parameter that admits class substitutions is a class or interface type for this rule; the generic body is rejected once.

title: Unmarked using var over an owned iteration variable of a Drain loop is rejected
rule: An unmarked `using var y := x;` is a compile error when its right-hand side is a named owned binding whose declared type, nullability stripped, is a class or interface type: it says neither that y adopts x nor that it views it (spec 28.10, Adopting a named owned binding); `move x` adopts, a `var` or `const` binding views. An owned iteration variable is a named owned binding.

title: Unmarked using var over an `out owned` recipient read with `!` is rejected
rule: An unmarked `using var y := x;` is a compile error when its right-hand side is a named owned binding whose declared type, nullability stripped, is a class or interface type: it says neither that y adopts x nor that it views it (spec 28.10, Adopting a named owned binding); `move x` adopts, a `var` or `const` binding views. An `out owned` recipient is a named owned binding, and the null-forgiving read `x!` is classified as the bare `x`.

title: Unmarked using var over an `owned` nullable parameter read with `!` is rejected
rule: An unmarked `using var y := x;` is a compile error when its right-hand side is a named owned binding whose declared type, nullability stripped, is a class or interface type: it says neither that y adopts x nor that it views it (spec 28.10, Adopting a named owned binding); `move x` adopts, a `var` or `const` binding views. An `owned` parameter is a named owned binding; `x!` is classified as the bare `x`.

title: Unmarked using var over an owning-match arm binding is rejected
rule: An unmarked `using var y := x;` is a compile error when its right-hand side is a named owned binding whose declared type, nullability stripped, is a class or interface type: it says neither that y adopts x nor that it views it (spec 28.10, Adopting a named owned binding); `move x` adopts, a `var` or `const` binding views. An owning-match arm binding is a named owned binding.

title: Unmarked using var over a `??` of two parenthesized null-forgiving owned reads is rejected
rule: An unmarked `using var y := x;` is a compile error when its right-hand side is a named owned binding whose declared type, nullability stripped, is a class or interface type: it says neither that y adopts x nor that it views it (spec 28.10, Adopting a named owned binding); `move x` adopts, a `var` or `const` binding views. `(x)` and `x!` are classified as the bare `x`, in a `??` meet whose every arm is one.

title: Unmarked using var over a plain borrowed parameter pins and disposes nothing
rule: A `using var` initialized from a borrow does not assume a disposal obligation: at scope end no Dispose() is called, because the value is not owned by this scope; it only pins the source (spec 28.10, `using var` initialized from a borrow). A plain parameter is borrow state, so the pin disposes nothing and the caller's local is disposed once at its scope end, after END.

title: Unmarked using var over a `var` alias of an owned local pins and disposes nothing
rule: A `using var` initialized from a borrow does not assume a disposal obligation: at scope end no Dispose() is called, because the value is not owned by this scope; it only pins the source (spec 28.10, `using var` initialized from a borrow). A `var v := src` alias is a borrowing alias, so the pin disposes nothing and the owner disposes once.

title: Unmarked using var over a borrowing for-in loop variable pins and disposes nothing
rule: A `using var` initialized from a borrow does not assume a disposal obligation: at scope end no Dispose() is called, because the value is not owned by this scope; it only pins the source (spec 28.10, `using var` initialized from a borrow). A borrowing loop variable is borrow state; the two elements are disposed once each, by their owning array, after END.

title: Unmarked using var over an owned binding captured by a closure pins and disposes nothing
rule: A `using var` initialized from a borrow does not assume a disposal obligation: at scope end no Dispose() is called, because the value is not owned by this scope; it only pins the source (spec 28.10, `using var` initialized from a borrow). A captured owned binding inside a closure is in borrow state (spec 28.3), so the unmarked form is the borrow pin and the owner disposes once.

title: Unmarked using var over a string local pins and disposes nothing
rule: A `using var` initialized from a borrow does not assume a disposal obligation: at scope end no Dispose() is called, because the value is not owned by this scope; it only pins the source (spec 28.10, `using var` initialized from a borrow). A string is not a class-typed owned binding, so the form is a vacuous pin with nothing to dispose.

title: Unmarked using var over a generic borrowed parameter pins and disposes nothing
rule: A `using var` initialized from a borrow does not assume a disposal obligation: at scope end no Dispose() is called, because the value is not owned by this scope; it only pins the source (spec 28.10, `using var` initialized from a borrow). A plain parameter of type-parameter type is borrow state (only an `owned` bare type-parameter binding is covered).

title: Unmarked using var over an adopted owned local with `move` pins and disposes nothing

title: storing a parameter-sourced borrow into a field-held borrowing collection is admitted
rule: Storing a class-typed borrow into a borrowing collection follows the same shape as §28.3's borrowed-field rule — parameter-sourced and receiver-sourced borrows are admitted at the store site.

title: storing a scope-bound local's borrow into an outliving field-held collection is rejected
rule: A borrow of a scope-bound binding — an owned parameter included — stored into a collection that provably outlives that scope — the collection is a field, is reachable from one, escapes the method, or is a local of strictly wider scope — is rejected at the store site.

title: move on a borrowing collection slot is rejected — there is no ownership to transfer
rule: No other receiver admits it ... A copy, shared-reference or borrow slot, and a read-only view, admit none: ... the borrowing collections ... reject `move coll[i]` at compile time.

title: Array<T> and OwningArray<T> are distinct, unrelated types with no implicit conversion
rule: There is no implicit conversion between the two families; an OwningArray<Connection> is not an Array<Connection> and vice versa.

title: an OwningDictionary owns its values while its keys are classified as ordinary borrows
rule: For dictionaries the classification applies independently to the key slots and the value slots — an owning dictionary owns its values; its keys are value-like and classified per the borrowing column.

title: an owning collection over Type is rejected at instantiation
rule: In the element-category table, a runtime-managed reference element type — `string`, a function type, `Type` (§28.9) — is *rejected at instantiation* in the owning-family column: no holder acquires an obligation for such a value, so an owned element slot has nothing to own.

title: the same owning collection over a class element type is admitted
rule: The owning-family column admits a **class** element type: the slot owns its element and the container's `Dispose()` cascades to it, which is the family's defining behaviour.

title: an element borrow used after a dominating RemoveAt at its index draws the use-after-removal warning
rule: The compiler must warn when a local holding such a borrow is used after a call on the same collection binding that disposes the borrowed element and dominates the use on every path — `RemoveAt(i)` where the borrow was taken as `coll[i]` with the same index expression, and no structural operation on the same collection binding between the borrow and the kill.

title: using an element borrow after a dominating Clear on the same collection draws the warning
rule: The compiler must warn when a local holding such a borrow is used after a call on the same collection binding that disposes the borrowed element and dominates the use on every path — `Clear()`, which disposes every element.

title: an element borrow re-taken after the mutation is clean
rule: A borrow so produced is valid until its slot is mutated — an indexer-set, `Remove`/`RemoveAt`, `Clear()` or the collection's own disposal disposes the referent — and is not statically tracked per slot ... Re-take the borrow after the mutation, take the element out first through `PopAt`/`Pop`/`PopValue`, which leave no borrow behind, or mutate after the last use

title: an element-level indexer write on the collection does not draw the element-borrow warning
rule: A borrow so produced is valid until its slot is mutated — an indexer-set, `Remove`/`RemoveAt`, `Clear()` or the collection's own disposal disposes the referent — and is not statically tracked per slot

title: a RemoveAt at the borrow's index after an intervening Insert draws no warning
rule: A borrow so produced is valid until its slot is mutated — an indexer-set, `Remove`/`RemoveAt`, `Clear()` or the collection's own disposal disposes the referent — and is not statically tracked per slot: a use of it afterwards is a mid-scope kill under the checked-mode backstop (K4.1, §28.2)

title: GetOrAdd with a scope-bound key on a field-held dictionary is rejected at the store
rule: `GetOrAdd(key, factory)` (stdlib §4.8, §4.9) is a store under this rule at every call, whether or not the key is present: of `key`, and, into a borrowing value slot, of the factory's result, whose sources are what invoking the factory on `key` carries

title: GetOrAdd with a parameter-sourced key on a field-held dictionary is admitted
rule: `GetOrAdd(key, factory)` (stdlib §4.8, §4.9) is a store under this rule at every call, whether or not the key is present: of `key`, and, into a borrowing value slot, of the factory's result, whose sources are what invoking the factory on `key` carries

title: a direct FromCollectionLiteral copy of borrow-bearing elements into a field is rejected
rule: An inline array's `ToArray` (§15.1), range slicing (§15.6) and a direct `FromCollectionLiteral` call are shape (i)'s copies ... A copy is judged as a store of each placed value into the destination, at the call — at a class or interface element type under this rule, at a value type that holds borrows under §9.7's collection bullet

title: a direct FromCollectionLiteral copy into a local is admitted
rule: An inline array's `ToArray` (§15.1), range slicing (§15.6) and a direct `FromCollectionLiteral` call are shape (i)'s copies ... The destination is where the result lands (its binding, an unbound temporary's full expression, §28.3, or the field, collection or return slot it is placed in)

title: ToArray of a local collection of borrow-bearing records into a field is rejected
rule: (i) a method, constructor or `static` factory whose result is an `owned` collection ... copies into that result every element value it takes: from its receiver ... A copy is judged as a store of each placed value into the destination, at the call — at a class or interface element type under this rule, at a value type that holds borrows under §9.7's collection bullet

title: returning ToArray of a parameter's borrow-bearing records is rejected
rule: (i) a method, constructor or `static` factory whose result is an `owned` collection ... copies into that result every element value it takes: from its receiver ... A copy is judged as a store of each placed value into the destination, at the call — at a class or interface element type under this rule, at a value type that holds borrows under §9.7's collection bullet

title: Counter.Increment of a plain parameter key into a field-held counter is admitted
rule: (ii) a method of a borrowing-family collection or of a span view that declares no return copies into its receiver the values it takes from a parameter declared `IEnumerable<T>`, a read-only span over `T`, or a bare `T` — the many-element forms ... and the single-element stores `Add`, `Insert`, `Push`, `Enqueue` and `Counter<K>.Increment`, which creates its key's entry, each of which the element slot policy already reads as a store

title: the fill constructor copying a borrow-bearing record into a field is rejected
rule: (i) a method, constructor or `static` factory whose result is an `owned` collection — the constructed collection itself, for a constructor — copies into that result every element value it takes ... from each argument declared at one of them (`fill`)

title: a local copy and a receiver-sourced snapshot are admitted
