title: the block-bodied loader async lambda forwards an owned Result through its state machine
rule: `var loader: (string) -> OwningTask<Resource> := async lambda(path) => do return await LoadResourceAsync(path); end;` — "Pattern B return; the lambda's state machine forwards the owned Resource through."

title: the closed target return slot, not the body alone, picks Task<C> over OwningTask<C>
rule: (2) Otherwise a **closed target return slot** names it ... a fresh owned class result is admitted under either `Task<C>` (Pattern A, kind 1 — the task owns the result) or `OwningTask<C>` (Pattern B), so the target decides between them. ... a closed head binds nothing, so reading it is reading a declared type, not an inference.

title: await for consumes an async iterator's yielded values in order
rule: `await for` is valid only inside an async method or async lambda. It desugars analogously to `for`: it acquires an async enumerator with `await using`, calls `MoveNextAsync()` with `await` in a loop.

title: await for over IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T> yields an owned iteration variable
rule: Each iteration variable is owned; the §28.3 discharge rules apply on every exit edge of the loop body — the same rule as for synchronous `for` over `IOwningEnumerable<T>`.

title: with token passes a CancellationToken to GetAsyncEnumerator
rule: `await for` accepts an optional `with` clause to pass a `CancellationToken` to the async enumerator. The `with token` clause passes `token` as the argument to `GetAsyncEnumerator(token)`.

title: await for outside an async method is rejected
rule: `await for` is valid only inside an async method or async lambda.

title: await inside a source-written finally is rejected in an async iterator
rule: Inside an async iterator, `await` may not appear in a `finally` block — a compile error.

title: an await using var may not be live across a yield return
rule: An `await using var` whose static type is such a class (or is of **interface** static type) ... may not be **live across a `yield return`** in an async iterator: a compile error at the yield.

title: an await using var whose class has only an inherited destructor may not cross a yield
rule: For a class **without a synchronous fallback** — some level of its chain declares or overrides a non-`abstract` `DisposeAsync` and declares **no destructor** of its own, a destructor it only inherits being a base level's cleanup ... An `await using var` whose static type is such a class ... therefore **may not be live across a `yield return`** in an async iterator: a compile error at the yield.

title: a class whose DisposeAsync level declares its own destructor may cross a yield
rule: For types **with** a destructor, the synchronous-fallback path above remains the defined degraded behavior, unchanged.

title: an Object-typed await using var may not be live across a yield return
rule: An `await using var` whose static type is such a class (or is of **interface** static type ... or is `Object`: neither an interface nor `Object` can promise a destructor, and the disposal path is the run-time object's, so the runtime type's fallback posture is statically unknowable and such bindings are conservatively included ...) therefore **may not be live across a `yield return`** in an async iterator.

title: the same binding at its own class static type, which declares a destructor, may cross a yield
rule: A binding whose static type is any other class is admitted, even where it holds an object of a subclass without a synchronous fallback.

title: a cancelled with-token faults the in-flight MoveNextAsync before any value is yielded
rule: **Token routing in generated async iterators.** For a compiler-generated async iterator, the enumerator returned by the generated `GetAsyncEnumerator(token)` captures the token, and every `MoveNextAsync()` performs an implicit `token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` — on entry ... so a requested cancellation faults the in-flight `MoveNextAsync` task with `OperationCanceledException`.

title: a case expression awaiting inside an async iterator keeps its binding across yield and await
rule: `await` suspends the current async method until a task completes (§30.2, v0.340) and an async iterator may `await` between `yield return`s (§30.7, v0.340); a `case` arm's binding keeps its value across both: `q` = `T(3) + 3` = 33, then `z` = 33 gives `T(33) + 33` = 363.

title: awaiting inside the token source's using var scope discharges the source-outlives obligation
rule: **The `CancellationTokenSource` must outlive the settlement of every task observing one of its tokens.** ... Awaiting the call inside the source's `using var` scope discharges the obligation.

title: IsCancellationRequested observes a Cancel() call on the source
rule: `CancellationToken` observes the source's state; when `Cancel()` is called on the source, all tokens derived from it report `IsCancellationRequested == true`.

title: an exception thrown after an await faults the task and is re-raised by the caller's await
rule: An exception thrown after an `await` faults the task. Awaiting a faulted task re-raises the exception with the original stack trace preserved.

title: an exception thrown in the synchronous prefix faults the returned task
rule: An exception thrown in the synchronous prefix of an async method (before any `await`) faults the returned task, not the immediate caller.

title: a catch guard may not contain await
rule: Catch **guards** are the one exception: a `when` guard on a catch arm is evaluated synchronously during exception dispatch and may not contain `await` (a compile error, in async and sync methods alike).

title: await is unrestricted inside catch and finally bodies
rule: `await` has no syntactic restrictions on its placement inside `try`/`catch`/`finally` *bodies*. The state machine handles suspension across exception-handling boundaries correctly.

title: a fault escaping into an outer task stays live for every awaiter of the outer task
rule: An instance that an `await` or a `Result` read re-raised from a task ... and that then leaves the body ... faults the body's task, which does **not** become its owner: the instance stays owned by the task that owned it, the faulted task carries it as a **borrow**, and the faulted task **retains the operand task** whose fault it carries

title: an outer task whose fault is never re-raised disposes the retained fault instance at its disposal
rule: An operand the frame **owns** — an unbound temporary (`await Inner()`), a plain owned local, an `owned` parameter — **moves** into the faulted task's state as a kind-2 chained source does (§30.5): the temporary's deferred terminal-act disposal, the local's discharge and the parameter's dispose-at-terminal-state do not run for it, and the faulted task's teardown disposes it

title: a using var operand whose fault escapes is disposed at the faulted task's teardown
rule: A `using var`/`await using var` operand's disposal is **deferred** to the faulted task's teardown, as axiom A12 defers a chained source's.

title: a borrowed Pattern B operand whose fault escapes is retained by borrow, not disposed by the award
rule: A **borrowed** operand — a plain task parameter, a task read from a field or static storage, an owning-collection slot, a borrowing-iteration variable; a Pattern B operand among them, whose award spends it and disposes nothing (§30.5) — is retained by **borrow**

title: the WithCleanupAsync example -- await in a catch arm and in a finally, then a bare re-raise
rule: `await` has no syntactic restrictions on its placement inside `try`/`catch`/`finally` *bodies*. The state machine handles suspension across exception-handling boundaries correctly. ... a bare `throw;` faults the body's task, and awaiting that task re-raises the exception.

title: Task.WhenAll completes only after every input task has settled
rule: `Task.WhenAll` (all input forms) completes only after **every** input has settled — it never abandons laggards. If every input succeeded it completes successfully.

title: Task.WhenAny yields the index of the settled task
rule: `Task.WhenAny(tasks: Array<Task>): Task<int>` — completes when the first task completes, yielding the **index** of the winner in `tasks`.

title: the owning WhenAll overload aggregates OwningTask<T> results
rule: `Task.WhenAll<T>(owned tasks: OwningArray<OwningTask<T>>): OwningTask<OwningArray<T>> where T: class` — the caller transfers ownership of the array (and its tasks); the result is an owned array of owned elements.

title: WhenAny of an empty array raises ArgumentException synchronously
rule: `WhenAny` of an **empty** array raises `ArgumentException` **synchronously at the call site**, not as a faulted task.

title: discarding a Task with the discard statement is rejected
rule: `Task.FireAndForget` is the only supported way to discard a `Task` value — the discard form `_ := someAsyncCall();` is rejected at compile time because abandoning a `Task` reference would skip its continuation cleanup.

title: the anonymous using-var binding of a Task is rejected
rule: The two legal patterns for "I don't want to await this task" are `Task.FireAndForget(call())` and a named `using var t := call();` — the anonymous `using var _ := call();` is rejected with the discard.

title: a named using-var binding is the legal unsupervised abandonment form
rule: A named `using var t := call();` is legal (unsupervised): the task is disposed at scope end without blocking, and any exceptions it raises are silently swallowed.

title: Task.FireAndForget accepts the task and relinquishes ownership
rule: `Task.FireAndForget(owned task: Task)` registers a continuation that logs or handles any exception the task produces, then disposes the task; the calling code relinquishes ownership.

title: WhenAll re-raises the first non-successful input in input order
rule: Awaiting a non-successful `Task.WhenAll` re-raises the exception of the **first non-successful input in input order**, per the first-fault-no-aggregation posture; the other inputs' faults remain observable on those tasks individually.

title: a cancelled input counts as OperationCanceledException for WhenAll
rule: Awaiting a non-successful `Task.WhenAll` re-raises the exception of the first non-successful input in input order — a cancelled input counting as `OperationCanceledException`.

title: Task.FromResult at a class-typed T is rejected
rule: `Task.FromResult<T>(value: T): Task<T>` is restricted to non-class T; calling FromResult with a class-typed T is a compile error pointing to the owned variant.

title: Task.FromOwnedResult transfers the value to the awaiting context
rule: `Task.FromOwnedResult<T>(owned value: T): OwningTask<T> where T: class` — the caller transfers ownership to the task; awaiters consume the task under Pattern B, the await appearing in an owned-consuming context to which ownership transfers.

title: the borrowing WhenAll overload delivers results in input order, not completion order
rule: `Task.WhenAll<T>(tasks: Array<Task<T>>): Task<Array<T>>` ... If every input succeeded it completes successfully (for the generic form, with the results in input order).

title: TaskCompletionSource<T> completes a Task<T> imperatively for non-class T
rule: A `TaskCompletionSource<T>` produces a task whose state is controlled imperatively. For non-class T ... the produced `Task<T>` carries no ownership across the await boundary.

title: OwningTaskCompletionSource<T> transfers ownership of a class-typed result
rule: For class T ... the source takes ownership of the result on completion, and the eventual awaiter takes ownership through the `using var x := await ...` shape.

title: returning the source's Task property out of its own scope is a borrow escape
rule: The task never outlives its source, and there is no first-read ownership transfer ... returning `tcs.Task` *itself* out of the scope is the return of a borrow sourced at a local with no source that outlives the call — rejected by §28.3's borrowed-return rule.

title: TrySetResult returns false once the task is already in a terminal state
rule: The `Set*` methods complete the task; `TrySet*` returns `false` instead of throwing when the task is already in a terminal state.

title: a rejected TrySetResult disposes the result it was handed, leaving only the task's own
rule: If `TrySetResult` returns `false` because the task is already in a terminal state, the implementation disposes `result` before returning. The caller has no further obligation — ownership was transferred at the call, and the implementation is responsible for releasing it on every path.

title: SetResult with one argument is rejected on the non-generic TaskCompletionSource
rule: The non-generic TaskCompletionSource has the same shape as the generic one minus the result parameter on SetResult and TrySetResult, so SetResult and TrySetResult take no argument on it (the declared shape is public method SetResult(); and TrySetResult(): bool;). The stdlib declares the non-generic SetResult() and TrySetResult(): bool the same way (stdlib 6.6). A call SetResult(1) therefore has no matching overload.

title: TrySetResult with one argument is rejected on the non-generic TaskCompletionSource
rule: The non-generic TaskCompletionSource has the same shape as the generic one minus the result parameter on SetResult and TrySetResult, so SetResult and TrySetResult take no argument on it (the declared shape is public method SetResult(); and TrySetResult(): bool;). The stdlib declares the non-generic SetResult() and TrySetResult(): bool the same way (stdlib 6.6). A call TrySetResult(1) therefore has no matching overload.

title: SetCancelled with one argument is rejected on the generic TaskCompletionSource
rule: The generic TaskCompletionSource<T> declares SetCancelled() with no parameter (stdlib 6.6 and spec 30.11 show public method SetCancelled(); on the generic form), so a call SetCancelled(1) has no matching overload.

title: SetResult with two arguments is rejected on the generic TaskCompletionSource
rule: The generic TaskCompletionSource<T> declares SetResult(result: T) with one parameter (spec 30.11), so a call SetResult(1, 2) has no matching overload.

title: the zero-argument TrySetResult on the non-generic TaskCompletionSource is accepted and runs
rule: The non-generic TaskCompletionSource declares TrySetResult(): bool with no parameter (spec 30.11, stdlib 6.6), so a zero-argument call is the admitted form and it runs.

title: SetCancelled with one argument is rejected on the owning TaskCompletionSource
rule: OwningTaskCompletionSource<T> declares SetCancelled() with no parameter (spec 30.11, stdlib 6.6), so a call SetCancelled(1) has no matching overload.

title: Mutex.Acquire() lexically inside an async method is rejected
rule: The compiler rejects the blocking forms **lexically inside `async` methods and `async` lambdas** (there the async forms are strictly superior — `await m.AcquireAsync()`).

title: AcquireAsync is the admitted remedy for blocking acquisition inside async code
rule: The compiler rejects the blocking forms lexically inside `async` methods and `async` lambdas (there the async forms are strictly superior — `await m.AcquireAsync()`).

title: the Lock pattern with using var -- the guard's disposal is the release
rule: The `Lock` pattern with `using var`: `class BankAccount ... using var guard := _mutex.Acquire(); ... end Deposit; end BankAccount;` — the releasing of the lock is disposal of the `Lock`.

title: Domain.Spawn rejects a capturing lambda entry
rule: The compiler enforces at the call site: **the entry must be capture-free**: a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference. A capturing lambda or an instance method reference is rejected — captures and receivers are borrows of the origin domain.

title: Domain.Spawn admits a non-capturing lambda entry
rule: The entry must be capture-free: a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference.

title: Domain.Spawn admits a static method reference entry
rule: The entry must be capture-free: a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference.

title: Domain.Spawn rejects a non-sendable class-typed argument
rule: **Argument and result types must be sendable**, per the rules above. A **class** type is sendable iff it is transfer-closed: the class must be `sealed` ... or `closed`. Open classes are not sendable.

title: Domain.Spawn admits a sealed class-typed argument
rule: A **class** type is sendable iff it is transfer-closed: the class is `sealed`; or it is `closed` and every class in its hierarchy is itself transfer-closed.

title: a sealed class deriving from Exception is not sendable as a spawn argument
rule: The inherited state of a **compiler-known** class among the class's bases, direct or indirect (§12.4's opened classes), is not read as fields (stdlib §1): it satisfies this rule only where the base's own section states its inherited state transfer-compatible, and fails it otherwise.

title: the same sealed class with a string field and no compiler-known base is sendable
rule: A **class** type is sendable iff it is transfer-closed: the class is `sealed`, and every instance field, including inherited fields, is a sendable value type; `string`- or `Type`-typed; or an `owned` field whose declared type is a sendable class type.

title: the nullable form of a sendable record satisfies where T sendable
rule: A **nullable type** `V?` is sendable exactly where `V` is (§3.6 *Nullable forms*): `int?` and `Job?` for a sendable `Job` cross as `V` does, the absent value included

title: the nullable form of a borrow-bearing record does not satisfy where T sendable
rule: A **nullable type** `V?` is sendable exactly where `V` is (§3.6 *Nullable forms*) ... **Value types** are sendable iff they are not borrow-bearing (§9.7), not move-only (§15.3), and **every component type is sendable**

title: Domain.Spawn rejects an entry whose nested lambda captures an enclosing local
rule: The compiler enforces at the call site: the entry must be capture-free: a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference. A capturing lambda or an instance method reference is rejected. (v0.338 §30.14). A lambda may reference variables from its enclosing scope (§27.5), so an entry containing a lambda that references a method local captures it.

title: Domain.Spawn rejects an entry that captures a method parameter
rule: The compiler enforces at the call site: the entry must be capture-free: a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference. A capturing lambda or an instance method reference is rejected. (v0.338 §30.14). Data enters the new domain only through the explicit `arg` parameters.

title: Domain.Spawn rejects an entry that captures a for-loop variable
rule: The compiler enforces at the call site: the entry must be capture-free: a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference. A capturing lambda or an instance method reference is rejected. (v0.338 §30.14)

title: an async Domain.Spawn entry that captures a method local is rejected
rule: The entry must be capture-free: a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference. (v0.338 §30.14). An entry may be an `async` function: a capture-free `async` lambda or a static `async` method reference.

title: Domain.Spawn admits an entry whose nested lambda uses only the entry's own local
rule: The entry must be capture-free: a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference. A capturing lambda is one that references a variable of its enclosing scope (v0.338 §27.5). A local the entry declares itself is not captured by the entry. (v0.338 §30.14, §27.5)

title: Domain.Spawn admits a capture-free async entry that uses its own local
rule: An entry may be an `async` function: a capture-free `async` lambda or a static `async` method reference. (v0.338 §30.14). A local the entry declares itself is not a capture (v0.338 §27.5).

title: Channel<T> rejects a non-sendable class-typed element
rule: Channels are the only mutable objects reachable from more than one domain; they are compiler-known, internally synchronized, and their element type must be sendable (checked at instantiation per §3.6).

title: Send transfers ownership into the channel and Receive transfers it out
rule: A **channel** carries sendable values from one domain to another with ownership transfer at both ends: `Send` consumes the value in the sending domain; `Receive` produces it owned in the receiving domain.

title: Send transfers ownership into the channel and Receive transfers it out in send order
rule: **Ordering.** Items from one sender are received in the order sent ... **Closing.** Disposing the last `ChannelSender<T>` *closes* the channel: items already sent remain receivable (the channel drains).

title: a thrown owned exception is caught by a matching arm
rule: `throw expr` constructs and raises an exception; a thrown exception is caught by the first arm naming its class or a base of it.

title: throwing a primitive-typed operand is rejected
rule: `throw expr` requires `expr`'s static type, nullability not admitted, to be `Exception` or a class deriving from it; values of primitive type cannot be thrown — a compile error at the throw site.

title: throwing an Object-typed operand is rejected
rule: An `Object`-typed operand is likewise rejected (no interface derives from `Exception`, and an `Object` referent may be a boxed value); narrow to the exception class first.

title: throwing an interface-typed operand is rejected
rule: An interface-typed operand is likewise rejected — no interface derives from `Exception` — even when the runtime class implementing it does; narrow to the exception class first.

title: throwing the caught exception binding directly is rejected
rule: The throw operand is consumed as an owned value, so a borrowed class reference is not a valid operand; to re-raise the exception being handled, use the bare re-raise instead.

title: the bare re-raise is the admitted way to re-throw a caught exception
rule: To re-raise the exception being handled, use the bare re-raise (`throw`, valid only inside a catch arm body) rather than throwing the borrowed catch-arm binding.

title: the transfer marker at the marker-free throw position is rejected
rule: `throw` is a marker-free consuming position — `throw x;` — the keyword itself is the announcement, so `throw move x;` is rejected at the marker-free position, the same no-marker rule as an `owned` return.

title: throwing a named owned local is written unmarked
rule: `throw` is a marker-free consuming position: the correct spelling of a named owned binding as a throw operand is `throw x;`, with no `move`.

title: disposing the caught exception binding is rejected
rule: Inside a catch arm, the bound exception variable is a borrow of the in-flight exception; `Dispose()` requires an owning receiver, and a catch-arm binding is one of the borrow forms through which disposal is a compile error with no exception.

title: a closure over the caught exception assigned outside the arm is rejected
rule: A closure capturing the catch-arm binding may outlive the arm only when the closure's value can leave the arm; assigning it to a binding declared outside the arm is one such escape, and the counter-example is one assignment away from the confined-closure idiom.

title: a closure over the caught exception confined to the arm is admitted
rule: A closure over the catch-arm binding is confined to the arm — admitted, however many lambdas nest inside it — whenever its value stays inside the arm: bound to an arm-local and invoked there, nothing over the binding ever leaves.

title: a throw of an owned parameter bounded by Exception is caught by its catch arm
rule: the operand's static type, nullability not admitted, must be

title: a throw of an owned parameter bounded by a user Exception subclass is caught
rule: the operand's static type, nullability not admitted, must be

title: a generic class whose type parameter is bounded by Exception throws an owned argument
rule: the operand's static type, nullability not admitted, must be

title: a throw of a borrowed (non-owned) class parameter is rejected
rule: The operand is consumed as an owned value under the ownership rules below

title: a throw of a local copied from an owned parameter without move is rejected as borrowed
rule: an unmarked read of an owned binding is a borrow of the binding.

title: a throw of an owned parameter bounded only by class is rejected
rule: the operand's static type, nullability not admitted, must be

title: a throw of an owned parameter bounded by a class that does not derive from Exception is rejected
rule: the operand's static type, nullability not admitted, must be

title: a throw of an owned parameter with no bound is rejected
rule: the operand's static type, nullability not admitted, must be

title: a throw of an unnarrowed nullable owned operand is rejected
rule: nullability not admitted

title: a try statement with neither catch nor finally is rejected
rule: A `try` statement consists of a protected block, optionally followed by a `catch` block, optionally followed by a `finally` block. At least one of `catch` or `finally` must be present.

title: a try statement with only a finally is admitted
rule: If the `try` has only a `finally` (no `catch`), the catch block is omitted entirely, satisfying the at-least-one-of-catch-or-finally rule.

title: a broader arm listed first catches a more specific exception
rule: The arms are tried in order; the first arm whose pattern matches the thrown exception is selected, its body runs, and exception handling completes. Arms after the matched one are not considered.

title: a more specific arm listed first catches its own type
rule: The arms are tried in order; the first arm whose pattern matches the thrown exception is selected. Reordering the arms of s31_2_0003 so the more specific type is first changes which arm is selected.

title: finally runs when the protected block completes normally
rule: `finally` runs whether the protected block completed normally, was exited by an exception (caught or uncaught), or was exited by `return`.

title: finally runs when the protected block exits by return
rule: `finally` runs whether the protected block completed normally, was exited by an exception, or was exited by `return`.

title: return inside a finally block is rejected
rule: `return` inside a `finally` block is a compile error (§21.5, §21.7).

title: break inside a finally whose target loop encloses it is rejected
rule: Neither may exit a `finally` block: inside a `finally`, a `break` or `continue` — labeled or unlabeled — whose target loop lies outside the `finally` is a compile error, the same rule as `return` in a `finally`.

title: continue inside a finally whose target loop encloses it is rejected
rule: Neither may exit a `finally` block: inside a `finally`, a `break` or `continue` whose target loop lies outside the `finally` is a compile error — on the exception edge such a jump would silently discard the in-flight exception.

title: an owned local of the protected block is disposed before finally runs
rule: The `finally` is established at entry to the protected block: on the single establishment-ordered cleanup stack it ranks before anything the block itself establishes, so an owned local or `using var` declared inside the protected block is disposed before the `finally` runs on every exit edge.

title: a throw escaping a finally supersedes the in-flight exception
rule: A throw escaping a `finally` supersedes the in-flight exception: when a `finally` entered during exception propagation itself completes by throwing, the new exception replaces the one being handled, and the superseding exception propagates from the `try` statement as usual.

title: the superseding exception's SupersededChain records the lost exception
rule: At the instant of supersession, and before the superseded exception is disposed, the runtime appends to the superseding exception's `SupersededChain` an `ExceptionInfo` snapshot of the superseded exception itself — its type name, `Message`, and `StackTrace`.

title: a return out of a try body runs the inner finally and then the outer finally
rule: A `finally` "runs whether the protected block completed normally, was exited by an exception (caught or uncaught), or was exited by `return` — or by a `break` or `continue` targeting an enclosing loop" (§31.2, v0.340), and the cleanups run in reverse establishment order. So a `return` out of the inner `try` body runs the inner `finally` and then the outer `finally`, and the statements after the inner `try` — and after the outer `try` — are skipped.

title: a bare type arm matches without binding
rule: A catch arm's pattern may be a bare type, `IOException`: it matches any thrown exception that is an instance of the type, without binding.

title: a false guard skips the arm and falls through to the next
rule: Each pattern may be followed by an optional `when Expression` guard. The guard is evaluated only if the pattern matches; if the guard returns `false`, the arm is skipped and the next arm is considered.

title: a multi-type binding types at the nearest common base
rule: When binding, `name` has the static type of the nearest common base of the listed types — the most specific class that is a base of every listed type.

title: a binding over unrelated types types at Exception, not either listed type
rule: For alternatives sharing nothing more specific, the nearest common base is `Exception`; every listed type is `Exception`-derived, so the binding's static type is never narrower than that.

title: a catch arm naming a non-Exception-derived class is rejected
rule: With every throwable `Exception`-derived and inheritance single, an arm naming any other class type is provably dead — no thrown instance can ever match — and is a compile error naming this rule.

title: a catch arm naming Object is rejected
rule: `Object` itself is rejected by the same rule for the opposite reason — as the universal root it matches every throwable, and the spelling for that is the bare `Exception` arm; the remedy is to delete the arm or fix the type.

title: an interface-typed catch arm matches an implementing exception
rule: An interface-typed arm remains admissible — no interface derives from `Exception`, but an `Exception`-derived class may implement one, so the arm matches exactly the throwables whose class implements the interface.

title: an unconstrained generic parameter used as a catch-arm type is rejected
rule: A generic type parameter used as a catch arm's type must carry an `Exception`-derived class bound; a parameter that is unconstrained is a compile error at the arm, checked at the generic declaration.

title: a generic type parameter bounded by Exception matches the substituted type
rule: A generic type parameter is admissible as an arm's type when it carries an `Exception`-derived class bound; it matches exactly as the substituted type argument would.

title: an expression-form catch arm body discards its result
rule: A catch arm's body may be an expression: `=> SomeMethod(args)`; the expression's result is discarded.

title: a single-statement catch arm body ends with the statement's semicolon
rule: A catch arm's body may be a single statement: `=> Log(ex);` ends with the statement's `;` — the convenient form for a one-line arm body that is a statement.

title: a do...end block catch arm body holds several statements
rule: A catch arm's body may be a `do ... end` block: `=> do statements end`, used when the body contains multiple statements.

title: a specific arm before the catch-all handles its own type
rule: Arms are tried in order; the first match wins. The most specific exception types should appear first, ahead of a bare `Exception` catch-all.

title: a bare Exception arm at the end is the catch-all
rule: A bare `Exception` arm at the end is the catch-all: every throwable derives from `Exception`, so such an arm captures any thrown exception.

title: a non-exhaustive catch block draws no diagnostic
rule: A `catch` block need not be exhaustive. Exceptions not matched by any arm propagate to the enclosing handler. The compiler does not warn on non-exhaustive `catch` blocks — non-exhaustiveness is the normal case.

title: the bare re-raise expression re-throws with the stack trace preserved
rule: The bare re-raise re-throws the currently-handled exception with its stack trace preserved. As an expression: `throw` (without a semicolon) — the natural form for an arm body that does nothing but re-raise.

title: the bare re-raise statement re-throws after other statements in the arm
rule: As a statement: `throw;` (with the trailing semicolon), equivalent to the expression form followed by `;`, used inside `do ... end` blocks where the re-raise is one statement among several.

title: a bare re-raise outside a catch arm body is rejected
rule: Bare `throw` (either form) outside a catch arm body is a compile error. It is valid only inside a catch arm body.

title: a catch-all arm whose body is the unit value suppresses the exception
rule: To deliberately suppress all catchable exceptions in a block, use a bare-`Exception` arm whose body is the unit value `()`; the `()` body makes the suppression syntactically explicit.

title: a method that may throw needs no exception declaration
rule: Methods do not declare which exceptions they may raise. The compiler does not enforce that callers handle particular exception types. Any exception may propagate from any method call.

title: an exception propagates undeclared through several call frames
rule: Any exception may propagate from any method call; none of the intermediate methods in the chain need declare it.

title: an ArithmeticException arm catches an OverflowException
rule: The inheritance hierarchy is relevant for arm ordering: an arm pattern of `ArithmeticException` matches both `OverflowException` and `DivideByZeroException`.

title: an ArgumentException arm catches an ArgumentNullException
rule: The inheritance hierarchy is relevant for arm ordering: an arm pattern of `ArgumentException` matches `ArgumentNullException`.

title: ArgumentException.ParamName holds the supplied parameter name
rule: `ArgumentException` exposes `public readonly property ParamName: string?;` — the `(message, paramName)` constructor supplies it.

title: ArgumentException.ParamName is null when not supplied
rule: `public readonly property ParamName: string?;   // null when not supplied` — the `(message)`-only constructor leaves it null.

title: the (message, cause) constructor snapshots the cause into CauseChain
rule: The `(message, cause)` constructor borrows `cause` for the duration of the call and copies its type name, message, and stack-trace text into the new exception's `CauseChain`.

title: the cause instance is never retained after chaining
rule: The cause instance is never retained — consistent with §31.1's caught-exception-is-a-borrow rule, no ownership machinery is needed, and the full diagnostic chain survives independently of the cause instance.

title: no Exception constructor accepts a SupersededChain argument
rule: No constructor populates or accepts `SupersededChain` — the chain is runtime-populated exactly as `StackTrace` is, so no constructor's purity classification changes.

title: SupersededChain is empty on an exception that superseded nothing
rule: `SupersededChain` (v0.259 — empty when nothing superseded). It starts empty and shares the empty-array representation, so an exception that supersedes nothing allocates nothing.

title: throw with an operand may appear as the right operand of ??
rule: `throw` — with an operand, or the bare re-raise — may appear in any expression position, per §17.12's throw expression and its bottom type.

title: throw with an operand may appear as an if-expression branch
rule: `throw` — with an operand, or the bare re-raise — may appear in any expression position; the bottom type unifies with the other branch's type in an if-expression.

title: a well-formed extern block declaring several methods is admitted
rule: An `extern` block opens with `extern` followed by a string-literal library name, optionally a `convention` clause, and ends with `end;`; each entry inside is an ordinary method declaration -- visibility, name, parameters, return type -- followed by `;`, with no body and no per-method `end`.

title: an extern method entry omitting visibility defaults to internal
rule: `extern` declarations may be `public` or `internal`, following the rules for module-level declarations; omitting the keyword defaults to `internal`, the module-level default.

title: an empty extern block is a compile error
rule: Empty `extern` blocks are a compile error.

title: an extern method declared static is rejected
rule: They may not carry `static`, `virtual`, `override`, `abstract`, or `sealed`.

title: an extern block nested inside a class is rejected
rule: They are always module-level -- never members of classes.

title: an extern method is called unqualified from within its declaring module
rule: From within the same module, they are called by name without qualification.

title: a bare library name resolves per platform convention
rule: The library name is a bare identifier without extension. The runtime resolves it according to platform conventions.

title: a full path library name bypasses runtime resolution
rule: For libraries with non-conventional names, a full path may be used as the library name; this bypasses runtime resolution and loads the file directly.

title: the convention clause selects a non-default calling convention
rule: The default calling convention is the platform-standard C convention. For non-default conventions, the `convention` clause specifies which. `cdecl` and `stdcall` are universally accepted.

title: every integer type, float, double and bool are FFI-compatible parameter types
rule: Only the following types may appear in `extern` method signatures: All integer types and `float`, `double`. `bool` -- passed as a 1-byte value.

title: Ptr<T> is admitted as a parameter, a return type, and inside an FFI function type
rule: `Ptr<T>` -- a typed foreign address; admitted as a parameter, as a return type, and inside FFI function types, marshalling as the pointer it is.

title: CString is admitted as a parameter and an owned nullable return
rule: `CString` -- null-terminated UTF-8 byte sequence.

title: an inline array of an FFI-compatible scalar is admitted as an extern parameter by address
rule: Inline arrays `[N]T` where the element type is an FFI-compatible scalar ... Admitted as parameters only, by address.

title: the nullable boundary forms CString?, WString?, RawBytes? and a nullable function type are admitted
rule: Nullable boundary forms: `CString?`, `WString?`, `RawBytes?`, and nullable FFI function types are admitted as possibly-NULL pointers.

title: a Bezel string parameter type is rejected
rule: Not allowed: Bezel `string` (use `CString` or `WString`).

title: an enum parameter type is rejected
rule: Not allowed: ... enums (declare the underlying integer type and cast explicitly at the boundary).

title: Array<T> as a parameter type is rejected
rule: Not allowed: ... `Array<T>`, `OwningArray<T>` and the other collections.

title: a record that is not C-compatible is rejected as a parameter type
rule: Not allowed: ... records other than the §32.13 forms.

title: a nullable value type parameter is rejected
rule: Nullable value types are rejected: `int?`, `bool?`, `IntPtr?`, `Ptr<T>?`, and nullable record forms have no C representation.

title: a RawBytes extern return type is rejected
rule: A `RawBytes` extern return type is rejected (a C function returns one value, and the two-slot shape has no return convention).

title: an inline array extern return type is rejected
rule: `[N]T` as an extern return type is rejected (C functions do not return arrays; declare `Ptr<U>`, or a C-compatible record with an inline-array field, per the actual C signature).

title: an owning inline array is not admitted at an extern parameter
rule: Owning inline arrays and inline arrays of other element types are not admitted.

title: ref and out are admitted on FFI-compatible scalar extern parameters
rule: On extern parameters whose type is an FFI-compatible scalar ...: `ref p: T` -- C sees `T*`, receiving the address of the caller's storage. `out p: T` -- same address passing.

title: out owned is not admitted on an extern parameter
rule: Not admitted, with reasons: `out owned` (ownership transfer through an out-slot has no defined native contract).

title: an owned parameter is not admitted on an extern method
rule: Not admitted, with reasons: ... `owned` parameters (no native contract for consuming a Bezel-owned argument).

title: scoped is illegal on an extern parameter
rule: `scoped` function-typed parameters are illegal on `extern` declarations: neither the storage obligations nor the quiescence guarantee can be verified across the FFI boundary.

title: a temporary inline-array argument at an extern call site is rejected
rule: A temporary or otherwise non-assignable inline-array argument is a compile error.

title: a callback may not capture a binding passed out to the same extern call
rule: A callback argument of the same extern call may not capture a binding passed `out` to that call -- a compile error.

title: env as ordinary local variable name must compile
rule: `env` is not a keyword outside the bare-env-marker position; it may be used as an ordinary local variable name.

title: env: IntPtr as ordinary callback parameter name must compile
rule: A parameter named `env: IntPtr` with a type annotation is not the bare env-marker; the following `:` disambiguates. `env` is a regular parameter name in a function type inside an extern declaration.

title: CString cannot be constructed directly with new
rule: `CString`, `WString`, and `RawBytes` are FFI-boundary types. They cannot be constructed or manipulated directly in ordinary Bezel code; the standard library provides explicit conversion functions.

title: a caller-owned string return is discharged with using var
rule: Native functions returning a buffer the caller must free declare their return type as `owned CString` (or `owned CString?` when the function may return NULL); ownership transfers to the Bezel side and `using var` discharges it.

title: a borrowed IntPtr return is read with string.FromCStringPointer
rule: For native functions returning a string pointer that the caller does not own ... the FFI declaration's return type is `IntPtr`, not `CString`. The Bezel side reads through the pointer with `string.FromCStringPointer(p: IntPtr): string`, which copies into a fresh Bezel `string` without taking ownership of the original buffer.

title: IntPtr.Zero supports the null test
rule: `IntPtr.Zero` -- the null pointer (integer 0). `=` and `<>` for null tests.

title: IntPtr converts explicitly to and from long
rule: Explicit conversions to and from `long` and `ulong` are also compiler intrinsics: `IntPtr(longValue)` and `long(ptr)` use the standard explicit-conversion syntax and are not declared as operator overloads on the record.

title: IntPtr declares no arithmetic operator
rule: `IntPtr` is a compiler-intrinsic value type. Its members are: `IntPtr.Zero`, `=` and `<>` for null tests, and explicit conversions to and from `long` and `ulong`. `IntPtr` is opaque; no arithmetic operator is among them, and §25.4 admits no user-declared conversion or operator on it.

title: a static method reference is admitted at a plain callback parameter
rule: At a plain (un-`env`-paired) function-typed parameter, the callback must be a static method reference or a non-capturing lambda: both lower to a bare C function pointer with no environment.

title: a non-capturing lambda is admitted at a plain callback parameter
rule: At a plain (un-`env`-paired) function-typed parameter, the callback must be a static method reference or a non-capturing lambda.

title: a bound instance-method reference is rejected at a plain callback parameter
rule: A bound instance-method reference (`obj.Method`) and a capturing lambda are rejected there -- each carries an environment (the receiver / the captures) that a bare function pointer cannot represent.

title: a capturing lambda is rejected at a plain callback parameter
rule: A bound instance-method reference (`obj.Method`) and a capturing lambda are rejected there -- each carries an environment (the receiver / the captures) that a bare function pointer cannot represent.

title: a bound instance-method reference is admitted at an env-paired callback parameter
rule: The pair makes the callback parameter capture-admitting: any function value -- including a capturing lambda and a bound instance-method reference `this.OnRow` -- may be passed there.

title: a capturing lambda is admitted at an env-paired callback parameter
rule: The pair makes the callback parameter capture-admitting: any function value -- including a capturing lambda ... -- may be passed there.

title: env pairing does not combine with variadic(N)
rule: `env` pairing does not combine with `variadic(N)`: a variadic call's trailing-slot ABI is caller-shaped per call, and no corpus case pairs the two.

title: Interop.LastErrno is read synchronously before the error message is built
rule: `Interop.LastErrno()` reads the calling thread's C `errno` directly. It is valid only when read before the next extern call or runtime operation on the thread.

title: the symbol alias clause binds a declaration to a different symbol name
rule: The alias clause `:= symbol "name"`, written after the return clause, binds the declaration to the named symbol instead.

title: several declarations of different shapes may bind one symbol
rule: Several declarations, of any mix of shapes, may bind one symbol.

title: variadic(N) with N equal to the declared arity is the sound fixed-arity binding
rule: `N` equal to the arity is legal and load-bearing ("call this variadic symbol with zero variadic arguments" -- the only sound minimum-arity binding of a variadic symbol).

title: variadic(N) with N less than the declared arity passes the trailing parameters variadically
rule: `variadic(N)` on the symbol clause declares: the named symbol is a C-variadic function whose fixed parameters are the first N declared parameters; the remaining declared parameters pass in the symbol's variadic slots.

title: a float in a variadic position is rejected in favor of double
rule: Declaring `float`, `bool`, `byte`, `sbyte`, `short`, or `ushort` in a variadic position is a compile error naming the type to write ("C promotes `float` variadic arguments to `double`; declare the parameter as `double`").

title: Ptr<T> members are usable over admitted pointee types
rule: `T` is drawn from the FFI-pointee set: integer types, `float`, `double`, `bool`, `IntPtr`, `UIntPtr`, and C-compatible records.

title: Ptr<Ptr<T>> is not admitted
rule: `Ptr<Ptr<U>>` is not admitted (v1 decline; `Ptr<IntPtr>` plus explicit `FromIntPtr` re-typing expresses every `T**` shape).

title: Ptr<T> instantiated at a class type is rejected
rule: The pointee gate (per-instantiation): `T` is drawn from the FFI-pointee set; a class type is not a member of it.

title: Ptr<T> is admitted at a C-compatible record pointee
rule: `T` is drawn from the FFI-pointee set: integer types, `float`, `double`, `bool`, `IntPtr`, `UIntPtr`, and C-compatible records.

title: a record of only FFI-compatible scalar fields is C-compatible and admitted by address
rule: A record is C-compatible iff every field's type is an FFI-compatible scalar ... Admission -- by address: as `ref`/`out` extern parameters.

title: a record with a string field is not C-compatible and rejected as a ref parameter
rule: Everything else disqualifies: `string`, `char`, `decimal`, nullable types, enums, class/interface/function-typed fields.

title: a single-field record over an integer scalar is admitted directly by value
rule: Typed handles: the single-field admission. A C-compatible record with exactly one field, of integer or pointer scalar type, is FFI-compatible directly -- parameter, return, `ref`/`out`, and callback positions -- marshalling exactly as its field.

title: a single-field record over a double is not admitted directly by value
rule: Float/double single-field records join Stage D; `bool` is excluded to avoid pinning an aggregate-normalization rule nothing needs.

title: a qualifying Main in a dependency artifact is inert
rule: A public static method Main declared on a class in the root compilation is the entry point. A qualifying signature in a dependency artifact is inert — never selected, never a conflict, an ordinary method. `Dep` even declares two qualifying overloads, which would be a §33.5 ambiguity error in a root compilation, yet it compiles as a dependency and never perturbs `App`'s build.

title: a dependency's Main stays inert even when its class is used by the root
rule: Every Bezel executable has exactly one entry point: a `public static method Main` declared on a class in the root compilation. A qualifying signature in a dependency artifact is inert — never selected, never a conflict, an ordinary method — and that holds for a dependency class the root compilation actually references, not only for one it merely imports.

title: Main() with no parameters and no return type qualifies
rule: `public static method Main()` is one of the eight accepted entry-point signatures.

title: Main(args) with no return type qualifies
rule: `public static method Main(args: Array<string>)` is one of the eight accepted entry-point signatures.

title: Main(): int qualifies
rule: `public static method Main(): int` is one of the eight accepted entry-point signatures.

title: Main(args): int qualifies
rule: `public static method Main(args: Array<string>): int` is one of the eight accepted entry-point signatures.

title: async Main(): Task qualifies
rule: `public static async method Main(): Task` is one of the eight accepted entry-point signatures.

title: async Main(args): Task qualifies
rule: `public static async method Main(args: Array<string>): Task` is one of the eight accepted entry-point signatures.

title: async Main(): Task<int> qualifies
rule: `public static async method Main(): Task<int>` is one of the eight accepted entry-point signatures.

title: async Main(args): Task<int> qualifies
rule: `public static async method Main(args: Array<string>): Task<int>` is one of the eight accepted entry-point signatures.

title: a private static Main overload does not conflict with a qualifying one
rule: `Main` must be `public` and `static`. A signature outside the eight accepted forms does not qualify as an entry point; a method named `Main` with a non-qualifying signature is an ordinary method.

title: an instance Main overload does not conflict with a qualifying one
rule: An instance method named `Main` does not qualify. (A class may still declare a non-qualifying `Main` alongside a qualifying one.)

title: Environment.Exit unwinds nothing - no finally runs and no using var is disposed
rule: **The calling thread's stack is not unwound:** no `finally` block of any live frame runs, no `using var`, owned local, `owned` parameter or unbound owned temporary of any live frame is disposed, and no suspended frame of any domain resumes — their owned state is reclaimed by the process exit, not by disposal

title: Environment.Exit inside the exit pass ends the pass and leaves unreached statics undisposed
rule: **Inside the exit pass** — from a destructor the pass runs, or from a lazy static initializer a first touch there triggers (§22.13) — the call neither re-initiates the sequence nor is a no-op: it ends the pass where it stands, and the process exits at once with its `code` ... every static `owned` field and owning-inline-array slot the pass had not yet reached is reclaimed by the process exit, never disposed

title: a class declaring two qualifying Main overloads is rejected
rule: A program is ill-formed if more than one method qualifies as the entry point ... within a single class (one class declaring more than one of the eight signature shapes). A class that overloads `Main` with multiple qualifying signatures is rejected at compile time.

title: only one overload qualifying resolves the entry point cleanly
rule: A class may declare at most one qualifying `Main`; making the second overload non-qualifying (here, `private`) removes the conflict.

title: two classes each declaring a qualifying Main is rejected
rule: A program is ill-formed if more than one method qualifies as the entry point. This applies across classes (multiple classes each declaring a qualifying `Main`). Without disambiguation, the compiler produces an error listing every qualifying `Main` it found.

title: only one class declaring a qualifying Main resolves cleanly
rule: An instance method named `Main` does not qualify; making the second class's `Main` an instance method removes the cross-class conflict.

title: standard documentation tags on a type and its members are accepted
rule: Documentation comments use XML element syntax. Recognized tags include `<summary>`, `<param>`, `<returns>`, `<exception>`; the compiler preserves them in output metadata for documentation generators.

title: an unrecognized documentation tag is preserved, not rejected
rule: Unrecognized tags are preserved verbatim in the same metadata: recognition affects only how documentation tooling may render a tag, never compilation.

title: a documentation comment not immediately before a declaration still compiles
rule: Documentation comments are meaningful only immediately before a declaration; the compiler preserves comments but does not interpret their content or restrict their placement.

title: a documented entry point compiles and runs unaffected
rule: The compiler preserves documentation comments for documentation generators but does not interpret their content — compilation and runtime behavior are unaffected.

title: generic type parameters are documented with typemref and typemname tags
rule: Recognized tags include <typeparam>, <typeparamref>, and <paramref> — generic declarations are documented like any other.

title: additional recognized documentation tags are accepted
rule: Recognized tags include <remarks>, <example>, <see>, and <seealso>.

title: the triple-slash form is the designated doc comment syntax
rule: Three comment forms (§1.5): // ... line comment, /* ... */ block comment, /// ... documentation comment.

title: an empty documentation comment compiles
rule: Three comment forms (§1.5): `// ...` line comment, `/* ... */` block comment, `/// ...` documentation comment.

title: a choice type satisfies the value constraint
rule: `where T: value` substitutions are non-nullable value types: records, enums, choices, primitives, inline arrays, the unit type.

title: a nullable choice type does not satisfy the value constraint
rule: `where T: value` substitutions are non-nullable value types — records, enums, choices, primitives, inline arrays, the unit type. A nullable value type does not satisfy the constraint.

title: a choice declares payload-free, value-payload, and owned-payload cases together
rule: A choice declares zero or more positional payload fields per case; a case with no payload list is payload-free; the owned marker is admissible on a class-typed payload field.

title: a case name colliding with a member name is rejected
rule: Case names must be distinct within the choice; a case name may not collide with any member name of the choice (the §11.3 member rules apply with cases counted as members).

title: duplicate case names within one choice are rejected
rule: Case names are PascalCase by convention and must be distinct within the choice.

title: a payload field of the choice's own type is rejected
rule: A choice payload field may not, directly or transitively through value-typed components, have the declaring choice's own type: a value type cannot contain itself.

title: a payload transitively containing the choice's own type via a record is rejected
rule: A choice payload field may not, directly or transitively through value-typed components (record fields, inline-array elements, other choices' payloads), have the declaring choice's own type.

title: owned on a primitive-typed payload field is rejected
rule: The owned payload marker's admissibility follows §28.1's type requirement: admissible on class types, interface types, and bare type parameters; a compile error on any other type.

title: owned on a move-only-value payload field is admitted but redundant
rule: The owned payload marker is admitted-but-redundant on move-only value types (an owning inline array, or another owning choice).

title: a destructor in a choice body is rejected
rule: Choices cannot have destructors, constructors, instance fields, block-form or storage-backed properties, indexers, or nested types — the same restriction set as enums, plus one: a choice's instance storage is its cases' payloads.

title: a constructor in a choice body is rejected
rule: Choices cannot have destructors, constructors, instance fields, block-form or storage-backed properties, indexers, or nested types.

title: an instance field in a choice body is rejected
rule: Choices cannot have destructors, constructors, instance fields, block-form or storage-backed properties, indexers, or nested types.

title: a choice body admits exactly what an enum body admits
rule: A choice body may declare, after the case list, exactly what an enum body may: instance methods, expression-bodied read-only instance properties, static methods, static readonly fields, const members, and operator overloads.

title: a virtual method on a choice is rejected
rule: Choice members are statically dispatched; virtual and abstract are rejected as on enums and records.

title: override on a non-Object-virtual choice member is rejected
rule: override is admitted exactly where §10.5 admits it — the Object-virtual surface, spelled override or plain — and is rejected on every other member.

title: override ToString is admitted on a choice
rule: §10.5's Equals/GetHashCode/ToString replacement rule carries over for the boxable classifications, spelled override or plain.

title: a plain Equals/GetHashCode member is declarable on an owning choice
rule: A choice of any classification — owning and borrow-bearing included — may declare plain Equals(other: C): bool and GetHashCode(): int members, statically dispatched like every choice method; on a non-boxable classification they replace nothing and are reachable by static dispatch only.

title: a Result combinator is rejected at an owning receiver instantiation
rule: Map, MapError, AndThen, and UnwrapOr are admissible only where the receiver instantiation and the member's result instantiation are both value-like (§35.4 rule 3); the rejection lands at the use site under §3.6 rule 2, the diagnostic naming the classification.

title: a static owned readonly field is admitted in a choice body
rule: A choice body may declare static readonly fields, including static owned readonly.

title: a declared homogeneous `=` overload on a choice replaces the generated one
rule: A choice body may declare operator overloads; records, enums, and choices may overload = and <>, and a homogeneous overload disqualifies the choice from auto-hashable, §25.2's co-declaration rule then supplying the equality surface.

title: an override Equals taking Object? on a choice is rejected
rule: and an `Equals` taking `Object?` or `Object` rejected in either spelling, at every classification, as §10.5 rejects it on an enum

title: a plain Equals taking Object? on a choice is rejected
rule: and an `Equals` taking `Object?` or `Object` rejected in either spelling, at every classification, as §10.5 rejects it on an enum

title: an override Equals taking the choice's own type is admitted
rule: `override` admitted exactly where §10.5 admits it on an enum — `Equals` taking the choice's own type, `GetHashCode()` and `ToString()`

title: a choice overriding Equals(Object?) needs GetHashCode even with an own-typed Equals
rule: A type that overrides `Equals` must also override `GetHashCode`. The compiler enforces this (v0.338, §8.3).

title: qualified case construction resolves a payload-free and a payload case
rule: Construction is qualified, resolving exactly as enum constants do: FetchOutcome.NotModified for a payload-free case (a value expression, not a call), FetchOutcome.Failed(504, "upstream timeout") for a payload case.

title: a bare unqualified case name outside a declared-result position is rejected
rule: In expression position outside a declared-result position the qualified form is required, exactly as for enum constants outside their scrutinee.

title: a bare case construction in a declared-result position resolves against the declared type
rule: In a declared-result position — the top-level operand of a return statement in a body with a declared return type — where the declared type is a choice instantiation that declares a case named N, the form N(args) is a case construction.

title: generic choice construction omitting type arguments is rejected
rule: For a generic choice the type arguments are written at the construction; the declared type supplies the choice type and all its type arguments whole — the generic type with no arguments (Result.Ok(v)) remains an error.

title: generic choice construction with explicit type arguments is admitted
rule: For a generic choice the type arguments are written at the construction: Result<int, string>.Ok(value).

title: the declared-result case reading does not extend into a subexpression position
rule: The case reading takes exactly the declared-result group and does not extend beyond it — not to subexpression positions within a return operand: in return (if c then Ok(v) else Error(e)); the branches are operands of the (if) atom and resolve ordinarily.

title: a named owned binding to an owned payload slot requires the move marker
rule: An argument to an owned payload slot is an owned-consuming position: a named owned binding requires the call-site marker (move resp) and is left moved-from.

title: constructing a holds-borrows choice from a temporary is rejected
rule: An argument to a plain class- or interface-typed payload slot is a borrow, and §9.7's no-temporary-source rule applies verbatim: constructing a choice that holds borrows from a temporary bound to a borrow-carrying payload is rejected.

title: a qualified payload-free case written with an empty argument list is a compile error
rule: Construction is qualified, resolving exactly as enum constants do (§10.1): `FetchOutcome.NotModified` for a payload-free case (**a value expression, not a call**) (§35.3, v0.340). `Outcome.Nothing` is a value of type `Outcome`; a choice type is not callable (§27.1), so `Outcome.Nothing()` has no meaning and is a compile error (owner ruling #7048, reading 1).

title: a qualified payload-free case, a qualified payload case and a bare declared-result case are accepted
rule: Construction is qualified, resolving exactly as enum constants do (§10.1): `FetchOutcome.NotModified` for a payload-free case (**a value expression, not a call**) (§35.3, v0.340). `Outcome.Nothing` is a value of type `Outcome`; a choice type is not callable (§27.1), so `Outcome.Nothing()` has no meaning and is a compile error (owner ruling #7048, reading 1). Control for #7048: `Outcome.Nothing`, `Outcome.Got("x")` and a bare `Nothing` in a declared-result position (§35.3) are the accepted spellings.

title: a bare case construction whose argument count differs from the payload is the arity error
rule: Within a declared-result position whose type *is* such a choice, the case reading is **authoritative**: it wins over any same-named local, parameter, member, or type in scope (§35.3, v0.340). The member `Program.Got(a, b)` does not win over the case `Got(body)`, so `return Got(1, 2);` is a case construction that supplies 2 arguments for a one-field payload, an arity error.

title: a bare case construction in a declared-result position binds its argument against the payload type
rule: Within a declared-result position whose type *is* such a choice, the case reading is **authoritative** and "Payload arguments bind to the case's payload fields as to a parameter list" (§35.3, v0.340). The member `Program.Got(a: int)` does not win, and the `int` argument does not convert to the `string` payload `body`.

title: a same-named member does not win over a case in a declared-result position and the compiler warns
rule: Within a declared-result position whose type *is* such a choice, the case reading is **authoritative**: it wins over any same-named local, parameter, member, or type in scope, and the compiler warns on such shadowing (§35.3, v0.340). The member `Ok` would return `Error("member")`; the case `Ok(1)` is constructed instead, so the match prints `case 1`.

title: a local function value named like a case does not win over the case in a declared-result return
rule: the case reading is **authoritative**: it wins over any same-named local, parameter, member, or type in scope, and the compiler warns on such shadowing (§35.3, v0.340). The local `Got` (a lambda returning `NotModified`) is shadowed, so `return Got("x");` constructs the case with payload `x`.

title: a parameter or local named like the choice type does not disturb the declared-result case reading
rule: where the declared type — nullability stripped — is a choice instantiation `C<…>` (or non-generic choice `C`) that declares a case named `N`: the form `N(args)` is a case construction of `C<…>.N(args)`, and the bare identifier `N` is the payload-free case value `C<…>.N` (§35.3, v0.340). The parameter `Fetch: int` and the local `Result := 4` have the names of the choice types; the cases `NotModified`, `Got` and `Ok` are still constructed, and the payload `Ok(Result)` reads the local.

title: a case with the same name as its choice is constructed bare in a declared-result position
rule: where the declared type — nullability stripped — is a choice instantiation `C<…>` (or non-generic choice `C`) that declares a case named `N`: the form `N(args)` is a case construction of `C<…>.N(args)`, and the bare identifier `N` is the payload-free case value `C<…>.N` (§35.3, v0.340). The choice `Wrap` declares a case `Wrap(n)`: `return Wrap(n);` is the case construction `Wrap.Wrap(n)` and `return Empty;` the payload-free case.

title: a nested choice type is the declared result for bare case constructions
rule: where the declared type — nullability stripped — is a choice instantiation `C<…>` (or non-generic choice `C`) that declares a case named `N`: the form `N(args)` is a case construction of `C<…>.N(args)`, and the bare identifier `N` is the payload-free case value `C<…>.N` (§35.3, v0.340). The declared type `Outer.Inner` is a non-generic choice that declares `A` and `B`.

title: a generic choice instantiated by a generic class is the declared result for bare case constructions
rule: a written choice instantiation inside a generic body (`method M<T>(): Result<T, string>`) fires normally (§35.3, v0.340): the declared `Opt<T>` of `Holder<T>.Get` supplies the choice, so `No` and `Some(x)` are `Opt<T>.No` and `Opt<T>.Some(x)`.

title: a nullable declared choice result target-types through the stripped form
rule: A declared nullable `C<…>?` target-types through the stripped form and the result converts by §5.1's `T → T?` wrapping (§35.3, v0.340): `Ok(n)` and `Error("neg")` in a `Result<int, string>?` result are `Result<int, string>` cases wrapped to the nullable type, and `null` stays null.

title: a block-bodied property getter return is a declared-result position
rule: the top-level operand of a `return e;` statement in a body with a declared return type (§21.7); the expression body of a member or accessor checked against a declared type (§22.2, §23.2, §23.3) (§35.3, v0.340). The block getter of `F: Fetch` returns bare `NotModified` and `Got("blk")`.

title: an operator method expression body under a declared choice return is a declared-result position
rule: the expression body of a member or accessor checked against a declared type (§22.2 ...) (§35.3, v0.340): the operator `+` declares `Cmp`, so `More(a.n + b.n)` is `Cmp.More(...)`.

title: a method of the choice itself uses the bare case in a declared-result expression body
rule: where the declared type — nullability stripped — is a choice instantiation `C<…>` (or non-generic choice `C`) that declares a case named `N`: the form `N(args)` is a case construction of `C<…>.N(args)`, and the bare identifier `N` is the payload-free case value `C<…>.N` (§35.3, v0.340). Inside `Fetch`, `Reset(): Fetch => NotModified` is a declared-result expression body, so the bare name is the case value.

title: an ascribed lambda return in a declared-result position constructs bare cases
rule: a `return e;` statement or expression body checked against a lambda's return-type ascription (§27.3) is a declared-result position (§35.3, v0.340): the lambdas ascribed `Result<..>` construct `Ok(...)`/`Error(...)` bare, in the expression body and in the block body. The four iterations (4..7) give ids 4+5+6+7 = 22 and string lengths 2, 2, then `Error` -> 100, 100.

title: an async method returning a choice-bearing Task builds bare cases by return and expression body
rule: for an `async` body, the declared `Task<T>`'s result type, per §30.1's completion rule is the declared type (§35.3, v0.340): `Later` returns `Error(...)` or `Ok(...)` bare as `Task<Result<string, string>>`, and `Fe(n) => Ok(n)` is an expression body. For n = 0..3: `Error("even0")` -> 1, `Ok("odd1")` -> 4, 1, 4, total 10; `Fe(7)` is `Ok(7)`.

title: a generic method returning a generic choice builds an owned payload bare and frees it
rule: Payload-argument binding and ownership are exactly the qualified form's (§35.3, v0.340): `Ok(move x)` in `Wrap<T>(x: owned T): Result<T, string>` transfers the owned payload into the choice, which owns it, so the destructor of each `Res` runs once when `r` leaves its scope: for i = 0..2 the count is 3 and `k` = 3 x (1 + 3) + (0 + 1 + 2) = 15.

title: a bare case name as a field initializer is not target-typed
rule: The case reading takes exactly the declared-result group ... and does not extend beyond it: ... not to `var` initialization, typed local declarations, field initializers, default parameter values, or typed assignment targets (§35.3, v0.340); a field initializer is such a position. Outside the family a bare case name keeps its ordinary resolution, and `NotModified` names nothing.

title: a bare case name as a default parameter value is not target-typed
rule: The case reading takes exactly the declared-result group ... and does not extend beyond it: ... not to `var` initialization, typed local declarations, field initializers, default parameter values, or typed assignment targets (§35.3, v0.340); a default parameter value is such a position. Outside the family a bare case name keeps its ordinary resolution, and `NotModified` names nothing.

title: a bare case name as a typed assignment target value is not target-typed
rule: The case reading takes exactly the declared-result group ... and does not extend beyond it: ... not to `var` initialization, typed local declarations, field initializers, default parameter values, or typed assignment targets (§35.3, v0.340); a typed assignment to an existing local is such a position. Outside the family a bare case name keeps its ordinary resolution, and `NotModified` names nothing.

title: a bare case name in a yield return is not target-typed
rule: The declared-result position is "the top-level operand of a `return e;` statement" (§35.3, v0.340); a `yield return` operand is not one, so `NotModified` keeps its ordinary resolution and names nothing.

title: a bare case construction in an unascribed lambda block is not target-typed
rule: not to lambdas whose return type arrives only by target inference (no ascription written) (§35.3, v0.340): the block lambda has no ascription, so `Got("inner")` names nothing.

title: a bare case name in a lambda typed only by its target is not target-typed
rule: not to lambdas whose return type arrives only by target inference (no ascription written) (§35.3, v0.340): the target `() -> Fetch` supplies the type, with no ascription, so `NotModified` names nothing.

title: a qualified payload-free case written with an empty argument list in an expression body is rejected
rule: Construction is qualified ... `FetchOutcome.NotModified` for a payload-free case (a value expression, not a call). The qualified construction of a payload-free case is the case value itself; an argument list on it is the §35.5 arity error.

title: the same expression body with the payload-free case written as a value is admitted
rule: Construction is qualified ... `FetchOutcome.NotModified` for a payload-free case (a value expression, not a call).

title: a nested choice's payload-free case written with an empty argument list is rejected
rule: Construction is qualified ... `FetchOutcome.NotModified` for a payload-free case (a value expression, not a call). The qualification of a nested choice reads through the enclosing declaration, and the case value it names takes no argument list.

title: the same nested payload-free case written as a value is admitted
rule: Construction is qualified ... `FetchOutcome.NotModified` for a payload-free case (a value expression, not a call).

title: a generic choice's payload-free case written with an empty argument list is rejected
rule: For a generic choice the type arguments are written at the construction (Result<int, string>.Ok(value)) ... the same qualified-construction reading applies, and a payload-free case is a value expression, not a call.

title: the same generic payload-free case written as a value is admitted
rule: For a generic choice the type arguments are written at the construction (Result<int, string>.Ok(value)); a payload-free case is a value expression, not a call.

title: a payload-free case written with an empty argument list inside an interpolation hole is rejected
rule: Construction is qualified ... `FetchOutcome.NotModified` for a payload-free case (a value expression, not a call). The hole of an interpolated string is an ordinary expression position, and the case value it names takes no argument list.

title: the same payload-free case in an interpolation hole, written as a value, is admitted
rule: Construction is qualified ... `FetchOutcome.NotModified` for a payload-free case (a value expression, not a call). The hole is an ordinary expression position, so the qualified value form is what appears there.

title: a payload-free case written with an empty argument list as a match arm's result is rejected
rule: Construction is qualified ... `FetchOutcome.NotModified` for a payload-free case (a value expression, not a call). An arm's result expression resolves ordinarily, and the qualified case value it names takes no argument list.

title: the same match arm with the payload-free case written as a value is admitted
rule: Construction is qualified ... `FetchOutcome.NotModified` for a payload-free case (a value expression, not a call).

title: a payload-free case reached through a type alias and written with an empty argument list is rejected
rule: Construction is qualified ... `FetchOutcome.NotModified` for a payload-free case (a value expression, not a call). A type alias names the same choice, and the case value reached through it takes no argument list either.

title: the same aliased payload-free case written as a value is admitted
rule: Construction is qualified ... `FetchOutcome.NotModified` for a payload-free case (a value expression, not a call).

title: a payload-free case written with a non-empty argument list is rejected
rule: A payload case written bare, or a payload-free case written with an argument list, is the arity error §35.5 names on the pattern side.

title: a payload-free case written with an empty argument list as an initializer is rejected
rule: Construction is qualified ... `FetchOutcome.NotModified` for a payload-free case (a value expression, not a call). A nullable choice's declared form does not make its case value callable.

title: the same nullable choice initialized from the payload-free case value is admitted
rule: Construction is qualified ... `FetchOutcome.NotModified` for a payload-free case (a value expression, not a call). The value converts into the nullable form by §5.1's `T → T?` wrapping.

title: a payload-free case written with an empty argument list as an equality operand is rejected
rule: Construction is qualified ... `FetchOutcome.NotModified` for a payload-free case (a value expression, not a call). The comparison's right operand is an ordinary expression, and the qualified case value it names takes no argument list.

title: the same equality against the payload-free case value is admitted and false
rule: Construction is qualified ... `FetchOutcome.NotModified` for a payload-free case (a value expression, not a call). The generated `=` is true exactly when both operands have the same active case and every payload compares equal (§35.7).

title: a payload-free case written with an empty argument list as a lambda body is rejected
rule: Construction is qualified ... `FetchOutcome.NotModified` for a payload-free case (a value expression, not a call). The lambda's expression body is an ordinary expression, and the qualified case value it names takes no argument list.

title: the same ascribed lambda body with the payload-free case written as a value is admitted
rule: Construction is qualified ... `FetchOutcome.NotModified` for a payload-free case (a value expression, not a call).

title: a value-like choice is an ordinary copyable value
rule: A value-like choice is an ordinary copyable value type: every payload is a value, a string, a runtime-managed type, or (transitively) a value-like record or choice.

title: owning choice local-to-local assignment moves, unmarked, and `using var` adopts
rule: Owning choices are move-only value types: local-to-local assignment moves (unmarked — copies are impossible, so there is nothing for a marker to disambiguate); `using var` is admitted with pin-only effect.

title: an owning choice that holds borrows may not be a class field
rule: An owning choice that holds borrows may not be a class field: it is the only move-only kind that can hold borrows, and the store would let the borrows outlive their sources.

title: disposing an owning choice disposes the active case's owned payloads in declaration order
rule: Disposal is defined by the active case. Disposing an owning choice value disposes the active case's owned payloads in payload declaration order; payload-free and value-payload cases dispose nothing.

title: drop-on-overwrite disposes the displaced owning-choice value at the store
rule: Drop-on-overwrite is defined and automatic: whole-value reassignment of an owning-choice local or field disposes the displaced value per §28.7; the RHS is evaluated first, then the displaced value is disposed, then the new value is stored.

title: Task<T> declared over an owning choice is a compile error at the declaration
rule: No §30.5 producer row admits a move-only value result, so a Task<T> or OwningTask<T> declared over an owning choice is a compile error at the declaration.

title: an owning-choice local under plain var auto-disposes at scope end and warns
