rule: Owning choices are move-only value types; locals are auto-disposed at scope end with the must-use warning (K3.14). Disposal is defined by the active case: it disposes the active case's owned payloads.

title: using var over an owning choice suppresses the must-use warning
rule: `using var` is admitted over an owning choice — it locks reassignment and suppresses the must-use warning on that auto-drop, the auto-dispose running either way.

title: an owning choice may not be a record field
rule: Owning choices are move-only value types and every section 15.3 rule applies as written: no move-only value may be a record field (records support only copy semantics, not move semantics).

title: a value-like choice is copyable and may be a record field
rule: Otherwise the choice is value-like: every payload is a value, a `string`, a runtime-managed type, or transitively a value-like record or choice. A value-like choice is an ordinary copyable value type, so section 15.3's move-only record-field ban does not reach it.

title: a choice that holds borrows is forbidden as an async parameter
rule: Every choice that holds borrows — whatever its classification — is subject to section 9.7's borrow-lifetime rules, and is forbidden as an `async` method's parameter or result (section 30.1).

title: a value-like choice holds no borrows and is admitted as an async parameter
rule: A value-like choice never holds borrows (rule 3's construction), so section 30.1's ban on a borrow-bearing parameter of an `async` method does not reach it.

title: the borrowing match is the default and leaves the scrutinee unchanged
rule: Matching a choice value non-destructively is the default everywhere: a pattern binding is a borrow whose source is the scrutinee's source; the scrutinee retains its ownership state; the construct never moves from the scrutinee.

title: an owning match is triggered by an unbound owned temporary
rule: The owning match is triggered by an unbound owned temporary of owning-choice classification — a fresh construction, an owning-choice-returning call, a move result; it transfers the selected case's owned payloads into the arm's bindings and consumes the scrutinee value.

title: an owning match is triggered by a named owned binding under `case move`
rule: The owning match is triggered by a named owned binding under an explicit scrutinee transfer marker — case move outcome of ...; the consumed binding is left moved-from when the construct completes.

title: the move marker on a fresh-producer scrutinee is rejected
rule: The marker on a borrowed or fresh-producer scrutinee is an error: an unmarked read never silently consumes, and a fresh producer needs no marker.

title: the move marker on a borrowed scrutinee (`this`) is rejected
rule: What does not trigger an owning match: an unmarked named-binding scrutinee; a borrowed scrutinee of any provenance (field read, parameter, this).

title: a discarded owned payload is disposed at construct completion
rule: Payloads not transferred into bindings — discarded slots like Fetched(_) — are disposed when the construct completes, by the same unbound-temporary pass that disposes the container.

title: a payload case matched bare with no arity is rejected
rule: A payload case may not be matched bare: Fetched without parentheses is a compile error naming the arity — matching a payload while ignoring it is spelled visibly as Fetched(_).

title: a marked named slot is rejected (the marker is retired at v0.338)
rule: A named slot **never transfers** ... `move` is not a slot spelling (`Fetched(move response = var r)` is a compile error at the pattern naming the positional form — retired v0.338)

title: a marked named slot in a borrowing match is rejected
rule: A named slot **never transfers** ... `move` is not a slot spelling (`Fetched(move response = var r)` is a compile error at the pattern naming the positional form — retired v0.338)

title: an unmarked named slot does not transfer, so its binding cannot be moved
rule: A named slot **never transfers**: a getter may not return a fresh owned value (§28.6), so no slot read can mint an obligation, and in an **owning match** (§35.5) an owned or move-only value payload matched by a named slot is borrowed during the arm and disposed at construct completion by the standard §35.5 machinery, exactly as a discarded slot

title: an owning-match arm binding left owning auto-drops with the must-use warning
rule: In an owning match, an `owned`-payload binding is an **owned local of the arm body's scope** ...: falling off the arm still owning the value auto-drops it with the must-use warning naming the binding and the standard remedies.

title: the using var move adoption in a do-end arm is warning-free
rule: The standard remedies are `using var u := move r;` adoption in a `do … end` arm, an owned-consuming call, an explicit `r.Dispose()`, `_ := r;`.

title: an owned-consuming call is an expression-position arm's warning-free discharge
rule: In *expression-position* arms (which cannot contain statements, §19.2), the warning-free discharges are an owned-consuming call (`RenderOwned(move r)`) or §19.2's helper-method extraction.

title: every declared case covered by an irrefutable arm needs no `_` arm
rule: Coverage is counted per case name, one level deep — a payload-free case by a constant-style pattern, a payload case by a destructuring whose every slot is irrefutable. When every case is covered, no _ arm is required.

title: a refutable slot arm contributes nothing to exhaustiveness
rule: Guarded arms and refutable-slot arms contribute nothing to the static proof for choice scrutinees.

title: a value-like choice is auto-hashable and its `=` compares active case and payloads
rule: A value-like choice is auto-hashable when every payload field of every case is an admissible component type. The generated = is true exactly when both operands have the same active case and every corresponding payload compares equal by its type's =.

title: the generated ToString renders TypeName.CaseName with its payloads
rule: The generated ToString produces TypeName.CaseName(field1: value1, ...), and TypeName.CaseName for a payload-free case.

title: comparing a non-auto-hashable owning choice without declared operators is a use-site error
rule: A choice that is not auto-hashable — any borrow-bearing or owning choice — draws a use-site compile error on =, <>, and direct Equals/GetHashCode calls, unless the author declares the operators under §25.2's co-declaration rule.

title: co-declared equality operators on a move-only choice bind borrows
rule: On a move-only choice, = / <> operands and the Equals(T) parameter bind borrows — both operands stay live after the operation.

title: direct Equals and GetHashCode calls are admitted on an owning choice that declares them
rule: The exemption for **direct `Equals`/`GetHashCode` calls** is keyed on the declared **members**, not on the operators: a choice that declares plain `Equals(other: C): bool` or `GetHashCode(): int` admits THAT call on **every** classification, owning and borrow-bearing included — they resolve statically to the declared members, so the exemption is per member and needs no pair (v0.301).

title: a direct Equals call on an owning choice that declares no such member is rejected
rule: A choice that is **not** auto-hashable — any borrow-bearing or owning choice — draws §9.2's use-site compile error on `=`, `<>`, and direct `Equals`/`GetHashCode` calls, unless the author declares the member itself.

title: a `T?` payload at a generic choice argument renders `null` when absent
rule: The generated ToString produces TypeName.CaseName(field1: value1, ...), and TypeName.CaseName for a payload-free case — and §8.5's choice row fixes the head UNQUALIFIED ("Status.Active(code: 7)", not "Conf.Status.Active(code: 7)"). Each payload renders as its own ToString renders it. A `T?` payload is an admissible component (§9.2 admits `T?` where `T` is admissible, and §35.7 adds another auto-hashable choice as an admissible component — `Col?` is one), so the generated rendering exists and an absent payload renders as `null`.

title: a value-like choice boxes through interface conformance
rule: Value-like choices box per the general rule; the box is runtime-managed.

title: converting an owning choice to an interface is a rejected boxing conversion
rule: Owning choices cannot be boxed. The conformance declaration remains legal, but the conversion of an owning value to an interface or Object type is rejected at the conversion site.

title: calling Dispose on a choice value is rejected
rule: Dispose stays off the surface everywhere: choices do not implement IDisposable — an owning choice's disposal obligation is discharged by its holder, never by calling Dispose() on it.

title: an owning choice passed to Console.Error.WriteLine is a boxing and is rejected
rule: Owning choices cannot be boxed (spec 35.8, v0.350): boxing copies, and a move-only value cannot be copied. The conversion of an owning value to an interface or Object type is rejected at the conversion site. Console.WriteLine, Console.Write and TextWriter members take their argument as Object, so passing an owning choice there is such a conversion.

title: an owning choice passed to Console.Out.WriteLine is a boxing and is rejected
rule: Owning choices cannot be boxed (spec 35.8, v0.350): boxing copies, and a move-only value cannot be copied. The conversion of an owning value to an interface or Object type is rejected at the conversion site. Console.WriteLine, Console.Write and TextWriter members take their argument as Object, so passing an owning choice there is such a conversion.

title: an owning choice passed to Console.WriteLine by named argument is a boxing and is rejected
rule: Owning choices cannot be boxed (spec 35.8, v0.350): boxing copies, and a move-only value cannot be copied. The conversion of an owning value to an interface or Object type is rejected at the conversion site. Console.WriteLine, Console.Write and TextWriter members take their argument as Object, so passing an owning choice there is such a conversion.

title: an owning choice passed to StringBuilder.Append is a boxing and is rejected
rule: Owning choices cannot be boxed (spec 35.8, v0.350): boxing copies, and a move-only value cannot be copied. The conversion of an owning value to an interface or Object type is rejected at the conversion site. Console.WriteLine, Console.Write and TextWriter members take their argument as Object, so passing an owning choice there is such a conversion.

title: an owning choice passed to a user method taking Object is rejected at the conversion site
rule: Owning choices cannot be boxed (spec 35.8, v0.350): boxing copies, and a move-only value cannot be copied. The conversion of an owning value to an interface or Object type is rejected at the conversion site. Console.WriteLine, Console.Write and TextWriter members take their argument as Object, so passing an owning choice there is such a conversion.

title: an instantiation of a generic choice with an owning payload cannot be boxed (per instantiation)
rule: Owning choices cannot be boxed (spec 35.8, v0.350): boxing copies, and a move-only value cannot be copied. The conversion of an owning value to an interface or Object type is rejected at the conversion site. Console.WriteLine, Console.Write and TextWriter members take their argument as Object, so passing an owning choice there is such a conversion. For a generic choice the rule is per instantiation (spec 35.8, 3.6 rule 2): Rs<Res, string> is owning.

title: a nullable owning choice boxes as its non-nullable form and is rejected
rule: Owning choices cannot be boxed (spec 35.8, v0.350): boxing copies, and a move-only value cannot be copied. The conversion of an owning value to an interface or Object type is rejected at the conversion site. Console.WriteLine, Console.Write and TextWriter members take their argument as Object, so passing an owning choice there is such a conversion. A nullable value type boxes as its non-nullable form (spec 8.6 Nullable value-type boxing), so OC2? is the owning choice OC2 at the conversion.

title: an owning choice with a declared ToString renders through it; a match reads the other case
rule: An owning choice cannot be boxed, but a ToString() call at its own static type is not a boxing: a declared ToString member is called in place on the borrowed storage (spec 35.8 and 8.5, v0.350).

title: a generic function over an unconstrained T prints a value-like instantiation (int) through Object
rule: Boxing is per instantiation (spec 35.8, 3.6 rule 2, v0.350): at T = int the value-like int boxes normally and prints.

title: an owning choice that declares ToString is still not boxable: StringBuilder.Append(bx.W) is rejected
rule: Owning** choices **cannot be boxed**

title: an owning choice passed to StringBuilder.Append by named argument value is rejected
rule: Owning** choices **cannot be boxed**

title: a payload-free case of an owning choice (declared owned Array<int> payload) is not boxable either
rule: Owning** choices **cannot be boxed**

title: an owned-field receiver chain does not exempt an owning-choice Append argument from the boxing rule
rule: Owning** choices **cannot be boxed**

title: value-like choices box at StringBuilder.Append, plain, nullable, generic and string-payload alike
rule: **Value-like** choices box per the general rule; the box is runtime-managed.

title: assigning null into an owned-state C? location disposes the displaced value
rule: For an owning C, x := null; on an owned C? location is drop-on-overwrite — the displaced value's payloads are disposed.

title: default(C?) is a valid null move-only value for an owning C
rule: For an owning C, the wrapper C? is itself move-only, and default(C?) is a valid null move-only value, on the precedent of §17.11's owning-inline-array form.

title: default(C) is a compile error for every choice type
rule: default(C) is a compile error for every choice type — no choice is defaultable: a sum yields no distinguished zero.

title: choices never satisfy where T: new()
rule: Choices never satisfy the value-type arm of where T: new() — a consequence of the property: no choice is defaultable.

title: nameof on a choice case yields the case's bare identifier
rule: nameof(FetchOutcome.Failed) yields "Failed".

title: a generic choice's classification is evaluated per instantiation
rule: Classification is evaluated per instantiation: a choice with Ok(owned value: T) is value-like at T = int (marker erased, payload an admissible value) and owning at T = Connection (marker means owned).

title: choices are invariant in their type parameters
rule: No variance. Variance attaches to interface and function-type parameters only; choices, like records and classes, are invariant. A Result<Derived, E> is not a Result<Base, E>; the conversion is an explicit re-wrap by match.

title: a generic choice at a borrow-bearing record payload is borrow-bearing and = is rejected
rule: An *unmarked* bare-type-parameter payload is classification-neutral at a runtime-managed substitution and at a copyable value substitution that carries no borrow ... and **borrow-carrying** at a class or interface substitution and at a value substitution that holds borrows (... so `Opt<Pair>` over `record Pair(It: Item)` is borrow-bearing by rule 2 and draws §35.7's use-site error on `=`)

title: the same generic choice at a borrow-free record payload is value-like and compares
rule: An *unmarked* bare-type-parameter payload is classification-neutral at a runtime-managed substitution and at a copyable value substitution that carries no borrow ... and **borrow-carrying** at a class or interface substitution and at a value substitution that holds borrows (... so `Opt<Pair>` over `record Pair(It: Item)` is borrow-bearing by rule 2 and draws §35.7's use-site error on `=`)

title: a borrow-bearing choice is never sendable
rule: Borrow-bearing choices are never sendable (they carry origin-domain borrows).

title: an owning choice is not directly sendable
rule: Owning choices are not directly sendable — the §30.14 move-only exclusion, unchanged.

title: an owning-choice field of a transfer-closed class is admitted when the choice holds no borrows
rule: §30.14's transfer-closure rule 2 admits an owning-choice-typed field of a transfer-closed class when the choice holds no borrows and every payload field of every case is transfer-compatible.

title: a choice type in an extern signature is rejected
rule: Choices are not FFI-compatible: the honest C spelling of a sum carries real ABI questions the language does not promise to resolve.

title: ReadKey is the assert-shaped throwing tier at end of input
rule: Console.ReadKey() blocks for one key and raises EndOfStreamException at end of input; per the failure-signal rule, end of input is band 2's expected absence, but ReadKey stays the throwing tier because absence there is a bug at its call sites.

title: ReadKeyOrNull is the *OrNull twin, answering the same absence with null
rule: The *OrNull convenience tier answers the same expected-absence condition its throwing twin raises on; Console.ReadKeyOrNull() returns null at end of input where Console.ReadKey() raises EndOfStreamException.

title: a negative constructor magnitude raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException
rule: Every constructor parameter that states a magnitude -- capacity, size, length -- raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException when passed a negative value; StringBuilder(capacity) is one of the named members.

title: a zero constructor magnitude is valid, not a fault
rule: Negative magnitudes fault; zero is valid -- a magnitude-taking constructor such as StringBuilder(capacity) constructs successfully at capacity zero, and the instance is fully usable afterward.

title: Try shape (c) assigns default(T) to the out parameter on the false path
rule: Try shape (c) -- bool + non-nullable value-typed out -- assigns default(T) to the out parameter when the operation declines. Convert.TryToInt32 is this shape over a concrete value-type payload.

title: Try shape (c) assigns the parsed value on the true path
rule: Try shape (c) assigns the real, non-default value to the out parameter when the operation succeeds; Convert.TryToInt32 returns true and the parsed integer on well-formed input.

title: ReadLine returns null at end of input
rule: Console.ReadLine() returns null at end of input.

title: WriteLine(Object) invokes the argument's ToString override
rule: The Object overloads of Console.Write/WriteLine invoke ToString().

title: Write does not append a line terminator, unlike WriteLine
rule: Console.Write(value) writes value with no terminator; consecutive Write calls land on the same output line, unlike WriteLine which terminates it.

title: Out exposes the process's standard-output stream
rule: Console is a static class providing process-level standard output, and Out is a readonly TextWriter property over it; a file that imports a module may call the public members of a value reachable through its surface without importing the value's own declaring module (System.IO).

title: Round uses banker's rounding at a midpoint
rule: Math.Round(x, digits) rounds using banker's rounding; a midpoint such as 2.5 rounds to the nearest even integer, 2, not 3.

title: Clamp raises ArgumentException when low exceeds high
rule: Math.Clamp<T>(value, low, high) raises ArgumentException when low is greater than high.

title: DivRem raises DivideByZeroException when the divisor is zero
rule: Math.DivRem(a, b, out remainder) raises DivideByZeroException when b = 0, the same fault the / operator raises.

title: Sign yields 0 for NaN rather than -1 or 1
rule: Math.Sign<T>(x) is two < tests against T.Zero(), so a NaN operand yields 0.

title: Fmod and IEEERemainder may disagree in sign on the same operands
rule: Fmod(x, y) returns a result with the same sign as x; IEEERemainder(x, y) may have the opposite sign from x -- unlike Fmod.

title: the decimal overload of Abs returns a decimal
rule: The declaration "public static pure method Abs(x: decimal): decimal;" returns a decimal, and a decimal times `0m` is the decimal zero, which renders `0`.

title: Floor of a negative decimal rounds toward negative infinity
rule: The declaration "public static pure method Floor(x: decimal): decimal;" rounds "toward negative infinity", each result an "integral value; exact, never faults". Floor(-1.5m) is -2.

title: Ceiling of a negative decimal rounds toward positive infinity
rule: The declaration "public static pure method Ceiling(x: decimal): decimal;" rounds "toward positive infinity", each result an "integral value; exact, never faults". Ceiling(-1.5m) is -1.

title: Truncate of a negative decimal rounds toward zero
rule: The declaration "public static pure method Truncate(x: decimal): decimal;" is commented "Truncate is toward zero." Truncate(-1.5m) is -1.

title: Sign of a negative decimal is -1
rule: public static method Sign<T>(x: T): int where T: INumber<T>; returns "-1, 0, or 1", and "The primitive numeric tower (`byte`…`ulong`, `float`, `double`, `decimal`) conforms to the standard-library `INumber<T>`" ([§11.8]); Sign(-0.5m) is -1.

title: Max<decimal> over byte operands returns the decimal maximum
rule: `Max(a, b)` returns `a` when `a.CompareTo(b) >= 0` and `b` otherwise ...

title: Sign of an unsigned operand above the signed maximum is 1 and of a zero one is 0
rule: public static method Sign<T>(x: T): int where T: INumber<T>; -1, 0, or 1: two `<` tests against.

title: Sign inside a generic body compares in the instantiated unsigned or signed type
rule: public static method Sign<T>(x: T): int where T: INumber<T>; -1, 0, or 1: two `<` tests against ... that obligation is what entitles a `where T: INumber<T>` or `where T: ISteppable<T>` body to all four comparisons (§25.2, *Type-parameter operands*).

title: Max, Min and Clamp in a generic body order uint and byte arguments by their unsigned CompareTo
rule: Ordering throughout is T's CompareTo (§2.8). Min(a, b) returns a when a.CompareTo(b) <= 0 and b otherwise; Max(a, b) returns a when a.CompareTo(b) >= 0 and b otherwise.

title: a reordered named argument on a Math member binds to the parameter it names
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares `Round(x: double, digits: int := 0): double` and `IEEERemainder(x: double, y: double): double`. §22.5: naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs - so `Round(digits := 3, x := 2.5)` is `Round(x: 2.5, digits: 3)` and renders 2.5, and `IEEERemainder(y := 4, x := 10)` is `IEEERemainder(x: 10, y: 4)`, which is 10 - 2*4 = 2 (the integer n nearest 10/4 is 2).

title: a Math member's supplied arguments run once each, in call-site textual order
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares `Pow(x: double, y: double): double`. §22.5, Evaluation order: a call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order - left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs. In `Pow(y := Next("y", 1), x := Next("x", 2))` the `y` expression runs first, the `x` expression second, each once - and the call is `Pow(x: 2, y: 1)`, which is 2.

title: Min's supplied arguments run once each, in call-site textual order
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares `Min<T>(a: T, b: T): T where T: IComparable<T>`, and `Min(a, b)` returns `a` when `a.CompareTo(b) <= 0` and `b` otherwise. §22.5, Evaluation order: a call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order - left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs. In `Min(b := Next("b", 2), a := Next("a", 1))` the `b` expression runs first, the `a` expression second, each once, and the call is `Min(a: 1, b: 2)`, which returns 1.

title: Clamp's supplied arguments run once each, in call-site textual order
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares `Clamp<T>(value: T, low: T, high: T): T where T: IComparable<T>`, and `Clamp(value, low, high)` returns `high` when the value compares greater than `high`. §22.5, Evaluation order: a call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order - left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs. In `Clamp(high := Next("h", 10), low := Next("l", 0), value := Next("v", 100))` the `high` expression runs first, then `low`, then `value`, each once, and the call is `Clamp(value: 100, low: 0, high: 10)`, which returns 10.

title: Math.Abs of a long argument resolves to the long overload and yields the long value
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares `Abs(x: int): int` and `Abs(x: long): long`. A `long` argument is an exact match for the `long` overload - §22.6: "an exact match is the only relation that distinguishes one applicable candidate from another at an argument position" - so the call resolves to `Abs(x: long): long` and its result is the long 2147483648, not an `int` overflow.

title: Math.Abs of a long constant plus an int operand promotes to long
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares `Abs(x: long): long`, and the `long` argument is an exact match for it (§22.6), so the result is a `long`. §6.2's mixed-type arithmetic: "the smaller-range operand is implicitly promoted to the larger type ... The result has the larger type" - so the sum is 4000000000, a value that does not fit an `int`.

title: Math.Abs of a long local plus an int operand promotes to long
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares `Abs(x: long): long`; a `long` argument is an exact match for it whatever its provenance (§22.6), so the result is a `long` and §6.2's promotion makes the sum 4000000000. This is the non-constant twin of l2_2_0020, which differs by the argument's provenance alone.

title: Math.Round admits a constant long argument at its int digits parameter
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares `Round(x: double, digits: int := 0): double`. §5.1's constant narrowing: "An expression of integer type that is a compile-time constant implicitly converts to any integer type whose range contains its value" - the constant `2L` reaches the `digits: int` parameter, and the call rounds 3.14159 to two digits.

title: Math.Round refuses a non-constant long argument at its int digits parameter
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares `Round(x: double, digits: int := 0): double`. §5.1's constant narrowing "applies to constants only" - "for non-constant expressions the conversion table and the never-implicit list above govern unchanged" - and the table admits no `long` to `int` row, so the sole candidate of §22.6 is inapplicable and the call is a compile error. This is the non-constant twin of l2_2_0022, which differs by the argument's provenance alone.

title: Math.Round admits a constant uint argument at its int digits parameter
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares `Round(x: double, digits: int := 0): double`. §5.1's constant narrowing is value-based and works "across signedness" - "a `uint`-typed constant `7` is admissible where `int` is expected" - so the `uint` constant `2U` reaches the `digits: int` parameter.

title: Math.Round refuses a constant uint argument that does not fit the int digits parameter
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares `Round(x: double, digits: int := 0): double`. §5.1's constant narrowing ends: "A constant whose value does not fit the target's range is a **compile error** at the conversion site - never a silent truncation." The `uint` constant 3000000000 does not fit an `int`, so the sole candidate of §22.6 is inapplicable and the call is a compile error.

title: Math.Abs refuses a bool argument
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares `Abs` for `int`, `long`, `double` and `decimal`. §5.1's never-implicit list bars the only conversion that could reach one of them: "Between integers and `bool`". So no candidate of §22.6 is applicable and the call is a compile error.
check: must be an `int`, a `long`, a `double` or a `decimal`

title: Math.Abs refuses a string argument
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares `Abs` for `int`, `long`, `double` and `decimal`. §5.1's implicit-conversion table admits no conversion to a `string` (and none from a `string` to a numeric type), so no candidate of §22.6 is applicable and the call is a compile error.
check: must be an `int`, a `long`, a `double` or a `decimal`

title: Math.Pow refuses a string argument at its double parameter
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares `Pow(x: double, y: double): double`. §5.1's implicit-conversion table admits no conversion from a `string` to a `double`, so no candidate of §22.6 is applicable and the call is a compile error.

title: Math.Floor of a byte argument is ambiguous and refused
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares `Floor(x: double): double` and `Floor(x: decimal): decimal`. §5.1's conversion table admits a `byte` at both `double` and `decimal`, and the argument matches neither parameter type exactly, so the two candidates are equally ranked at that position (§22.6: "two candidates that both require an implicit conversion at the same position are equally ranked there") and the call is ambiguous — "a compile error".

title: Math.Abs/Min/Clamp accept a double? narrowed by an early return
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares Abs(x: double), Min<T>, Clamp<T>. §7.4 (v0.350): narrowing is flow-sensitive and "a null test ... `x <> null` ... narrowing the true branch"; a narrowed nullable local has the non-nullable type, so a stdlib parameter of the underlying type accepts it. After `if e = null then return; end;` the surviving path is narrowed ("an early exit", §7.4), so the calls type-check and compute -2.5 -> 2.5, Min(-2.5, 0.5) -> -2.5, Clamp(-2.5, -1.0, 1.0) -> -1.

title: Math.Abs/Max/Floor accept a double? narrowed on the else branch of `is null`
rule: stdlib §2.2 Abs/Max/Floor/Sqrt over double. §7.4 (v0.350): narrowing is flow-sensitive and "a null test ... `x <> null` ... narrowing the true branch"; a narrowed nullable local has the non-nullable type, so a stdlib parameter of the underlying type accepts it. "x = null or x is null (narrowing the *false* branch)": the else branch of `e is null` has `e` non-null: Abs(-2.5) -> 2.5, Max(-2.5, -9.0) -> -2.5, Floor(-2.5) -> -3.

title: Math.Abs/Max/Min/Clamp/Floor/Ceiling/Truncate accept a narrowed decimal?
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares the decimal overloads Abs, Floor, Ceiling, Truncate and the generic Min/Max/Clamp. §7.4 (v0.350): narrowing is flow-sensitive and "a null test ... `x <> null` ... narrowing the true branch"; a narrowed nullable local has the non-nullable type, so a stdlib parameter of the underlying type accepts it. With m = -2.5m: Abs 2.5, Max(m, 1.5m) 1.5, Min -2.5, Clamp(m, -1.5m, 1.5m) -1.5, Floor -3, Ceiling -2, Truncate (toward zero) -2.

title: Math.Abs and DivRem accept an int? narrowed non-null
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares Abs(x: int) and DivRem(a: int, b: int, out remainder: int) "returns the quotient". §7.4 (v0.350): narrowing is flow-sensitive and "a null test ... `x <> null` ... narrowing the true branch"; a narrowed nullable local has the non-nullable type, so a stdlib parameter of the underlying type accepts it. For -7: Abs 7; DivRem(-7, 2) quotient -3 (truncated toward zero, §6.1) with remainder -1.

title: Math.Abs and Math.Max accept a long? narrowed non-null
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares Abs(x: long). §7.4 (v0.350): narrowing is flow-sensitive and "a null test ... `x <> null` ... narrowing the true branch"; a narrowed nullable local has the non-nullable type, so a stdlib parameter of the underlying type accepts it. Abs(-9000000000) is 9000000000 and Max(-9000000000, 5L) is 5.

title: Math.Abs of a readonly double? field narrowed by a null test
rule: Narrowing applies to locals and `readonly` fields only (§7.4, v0.350): "no call, `await` or closure invalidates the fact" on a readonly-field carrier. After `if c.g <> null`, `c.g` is double for Abs(2.5) -> 2.5 and Max(2.5, 1.0) -> 2.5, with a call (`Max`) between the test and the second use.

title: Math.Max and Math.Min over byte are generic and need no cast
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares `Max<T>`/`Min<T>` with `T: IComparable<T>`; a `byte` binds T exactly (§14.5), so unlike the non-generic Abs/Floor overloads (§22.6) no ambiguity arises. Max(200, 3) is 200, Min is 3.

title: Math.Abs of a byte? narrowed non-null is ambiguous and refused
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares only Abs(int), Abs(long), Abs(double), Abs(decimal). §5.1 admits a `byte` at more than one of them and it matches none exactly, so the candidates are equally ranked (§22.6: "two candidates that both require an implicit conversion at the same position are equally ranked there") and the call is ambiguous, a compile error. Narrowing a `byte?` (§7.4) yields a plain `byte`, which does not change that.

title: Math.Abs of a short is ambiguous and refused
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares only Abs(int), Abs(long), Abs(double), Abs(decimal). §5.1 admits a `short` at more than one of them and it matches none exactly, so the candidates are equally ranked (§22.6: "two candidates that both require an implicit conversion at the same position are equally ranked there") and the call is ambiguous, a compile error.

title: Math.Abs of a char is ambiguous and refused
rule: stdlib §2.2 declares only Abs(int), Abs(long), Abs(double), Abs(decimal). §5.1 admits a `char` at more than one of them and it matches none exactly, so the candidates are equally ranked (§22.6: "two candidates that both require an implicit conversion at the same position are equally ranked there") and the call is ambiguous, a compile error.

title: ToInt32 raises FormatException on a non-numeric string
rule: Convert.ToInt32(value) raises FormatException when the string is not a well-formed representation of the target type.

title: ToInt32 raises OverflowException when the value does not fit
rule: Convert.ToInt32(value) raises OverflowException when the value does not fit the target type.

title: ToString(value, toBase) rejects a base outside {2, 8, 10, 16}
rule: Convert.ToString(value, toBase) accepts only bases 2, 8, 10, and 16, raising ArgumentException otherwise.

title: ToBoolean accepts "true"/"false" case-insensitively
rule: Convert.ToBoolean(value) accepts exactly "true"/"false", case-insensitively -- Boolean.Parse's contract.

title: a reordered named argument on a Convert member binds to the parameter it names
rule: stdlib §2.3 declares `ToString(value: int, toBase: int): string` and `ToString(value: int): string`, and states that `ToString(value, toBase)` returns the text `value.ToString(toBase)` returns (§9.1), whose radix digits are lower-case. §22.5: naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to - so `ToString(toBase := 16, value := 255)` is `ToString(value: 255, toBase: 16)` and renders "ff", while the one-argument form renders the value's own no-format text, "255".

title: a Convert member's supplied arguments run once each, in call-site textual order
rule: stdlib §2.3 declares `ToString(value: int, toBase: int): string` and states that the result is the text `value.ToString(toBase)` returns (§9.1), whose radix digits are lower-case. §22.5, Evaluation order: a call's supplied argument expressions are evaluated in call-site textual order - left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs. In `ToString(toBase := Next("tb", 16), value := Next("v", 255))` the `toBase` expression runs first, the `value` expression second, each once, and the call renders "ff".

title: Convert.ToString of a long argument resolves to the long overload and renders the value
rule: stdlib §2.3 declares `ToString(value: long): string` among the one-argument forms, and states that "where that selects an overload the text is the converted value's". A `long` argument is an exact match for the `long` overload (§22.6), so the call renders the value's own no-format text.

title: Convert.ToString refuses a string argument
rule: stdlib §2.3 declares `ToString` for `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` and `bool` - there is no `string` overload, the `To*` parsing forms take the `string` and the rendering forms do not - and §5.1's table admits no conversion from a `string` to any of them, so no candidate of §22.6 is applicable and the call is a compile error.
check: must be an `int`, a `long`, a `float`, a `double`, a `decimal` or a `bool`

title: Convert.ToString of a uint argument is ambiguous and refused
rule: stdlib §2.3: "A `char` and the integer types other than `int` and `long` each convert to two or more of these parameter types and match none exactly, so the call is ambiguous and a compile error (§22.6)" - and §5.1's constant narrowing reaches a candidate only as a conversion, "never as an exact match". A `uint` is an integer type other than `int` and `long`, so `ToString(5U)` is ambiguous and refused.

title: Convert.ToString of a uint variable is ambiguous and refused
rule: stdlib §2.3: "A `char` and the integer types other than `int` and `long` each convert to two or more of these parameter types and match none exactly, so the call is ambiguous and a compile error (§22.6)". A `uint` reaches `long`, `float`, `double` and `decimal` (§5.1's conversion table) and matches none of the one-argument forms exactly, so the one-argument `ToString` call on a `uint` variable is ambiguous.

title: Convert.ToString of a ulong variable is ambiguous and refused
rule: stdlib §2.3: "A `char` and the integer types other than `int` and `long` each convert to two or more of these parameter types and match none exactly, so the call is ambiguous and a compile error (§22.6)". A `ulong` reaches only `float`, `double` and `decimal` (§5.1's conversion table) — two or more of them — and matches none of the one-argument forms exactly, so the call is ambiguous.

title: Convert.ToString of a byte value with a toBase is ambiguous and refused
rule: stdlib §2.3: "A `char` and the integer types other than `int` and `long` each convert to two or more of these parameter types and match none exactly, so the call is ambiguous and a compile error (§22.6)". A `byte` reaches `int`, `long`, `float`, `double` and `decimal` (§5.1's conversion table) and matches neither of the two-argument forms' value parameters (`int` and `long`) exactly, so the two-argument `ToString` call on a `byte` is ambiguous.

title: Convert.ToString of a uint constant with a toBase is ambiguous and refused
rule: stdlib §2.3: "A `char` and the integer types other than `int` and `long` each convert to two or more of these parameter types and match none exactly, so the call is ambiguous and a compile error (§22.6)". A `uint` constant reaches the `int` form by §5.1's constant narrowing, which "is graded as any other conversion is, never as an exact match", and reaches the `long` form by the admitted `uint` → `long` widening; the two candidates therefore both convert at the value position and are equally ranked there (§22.6), so the call is ambiguous.

title: Convert.ToString of a ulong value with a toBase reaches no candidate
rule: stdlib §2.3 declares the two-argument forms as `ToString(value: int, toBase: int)` and `ToString(value: long, toBase: int)`. A `ulong` reaches neither `int` nor `long` (§5.1: "Between signed and unsigned types of the same or narrower width ... is never implicit", and the `ulong` → `long` widening is not among the admitted ones), so no candidate is applicable at the value position and §22.6's rule applies: "If no candidate is applicable at all ... the call is a compile error with no candidates cited".

title: an explicit cast to one parameter type resolves the ambiguous Convert.ToString
rule: stdlib §2.3: "the remedy is an explicit cast to one parameter type, or the value's own `ToString()`". §22.6 agrees: "The caller resolves the ambiguity by adding an explicit cast (§5.2) to an argument so that exactly one candidate becomes an exact match". Casting the `byte` value to `int` makes the `int` form an exact match, so the call renders the value.

title: the value's own ToString is the other remedy for the ambiguous Convert.ToString
rule: stdlib §2.3: "the remedy is an explicit cast to one parameter type, or the value's own `ToString()`, which renders it in its own type". The `byte` value's own no-format `ToString()` renders it in its own type, so the `byte` is rendered without the ambiguous `Convert.ToString` call.

title: Convert.ToString of a bool renders True
rule: stdlib §2.3: "Each one-argument `ToString` returns the text the value it receives renders as under its own no-format `ToString()`", and the section's own example: "`Convert.ToString(true)` is `"True"`". A `bool` renders `True`/`False` (§8.5).

title: Convert.ToString with a runtime toBase renders the radix form
rule: stdlib §2.3: "`ToString(value, toBase)` returns the text `value.ToString(toBase)` returns (§9.1)". §9.1: "`ToString(radix)` emits the **lower-case** digits". The `toBase` is a run-time value here, and the rendered text is the radix form, not the decimal form.

title: an un-narrowed nullable toBase reaches no Convert.ToString candidate
rule: stdlib §2.3 declares `ToString(value: int, toBase: int)` and `ToString(value: long, toBase: int)`. §5.1's nullable conversions lift an implicit conversion to the nullable forms only — "`S?` implicitly converts to `T?` whenever `S` implicitly converts to `T`" — so an `int?` converts to neither `int` nor `long`, and §22.6's rule applies: "If no candidate is applicable at all ... the call is a compile error with no candidates cited". The local is never narrowed: its initializer is a nullable-typed expression, which §7.4 does not narrow.

title: a narrowed nullable toBase renders the radix form
rule: stdlib §2.3: "`ToString(value, toBase)` returns the text `value.ToString(toBase)` returns (§9.1)". §22.6: "The argument's static type is its type at the call: a read of a binding §7.4 has narrowed non-null is of its non-nullable type". The narrowed `r` is an `int` at the call, so the `int` form is applicable and the radix form is rendered.

title: Convert.ToString of a uint value with a toBase widens to the long form
rule: stdlib §2.3 declares `ToString(value: int, toBase: int)` and `ToString(value: long, toBase: int)`, and "where that selects an overload the text is the converted value's". §5.1 admits the `uint` → `long` widening and never the `uint` → `int` conversion, so exactly one candidate is applicable and the value is rendered in the radix, in §9.1's lower-case digits.

title: a named Convert.ToString binds each parameter by name and renders the radix form
rule: stdlib §2.3: "`ToString(value, toBase)` returns the text `value.ToString(toBase)` returns (§9.1)". §22.5: "Named arguments may appear in any order after positional arguments. Each supplied argument binds exactly one parameter". The named spelling binds `value` and `toBase` to the two parameters, and the rendered text is the radix form.

title: Convert.ToDouble raises FormatException for the spellings the double input grammar forbids
rule: The `To*` methods raise `FormatException` when the string is not a well-formed representation of the target type and `OverflowException` when the value does not fit — the same contract as the §9 per-type `Parse` family these conversions mirror

title: Convert.TryToDouble returns false exactly where Convert.ToDouble raises
rule: `Try` forms return `false` in exactly the cases the throwing forms would raise; the `out` parameter receives the default value.

title: Convert.ToString of a narrowed long? renders decimal, and base 16 in lower case
rule: stdlib §2.3: Convert.ToString(value: long) and ToString(value: long, toBase: int); the radix form "emits the same text as ToString(radix)" which emits "the lower-case digits" (§9.1). §7.4 (v0.350): narrowing is flow-sensitive and "a null test ... `x <> null` ... narrowing the true branch"; a narrowed nullable local has the non-nullable type, so a stdlib parameter of the underlying type accepts it. long.MaxValue renders 9223372036854775807 and 7fffffffffffffff.

title: Convert.ToString of narrowed nullable long and int with base arguments
rule: stdlib §2.3 ToString(value, toBase) returns the text value.ToString(toBase) returns: for a negative value "a `-` for a negative value followed by the magnitude's digits" (§9.1), lower-case. -255 base 16 is -ff, 5 base 2 is 101. §7.4 (v0.350): narrowing is flow-sensitive and "a null test ... `x <> null` ... narrowing the true branch"; a narrowed nullable local has the non-nullable type, so a stdlib parameter of the underlying type accepts it.

title: Convert.ToInt32 of a long is refused: the only overload takes a string
rule: stdlib §2.3 declares only `ToInt32(value: string): int`; a `long` argument does not convert to `string` (§5.1), so no overload applies and the call is a compile error.

title: Convert.ToString(int) and ToString(int, 16) assigned to locals in a loop
rule: Convert.ToString(value: int) returns the text the int renders as under its own ToString(); ToString(value, toBase) returns the text value.ToString(toBase) returns, so base 16 renders 255 as ff (stdlib 2.3, 9.1).

title: Convert.ToString with base 2 and no base inside one interpolated string
rule: Convert.ToString(value: int) returns the text the int renders as under its own ToString(); ToString(value, toBase) returns the text value.ToString(toBase) returns, so base 2 renders 99 as 1100011 (stdlib 2.3, 9.1).

title: Convert.ToString results returned from methods and concatenated
rule: Convert.ToString(value: int) returns the text the int renders as under its own ToString(); ToString(value, toBase) returns the text value.ToString(toBase) returns, so base 16 renders 255 as ff (stdlib 2.3, 9.1).

title: Convert.ToString results stored into a string field and reassigned
rule: Convert.ToString(value: int) returns the text the int renders as under its own ToString(); ToString(value, toBase) returns the text value.ToString(toBase) returns, so base 16 renders 255 as ff (stdlib 2.3, 9.1).

title: Convert.ToString results through the null-coalescing operator and a null guard
rule: Convert.ToString(value: int) returns the text the int renders as under its own ToString(); ToString(value, toBase) returns the text value.ToString(toBase) returns, so base 16 renders 255 as ff (stdlib 2.3, 9.1).

title: Get returns null when the variable is absent
rule: Environment.Get(name) returns null when the variable is absent.

title: Set(name, null) removes the variable
rule: Environment.Set(name, value) with value = null removes the variable.

title: Set raises ArgumentException for an empty variable name
rule: Environment.Set(name, value) raises ArgumentException when name is empty, or contains "=".

title: GetInt conflates a malformed value with an absent one, returning null
rule: Environment.GetInt(name) returns null when the variable is absent OR malformed -- deliberately conflated.

title: DateTime's no-format ToString renders ISO 8601
rule: The no-argument DateTime.ToString() renders the round-trippable ISO 8601 form yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ss.

title: an invalid DateTime component raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException
rule: The DateTime constructors raise ArgumentOutOfRangeException on invalid components, such as a month outside 1..12.

title: Parse accepts the date-only form with zero time components
rule: DateTime.Parse accepts the date-only form yyyy-MM-dd, with time components zero.

title: Parse raises FormatException on a non-conforming string
rule: DateTime.Parse accepts exactly the round-trip form, its fractional- seconds extension, and the date-only form; any other input raises FormatException.

title: ParseOrNull returns null exactly where Parse raises
rule: DateTime.ParseOrNull(s) returns null exactly where Parse(s) raises; otherwise the parsed value.

title: TimeSpan subtraction computes the elapsed duration
rule: TimeSpan declares operator -(a, b): TimeSpan; subtracting one hour from one day leaves a TimeSpan whose TotalHours is 23.

title: a temporal format pattern preserves non-specifier characters literally
rule: In a temporal pattern, every character that does not begin one of the yyyy/MM/dd/HH/mm/ss/fff specifiers is a literal, copied to the output verbatim.

title: adding past MaxValue raises OverflowException
rule: DateTime's Add* family raises OverflowException when the result falls outside MinValue..MaxValue.

title: DateTime.Parse reads the round-trip form and renders it back
rule: stdlib §2.5's parse contract: "`DateTime.Parse` accepts exactly the type's own rendered forms — the round-trip form `yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ss`, optionally extended with a fractional-seconds tail `.fff`, and the date-only form `yyyy-MM-dd` (time components zero)". The no-argument `ToString()` renders the round-trippable ISO 8601 form `yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ss`.

title: TimeSpan.MinValue and MaxValue are FromTicks of the long extremes and render in the constant form
rule: `MinValue` is `FromTicks(long.MinValue)` and `MaxValue` is `FromTicks(long.MaxValue)`; `TimeSpan.MinValue` renders `-10675199.02:48:05.4775808` (2.18, the `TimeSpan` constant form). The no-format `ToString()`, `ToString("c")` produce this one rendering.

title: TimeSpan comparison of the extremes, interpolation holes, and unary negation of MinValue
rule: `CompareTo` is tick order; an interpolation hole with or without `:c` produces the constant-form rendering; the unary `-` on a `TimeSpan` raises `OverflowException` on `MinValue`.

title: DateTime, DateOnly and TimeOnly constructors admit every arity and naming they declare
rule: DateTime declares `constructor(year, month, day)` and `constructor(year, month, day, hour, minute, second, millisecond := 0, kind := ...)`; `DateOnly` declares `constructor(year, month, day)`; `TimeOnly` declares `constructor(hour, minute, second := 0, millisecond := 0)`. Named arguments may appear in any order after positional ones and every parameter without a default must be bound (spec 22.5).

title: DateTime() is rejected: DateTime declares no parameterless constructor
rule: Every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; a construction that binds no declared constructor of the type is a compile error (spec 22.5, 22.6). DateTime declares no parameterless constructor.

title: DateTime(2024) is rejected: a one-argument DateTime construction matches no declared constructor
rule: Every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; a construction that binds no declared constructor of the type is a compile error (spec 22.5, 22.6). A one-argument DateTime construction matches no declared constructor.

title: DateTime(2024, 3) is rejected: a two-argument DateTime construction matches no declared constructor
rule: Every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; a construction that binds no declared constructor of the type is a compile error (spec 22.5, 22.6). A two-argument DateTime construction matches no declared constructor.

title: DateTime(2024, 3, 4, 5) is rejected: hour without minute and second matches no constructor
rule: Every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; a construction that binds no declared constructor of the type is a compile error (spec 22.5, 22.6). A four-argument DateTime construction (hour without minute and second) matches no declared constructor.

title: DateTime(2024, 3, 4, 5, 6) is rejected: a five-argument form without second matches no constructor
rule: Every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; a construction that binds no declared constructor of the type is a compile error (spec 22.5, 22.6). A five-argument DateTime construction (no second) matches no declared constructor.

title: DateTime with nine arguments is rejected: it exceeds the longest declared constructor
rule: Every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; a construction that binds no declared constructor of the type is a compile error (spec 22.5, 22.6). A nine-argument DateTime construction exceeds the longest declared constructor.

title: DateOnly() is rejected: DateOnly declares no parameterless constructor
rule: Every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; a construction that binds no declared constructor of the type is a compile error (spec 22.5, 22.6). DateOnly declares no parameterless constructor.

title: DateOnly(2024) is rejected: a one-argument DateOnly construction matches no declared constructor
rule: Every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; a construction that binds no declared constructor of the type is a compile error (spec 22.5, 22.6). A one-argument DateOnly construction matches no declared constructor.

title: DateOnly(2024, 3) is rejected: a two-argument DateOnly construction matches no declared constructor
rule: Every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; a construction that binds no declared constructor of the type is a compile error (spec 22.5, 22.6). A two-argument DateOnly construction matches no declared constructor.

title: DateOnly with four arguments is rejected: it exceeds the declared constructor
rule: Every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; a construction that binds no declared constructor of the type is a compile error (spec 22.5, 22.6). A four-argument DateOnly construction exceeds the declared constructor.

title: TimeOnly() is rejected: TimeOnly declares no parameterless constructor
rule: Every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; a construction that binds no declared constructor of the type is a compile error (spec 22.5, 22.6). TimeOnly declares no parameterless constructor.

title: TimeOnly(1) is rejected: a one-argument TimeOnly construction leaves the required minute unbound
rule: Every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; a construction that binds no declared constructor of the type is a compile error (spec 22.5, 22.6). A one-argument TimeOnly construction leaves the required minute unbound.

title: TimeOnly with five arguments is rejected: it exceeds the declared constructor
rule: Every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; a construction that binds no declared constructor of the type is a compile error (spec 22.5, 22.6). A five-argument TimeOnly construction exceeds the declared constructor.

title: TimeOnly(1, millisecond := 5) is rejected: the required minute is left unbound
rule: Every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; a construction that binds no declared constructor of the type is a compile error (spec 22.5, 22.6). Naming only millisecond after hour leaves the required minute unbound.

title: TimeOnly(hour := 1) is rejected: naming only hour leaves the required minute unbound
rule: Every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; a construction that binds no declared constructor of the type is a compile error (spec 22.5, 22.6). Naming only hour leaves the required minute unbound.

title: TimeOnly(minute := 1, second := 2) is rejected: the required hour is left unbound
rule: Every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; a construction that binds no declared constructor of the type is a compile error (spec 22.5, 22.6). Naming minute and second leaves the required hour unbound.

title: DateTime(year := 1, month := 2, hour := 3) is rejected: it binds no declared constructor
rule: Every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; a construction that binds no declared constructor of the type is a compile error (spec 22.5, 22.6). Naming year, month and hour binds no declared DateTime constructor (day, minute and second are unbound).

title: DateTime, DateOnly, TimeOnly constructors bind named and defaulted arguments by parameter
rule: DateTime declares `constructor(year, month, day, hour, minute, second, millisecond := 0, kind := ...)`; `TimeOnly` declares `constructor(hour, minute, second := 0, millisecond := 0)`; a named argument binds the parameter of that name in any order (spec 22.5), and an omitted defaulted parameter takes its default (0).

title: The eight-argument DateTime keeps its Kind; DateOnly takes named year, month, day in any order
rule: DateTime declares `constructor(..., millisecond := 0, kind := DateTimeKind.Unspecified)`, so the eighth positional argument is `kind`; named `DateOnly(day := 2, month := 5, year := 2000)` binds each parameter by name (spec 22.5) and renders `yyyy-MM-dd`.

title: DateOnly with named year and month but no day is rejected
rule: Every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name (spec 22.5); `DateOnly(year, month, day)` has no default for `day`.

title: TimeSpan * double: range, NaN and double-precision edges
rule: stdlib §2.5 (TimeSpan `operator *`): "computes over Ticks in double; OverflowException on a product outside the tick range or a NaN operand (pinned)"; the tick range is long.MinValue..long.MaxValue. Each row's product is formed from the tick count converted to double: an out-of-range product, an infinite product and a NaN operand raise OverflowException; in-range products (including exactly long.MinValue) return the tick count; 2^53+1 ticks times 1.0 loses the low bit in double.

title: TimeSpan / double: zero divisor, NaN, range and tiny-divisor edges
rule: stdlib §2.5 (TimeSpan `operator /`): "same computation model and OverflowException rule as *; DivideByZeroException on divisor = 0.0". The divisor 0.0 or -0.0 (equal to 0.0) raises DivideByZeroException; a NaN divisor or a quotient outside the tick range raises OverflowException; a quotient that is an in-range double is converted to ticks.

title: Repeated TimeSpan * double and / double throws and results stay consistent over 100 rounds
rule: stdlib §2.5 (TimeSpan `operator *`): "computes over Ticks in double; OverflowException on a product outside the tick range or a NaN operand (pinned)"; the tick range is long.MinValue..long.MaxValue. stdlib §2.5 (TimeSpan `operator /`): "same computation model and OverflowException rule as *; DivideByZeroException on divisor = 0.0". Per round: Max*2.0 -> Overflow, 100/0.0 -> DivideByZero, 100*NaN -> Overflow, 100*3.0 -> 300 (no throw). 100 rounds: ov=200 dz=100 ok=100.

title: DateTime Add/Subtract/AddDays and the + and - operators with a TimeSpan agree
rule: stdlib §2.5 declares DateTime.Add(span), Subtract(span), Subtract(other), AddDays(days) and the operators `d + t`, `t + d`, `d - t`, `a - b`. From 2024-01-31: +1 day is day 1 (Feb 1); -1 day is day 30; the difference is 864000000000 ticks (10,000,000 ticks per second times 86,400, §2.5); AddDays(2.0) is day 2.

title: TimeSpan and DateTime members work on method parameters
rule: stdlib §2.5: CompareTo is tick order, ToString() is the constant "c" form (§2.18), Hours/TotalSeconds/Ticks as declared. For 3 hours against 1 hour: CompareTo is positive, "03:00:00", Hours 3, TotalSeconds 10800, adding to 2024-01-31 keeps day 31, and the difference is 108000000000 ticks.

title: TimeSpan has no Duration member and the call is refused
rule: stdlib §2.5 declares no `Duration` on TimeSpan (the members are those listed there); a member the type does not declare is a compile error (§22.1).

title: DateTime.DayOfWeek chained off every receiver shape yields the day of that date
rule: DateTime.DayOfWeek is a property of type DayOfWeek, an enum over byte with Sunday = 0 through Saturday = 6 (stdlib 2.5); 2024-03-15 is a Friday, value 5. The property read applies to any DateTime-typed receiver expression: field, property, call result, chained call, index, loop variable, record field, lambda parameter, out variable, generic field, narrowed nullable and map value.

title: A DayOfWeek value supports equality, hashing, casts, array and map keys, and case patterns
rule: DateTime.DayOfWeek is a property of type DayOfWeek, an enum over byte with Sunday = 0 through Saturday = 6 (stdlib 2.5); 2024-03-15 is a Friday, value 5. Enum values compare with = and <>, convert explicitly to their underlying integers (spec 5.4) and match case constants.

title: DateOnly binds positional then named arguments, and all-named arguments in reverse order
rule: public constructor(year: int, month: int, day: int);   // ArgumentOutOfRangeException on invalid

title: TimeOnly binds trailing named arguments and a mix of positional and named arguments
rule: public constructor(hour: int, minute: int, second: int := 0, millisecond: int := 0);

title: DateTime and TimeOnly named arguments are matched by name whatever their written order
rule: millisecond: int := 0, kind: DateTimeKind := DateTimeKind.Unspecified); ... public constructor(hour: int, minute: int, second: int := 0, millisecond: int := 0);

all:throw ok ok throw throw
throw ok ok throw

rule: ArgumentOutOfRangeException on invalid components

title: an ArgumentException catch arm and an Exception catch arm both receive the out-of-range DateTime
rule: so that an `ArgumentException` catch arm covers the whole argument-validation family

title: a DateTime constructor argument produced by an await raises on an invalid month in an async method
rule: ArgumentOutOfRangeException on invalid components

title: an iterator yielding DateTime constructions raises mid-sequence and the loop sees the earlier values

title: Empty equals default(Guid)
rule: Guid.Empty is the all-zero UUID -- the same value default(Guid) produces.

title: Parse raises FormatException on a malformed string
rule: Guid.Parse(s) accepts the "D" and "N" renderings; FormatException otherwise.

title: ParseOrNull returns null for the same malformed string Parse rejects
rule: Guid.ParseOrNull(s) returns null exactly where Parse(s) raises; otherwise the parsed value.

title: FromByteArray requires exactly 16 bytes
rule: Guid.FromByteArray(bytes) requires Count = 16, raising ArgumentException otherwise.

title: new Guid(...) is rejected -- Guid declares no constructor
rule: Guid declares no constructor, so new Guid(...) is a compile error at any argument list.

title: Guid.Parse reads the D rendering of the all-zero UUID
rule: stdlib §2.6 declares `public static method Parse(s: string): Guid;` with the comment "accepts the "D" and "N" renderings (§2.18); FormatException otherwise", and §2.18's `Guid` row reads "`D` (hyphenated, lowercase), `N` (no hyphens) | no-format = `D`". The all-zero D rendering parses, and the value it yields is `Guid.Empty` — "the all-zero UUID" (§2.6).

title: Guid.ToString("D") renders the hyphenated lowercase D form
rule: | `Guid` | `D` (hyphenated, lowercase), `N` (no hyphens) | no-format = `D` |

title: Guid? members after each narrowing form render the canonical D and N forms
rule: A Guid? is a nullable value; a member access on it requires narrowing it to non-null first (spec 7.4): guard with a null test, a pattern, ! or ?. ; Guid.ToString() renders the canonical form and ToString("N") the 32-digit form (stdlib 2.6, 2.18).

title: A member access on a Guid? that is not narrowed is rejected
rule: A member access on a nullable value requires narrowing it to non-null first (spec 7.4); Guid? is nullable, so g.ToString() without a guard is a compile error.

title: Guid.TryParse accepts the D and N forms and assigns the zero Guid on failure
rule: Guid.TryParse accepts the D and N renderings and fails otherwise (stdlib 2.6); the out parameter is a non-nullable value-typed out, so failure assigns default(Guid), the all-zero value, never the previous contents (stdlib 1 shape (c), spec 22.3).

title: Guid.FromByteArray raises ArgumentException for 15 and 17 bytes and reads 16 zero bytes as Empty
rule: borrows; raises ArgumentException unless Count = 16

title: two Random instances constructed with the same seed agree
rule: Random is seeded; constructing it with an explicit seed determines its output sequence, as distinct from the default constructor's system-time-based seed.

title: Next(maxValue) returns a value in 0..<maxValue
rule: Random.Next(maxValue) returns a value in the range 0..<maxValue.

title: Next(maxValue) rejects a negative maxValue
rule: Random.Next(maxValue) raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException when maxValue < 0.

title: Next(minValue, maxValue) rejects minValue greater than maxValue
rule: Random.Next(minValue, maxValue) raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException when minValue > maxValue.

title: Random is sendable and a moved instance continues its sequence
rule: `Random` is **sendable**, on the sendable form's copy-state ground. A moved instance continues its sequence in the receiving domain.

title: Random seeds given as byte, uint, char or named long produce the stream of the equal long seed
rule: two instances constructed with the same seed and driven with the same calls produce the same values

title: a class declaring IComparable<T> must supply CompareTo
rule: IComparable<T> declares method CompareTo(other: T): int; a class whose inheritance clause lists IComparable<T> must implement it.

title: a class implementing CompareTo satisfies IComparable<T>
rule: IComparable<T> declares method CompareTo(other: T): int; a class supplying it satisfies the interface's inheritance-clause declaration.

title: CompareTo's sign convention drives a where T: IComparable<T> caller
rule: a.CompareTo(b) returns negative if a < b, zero if equal, positive if a > b; a generic caller constrained on IComparable<T>, such as Math.Min, relies on this convention to select the lesser value.

title: a record's auto-generated equality does not by itself satisfy IEquatable<T>
rule: A record conforms to an interface only when it lists that interface in its inheritance clause and declares matching members; a plain record with no such clause does not conform to IEquatable<T>, whatever equality operators it auto-generates.

title: a record listing IEquatable<T> satisfies it with no written Equals
rule: Records implement this implicitly -- once a record lists IEquatable<T> in its inheritance clause, the auto-generated Equals(T) counts as declaring the matching member, with no explicit body needed.

title: a class implements IEquatable<T> by writing Equals(T) itself
rule: classes may implement IEquatable<T> for type-safe equality without boxing -- unlike a record's synthesized member, a class supplies Equals(other: T): bool by hand.

title: user code may not implement Dispose() directly
rule: Every class implicitly implements IDisposable; user code does not implement it directly -- a class or record declaring a member named Dispose, at any parameter list, is a compile error at that declaration.

title: a destructor is the customization point for disposal, not Dispose()
rule: Every class implicitly implements IDisposable; user code does not implement it directly -- the customization points are a destructor and owned fields.

title: where T: IDisposable admits every class implicitly
rule: Every class implicitly implements IDisposable, so the constraint where T: IDisposable admits every class -- with no interface declared.

title: where T: IDisposable admits no record
rule: The constraint where T: IDisposable admits every class, no records -- records cannot implement IDisposable.

title: IAsyncDisposable is implemented explicitly with an async DisposeAsync
rule: IAsyncDisposable is implemented explicitly by classes that need asynchronous cleanup; implementations declare a method matching DisposeAsync(): Task and add async -- async never appears on the interface declaration itself. A class implementing IAsyncDisposable also declares a destructor for the synchronous fallback path.

title: where T: IDisposable admits a user interface that extends IDisposable
rule: stdlib §2.10 (v0.345): "The constraint `where T: IDisposable` admits every class … and the interfaces that extend `IDisposable` directly or transitively — including `IAsyncDisposable`, `IEnumerator<T>`, `IAsyncEnumerator<T>`, and **user-defined interfaces that list `IDisposable` in their extension clause**."  The argument here is bound at the INTERFACE's static type, so it is the interfaces clause — not the "every class" clause — that decides this call.

title: where T: IDisposable admits an IEnumerator
rule: stdlib §2.10 (v0.345): "The constraint `where T: IDisposable` admits every class … and the interfaces that extend `IDisposable` directly or transitively — including `IAsyncDisposable`, **`IEnumerator<T>`**, `IAsyncEnumerator<T>` …"

title: where T: IDisposable admits an IAsyncDisposable
rule: stdlib §2.10 (v0.345): "The constraint `where T: IDisposable` admits every class … and the interfaces that extend `IDisposable` directly or transitively — including **`IAsyncDisposable`**, `IEnumerator<T>`, `IAsyncEnumerator<T>` …"  The argument here is bound at the `IAsyncDisposable` static type, so it is the interfaces clause that decides this call.

title: Subscription, obtained from a registration call, disposes with using var
rule: Subscription has no public constructor and is obtained from a registration call, such as CancellationToken.Register; it is auto-imported, needing no explicit import statement.

title: new Subscription() is rejected -- no public constructor
rule: Subscription has no public constructor; it is obtained only from a registration call.

title: FloatToInt32Bits/Int32BitsToFloat round-trip a float exactly
rule: Int32BitsToFloat interprets the integer's bit pattern as a float; the bit patterns are preserved exactly, so FloatToInt32Bits followed by Int32BitsToFloat reproduces the original value.

title: DoubleToInt64Bits/Int64BitsToDouble round-trip a double exactly
rule: These are pure bit-reinterpretation operations: the bit patterns are preserved exactly, so DoubleToInt64Bits followed by Int64BitsToDouble reproduces the original value.

title: Reinterpret views the same bits under a different type, not a value
rule: Reinterpret copies the value's bits unchanged -- it never raises and never alters the bit pattern, unlike a value-converting cast.

title: a NaN bit pattern is preserved exactly through a round trip
rule: For NaN values, the specific bit pattern (signaling vs quiet, payload bits) is preserved -- not merely a canonical NaN value.

title: Type.Name renders the unqualified declared identifier
rule: Name renders named components unqualified — for a named non-generic type, Name is the declared identifier alone.

title: Type.FullName renders the module-qualified path
rule: FullName renders every named component qualified by its declaring module path — for a top-level type, the module then the identifier ("BankingApp.BankAccount").

title: a keyword-aliased type renders its lowercase keyword in FullName
rule: The keyword-aliased types render as their lowercase keyword in both Name and FullName ("typeof(int).FullName = \"int\""), a recorded exception to qualification.

title: a generic instantiation's FullName recurses through its arguments
rule: A generic instantiation renders the head followed by "<", its arguments joined by ", ", and ">", each argument rendered recursively in the same property's form (the document's own worked example).

title: BaseType of a class with no explicit base is the Object Type
rule: BaseType is null only for Object, interface types, value types, and function types; a class declared with no base clause still resolves a non-null BaseType, terminating the chain at Object.

title: EnumNames on a non-enum Type raises InvalidOperationException
rule: Enum metadata (EnumNames, EnumValues) is valid only when IsEnum; on any other Type, accessing either property raises InvalidOperationException.

title: Type is sendable, so Channel<Type> is an admitted instantiation
rule: `Type` is **sendable**: it crosses a domain boundary as a shared reference, as `string` does.

title: a static readonly field of type Type is warning-free
rule: `Type` joins language spec §22.12 rule 4's warning-suppression set — a `static readonly` field or auto-property of type `Type` is warning-free.

title: a record declaring both serialization interfaces needs no body
rule: A record that declares : ISerializable and/or : IDeserializable and satisfies the synthesis-eligibility rule has the bodies generated by the compiler — the hand-written forms are unnecessary for the common case.

title: a serialized rename beginning with $ is a compile error
rule: Field names beginning with $ are reserved for the identity mapping ($id, $ref, $type, $case); a serialized "<name>" rename whose name begins with $ is a compile error at the conformance declaration.

title: a hand-written Deserialize for a value-type target returns plain T
rule: For a value-type target (a record, enum, or value-like choice) the recognized Deserialize factory returns a plain by-value T with no owned modifier.

title: owned on a value-type target's Deserialize return is rejected
rule: owned on a record, enum, or choice return is a compile error (language spec §28.1's type requirement); the recognized factory for a value-type target must not spell owned.

title: a hand-written Deserialize for a class target returns owned T
rule: The owned modifier appears exactly when the declaring type is a class — a class instance is an owned heap value transferred to the caller.

title: a class target's Deserialize without owned is rejected
rule: The owned modifier appears exactly when the declaring type is a class; a class's recognized Deserialize factory that omits owned is rejected — a plain class-typed return reads as a borrow, and a static method's borrow-shaped return of a fresh value is rejected.

title: Json.ToText / Json.Parse round-trip a value-type record
rule: Json.ToText<T> / Json.Parse<T> are defined as the corresponding agent sequence, producing and consuming the type's synthesized JSON encoding.

title: Json.Parse<T> rejects a class-typed T at compile time
rule: Parse<T> requires an IDeserializable-conforming value-type target and rejects a class-typed T at compile time, directing to ParseOwned<T>.

title: writing a non-finite float raises SerializationException
rule: WriteFloat produces a JSON number, with non-finite values (NaN, ±Infinity) raising SerializationException — JSON has no representation for them.

title: a JSON-raised SerializationException carries a null Offset
rule: SerializationException locates the fault through Offset (binary) or Line/Column (JSON); the other format's properties are null on each instance.

title: an unknown field raises SerializationException by default
rule: A field present in the input that matches no declared component is, by default (IgnoreUnknownFields = false), a SerializationException — the strict default.

title: the JSON deserializer raises SerializationException on a number that rounds to a non-finite value
rule: a number whose value, so rounded, is not finite (`1e999`, `-1e999`) raises `SerializationException` located at the number, so a document never reads back a non-finite value `WriteFloat` could not have written.

title: the JSON deserializer raises SerializationException on a fragment that is not a JSON number
rule: **Errors.** Malformed input, type mismatches (a `ReadInt` when the next token is a string), and depth-limit violations raise `SerializationException` (declared in `System.Serialization`); a JSON number has the shape the input grammar of [§9.2](#sec-double-and-float) admits, and that grammar admits no bare point.

title: the JSON deserializer raises SerializationException on every malformed number
rule: **Errors.** Malformed input, type mismatches (a `ReadInt` when the next token is a string), and depth-limit violations raise `SerializationException` (declared in `System.Serialization`).

title: ReadFloat raises SerializationException on a point with no digits after it
rule: **Errors.** Malformed input, type mismatches (a `ReadInt` when the next token is a string), and depth-limit violations raise `SerializationException` (declared in `System.Serialization`); a JSON number has the shape the input grammar of [§9.2](#sec-double-and-float) admits, and that grammar admits a `.` only when one or more digits follow it.

title: disposing a cloned handle does not dispose the underlying value
rule: N handles jointly own one underlying value; the last handle's disposal disposes it — Clone() increments the count, and disposing one handle while another lives leaves the value alive.

title: Get() returns a borrow of the underlying value
rule: Shared<T>.Get() returns a borrow of the underlying value, sourced from the handle, valid while that handle lives.

title: Weak<T>.TryUpgrade succeeds while the value is still alive
rule: TryUpgrade returns a new strong handle if the value is still alive, null otherwise (Try shape (b)).

title: Weak<T>.TryUpgrade fails once the value has been disposed
rule: TryUpgrade returns null once the underlying value is no longer alive — Weak<T> does not keep the value alive, and after the last Shared handle disposes it, upgrading fails.

title: Shared<T> rejects a value-typed T at instantiation
rule: Shared<T> requires where T: class — proper class types only; a runtime-managed or value-typed T is rejected at instantiation.

title: TypeInitializationException.InnerException carries the original
rule: TypeInitializationException.InnerException carries the original exception that escaped the static initializer.

title: every subsequent access to a failed type raises the same exception
rule: Raised on access to a static member of a type whose static initialization failed — every subsequent access raises TypeInitializationException, not just the first.

title: integer Dn pads with leading zeros to n digits
rule: Integers admit D/Dn decimal, n = min digits, zero-padded.

title: integer X renders uppercase hex with no grouping separators
rule: Integers admit X/x hex (upper/lower), no grouping separators (no culture).

title: integer B renders binary digits
rule: Integers admit B binary.

title: floating F with no digit count defaults to 2 decimals
rule: Floating admits F/Fn fixed-point, n decimals, default 2.

title: floating P scales by 100 and appends a percent suffix
rule: Floating admits P/Pn percent (×100, % suffix).

title: decimal F2 rounds a midpoint half-to-even
rule: For a decimal operand, digit reduction under F/Fn rounds a midpoint half-to-even (banker's rounding): 0.125m under F2 renders "0.12".

title: a temporal pattern's non-specifier characters are literals
rule: In a temporal pattern, every character that does not begin one of the specifiers is a literal, copied to the output verbatim — T, Z, -, :, space, and any other non-specifier character alike.

title: a format spec on char is a compile error
rule: bool, char, string take none of the specifier vocabulary — a format spec on these is a compile error.

title: an unrecognized specifier raises FormatException
rule: The specifier vocabulary is invariant-culture only; an unrecognized specifier raises FormatException (strict-fault, as everywhere).

title: an unrecognized specifier in an interpolation hole raises FormatException
rule: An unrecognized specifier raises `FormatException` ([stdlib §2.18]). `c` is the TimeSpan constant form ("`c` renders the span's magnitude behind at most one sign"), so the specifier `g` in the hole is unrecognized and the interpolation throws before the next statement runs.

title: the TimeSpan constant form renders the documented examples
rule: `TimeSpan.FromMinutes(90.5)` renders `01:30:30` and "`TimeSpan.FromDays(1.5)` renders `1.12:00:00`" ([stdlib §2.18]); "The no-format `ToString()`, `ToString("c")` and an interpolation hole with or without `:c` produce this one rendering" ([stdlib §2.18]).
