A one-tick span renders its sub-second remainder as seven digits, and a minus sign is shown for a negative span.

title: the lower-case x specifier renders lower-case hex
rule: stdlib §2.18's integer row: "`X`/`x` hex (upper/lower, `Xn` pads)". The `x` specifier of 255 is the lower-case `ff`.

title: the X specifier pads to the stated digit count
rule: stdlib §2.18's integer row: "`X`/`x` hex (upper/lower, `Xn` pads)". `X4` pads 255 to four hex digits.

title: a user-defined IFormattable defines its own specifier vocabulary
rule: stdlib §2.18: "A **user-defined** `IFormattable` implementation defines its own specifier vocabulary — the table below governs only the intrinsic types ... (`money` above is such a user type defining its own `"C2"`; the intrinsic vocabulary deliberately has no `C`)". The interpolation hole dispatches the spec to the user's own `ToString`.

title: a format spec on a non-conforming operand is a compile error
rule: stdlib §2.18: "The primitive and temporal types are **intrinsically formattable** (they behave as conforming implementations without declaring the interface); a format spec on any other non-conforming operand is a compile error." The plain class below conforms to nothing that takes a format, so the hole's spec is a compile error.

title: a non-finite double renders NaN, Infinity or -Infinity
rule: stdlib §2.18: "The no-format `ToString()` and every floating specifier ... render a NaN as `NaN`, positive infinity as `Infinity` and negative infinity as `-Infinity` — the names of the `NaN`, `PositiveInfinity` and `NegativeInfinity` constants (§9.2) — with no digits, no exponent and no `%` suffix".

title: the intrinsic vocabulary has no C specifier
rule: stdlib §2.18: "`C` (currency) deliberately does not exist — currency formatting is culture by definition" and "An unrecognized specifier raises `FormatException`". `C` is not in the intrinsic vocabulary, so it is an unrecognized specifier.

title: the no-format ToString of an unsigned value keeps its value
rule: stdlib §9.1: "The no-format `ToString()` ... emits the text `ToString(10)` emits", and §2.18's integer row gives the decimal spelling of an integer. 4000000000 is a `uint` value and its decimal text is 4000000000 — the value, not the reinterpretation of its bits.

title: the D specifier of an unsigned value keeps its value
rule: stdlib §2.18's integer row: "`D`/`Dn` decimal (n = min digits, zero-padded)". The `D` spelling of 4000000000 is its decimal text.

title: a run-time format string renders as the literal spelling of the same format
rule: stdlib §9.1 declares `public pure method ToString(format: string): string` — one member, taking the format as a value — and §2.18's integer row gives the rendering of `D`/`Dn`. The format is the same string whichever spelling supplies it, so the two renderings agree.

title: an interpolation hole renders a non-finite double as Infinity
rule: stdlib §2.18's non-finite paragraph: "The no-format `ToString()` and every floating specifier ... render a NaN as `NaN`, positive infinity as `Infinity` and negative infinity as `-Infinity` ... with no digits, no exponent and no `%` suffix: `$"{1.0 / 0.0}"` and `(1.0 / 0.0).ToString("P2")` both render `"Infinity"`." The hole dispatches to the value's own rendering (language spec §18.5), so `$"{1.0 / 0.0}"` renders `Infinity`.

title: a non-finite float renders NaN, Infinity or -Infinity
rule: stdlib §2.18's non-finite paragraph governs `double` and `float` alike: "Non-finite `double` and `float` values. The no-format `ToString()` and every floating specifier ... render a NaN as `NaN`, positive infinity as `Infinity` and negative infinity as `-Infinity` — the names of the `NaN`, `PositiveInfinity` and `NegativeInfinity` constants (§9.2) — with no digits, no exponent and no `%` suffix".

title: a floating specifier renders a non-finite double as its name, with no percent suffix
rule: stdlib §2.18's non-finite paragraph: "every floating specifier (`F`, `E`, `G` and `P`, with or without a digit count, and `R`) render a NaN as `NaN`, positive infinity as `Infinity` and negative infinity as `-Infinity` ... with no digits, no exponent and no `%` suffix". The `P` specifier of an infinity carries no `%` suffix, so `$"{1.0 / 0.0:P2}"` renders `Infinity`.

title: the NaN round trip yields NaN, equal to the original under =
rule: stdlib §2.18's non-finite paragraph: "`Parse` reads each of the three back (§9.2); for a NaN the round trip yields `NaN`, equal to the original under `=` (language spec §4.3.1), and does not carry its sign or payload bits". Language spec §4.3.1: "`NaN = NaN` is **true**."

title: a NaN from an operation renders NaN like the NaN constant
rule: stdlib §2.18's non-finite paragraph: "Every NaN renders `NaN`, whatever its sign bit and payload." A NaN produced by an operation — here `Math.Sqrt` of a negative argument, IEEE 754 per language spec §6.3 — renders the same name as the `double.NaN` constant.

title: the no-format ToString of a double is the shortest string that parses back
rule: stdlib §2.18's floating row: "`R` and the **no-format `ToString()`** both produce the shortest string that parses back to the identical value — of several such, the one nearest it (round-trip guarantee)". One third renders `0.3333333333333333` and one tenth renders `0.1`.

title: an unrecognized specifier on an integer raises FormatException
rule: The specifier vocabulary is invariant-culture only — Bezel has no culture machinery, and formatted output is identical on every platform. An unrecognized specifier raises `FormatException` (strict-fault, as everywhere).

title: a format spec on a bool is a compile error
rule: stdlib §2.18 (v0.345), specifier table: "| `bool`, `char`, `string` | *(none)* | a format spec on these is a compile error".

title: a format spec on a bool in an interpolation hole is a compile error
rule: stdlib §2.18 (v0.345), specifier table: "| `bool`, `char`, `string` | *(none)* | a format spec on these is a compile error" — the interpolation hole dispatches its spec to the same vocabulary.

title: a format spec on a string in an interpolation hole is a compile error
rule: stdlib §2.18 (v0.345), specifier table: "| `bool`, `char`, `string` | *(none)* | a format spec on these is a compile error" — the interpolation hole dispatches its spec to the same vocabulary.

title: a format spec on a string passed to ToString is a compile error
rule: stdlib §2.18 (v0.345), specifier table: "| `bool`, `char`, `string` | *(none)* | a format spec on these is a compile error" — `string` declares no `ToString(format)` form.

title: a user record conforming to INumber<T> is usable through the constraint
rule: User types conform to INumber<T> by declaring and supplying the statics — a conformer's `<` with the rest of §25.2's complete group — and at a value conformer the operator witnesses are unmarked, matching the erased signatures.

title: char conforms to ISteppable<char> through T.Step
rule: char conforms to ISteppable<char>, witnessed by the compiler- provided conformance; ISteppable<T>.Step(value, by) advances in T's space.

title: bool conforms to none of INumber, ISteppable, IParsable
rule: bool conforms to none — deliberately: its Parse/TryParse are plain static members, not witnesses.

title: string conforms to none of INumber, ISteppable, IParsable
rule: string conforms to none of the three static abstractions — concatenation is not addition, and parsing a string to a string is meaningless.

title: a user class implementing ICollectionLiteralTarget is a literal target
rule: A user class declares exactly one of ICollectionLiteralTarget<TSelf, T> / IOwningCollectionLiteralTarget<TSelf, T>, at TSelf = itself, and supplies FromCollectionLiteral — the sequence-literal target.

title: IsOk() is true for the Ok case
rule: IsOk() distinguishes Ok from Error by case, compiler-provided.

title: Map transforms the Ok payload
rule: Map(f) ... maps Ok(v) to Ok(f(v)).

title: Map passes Error through unchanged
rule: Map(f) passes Error(e) through unchanged.

title: MapError transforms the Error payload
rule: MapError(f) ... maps Error(e) to Error(f(e)).

title: AndThen sequences a second fallible step on Ok
rule: AndThen(f) ... returns f(v) on Ok(v) and passes Error(e) through.

title: UnwrapOr returns the fallback on Error
rule: UnwrapOr(fallback) ... returns v on Ok(v) and fallback on Error(_).

title: UnwrapOr's fallback argument is evaluated eagerly
rule: UnwrapOr's argument is an ordinary value argument, not a deferred computation — it is evaluated at the call site, before the call, on the Ok path exactly as on the Error path.

title: Map is unreachable at an owning Result instantiation
rule: Map/MapError/AndThen/UnwrapOr are conditionally-admitted members, admissible only where the receiver instantiation is value-like; a borrow-bearing or owning receiver is rejected at the use site.

title: a ScopeGuard runs its action at disposal unless dismissed
rule: ScopeGuard's constructor runs the action at disposal unless dismissed.

title: Dismiss() suppresses the guard's action
rule: Dismiss() disarms the guard; after Dismiss() it is a no-op — the action does not run at disposal.

title: a ScopeGuard's action runs on the throwing edge
rule: On any throwing edge the guard's disposal runs the undo — a using var's dispose runs on the exception edge exactly as on the normal one.

title: IsDismissed defaults to False before Dismiss() is called
rule: IsDismissed exists for assertions and tests; a fresh guard is not dismissed.

title: Dismiss() is idempotent
rule: Dismiss() disarms; idempotent — a second call raises nothing.

title: Append returns this, enabling chained calls
rule: Methods return this to allow chaining; per-type Append overloads behave as Append(value.ToString()).

title: Remove raises IndexOutOfRangeException outside 0..Length
rule: stdlib §3.1's Contracts paragraph: "`Insert` and `Remove` raise `IndexOutOfRangeException` when the index or the `(startIndex, length)` window falls outside `0..Length`". The `(startIndex, length)` window `(10, 1)` over a builder whose `Length` is 5 falls outside `0..5`, so the call raises.

title: Replace with an empty oldValue raises ArgumentException
rule: Replace raises ArgumentException when oldValue is empty.

title: a negative capacity raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException
rule: Negative magnitudes fault — StringBuilder(capacity) raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException when passed a negative value.

title: AppendFormat raises FormatException on a hole index outside args
rule: AppendFormat's format string contains literal text and holes {n} — n a zero-based index into args; a hole index outside args raises FormatException.

title: StringBuilder is sendable and a moved builder keeps its contents
rule: `StringBuilder` is **sendable**, on the sendable form's copy-state ground. A moved builder keeps its contents.

title: a StringBuilder's Length reads its character count
rule: `Length` measures a fixed or contiguous extent — text (`String`, `StringBuilder`, `ReadOnlyStringSpan`) (stdlib §1, Count vs Length); StringBuilder declares `Length: int`. A StringBuilder holding the three characters abc has a Length of 3.

title: a StringBuilder member call that supplies fewer arguments than the member declares is rejected
rule: stdlib §3.1 declares `Replace(oldValue: string, newValue: string): StringBuilder` - two parameters, neither carrying a default. §22.5: every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; leaving one unbound makes the candidate inapplicable, so §22.6's arity filtering rejects the call.

title: a char argument to a StringBuilder member's string parameter is rejected
rule: stdlib §3.1 declares `Replace(oldValue: string, newValue: string): StringBuilder`. §5.1's implicit-conversion table lists a `char` as converting to `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`, `float`, `double` and `decimal` - never to `string` - so no candidate of §22.6 is applicable and the call is a compile error.

title: an int argument to a StringBuilder member's string parameter is rejected
rule: stdlib §3.1 declares `Replace(oldValue: string, newValue: string): StringBuilder`. §5.1's implicit-conversion table lists an `int` as converting to `long`, `float`, `double` and `decimal` - never to `string` - so no candidate of §22.6 is applicable and the call is a compile error.

title: the null-conditional spelling of a StringBuilder member call is rejected for the same arity reason
rule: stdlib §3.1 declares `Replace(oldValue: string, newValue: string): StringBuilder` - two parameters, neither carrying a default. §22.5: every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; leaving one unbound makes the candidate inapplicable, so §22.6's arity filtering rejects the call. The `?.` spelling of §7.5 decides whether the call happens on a null receiver; it does not change the member's declared arity.

title: an Array<int> argument to AppendFormat's Array<Object> parameter is rejected
rule: stdlib §3.1 declares `AppendFormat(format: string, args: Array<Object>): StringBuilder`. §12.9: classes, records, and concrete generic types are always invariant, so `Array<int>` is not `Array<Object>`; §5.1's reference conversions admit no such assignment, and §22.6 finds no applicable candidate.

title: an Object-typed argument to a StringBuilder member's string parameter is rejected
rule: stdlib §3.1 declares `Replace(oldValue: string, newValue: string): StringBuilder`. §5.1's reference conversions run from a type to a WIDER one - class to base class, transitively up to `Object`, and any type to `Object` - never from `Object` to a narrower one, so an `Object` reference converts to no `string`. No candidate of §22.6 is applicable and the call is a compile error.

title: a named argument to a StringBuilder member binds to the parameter it names
rule: stdlib §3.1 declares `Replace(oldValue: string, newValue: string): StringBuilder`. §22.5: named arguments may appear in any order after positional arguments, and each supplied argument binds exactly one parameter - so `Replace(oldValue := "l", newValue := "L")` binds "l" to oldValue and "L" to newValue, and the builder holds the text with its first "l" replaced.

title: a runtime long argument to a StringBuilder member's int parameter is rejected
rule: stdlib §3.1 declares `Insert(index: int, value: string): StringBuilder`. §5.1's implicit-conversion table admits a `long` only to `float`, `double` and `decimal`, and its constant narrowing reaches a narrower integer type only for a compile-time constant - a run-time integer value never narrows implicitly. No candidate of §22.6 is applicable and the call is a compile error.

title: a user-declared StringBuilder's own member is checked against its own declaration
rule: §22.5: every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name; leaving one unbound makes the candidate inapplicable, so §22.6 rejects the call. A user-declared type's member surface is its own declaration, not the built-in surface of stdlib §3.1 - and the arity rule applies to it unchanged.

title: a constant long argument to a StringBuilder member's int parameter narrows and is admitted
rule: stdlib §3.1 declares `Insert(index: int, value: string): StringBuilder`. §5.1's constant narrowing: an expression of integer type that is a compile-time constant implicitly converts to any integer type whose range contains its value, across signedness - so the constant `1L` reaches an `int` parameter. This is the accepting counterpart of the run-time `long` argument, which §5.1's conversion table does not reach.

title: StringBuilder.Insert raises IndexOutOfRangeException when the index is outside 0..Length
rule: stdlib §3.1's Contracts paragraph: "`Insert` and `Remove` raise `IndexOutOfRangeException` when the index or the `(startIndex, length)` window falls outside `0..Length`". §4.6 counts a length in code points - "`s.Length` returns the number of code points in `s`" - so a builder holding one non-ASCII code point has `Length` 1, and the index 2 lies outside `0..1`: the call raises rather than inserting.

title: StringBuilder.Insert with an index equal to the builder's Length is admitted
rule: stdlib §3.1's Contracts paragraph: "`Insert` and `Remove` raise `IndexOutOfRangeException` when the index or the `(startIndex, length)` window falls outside `0..Length`". The bound `0..Length` is INCLUSIVE at both ends and §4.6 counts a length in code points - "`s.Length` returns the number of code points in `s`" - so an index equal to the builder's code-point length is inside the bound and the call is admitted rather than raising: the admitting twin of l3_1_0058, which differs by the index alone.

title: StringBuilder.Replace with an empty oldValue raises ArgumentException, builder unchanged
rule: `Replace` raises `ArgumentException` when `oldValue` is empty.

title: StringBuilder.Replace raises ArgumentException for an empty oldValue passed by name in swapped order
rule: `Replace` raises `ArgumentException` when `oldValue` is empty. The parameters are `oldValue` and `newValue`, so the empty value is the `oldValue` whatever the order the named arguments are written in.

title: StringBuilder.Replace with integer arguments is rejected
rule: public method Replace(oldValue: string, newValue: string): StringBuilder;

title: StringBuilder.Remove with a string startIndex is rejected
rule: public method Remove(startIndex: int, length: int): StringBuilder;

title: StringBuilder.Insert with one argument is rejected
rule: public method Insert(index: int, value: string): StringBuilder;

title: StringBuilder.Insert with a string index is rejected
rule: public method Insert(index: int, value: string): StringBuilder;

title: StringBuilder.Insert with three arguments is rejected
rule: public method Insert(index: int, value: string): StringBuilder;

title: StringBuilder.Insert accepts fresh string producers at the start, the end and mid-string, 150 loops
rule: public method Insert(index: int, value: string): StringBuilder; ... `Insert` and `Remove` raise `IndexOutOfRangeException` when the index or the `(startIndex, length)` window falls outside `0..Length`; `Replace` raises `ArgumentException` when `oldValue` is empty.

title: StringBuilder.Replace accepts fresh string producers, empty new text and named arguments
rule: public method Replace(oldValue: string, newValue: string): StringBuilder; ... `Insert` and `Remove` raise `IndexOutOfRangeException` when the index or the `(startIndex, length)` window falls outside `0..Length`; `Replace` raises `ArgumentException` when `oldValue` is empty.

title: StringBuilder Insert and Replace raise on a bad index or an empty old value from fresh producers
rule: `Insert` and `Remove` raise `IndexOutOfRangeException` when the index or the `(startIndex, length)` window falls outside `0..Length`; `Replace` raises `ArgumentException` when `oldValue` is empty.

title: UTF8 round-trips GetBytes and GetString
rule: GetBytes(s: string) / GetString(bytes) form a round trip for well-formed input.

title: ASCII.GetBytes raises FormatException above U+007F
rule: ASCII is strict seven-bit; GetBytes raises FormatException on any code point above U+007F.

title: UTF8.GetString raises FormatException on malformed bytes
rule: Malformed or unrepresentable input is a defined fault — GetString raises FormatException when the input bytes are not a well-formed sequence; no replacement characters are produced.

title: UTF8.Name is "utf-8"
rule: UTF8's Name is "utf-8".

title: UTF8.GetBytes never emits a byte-order mark
rule: GetBytes never emits a byte-order mark.

title: each standard encoding reports its Name through parameters, fields, array elements and conditionals
rule: Stdlib §3.2: "`UTF8` (`Name` = `"utf-8"`)", "`UTF16` (`Name` = `"utf-16le"`)", "`UTF32` (`Name` = `"utf-32le"`)", "`ASCII` (`Name` = `"us-ascii"`)". The singletons are `Encoding`-typed values (the concrete subclasses are not public API), so `Name` reads the same through a parameter, a class field, an array element and a conditional.

title: Encoding.GetBytes has no overload taking an Array<char>
rule: Stdlib §3.2 declares `GetBytes(s: string)`, `GetBytes(s: string, destination: Span<byte>)`, `GetBytes(s: ReadOnlyStringSpan)` and `GetBytes(s: ReadOnlyStringSpan, destination: Span<byte>)`; none takes an `Array<char>`, and §5.1 has no implicit conversion from `Array<char>` to `string` or a string span, so the call has no applicable overload.

title: Encoding.GetByteCount has no overload taking an int
rule: Stdlib §3.2 declares `GetByteCount(s: string)` and `GetByteCount(s: ReadOnlyStringSpan)` only; `int` converts to neither (§5.1), so `GetByteCount(5)` has no applicable overload.

title: GetByteCount over a string returned by a call counts the UTF-8 bytes
rule: Stdlib §3.2: `GetByteCount(s: string): int`, and "`UTF8` ...: bytes are the UTF-8 form of the string's code points": `"aé"` is U+0061 (1 byte) and U+00E9 (2 bytes), so the count is 3, for a string that is a call result.

title: the span-source encode forms agree on a window of a string
rule: Stdlib §3.2: the span-source encode overloads have "identical contract to the string forms over the span's code-point range (`GetByteCount` and `GetBytes` agree ...)". The window `(1, 2)` of `"aé€z"` is `é€`, U+00E9 as C3 A9 and U+20AC as E2 82 AC: `GetBytes(s, destination)` returns 5, the allocating `GetBytes(s)` holds 5 bytes, `GetByteCount` is 5, and the destination begins C3 A9 E2.

title: the span-source encode forms keep the strict fault model of the string forms
rule: Stdlib §3.2: the span-source encode overloads carry "the same strict fault model, `FormatException` possible only for `ASCII`", and `GetBytes(s, destination)` raises `IndexOutOfRangeException` if the destination is too short. The window `"aé"` holds U+00E9, which `ASCII` cannot represent; the one-byte destination cannot hold `é€`.

title: ReadOnlyStringSpan is not borrow-bearing and may sit in a field
rule: ReadOnlyStringSpan is a deliberate exception among the spans — its only reference field is a string, so it may sit in fields and cross await.

title: Slice returns the requested sub-range
rule: Slice(start, length) constructs a new ReadOnlyStringSpan over the requested range.

title: IndexOf of an empty needle returns 0
rule: The empty span or string is a valid needle: IndexOf of an empty needle returns 0.

title: the indexer raises IndexOutOfRangeException outside 0..Length
rule: span[i] throws IndexOutOfRangeException when i < 0 or i >= Length.

title: a zero-length receiver never contains a non-empty needle
rule: A zero-length receiver is well-defined: every non-empty needle is not found — Contains returns false.

title: ReadOnlyStringSpan.SequenceEqual takes the array-backed char span
rule: public pure method SequenceEqual(other: ReadOnlyArraySpan<char>): bool; ... `SequenceEqual(other)` returns `true` if the two spans have the same length and matching code points at every position.

title: Array<T>.Dispose() does not dispose its stored elements
rule: Element disposal is never performed by or through a borrowing collection: a holder that owns its elements uses the owning family, whose Dispose() cascades; the borrowing family's Dispose() is a no-op.

title: Array<T>.Remove removes the borrow without disposing the element
rule: ICollection<T>'s Remove/Clear/RemoveAt on a borrowing collection remove without disposing; the element's holder, if any, keeps its disposal obligation.

title: IsReadOnly is false on a mutable borrowing collection
rule: IsReadOnly is false for every standard collection implementing ICollection<T> (Array<T>, LinkedList<T>, Set<T>, Dictionary<K, V>).

title: IList<T> is a reachable abstraction over Array<T>'s mutation surface
rule: IList<T>: IReadOnlyList<T>, ICollection<T> declares the settable indexer and Insert(index, item); Array<T> conforms to IList<T>, so a generic helper written against the interface reaches those members.

title: an ICollection's Count reads the number of elements
rule: `public interface IReadOnlyCollection<out T>: IEnumerable<T>` declares `pure readonly property Count: int;` (stdlib §4.1), and ICollection<T> extends it. After two Add calls an Array<int> reached through ICollection<int> has Count 2.

title: IsReadOnly reads false through an ICollection-typed receiver
rule: IsReadOnly is `false` for every standard collection implementing `ICollection<T>` (`Array<T>`, `LinkedList<T>`, `Set<T>`, `Dictionary<K, V>`) (stdlib §4.1, v0.340). `ICollection<T>` declares `readonly property IsReadOnly: bool` (§4.1), and §26.5 rule 1 commits instance resolution to the head's declared member, so the `Array<int>` (§4.4) behind an `ICollection<int>`-typed receiver answers `false` — the value the concrete receiver gives, read through the interface.

title: Contains reads true through an IList-typed receiver
rule: `ICollection<T>` declares `method Contains(item: T): bool` (stdlib §4.1, v0.340), and `IList<T>: IReadOnlyList<T>, ICollection<T>` (§4.1) inherits it; §26.5 rule 1 commits instance resolution to the head's declared member, so the `Array<int>` (§4.4) holding 1, 2, 3 behind an `IList<int>`-typed receiver answers `true` for `Contains(2)`.

title: Count reads the element count through an IList-typed receiver
rule: `IReadOnlyCollection<out T>: IEnumerable<T>` declares `pure readonly property Count: int` (stdlib §4.1, v0.340), and `IList<T>: IReadOnlyList<T>, ICollection<T>` inherits it; §26.5 rule 1 commits instance resolution to the head's declared member, so the `Array<int>` (§4.4) holding 1, 2, 3 behind an `IList<int>`-typed receiver answers `3`.

title: Add is not a member of IReadOnlyList and the call is a compile error
rule: `public interface IReadOnlyList<out T>: IReadOnlyCollection<T>` declares only `readonly property [i: int]: T;` (stdlib §4.1, v0.340) — the indexer, plus the `Count` property and `GetEnumerator` it inherits. `Add` is declared on `ICollection<T>` (§4.1), which `IReadOnlyList<T>` does not extend, and no stdlib §5 extension operator is named `Add`; §26.5 rule 1 commits instance resolution to the head's declared member and rule 2 finds no applicable extension, so the call is a compile error.

title: Insert is not a member of ICollection and the call is a compile error
rule: `public interface ICollection<T>: IReadOnlyCollection<T>` declares `readonly property IsReadOnly: bool`, `method Add(item: T)`, `method Clear()`, `method Contains(item: T): bool` and `method Remove(item: T): bool` (stdlib §4.1, v0.340) — `Insert` is declared on `IList<T>` (§4.1) alone, and `ICollection<T>` does not extend it; no stdlib §5 extension operator is named `Insert`, so §26.5 rule 1 finds no instance member and rule 2 finds no extension: the call is a compile error.

title: IndexOf is not a member of IList and the call is a compile error
rule: `public interface IList<T>: IReadOnlyList<T>, ICollection<T>` declares `property [i: int]: T` and `method Insert(index: int, item: T)` (stdlib §4.1, v0.340) over the members it inherits — `IndexOf` is declared on the concrete `Array<T>` (§4.4) alone, and `IList<T>` does not declare it; no stdlib §5 extension operator is named `IndexOf`, so §26.5 rule 1 finds no instance member and rule 2 finds no extension: the call is a compile error.

title: IsReadOnly reads false through an IList-typed receiver
rule: IsReadOnly is `false` for every standard collection implementing `ICollection<T>` (`Array<T>`, `LinkedList<T>`, `Set<T>`, `Dictionary<K, V>`) (stdlib §4.1, v0.343). `IList<T>` extends `ICollection<T>` (§4.1), so it inherits the `readonly property IsReadOnly: bool` §4.1 declares on `ICollection<T>`; §26.5 rule 1 commits instance resolution to the head's declared member, so the `Array<int>` (§4.4) holding 1, 2, 3 behind an `IList<int>`-typed receiver answers `false` — the value the concrete receiver gives, read through the interface.

title: IOwningCollection<T>.Add takes owned and transfers ownership in
rule: IOwningCollection<T> declares method Add(owned item: T); the mutating methods of the owning family take owned parameters and take ownership of the new element.

title: IOwningCollection<T>.Clear disposes every element
rule: IOwningCollection<T> declares method Clear(); // disposes every element — the interface-level contract every owning collection shares.

title: IOwningCollection<T>.Remove disposes the removed element
rule: IOwningCollection<T> declares method Remove(item: T): bool; // disposes the removed element — the borrow-taking query removes and disposes what it finds.

title: OwningArray<string> is rejected at the instantiation site
rule: The where T: class constraint is enforced at the instantiation site: a runtime-managed reference type such as string has no disposal obligation and is rejected where the owning family requires a class or interface element type.

title: OwningArray<Widget> is admitted at a class element type
rule: The where T: class constraint on the owning family is satisfied by a concrete class type; a class-typed instantiation is admissible where a runtime-managed type is not.

title: OwningDictionary<K, V> rejects a value-typed V at instantiation
rule: OwningDictionary<K, V> requires where V: class (the value type is owned); a value-typed V has no disposal obligation and is rejected at the instantiation site, keys being unconstrained.

title: OwningLinkedList<T> rejects a function-typed T at instantiation
rule: Runtime-managed reference types (string, function values) are rejected at the owning family's instantiation site, alongside value-typed elements — ownership only makes sense for class-typed values.

title: Insert is not a member of IOwningCollection and the call is a compile error
rule: `public interface IOwningCollection<T>: IReadOnlyCollection<T>, IDisposable` declares `IsReadOnly`, `Add`, `Clear`, `Contains`, `Remove` and `Dispose` (stdlib §4.2, v0.340) — `Insert` is declared on `IOwningList<T>` (§4.2) alone, which `IOwningCollection<T>` does not extend; no stdlib §5 extension operator is named `Insert`, so §26.5 rule 1 finds no instance member and rule 2 finds no extension: the call is a compile error.

title: a read-only helper accepts both a borrowing and an owning collection
rule: The two hierarchies share IEnumerable<T>, IReadOnlyCollection<T>, and IReadOnlyList<T> as common ancestors; a function that wants to read elements without taking ownership accepts one of these interfaces, and both borrowing and owning collections of T conform.

title: OwningArray<T> does not implicitly convert to Array<T>
rule: The two hierarchies do not share mutating interfaces, and there is no implicit conversion between the families — an OwningArray<T> is not an Array<T>.

title: IList<T> and IOwningList<T> are unrelated types
rule: IList<T> (borrowing) and IOwningList<T> (owning) are unrelated types with no subtyping; code that abstracts over "any mutable list" must pick one.

title: OwningArray<T> conforms to IOwningList<T>, its own mutating family
rule: The mutating interfaces do not cross families; OwningArray<T> does implement IOwningList<T>, its own family's mutable abstraction.

title: Drain() is the route from the owning family to ownership-transferring iteration
rule: For draining iteration that transfers ownership, the owning collections expose Drain() returning IOwningEnumerable<T>; default iteration stays borrowing, and the owning path is taken only at static type IOwningEnumerable<T>.

title: Array<T>(capacity) reserves storage without adding elements
rule: constructor(capacity: int); // empty (Count = 0), storage reserved

title: Array<T>(size, fill) fills every slot with the given value
rule: constructor(size: int, fill: T); // Count = size, every slot = fill (v0.165, #1375)

title: IndexOf finds the first occurrence at or after startIndex
rule: method IndexOf(item: T, startIndex: int := 0): int; // first occurrence at or after startIndex, or -1 (v0.228).

title: IndexOf with startIndex equal to Count is legal and returns -1
rule: 0 <= startIndex <= Count required, IndexOutOfRangeException otherwise; startIndex = Count is legal and returns -1.

title: IndexOf raises when startIndex exceeds Count
rule: 0 <= startIndex <= Count required, IndexOutOfRangeException otherwise.

title: Sorted() natural order requires T: IComparable<T>, checked at the call
rule: method Sorted(): owned Array<T>; // natural order; admitted only where T: IComparable<T>, checked at the call's instantiation (v0.275).

title: Sorted natural order is rejected for a non-IComparable element type
rule: The parameterless natural-order Sort/Sorted is a conditionally admitted member: admitted only where T: IComparable<T>, with the condition decided after substitution and the rejection reported at the call, never at the declaration.

title: Sorted leaves the receiver unchanged and returns a fresh copy
rule: The past-participle form (Sorted) leaves the receiver unchanged and returns a fresh owned Array<T> with the elements in the new order.

title: Sort mutates the receiver in place and returns nothing
rule: The imperative-verb form (Sort) mutates the receiver in place and returns nothing.

title: structurally mutating an Array<T> inside its own sort comparer raises
rule: Structurally mutating a collection from inside its own sort comparer raises InvalidOperationException (the loud-failure discipline, extended from enumerator invalidation to sort callbacks).

title: a fresh producer stored via Array<T>.Add warns rather than rejects
rule: On the borrowing family a fresh producer via Add/Insert/indexer-set is admitted but warns: the temporary dies at the statement's end and the stored slot dangles.

title: a fresh non-trivial-dispose element inside an Array<T> literal is a hard error
rule: For borrowing-family targets, an element expression that is a fresh producer of non-trivial-dispose class type is rejected at the literal site — the temporary would be disposed at the end of the declaration statement, leaving the collection holding a dangling borrow from birth.

title: a bound source in an Array<T> literal is admitted, unlike a fresh producer
rule: The remedy for a fresh producer inside a borrowing-family literal names the source first: bind the source to a named holder, whose borrow is then admitted at the literal site.

title: Array<T>.Remove's result is a bool, usable in a condition
rule: public method Remove(item: T): bool; (stdlib §4.4 Array<T>)

title: Array<T>.Remove result is bool and does not convert to int
rule: public method Remove(item: T): bool; (stdlib §4.4 Array<T>)

title: IndexOf's defaulted startIndex is 0 and the first match is found
rule: `public method IndexOf(item: T, startIndex: int := 0): int;` (stdlib §4.4, v0.340) — the first occurrence at or after `startIndex`, or -1. The call omits the optional `startIndex`, so the default 0 applies and the search starts at the first slot: the elements 1, 2, 3 hold 2 at index 1.

title: Array<int>.Sorted(a) static form is rejected: Sorted is an instance member
rule: Array<T> declares `Sorted()` and `Sorted(comparer)` as instance methods returning a fresh owned Array<T> and declares no static members; an undeclared static is an error (stdlib 4.4; spec 22.1).

title: Array LastIndexOf returns the last occurrence on bool, long, double and short arrays, or -1
rule: public method LastIndexOf(item: T): int;      // last occurrence, or -1.

title: OwningArray<T>.Add transfers ownership; a fresh producer is warning-free
rule: OwningArray<T> owns each element; Add takes ownership. On the owning family a fresh producer is idiomatic and warning-free: pool.Add(new Connection("a"));

title: the OwningArray<T> indexer setter disposes the previous slot value
rule: The indexer getter produces a borrow of the slot's owned element; the setter takes ownership and disposes the previous value first — property [i: int]: T get; set(owned);

title: OwningArray<T>.RemoveAt disposes the removed element
rule: RemoveAt(index: int); // disposes the removed element

title: OwningArray<T>.Clear disposes every element
rule: Clear(); // disposes every element — the array's own Dispose() cascades the same way.

title: PopFirst takes an element out without disposing it
rule: PopFirst(): owned T; // = PopAt(0); raises if empty. Drain methods transfer ownership of elements out of the collection.

title: PopFirst raises when the array is empty
rule: PopFirst(): owned T; // = PopAt(0); raises if empty.

title: TryPopLast reports false on an empty array and assigns null
rule: TryPopLast(out owned item: T?): bool; // v0.171: the false path assigns null.

title: Drain() yields owned elements and leaves the array empty
rule: Drain(): IOwningEnumerable<T>; // iteration drains the source. A for var x in arr.Drain() do ... end loop has owned iteration variables and consumes the array's elements.

title: an undischarged owning-drain iteration variable auto-drops with the must-use warning
rule: The spec §28.3 discharge rules apply per iteration in the drain loop; an undischarged element auto-drops at the body's end with the must-use warning.

title: move arr[i] takes ownership and leaves the slot moved-from
rule: To take an element out, use PopAt(i) ... or move arr[i] (returns owned T and leaves the slot in moved-from state; the caller must reassign before the next exit point).

title: OwningArray<T>.AddRange drains its owned source argument
rule: AddRange(owned items: OwningArray<T>); // drains items into self.

title: OwningArray<T> declares no Sorted() — no owning copy is expressible
rule: OwningArray<T> declares no copy-forms of its own — no Reversed, no Sorted, no ToArray — because no owning copy is expressible: it would either double-own each element or drain the source.

title: ToArray() is reachable on OwningArray<T> as a borrowing snapshot extension
rule: What is reachable, and is not an owning copy, is the LINQ ToArray() extension on IEnumerable<T>: it resolves on an OwningArray<T> receiver and returns an owned Array<T> — a borrowing snapshot whose slots hold borrows of the elements this array still owns.

title: OwningArray<T>.Remove on a bound element has a bool result
rule: public method Remove(item: T): bool;                   // borrow-taking query; (stdlib §4.5 OwningArray<T>)

title: LinkedList<T>.AddLast returns a node borrowing the list
rule: method AddLast(item: T): LinkedListNode<T>; LinkedListNode<T> instances are owned by their containing LinkedList<T>; methods returning LinkedListNode<T> return a borrow whose lifetime is the list's lifetime.

title: LinkedList<T>.RemoveFirst removes without disposing the element
rule: LinkedList<T> is a borrowing collection (ICollection<T>); RemoveFirst/RemoveLast/RemoveNode remove without disposing, per the borrowing-family rule (spec §28.11).

title: a sequence literal constructs a LinkedList<T> in head-to-tail order
rule: A LinkedList<T> may be constructed with a sequence literal; textual order is head-to-tail: `using var l: LinkedList<int> := [10, 20, 30];` produces a list whose First is 10 and Last is 30.

title: LinkedList<T>.Add appends at the tail, equivalent to AddLast
rule: Plus the standard ICollection<T> operations: Add (appends at the tail, = AddLast — v0.195).

title: OwningLinkedList<T>.AddLast takes ownership of its argument
rule: method AddLast(owned item: T): LinkedListNode<T>; a fresh producer into the owning family is idiomatic and warning-free.

title: OwningLinkedList<T>.RemoveFirst disposes the removed element
rule: RemoveFirst(); // disposes — the owning list's removal methods dispose the element they remove.

title: OwningLinkedList<T>.PopFirst transfers ownership out without disposing
rule: To take an element out, use RemoveNode (which disposes), PopFirst / PopLast (transfer ownership to caller), or Drain().

title: OwningLinkedList<T> has no populate-from-source constructor
rule: There is no source constructor (v0.265): OwningLinkedList<T> declares constructor() and no populate-from-source form, deliberately — a borrowing source has no elements to give.

title: draining an owning array into an owning list, one element at a time
rule: Build an owning list from owned elements ... or add them one at a time, taking them out of the source as you go: for var c in src.Drain() do dst.AddLast(move c); end;

title: Dictionary<K,V> indexer raises KeyNotFoundException on a missing key
rule: Indexer dict[key] raises KeyNotFoundException if the key is not present.

title: Dictionary<K,V>.Add raises ArgumentException on a duplicate key
rule: Add(key, value) inserts and raises ArgumentException if the key is already present.

title: TryAdd reports false and makes no mutation on a duplicate key
rule: TryAdd(key, value): bool; // v0.282: false, no mutation if the key is present.

title: TryAdd leaves the existing value unchanged on a duplicate key
rule: TryAdd(key, value): bool; // false, no mutation if the key is present — the twin observation to l4_8_0003's boolean result.

title: dict[key] += 1 raises on an absent key; the compound form never inserts
rule: dict[key] += 1 desugars to a getter plus a setter, and the getter raises KeyNotFoundException on an absent key — the compound form updates, it never inserts.

title: there is no Set method on Dictionary<K,V> — writes go through the indexer
rule: There is no separate Set method — neither here nor on any other collection. A call to a Set method on any collection is rejected as an unknown member.

title: Dictionary<K,V>.Clear drops every entry without disposing keys or values
rule: Clear(); // drops every entry; disposes neither keys and values.

title: GetOrNull returns null for an absent key
rule: GetOrNull(key: K): V?; // v0.231 (§1 *OrNull tier): absent -> null.

title: a Dictionary<K,V> key type that is neither auto-hashable nor equality-declaring is rejected
rule: K must be hashable (spec §3.6/§8.3) — enforced at the instantiation site per §3.6 rule 2: a Dictionary<K, V> whose K is a record that is neither auto-hashable nor declares user equality is rejected with a diagnostic naming the property.

title: an auto-hashable record key is admitted at Dictionary<K,V>
rule: K must be hashable; an auto-hashable record — one whose storage is composed only of admissible component types — satisfies the constraint where the disqualified twin does not.

title: OwningDictionary<K,V>.Add disposes the passed value when the key is a duplicate
rule: Add(key: K, owned value: V); // ArgumentException if the key is present; the passed value was consumed at the call site and is disposed on that path (v0.195).

title: OwningDictionary<K,V>.TryAdd disposes the passed value on a duplicate key
rule: TryAdd(key: K, owned value: V): bool; // v0.282: false on duplicate, and the passed value is disposed on that path.

title: OwningDictionary<K,V>.Remove disposes the removed value
rule: Remove(key: K): bool; // disposes the removed value.

title: OwningDictionary<K,V>.Clear disposes every value
rule: Clear(); // disposes every value — the dictionary's Dispose() cascade handles the same disposal.

title: PopValue transfers ownership out without disposing
rule: PopValue(key: K): owned V; // raises if not present — the take form, in contrast with GetOrNull's look.

title: OwningDictionary<K,V> provides no default entry iteration
rule: Default for var entry in ownedDict do iteration is not provided on OwningDictionary<K, V> — the interface conformance is IDisposable only, not IOwningCollection<DictionaryEntry<K, V>>.

title: a fresh class-typed key into an OwningDictionary warns
rule: A class-typed key is held as a borrow exactly as Dictionary<K,V>'s is, and the fresh-store warning reaches that position: od[key] := v with a fresh key temporary dangles at the K8 boundary.

title: OwningDictionary<K,V>.GetOrAdd returns a borrow of the stored value
rule: GetOrAdd(key: K, factory: (K) -> owned V): V; // returns borrow — the dictionary stores the factory's value, taking ownership, and the call returns a borrow of the now-stored value.

title: OwningDictionary at a class-typed key is not sendable, whatever the key's own sendability
rule: Its keys are held as a borrowing map's are (spec §28.11), so the borrowing condition applies to them as well: `K`'s category is sendable-value, `string` or `Type`. At a class- or interface-typed `K` the map carries borrows and is not sendable, whatever `K`'s own sendability.

title: OwningDictionary at a string key and a sendable class value is sendable
rule: `OwningDictionary<K, V>`'s element type is `V`. Its keys are held as a borrowing map's are (spec §28.11), so the borrowing condition applies to them as well: `K`'s category is sendable-value, `string` or `Type`. `OwningDictionary<string, Session>` is sendable at a sendable `Session`.

title: Set<T>.TryAdd reports false on a duplicate element
rule: method TryAdd(item: T): bool; // returns whether added (false if duplicate).

title: OwningSet<T>.Add silently disposes the item on a duplicate
rule: When the caller passes owned item and the set already contains an equal element, Add returns () and disposes the passed-in item — the caller relinquished ownership at the call site.

title: OwningSet<T>.TryAdd disposes the passed item on a duplicate
rule: method TryAdd(owned item: T): bool; // returns whether added (false if duplicate; passed item is disposed).

title: OwningSet<T>.Pop finds the equal element and transfers ownership out
rule: Pop(query: T): owned T; // finds the equal element in the set, removes it, and returns ownership. The query and the stored element are equal by the set's Equals rule but may be distinct instances.

title: a Set<T> element type that is neither auto-hashable nor equality-declaring is rejected
rule: T must be hashable (spec §3.6/§8.3), enforced at the instantiation site per §3.6 rule 2 — same rule as Dictionary<K, V> keys.

title: Set<T>.Remove's result is a bool, usable in a condition
rule: method Remove(item: T): bool; (stdlib §4.10 Set<T>, ICollection<T>)

title: Set<T>.Remove result is bool and does not convert to int
rule: method Remove(item: T): bool; (stdlib §4.10 Set<T>, ICollection<T>)

title: OwningSet<T>.Remove on a bound element has a bool result
rule: method Remove(item: T): bool;              // disposes the removed element (stdlib §4.10 OwningSet<T>, IOwningCollection<T>)

title: OwningStack<T>.Pop transfers ownership out without disposing
rule: On the owning forms, Pop and Dequeue return ownership; the collection no longer holds the element.

title: Stack<T>.Clear drops every element and disposes nothing
rule: The borrowing forms also provide Clear(): it drops every element reference and disposes nothing, per the borrowing-family rule.

title: OwningQueue<T>.Clear disposes every element
rule: OwningStack<T>/OwningQueue<T>.Clear(); // disposes every element.

title: a Stack<T> literal is read bottom-to-top, so the last element pops first
rule: Stack<T>/OwningStack<T>: the literal lists elements bottom-to-top — the first element is pushed first (ends up at the bottom), the last element is on top (popped first). [1, 2, 3] pops 3, then 2, then 1.

title: a Queue<T> literal places the first element at the front
rule: Queue<T>/OwningQueue<T>: the first literal element is at the front of the queue (the next to be dequeued). [1, 2, 3] dequeues 1, then 2, then 3.

title: OwningStack<T>.Peek borrows the top element without removing it
rule: pure method Peek(): T; // borrow of top element — for class T on the owning forms, Pop and Dequeue transfer ownership, while Peek only borrows.

title: a Stack<int> iterates top-to-bottom, the order its elements pop in
rule: All four types iterate (via `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`) in take order — a stack top-to-bottom (pop order), a queue front-to-back (dequeue order); the owning forms iterate identically, yielding borrows.

title: IEnumerator<T>.Current is non-destructive and repeats without an intervening MoveNext
rule: IEnumerator<T>.Current is non-destructive -- it returns a borrow of the most-recently-yielded value, which the enumerator continues to own; reading it again without an intervening MoveNext yields the same value.

title: IEnumerable<T> is covariant, admitting an Array<Derived> where IEnumerable<Base> is expected
rule: IEnumerable<T> is covariant in T.

title: GetEnumerator() returns an owned IEnumerator<T> the caller must dispose
rule: GetEnumerator(): owned IEnumerator<T>; -- the caller takes ownership of the returned enumerator and must dispose it.

title: a second TakeCurrent without an intervening advance raises InvalidOperationException
rule: A second take without an intervening advance, or a take before the first advance/after exhaustion, raises InvalidOperationException.

title: TakeCurrent before the first advance raises InvalidOperationException
rule: A take before the first advance/after exhaustion raises InvalidOperationException.

title: an advanced-but-untaken element is disposed when the enumerator is disposed
rule: Between a successful advance and TakeCurrent() the enumerator owns the pending value -- a Dispose() after an advance whose value was never taken disposes it; an advanced-but-untaken element neither leaks nor reaches the consumer.

title: an undischarged owned for-loop variable over an owning source auto-drops with a warning
rule: A for var x in src do ... end where src is an IOwningEnumerable<T> produces owned iteration variables; where the body does not discharge x, the affine auto-drop disposes it at the iteration's scope end with the plain-var must-use warning.

title: disposing a drain-view frame does not dispose the collection; partial iteration leaves the remainder
rule: Every owning collection's Drain() mints a fresh drain-view frame -- a caller-owned enumerable over the collection, never the collection re-exposed -- so the frame's disposal at loop end never disposes the collection, and partial iteration leaves the undrained remainder in place.

title: a fresh GetOwningEnumerator() on a live drain view continues over the current remainder
rule: Each GetOwningEnumerator() call on a live view yields a fresh enumerator over the collection's current remainder -- a re-enumeration continues draining what remains, never replaying what already left.

title: a Span<T> may not outlive the OwningBuffer<T> source it borrows
rule: A borrow-bearing record value may not outlive the source of any borrow it contains; a Span<T>'s Buffer field carries a borrow of the OwningBuffer<T> it views, bounded by the source's lifetime.

title: a Span<T> is usable while its OwningBuffer<T> source stays live
rule: A borrow-bearing record value is admitted while the source of every borrow it contains is still live; Span<T> reads through the buffer for as long as the buffer is not disposed.

title: a Span<T> may not be constructed from an unbound temporary buffer
rule: A borrow-bearing record may not be constructed from a temporary bound to one of its borrow-carrying fields -- a fresh call result not bound to a named location has a lifetime ending at the construction expression, so the record would immediately outlive that source.

title: a Span<T> constructed from a named, bound buffer is admitted
rule: Bind the source to a named local whose scope outlives the record, and pass that -- the remedy for the no-temporary-source rule.

title: a Span<T> may not be stored in an instance field of a class
rule: A borrow-bearing record value may not be stored in an instance field of a class -- a class instance's lifetime is not bounded by any borrow source's scope, and the store is rejected statically.

title: a Span<T> may not be stored in a static field unless it is the null-source form
rule: A borrow-bearing record may not be stored in a static field of any type, except when every reference-typed field of the value is null; Span<T>'s Buffer field is a non-nullable reference, so no Span<T> value ever satisfies the null-source form.

title: OwningBuffer<T>'s indexer setter disposes the slot's previous value at class T
rule: The indexer's setter takes ownership of the assigned value and disposes whatever the slot previously held.

title: a slot moved-from via move buf[i] must be restored before the enclosing scope exits
rule: move buf[i] leaves the slot moved-from; the field-restoration rule of language spec 28.8.1 applies -- any slot moved-from must be reassigned before any exit edge, because auto-dispose on a moved-from slot is not defined.

title: a bare move buf[i] on a class-typed buffer slot stores null in the same step
rule: `move buf[i]` is admitted and produces an owned `T?` value, storing `null` into the slot in the same step; `move buf[i] with e` stores `e` instead (§28.8.1).

title: move buf[i] is not admitted for value-typed T
rule: For value-typed T, move buf[i] is not admitted -- values have no ownership to transfer, and are read with the plain indexer instead.

title: ReadOnlySpan<T> has no ToArray() member
rule: ReadOnlySpan<T> declared ToArray(): owned Array<T> from v0.222 until v0.277, which deleted it; the compiler never admitted the call, and the absence is now recorded -- there is no materializer on this family.

title: TryReadInt16LittleEndian returns false and leaves value default on a short span
rule: Read methods throw IndexOutOfRangeException if the span is shorter than the type being read; TryRead* variants return false instead of throwing and assign the out parameter to default(T) on the false path.

title: OwningBuffer<T> does not admit a runtime-managed reference type such as string
rule: What is not admitted. Runtime-managed reference types (string, function types) are not admitted as T -- they have no disposal obligation, so the owning semantics add nothing.

title: OwningBuffer<double> is sendable and its storage crosses with it
rule: `OwningBuffer<T>` is sendable iff its element type is a sendable class type or a sendable value type: its storage is part of the instance and crosses with it (`OwningBuffer<double>` is sendable; a buffer of a borrow-bearing record is not).

title: OwningBuffer at a non-sendable value element is not sendable
rule: `OwningBuffer<T>` is sendable iff its element type is a sendable class type or a sendable value type.

title: a buffer span compares with a writable array span passed through AsReadOnly
rule: Every span type declares it for its own type and for the read-only span of each heap backing — here `Span<T>`, `ReadOnlySpan<T>` and `ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>` ... — so a comparison across backings needs no common type, and a writable span passed as the argument converts by `.AsReadOnly()`.

title: a buffer span's SequenceEqual does not take a writable array span
rule: Every span type declares it for its own type and for the read-only span of each heap backing — here `Span<T>`, `ReadOnlySpan<T>` and `ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>` ... — so a comparison across backings needs no common type, and a writable span passed as the argument converts by `.AsReadOnly()`.

title: at a class T a buffer span compares with a non-nullable array span and a null slot equals nothing
rule: The overloads are declared at the receiver's own `T`: at a class `T` the buffer span's `T?` slots compare with an array span's `T` slots, `Equals` null-safe on the nullable side, so a null slot equals no element.

title: OwningBuffer at a sendable class element is sendable
rule: `OwningBuffer<T>` is sendable iff its element type is a sendable class type or a sendable value type: `OwningBuffer<sealed_class>` accepts.

title: OwningBuffer at a borrow-bearing record element is not sendable
rule: `OwningBuffer<T>` is sendable iff its element type is a sendable class type or a sendable value type: a buffer of a borrow-bearing record is not sendable.

title: an OwningBuffer's Length reads its stored extent
rule: `public pure readonly property Length: int;    // stored extent, immutable once` (stdlib §4.14, OwningBuffer<T>, no IEnumerable conformance). A buffer constructed with length 4 has a stored extent of 4.

title: move is not admitted through an ArraySpan<T> indexer for any T
rule: move arrSpan[i] is not admitted for any T -- borrowed slots have no ownership to transfer; the plain indexer-get is the only read form.

title: writing through an ArraySpan<T> stores a borrow with no disposal of the previous slot
rule: For class T, the assigned value is a borrow -- no ownership transfer; the previous slot contents are not disposed (they were borrows, not owned values). This differs from Span<T>'s class-T setter.

title: an ArraySpan<T> may not be constructed from an unbound temporary array
rule: A borrow-bearing record may not be constructed from a temporary bound to one of its borrow-carrying fields; ArraySpan<T>'s Source field carries a borrow of the Array<T>, so a fresh unbound array is rejected.

title: an ArraySpan<T> constructed from a named, bound array is admitted
rule: Bind the source to a named local whose scope outlives the record, and pass that -- the remedy for the no-temporary-source rule, applied to the Array<T>-backed span family.

title: ArraySpan<T>.Fill assigns the value to every slot, for class and value T alike
rule: Unlike Span<T> (whose mutation API splits by T's category), ArraySpan<T> provides a single uniform mutation surface for all T -- admissible because Array<T> slots do not own their contents.

title: neither ArraySpan<T> nor ReadOnlyArraySpan<T> declares ToArray()
rule: No ToArray() on either span family -- neither materializes; a view on this side is over an Array<T>, which already carries ToArray() and Slice, so materialization is reachable through the source instead.

title: a writable array byte span reads the read tier through AsReadOnly
rule: the §4.14 endianness-aware read tier — every `Read*{Little,Big}Endian`/`TryRead*` form — is declared again as `extension ReadOnlyArraySpan<byte>`, member for member and with identical semantics (`ArraySpan<byte>` reads through `AsReadOnly()`, as `Span<byte>` does)

title: the byte read tier is not declared on a writable array byte span
rule: the §4.14 endianness-aware read tier — every `Read*{Little,Big}Endian`/`TryRead*` form — is declared again as `extension ReadOnlyArraySpan<byte>`, member for member and with identical semantics (`ArraySpan<byte>` reads through `AsReadOnly()`, as `Span<byte>` does)

title: a buffer span's SequenceEqual takes an array span of the other backing
rule: `SequenceEqual` is declared on each span type for its own type and for the read-only span of each heap backing (§4.14, §4.15; §3.3 for `char`)

title: a parameter declared at the retired read-only span interface is rejected
rule: Retired. There is no `IReadOnlySpan<TElement>`.

title: a member over either heap backing declares one overload per read-only span type
rule: A member that accepts a read-only span of either heap backing declares two overloads, `(ReadOnlySpan<T>)` and `(ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>)`, each the direct-dispatch path; a writable span passes `.AsReadOnly()`.

title: SortedDictionary<K, V> iterates entries in ascending key order regardless of insertion order
rule: A comparison-ordered associative collection: iteration visits entries in ascending key order.

title: Add on a present key raises ArgumentException
rule: method Add(key: K, value: V); // v0.282: ArgumentException if the key is present -- the duplicate-is-a-bug tier.

title: TryAdd on a present key returns false and does not mutate
rule: method TryAdd(key: K, value: V): bool; // v0.282 (shape (d)): false and no mutation if present.

title: FirstKey on an empty SortedDictionary raises InvalidOperationException
rule: pure readonly property FirstKey: K; // least key; InvalidOperationException if empty.

title: the indexer get raises KeyNotFoundException on an absent key
rule: property [key: K]: V; // get: KeyNotFoundException if absent.

title: structurally modifying a SortedDictionary during iteration raises InvalidOperationException
rule: Iteration is O(n) in ascending key order, one live pass at a time; structural modification during iteration raises InvalidOperationException.

title: SortedSet<T> iterates in ascending order regardless of insertion order
rule: A comparison-ordered set: membership by CompareTo-equality, iteration in ascending order.

title: Add on an already-present element is a silent no-op
rule: As with Set<T>, adding an equal element leaves the set unmodified -- Add returns () and discards silently.

title: TryAdd on an already-present element returns false
rule: method TryAdd(item: T): bool; // false if an equal item is present.

title: First on an empty SortedSet raises InvalidOperationException
rule: pure readonly property First: T; // least; InvalidOperationException if empty.

title: reassigning a SortedSet<int> local leaves the new set in ascending order
rule: A comparison-ordered set: membership by `CompareTo`-equality, iteration in ascending order.

title: a SortedSet of a class element iterates in CompareTo order after the set is reassigned
rule: A comparison-ordered set: membership by `CompareTo`-equality, iteration in ascending order.

title: FrozenArray<T>.From(owned buffer) steals a value-typed buffer's storage
rule: static method From(owned buffer: OwningBuffer<T>): owned FrozenArray<T>; // VALUE-TYPED T ONLY: O(1) -- steals the storage; the buffer is consumed.

title: FrozenArray<T>.From(items) copies and is the only construction form for string
rule: static method From(items: Array<T>): owned FrozenArray<T>; // Copies; the only construction form for T = string.

title: FrozenArray<T> has no indexer setter -- deeply immutable after construction
rule: public property [i: int]: T get; end; -- FrozenArray<T> declares no mutating member, so no writer can exist after construction.

title: freezing a buffer with a live span local over it is rejected by the consume-site freeze
rule: A live local of borrow-bearing record type counts as a live local borrow of every held borrow's source: var s := buf.AsSpan(); freezes buf against FrozenArray<T>.From(move buf) -- and every other consume -- for as long as s is live, a borrow being live at a consume site when some path from the site reaches a later use of it.

title: ToArray() returns a fresh mutable copy out of a FrozenArray<T>
rule: method ToArray(): owned Array<T>; // fresh mutable copy back out.

title: a static owned readonly FrozenArray<T> is a sound all-domains singleton
rule: A static owned readonly FrozenArray<T> is a sound all-domains singleton and draws no language spec 22.12 rule-4 warning (rule 4's warning-suppression set, the v0.186 ruling); mutable statics of it remain rejected.

title: From over a borrowed Array<string> parameter copies: a later write to the source misses the copy
rule: public static method From(items: Array<T>): owned FrozenArray<T>; Copies; the only construction form for T = string. Construction consumes or copies its source — after either, no writer can exist.

title: From at T = string inside a generic body copies a borrowed source like the non-generic call
rule: public static method From(items: Array<T>): owned FrozenArray<T>; Copies; the only construction form for T = string. Construction consumes or copies its source — after either, no writer can exist.

title: Increment on an absent key creates it at delta
rule: method Increment(key: K, delta: int := 1); // absent key is created at delta.

title: CountOf returns 0 for an absent key
rule: method CountOf(key: K): int; // 0 when absent.

title: Contains distinguishes a present-at-zero key from an absent one
rule: method Contains(key: K): bool; // distinguishes present-at-zero from absent; enables key in tally.

title: a key decremented to zero or below is not removed and still counts toward Count
rule: A key decremented to zero or below is not removed -- it keeps its position, counts toward Count, and CountOf returns its possibly negative value; only Remove deletes it.

title: Counter<K> iterates its entries in insertion order
rule: Counter<K> implements IEnumerable<DictionaryEntry<K, int>>; iteration is insertion-ordered, exactly as Dictionary.

title: Increment on an existing key updates in place and preserves its insertion position
rule: Increment on an existing key updates in place and preserves its position.

title: Counter<string> is sendable and crosses as a channel element
rule: `Counter<K>` is sendable iff `K`'s element category (language spec §28.11) is sendable-value, `string` or `Type`, the borrowing maps' key condition. `Counter<string>` is sendable.

title: Counter at a class-typed key is not sendable, though the key class is
rule: `Counter<string>` is sendable; a `Counter<K>` at a class- or interface-typed `K` carries borrows and is not.

title: Insert mints a handle, GetOrNull reads the stored value as a borrow, and the map's disposal cascades
rule: Insert(owned value: T): SlotHandle takes ownership and mints a handle; GetOrNull(handle) returns a borrow of the stored value when the handle is live; disposing the map disposes every value it still holds.

title: Remove disposes the value and the handle reads absent afterwards
rule: Remove(handle) disposes the value and returns true; a handle whose slot has been vacated reads as absent — Contains is false and GetOrNull is null — for the rest of the map's life.

title: a stale handle after slot reuse reads absent while the new handle for the same slot reads live
rule: Insert reuses the most recently vacated slot; a handle is live iff its slot holds a value and the slot's generation equals the handle's Generation, so a handle minted before the slot was vacated never reads a later occupant of its slot.
check: all:disposed a\nFalse True False True\ndisposed b

title: Clear disposes every value in descending Index and keeps the map usable
rule: Clear() disposes every value in descending Index and keeps the emptied map.

title: disposing the map disposes its values in descending Index
rule: The map's own Dispose() disposes the values in descending Index — the ordered families' reverse-storage-order rule of spec §28.11, storage order here being slot order — then releases the storage.

title: Drain yields owned values in ascending Index and vacates each slot as it goes
rule: Drain() returns an IOwningEnumerable<T> whose iteration transfers each value to the consumer in ascending Index and vacates its slot; after full iteration the map is empty.

title: a handle minted by another map raises ArgumentException
rule: Every handle-taking member raises ArgumentException when the handle was minted by a different OwningSlotMap<T> instance — a caller bug, not an expected absence.

title: an unmarked read of an owned binding at Insert's owned position is rejected
rule: Insert(owned value: T) takes ownership: a fresh producer or a moved binding, never an unmarked read of an owned binding (spec §28.3 K3.3 — an owned argument is spelled `move x` at the call site).

title: a moved owned binding at Insert's owned position compiles warning-free
rule: Insert(owned value: T) takes ownership: a fresh producer or a moved binding is admitted, and the moved binding needs no other discharge.

title: Dispose through the borrow GetOrNull returns is rejected
rule: Get, GetOrNull and TryGetValue produce borrows sourced from the map; disposing through such a borrow is spec §28.6's compile error — the map owns the value, and Remove/PopValue are the forms that release it.

title: default(SlotHandle) denotes a slot of no map and raises ArgumentException
rule: A default(SlotHandle) (spec §17.11) denotes a slot of no map and takes the same fault as a handle minted by a different OwningSlotMap<T> instance: every handle-taking member raises ArgumentException — no map ever mints it.

title: Where's predicate is not invoked until the query is enumerated
rule: All are lazy unless documented otherwise. Callback retention: a predicate passed to a lazy operator is retained by the returned query value until enumeration, not invoked at the call.

title: a bound lazy query enumerated twice is a compile error
rule: A lazy query is single-consumption -- it may be enumerated at most once; a second enumeration is a compile error where the flow analysis can see it statically.

title: passing a query as an IEnumerable<T> argument transfers its single-enumeration right
rule: Passing the query as an IEnumerable<T> argument transfers the single-enumeration right to the callee; inside a callee a plain IEnumerable<T> parameter is statically untracked, so a re-enumeration there is enforced only by the runtime InvalidOperationException guard.

title: composing a further deferred operator spends the source query's enumeration right
rule: Applying a further deferred operator (var q2 := q.Select(f);) spends the binding q's enumeration right -- using q afterwards as a query is a static error where visible.

title: materializing with ToArray() produces a result that may be enumerated more than once
rule: To enumerate the results more than once, materialize first -- using var ys := xs.Where(...).ToArray(); produces an owned Array<T>, which, like any collection, may be enumerated any number of times.

title: Take clamps a negative count to zero
rule: Take/Skip clamp -- a negative count behaves as 0, and a count beyond the source takes everything / skips everything; they are range operations, not magnitude constructors.

title: Zip ends when either input sequence ends
rule: Zip ends when either input ends.

title: an OrderBy result mints a single-consumption frame by its lazy-query kind
rule: Each deferred operator call mints a caller-owned query frame; where the declared type is one of stdlib section 5's derived interfaces instead (the OrderBy/OrderByDescending/ThenBy/ThenByDescending quartet's IOrderedEnumerable<T>), the operator is the same minting member by its lazy-query kind.

title: OrderBy composed with ThenBy is stable at every tier
rule: The OrderBy family is STABLE; ThenBy/ThenByDescending break ties left by the preceding key while preserving encounter order among equal elements.

title: ToDictionary raises ArgumentException on a duplicate key
rule: ToDictionary (both overloads) raises ArgumentException on a duplicate key -- Dictionary.Add semantics; silent last-wins would mask a defective key selector.

title: GroupBy materializes fully on its first enumeration, one key-selector call per element
rule: GroupBy is lazy until its first enumeration, then materializes fully -- no complete group can exist before the source is exhausted, so the operator buffers.

title: Sum() accumulates in the element's own type and is overflow-checked in it
rule: Sum now returns the element's own type, so a narrow integer element type accumulates in that type and is overflow-checked in it -- bytes.Sum() over an Array<byte> raises OverflowException past 255.

title: ToDictionary keyed by a function type is a compile error
rule: ToDictionary states `where TKey: hashable` as an ordinary member-level where clause on its own type parameter, the ordinary constraint form of language spec 14.2. A function type is not hashable (spec 3.6 clause (e): a lambda equals only itself), so a key selector returning one fails the constraint at the call site -- the diagnostic names the constraint, the argument and the parameter it turns on.

title: GroupBy keyed by a function type is a compile error
rule: GroupBy states `where TKey: hashable` as an ordinary member-level where clause on its own type parameter, the ordinary constraint form of language spec 14.2 -- the same requirement ToDictionary states on its TKey. A function type is not hashable (spec 3.6 clause (e)), so a key selector returning one fails the constraint at the call site.

title: GroupBy and ToDictionary keyed by a hashable type still work
rule: The `where TKey: hashable` member-level constraint on GroupBy and both ToDictionary overloads excludes a function type and a non-hashable record; it admits every hashable key type, which is the acceptance twin of the two rejection rows above. A gate that fired on any key selector rather than on the failing TKey would reject this program.

title: GroupBy on a string key puts each distinct key in one group, counting its equal elements together
rule: Groups appear in first-occurrence-of-key order; elements within a group in source order. (stdlib [§5]); one group per distinct key, the string key compared by content ("A reference type with content-based equality." [§4.6]), so the two `aa` elements share one group.

title: GroupBy merges a string key built at run time with an equal literal key
rule: Groups appear in first-occurrence-of-key order; elements within a group in source order. (stdlib [§5]); a string is compared by content ("A reference type with content-based equality." [§4.6]), so the concatenated key `ax` and the literal `ax` fall in one group.

title: GroupBy keeps a string key and a longer string that extends it in separate groups
rule: Groups appear in first-occurrence-of-key order; elements within a group in source order. (stdlib [§5]); a string key is compared by its whole content ("A reference type with content-based equality." [§4.6]), so `ab` and `abc` are distinct keys and never share a group.

title: an IGrouping parameter answers Count() and Key in a per-group call
rule: public method GroupBy<TKey>(key: (T) -> TKey): IEnumerable<IGrouping<TKey, T>> where TKey: hashable; (stdlib §5) groups the array. "public interface IGrouping<TKey, T>: IEnumerable<T>" and "readonly property Key: TKey;" (stdlib §5) type the parameter and its key, and "public method Count(): int;" (stdlib §5) is the count. The groups of [1, 2, 2, 3] have keys 1, 2, 3 and counts 1, 2, 1, so `Sz` returns 2, 4 and 4.

title: a GroupBy materialized by ?.ToArray() lists groups in first-occurrence order with element sums
rule: public method GroupBy<TKey>(key: (T) -> TKey): IEnumerable<IGrouping<TKey, T>> where TKey: hashable; ([§5]). "Groups appear in first-occurrence-of-key order; elements within a group in source order." ([§5]). "`x?.M` returns null if `x` is null; otherwise it performs the access" ([§7.5]) keeps the array non-null here.

title: a grouping declares only Key, so an access to any other member name is refused
rule: public interface IGrouping<TKey, T>: IEnumerable<T> declares "readonly property Key: TKey;" and no other property, so the access `g.Foo` names no member of the grouping ([§5]).

title: a grouping-typed parameter does not expose a member only the implementing class declares
rule: A class implements an interface implicitly: by declaring matching public members ([§11.2]). The parameter is typed "public interface IGrouping<TKey, T>: IEnumerable<T>", whose declared surface is "readonly property Key: TKey;" ([stdlib §5]); the `Extra` property that only `MyG` declares is not on that surface, so `g.Extra` names no member and is refused.

title: Contains reaches the §5 operator on an IReadOnlyList-typed receiver
rule: §5 declares `public extension IEnumerable<T> where T: hashable` with `public method Contains(value: T): bool;` (stdlib §5, v0.340). `IReadOnlyList<T>` declares no instance member named `Contains` — `Contains` is declared on `ICollection<T>` (stdlib §4.1), which `IReadOnlyList<T>` does not extend — so §26.5 rule 1 does not commit instance resolution and rule 2 reaches the §5 extension block over `IEnumerable<T>`, whose block parameter is inferred as `int` and whose `where T: hashable` constraint is satisfied. `Contains(3)` over the elements 1, 2, 3 is therefore `true`.

title: element accessors First, Last, ElementAt, Min and Max resolve on IList and IReadOnlyList receivers
rule: The section 5 operators are extension methods on IEnumerable<T>; IReadOnlyList<T> and IList<T> extend IEnumerable<T> (stdlib 4.1), and neither interface declares a member of the called name, so the extension is reached. a is [5, 3, 8, 1].

title: Sum, Average, Any and All resolve on IList and IReadOnlyList receivers
rule: The section 5 operators are extension methods on IEnumerable<T>; IReadOnlyList<T> and IList<T> extend IEnumerable<T> (stdlib 4.1), and neither interface declares a member of the called name, so the extension is reached. a is [5, 3, 8, 1]; Average over int elements returns double.

title: Contains reaches the instance member on IList and the extension on IReadOnlyList
rule: ICollection<T> (and so IList<T>) declares Contains(item: T), which an extension cannot shadow; IReadOnlyList<T> declares none, so the section 5 Contains(value: T) extension (T: hashable) is reached. Both answer true for 3 in [5, 3, 8, 1].

title: predicate and selector operator forms resolve on list interfaces
rule: The section 5 operators are extension methods on IEnumerable<T>; IReadOnlyList<T> and IList<T> extend IEnumerable<T> (stdlib 4.1), and neither interface declares a member of the called name, so the extension is reached. a is [5, 3, 8, 1]; Average with an int selector returns double.

title: Count(predicate) on an IReadOnlyList is rejected: the Count property blocks the extension
rule: An instance member blocks a same-named extension by name, any arity (spec 26.5 rule 1); the spelling that reaches the operator pipeline is r.Where(pred).Count().

title: ToArray on an IList receiver returns a fresh copy independent of the source
rule: ToArray() returns a fresh Array<T> containing the materialized sequence (stdlib 5); ToArray is not declared by IList<T>, so the extension is reached, and writing the copy does not write the source.

title: ToArray on an IReadOnlyList receiver returns a fresh copy of the elements
rule: ToArray() returns a fresh Array<T> containing the materialized sequence (stdlib 5), reachable on IReadOnlyList<T> receivers.

title: the null-conditional call of ToArray on a nullable list interface yields null for a null receiver
rule: ?. short-circuits on a null receiver (spec 7.5); on a non-null IList<int>? the section 5 ToArray() extension is reached, so the count is 3 for [1, 2, 3] and 0 through ?? for the null receiver.

title: null-conditional First, Sum, Any and ToArray on nullable list interfaces take the null branch
rule: ?. short-circuits on a null receiver (spec 7.5); on non-null receivers the section 5 operators are reached through IList<int>? and IReadOnlyList<int>?.

title: a field and a method result typed as a list interface reach the section 5 operators
rule: The section 5 operators are extension methods on IEnumerable<T>; IList<T> and IReadOnlyList<T> extend it (stdlib 4.1), so they resolve on a field read, a call result and a property read alike.

title: ToArray over an IReadOnlyList of class elements borrows the elements
rule: ToArray() gives the result a new container, never a new owner for the elements (stdlib 5, what materialization copies); an OwningArray<C> that outlives the call is viewed as IReadOnlyList<C> and its elements are readable through the copy.

title: a user interface named IList shadows the library interface and its own members resolve
rule: Auto-imported names may be shadowed by a declaration in the module (spec 2.3); on a receiver of the user's own IList<string> its instance members First, ToArray, Contains and Sum are the ones called.

title: assigning the int result of First on an IList of int to a string local is rejected
rule: First() returns T (stdlib 5), here int; an int does not convert implicitly to string (spec 5.1), so the initializer is a type error.

title: First with three arguments on an IReadOnlyList is rejected
rule: First is declared with no parameters and with one predicate parameter (stdlib 5); no overload takes three arguments.

title: Zip with one argument on an IReadOnlyList is rejected
rule: Zip<U, R>(other, combine) takes two arguments (stdlib 5); a call with one has no applicable overload.

title: ElementAt with two arguments on an IReadOnlyList is rejected
rule: ElementAt(index: int) takes exactly one argument (stdlib 5).
