title: Contains on an IReadOnlyList of a record with a function-typed component is rejected
rule: The Contains(value: T) extension is declared where T: hashable (stdlib 5); a record with a function-typed component is not hashable, so the extension is not applicable to IReadOnlyList<Fn>.

title: Sum and Max over long list interfaces keep the element type long
rule: Sum() is the INumber<T> generic returning the element's own type (stdlib 5.1) and Max() returns T; over long elements 5000000000 + 3 + 8 does not wrap, and the result passes as a long argument.

title: Average, Sum and Max over double list interfaces keep the element type double
rule: Average over double returns double and Sum() returns the element's own type (stdlib 5, 5.1); for [1.5, 2.5] the average is 2, the sum 4 and twice the maximum 5.

title: First, Last and ElementAt over string list interfaces return strings
rule: First, Last and ElementAt return T (stdlib 5), here string, so string members apply to the result.

title: selector Sum and Max and predicate First and Last resolve on list interfaces
rule: The section 5 operators are extension methods on IEnumerable<T>; IReadOnlyList<T> and IList<T> extend IEnumerable<T> (stdlib 4.1), and neither interface declares a member of the called name, so the extension is reached. a is [5, 3, 8, 1].

title: operator results interpolate, combine and condition like ordinary expressions
rule: The section 5 operators return ordinary typed values (stdlib 5): First() on IReadOnlyList<int> is an int, Sum() on IList<int> is an int; a is [5, 3, 8, 1].

title: Contains, Any and All with string elements resolve on list interfaces
rule: Contains(value: T) is declared where T: hashable and string is hashable; Any(predicate) and All(predicate) are section 5 quantifiers; sa is ["ab", "cde"].

title: Min with a selector and Average with a selector over int list interfaces
rule: Min<U>(selector) returns U and Average(selector: (T) -> int) returns double (stdlib 5); a is [5, 3, 8, 1].

title: ToArray of a list interface and of a string list interface produce independent arrays
rule: ToArray() returns a fresh Array<T> (stdlib 5): writing the copy leaves the source unchanged, and a string list copies to an Array<string> with the same count.

title: Count(predicate) on an IList receiver is rejected because the Count property blocks the extension
rule: An instance member blocks a same-named extension by name, any arity (spec 26.5 rule 1); IList<T> declares the property Count (stdlib 4.1), so no section 5 Count operator is reachable through it.

title: Count(predicate) as an argument of a nested call on an IList receiver is rejected
rule: An instance member blocks a same-named extension by name, any arity (spec 26.5 rule 1); the rejection holds when the call is an argument of Math.Max, not only at statement level.

title: Count(predicate) on a Dictionary is rejected because the Count property blocks the extension
rule: An instance member blocks a same-named extension by name, any arity (spec 26.5 rule 1); Dictionary<K, V> declares the property Count (stdlib 4), so no section 5 Count operator is reachable through it.

title: Count(predicate) on a Set receiver is rejected because the Count property blocks the extension
rule: An instance member blocks a same-named extension by name, any arity (spec 26.5 rule 1); Set<T> declares the property Count (stdlib 4), so no section 5 Count operator is reachable through it.

title: A user extension named Count on a class without a Count member is called
rule: Only an instance member blocks an extension (spec 26.5 rule 1); Bag declares no Count, so the user extension Count(predicate) is selected.

title: A local variable named Count of function type is called, not resolved as the LINQ operator
rule: Only an instance member blocks an extension (spec 26.5 rule 1); a call whose callee is a plain local name is a call of that local (spec 22), with no receiver to block or extend.

title: A parameter named Count of function type is called inside the method
rule: Only an instance member blocks an extension (spec 26.5 rule 1); a call whose callee is a parameter name is a call of that parameter.

title: A function-typed parameter named Count is called with the IList Count property as its argument
rule: Only an instance member blocks an extension (spec 26.5 rule 1); Count(l.Count) calls the parameter with the property value 3, and 3 * 2 = 6.

title: Count(predicate) and Count() on an IEnumerable receiver count the matching and all elements
rule: IEnumerable<T> declares no Count member, so the section 5 operators Count(predicate) and Count() apply (stdlib 5, spec 26.5).

title: The IList Count property is accepted as a nested call argument
rule: Only an instance member blocks an extension (spec 26.5 rule 1); l.Count is a property read, not a Count call, so it is an ordinary int argument.

title: The IList Count property is accepted inside a lambda body and as a Math.Max argument
rule: Only an instance member blocks an extension (spec 26.5 rule 1); l.Count is a property read of 3, so f(1) is 4 and Math.Max(3, 2) is 3.

title: Sum() on an empty source returns the zero of its result type
rule: Sum without a selector is the constrained generic; on an empty source Sum (both forms) returns the zero of its result type.

title: Min() on an empty source raises InvalidOperationException
rule: Min and Max without a selector are generic over comparable types; Min()/Max() -- selector and no-selector forms alike -- throw InvalidOperationException on an empty source.

title: MinOrNull() on an empty source returns null
rule: method MinOrNull(): T?; // null if empty.

title: Sum() accumulates an interface-typed receiver in the element's own type
rule: §5.1 declares `public extension IEnumerable<T> where T: INumber<T>` with `public method Sum(): owned T;` (stdlib §5.1, v0.340) — an accumulator over `T.Zero()` and `+`. `IList<T>` declares no instance member named `Sum`, so §26.5 rule 1 does not commit instance resolution and rule 2 reaches the §5.1 extension block over `IEnumerable<T>`, whose block parameter is inferred as `int`. The sum of the elements 1, 2, 3 accumulates in `int` itself and is 6.

title: CancellationTokenSource.IsCancellationRequested agrees with its Token's property
rule: CancellationTokenSource.IsCancellationRequested and source.Token.IsCancellationRequested always return the same value: the source's property is a convenience equivalent to source.Token.IsCancellationRequested.

title: Register on an already-cancelled token fires the callback synchronously
rule: If the token is already in the cancelled state at the moment Register is called, the callback is invoked synchronously on the calling thread before Register returns.

title: ThrowIfCancellationRequested raises OperationCanceledException once cancelled
rule: Cancellation surfaces as OperationCanceledException (language spec §30.8); the generated async iterator's implicit token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested() "faults the in-flight MoveNextAsync task with OperationCanceledException" on a requested cancellation (language spec §30.7), which is the call's own effect.

title: Register on a published static source raises InvalidOperationException
rule: A source is published at a static readonly field of the type; on a published source, Register raises InvalidOperationException.

title: CancellationToken.None is never cancelled and never raises
rule: CancellationToken.None has no source and is never in the cancelled state, so ThrowIfCancellationRequested never raises on it.

title: Register on an unpublished source invokes the callback on Cancel
rule: Register invokes the callback when cancellation is requested; the returned Subscription removes the registration when disposed.

title: disposing a source performs a full Cancel before severing registrations
rule: Disposal performs a full Cancel() (v0.195): registered callbacks that have not yet run are invoked synchronously on the disposing thread before the registration list is severed.

title: a parent already cancelled at creation cancels the linked source at once
rule: A parent already cancelled at creation cancels the linked source before CreateLinked returns — the same race-free synchronous policy as Register on a cancelled token.

title: cancelling a parent cancels the linked source
rule: The linked source enters the cancelled state when any parent token cancels or its own Cancel()/CancelAfter() fires, whichever happens first.

title: Register on a linked child of a published parent raises
rule: A linked child of a published parent is published; on a published source, Register raises InvalidOperationException.

title: TryAcquire succeeds immediately on an uncontended Mutex
rule: TryAcquire(timeout) returns owned Lock? — an owned Lock on success or null on timeout.

title: TryAcquire(TimeSpan.Zero) returns null while the mutex is already held
rule: TryAcquire(timeout) returns owned Lock? — an owned Lock on success or null on timeout (§6.2). Mutex is non-reentrant — "a holder re-acquiring waits on itself, whatever the acquisition form" — is language spec §30.12's sentence, not §6.2's.

title: Semaphore.TryAcquire fails once the permit count is exhausted
rule: constructor(initialCount: int); ... TryAcquire(timeout: TimeSpan): owned SemaphoreToken?

title: releasing a SemaphoreToken restores a permit for the next Acquire
rule: SemaphoreToken — destructor; // releases the held permit

title: Atomic<T>.Exchange atomically replaces Value and returns the previous value
rule: Exchange(value) atomically replaces Value with value and returns the previous value.

title: AtomicInteger<T>.Increment returns the post-increment value
rule: Increment(): T; // returns post-increment value

title: AtomicInteger<T>.Add raises OverflowException on overflow
rule: Increment, Decrement, and Add perform the operation atomically ... an operation whose mathematical result is not representable in T raises OverflowException.

title: Subscribe then Raise invokes the handler with the payload
rule: Subscribe registers a handler and returns an owned Subscription; Raise invokes handlers in subscription order.

title: Raise with zero subscribers is a no-op
rule: With zero subscribers, both methods are no-ops — no null check, no ?., no Invoke indirection.

title: a synchronous handler exception stops later handlers — first error wins
rule: If a synchronous handler throws, subsequent handlers are not invoked and the exception propagates out of Raise to the raiser.

title: SharedEventSource.Subscribe rejects a capturing handler
rule: Every subscribe position of the pair admits only capture-free handlers — a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference.

title: SharedEventSource.Subscribe accepts a capture-free handler
rule: Every subscribe position of the pair admits only capture-free handlers — a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference.

title: Raise invokes handlers in subscription order
rule: Raise and RaiseAsync invoke handlers in subscription order, over a snapshot of the subscriber list taken when the raise begins.

title: a handler subscribing during a raise affects only the next raise
rule: Raise invokes handlers over a snapshot of the subscriber list taken when the raise begins (v0.163): a handler that subscribes or unsubscribes during the raise affects the next raise, never the in-flight pass.

title: disposing the Subscription removes the handler
rule: Subscribe registers a handler and returns an owned Subscription; disposing the subscription removes the handler.

title: the producer-side += form registers a handler on the readonly source field
rule: The producer-side `_clicked += h` spelling remains available on the `readonly` field because the subscription forms neither read nor assign the operand; `lhs += h` rewrites to `lhs.Add(h)`.

title: EventSource of unit provides a no-argument Raise overload
rule: No-payload events use `EventSource<()>`; both `EventSource<()>` and `SharedEventSource<()>` provide a convenience `Raise()` overload that takes no arguments, equivalent to `Raise(())`.

title: RaiseAsync awaits each handler's task before invoking the next
rule: RaiseAsync returns a Task that completes when every handler's task completes; each handler's task is awaited before the next is invoked.

title: a faulted async handler stops later handlers and propagates from RaiseAsync
rule: If an asynchronous handler's task faults, subsequent handlers are not invoked and the exception propagates from the awaited RaiseAsync.

title: a cancelled async handler task behaves exactly as a fault
rule: If an asynchronous handler's task is cancelled, the behavior is the same as a fault: subsequent handlers are not invoked and OperationCanceledException propagates from the awaited RaiseAsync.

title: the source classes are invariant in their payload type
rule: The source classes are invariant — `Raise(payload: T)` places T in input position; an exposed source is simply invariant, as its signature dictates.

title: a covariant IEvent face over a narrower source is directly declarable
rule: IEvent<T> and IAsyncEvent<T> are covariant in T (`out T`). Covariant exposure is directly declarable by the pattern: an EventSource<Dog> field behind a `property Sightings: IEvent<Animal>` face.

title: SharedEventSource does not implement IEvent
rule: SharedEventSource<T> deliberately does not implement IEvent<T> — an upcast would launder the capture-free requirement through IEvent<T>.Subscribe's capture-admitting `scoped` signature.

title: the ISharedEvent face subscribes and receives a raise
rule: SharedEventSource<T> implements ISharedEvent<T>, whose Subscribe admits a capture-free handler and returns an owned Subscription; Raise is a synchronized snapshot-raise whose handlers run on the raising domain.

title: a handler capturing a constructor parameter other than this is rejected
rule: A captured constructor parameter other than `this` is not admitted where it contributes a borrow source (spec §28.3) — a class-, interface- or plain function-typed parameter, or an `owned` one: such a parameter is a borrow of a caller local and does not provably outlive the constructed object (v0.301).

title: a handler capturing this is admitted when the Subscription is an owned field
rule: Storing a Subscription in an owned field of `this` resolves the bounding object to `this` (spec §28.14 form 3), so a handler capturing `this` (or state reached through it) is admitted regardless of how the publisher was reached.

title: an EventSource over an owning choice is rejected at its naming
rule: **A move-only payload is not admitted at the source classes.** `EventSource<T>` and `AsyncEventSource<T>` admit no move-only value type (language spec §15.3 — an owning inline array or an owning choice) as `T`: a compile error at the instantiation site, through any chain of user declarations

title: an EventSource over a copyable choice is admitted
rule: `EventSource<T>` and `AsyncEventSource<T>` admit no move-only value type (language spec §15.3 — an owning inline array or an owning choice) as `T`

title: instantiating TaskCompletionSource<T> with a class T is rejected
rule: For non-class T (copyable value types, string, runtime-managed reference types). Instantiating with a class T is a compile error pointing to OwningTaskCompletionSource<T>.

title: OwningTaskCompletionSource<T> is the admitted spelling for a class T
rule: For class T. Result is transferred via `owned` parameter; produced task is Pattern B. OwningTaskCompletionSource<T> where T: class.

title: SetException's owned exception is re-raised to the awaiter
rule: Fault-path ownership (v0.179). SetException/TrySetException (all forms) take the exception owned: the produced task becomes the single owner of its fault exception (awaiters borrow it on re-raise).

title: disposing the source before completion faults the produced task
rule: destructor; // disposes the produced task, faulting it first if the source is disposed before completion.

title: a caught exception borrow cannot feed SetException's owned parameter
rule: A caller that holds only a caught borrow (spec §31.1) constructs a fresh cause-chained exception instead: tcs.SetException(new Exception(ex.Message, ex));

title: a fresh cause-chained exception is the admitted spelling from a catch arm
rule: A caller that holds only a caught borrow (spec §31.1) constructs a fresh cause-chained exception instead: tcs.SetException(new Exception(ex.Message, ex));

title: WhenAny yields the index of the first task to settle and never re-raises its fault
rule: WhenAny(tasks: Array<Task>): Task<int>; // index of the first task to SETTLE — success, fault, or cancellation; never re-raises the winner's fault (inspect tasks[i]).

title: the owning WhenAll overload produces an owned array holding each task's result
rule: Task.WhenAll<T>(owned tasks: OwningArray<OwningTask<T>>): OwningTask<OwningArray<T>> where T: class — aggregates OwningTask<T> results into an owned array of owned elements.

title: Spawn's value-typed result crosses the join as a plain Task<R>
rule: Spawn<R>(entry: () -> R): owned Task<R> where R: sendable, notnull; // Value-typed or string result (Pattern A).

title: Spawn's class-typed result transfers ownership to the awaiter
rule: Class-typed result: ownership transfers to the awaiter (Pattern B). Spawn<R>(entry: () -> owned R): owned OwningTask<R> where R: sendable, class;

title: a fault in the entry surfaces at the join as DomainFaultedException
rule: DomainFaultedException ... Message carries the original exception's message text.

title: CancellationToken cannot cross a domain boundary as a spawn argument
rule: A CancellationToken never crosses a domain boundary itself: it is a borrow-bearing record and not sendable.

title: a sendable value type crosses the spawn boundary as a copy
rule: A CancellationToken never crosses a domain boundary itself: it is a borrow-bearing record and not sendable.

title: T must be sendable; a non-sendable class T is rejected
rule: T must be sendable; the instantiation is rejected otherwise (language spec §3.6).

title: a sealed class with sendable fields admits Channel<T>
rule: T must be sendable; the instantiation is rejected otherwise (language spec §3.6).

title: items from one sender are received in per-sender FIFO order
rule: Ordering. Per-sender FIFO; cross-sender interleaving is an unspecified consistent total order; each item is received exactly once.

title: after the last sender closes, drained receives raise ChannelClosedException
rule: Closing. Disposing the last sender closes the channel; buffered items remain receivable, and after the drain Receive raises ChannelClosedException.

title: Close() from the receiving end is idempotent
rule: Close() is idempotent: on an already-closed channel it is a no-op, and later sender disposals remain no-ops with respect to the closed state.

title: TryReceive returns false for both empty-open and drained-closed; IsClosed distinguishes
rule: TryReceive returns false for both empty-open and drained-closed; consult IsClosed to distinguish.

title: synchronous Send on a full bounded channel raises ChannelFullException
rule: on a FULL bounded channel raises ChannelFullException (v0.174); ChannelClosedException if closed

title: ReceiveAll completes normally on drained-and-closed
rule: ReceiveAll() ... suspends while empty-and-open, and completes the enumeration normally on drained-and-closed — ChannelClosedException stops being control flow for the normal exit.

title: disposing the channel disposes undelivered items in reverse insertion order
rule: Disposing the Channel<T> closes it immediately and disposes every undelivered class-typed item in reverse insertion order; subsequent Send raises ChannelClosedException.

title: a mutable static Channel<T> field is rejected
rule: A mutable static Channel<T> field is rejected by language spec §22.12 rule 2 (v0.181).

title: a static readonly Channel<T> draws rule 4's confinement warning
rule: a static readonly Channel<T> draws rule 4's warning: the channel object is the single-consumer receiving end and must stay confined to one consuming domain.

title: Send on a closed channel raises ChannelClosedException
rule: Send(owned item: T); ... ChannelClosedException if closed.

title: disposing a pending Receive task deregisters without consuming an item
rule: Disposing a Receive task before an item has been dequeued into it deregisters the waiter; no message is consumed or lost — the next item goes to the next receive.

title: TaskScope may not be bound with a plain using var
rule: Consumption is await using only — a plain using var, or dropping the scope undisposed, is a compile error naming this rule: a synchronous destructor cannot await the drain.

title: await using is the admitted way to consume a TaskScope
rule: Consumption is await using only — a plain using var, or dropping the scope undisposed, is a compile error naming this rule.

title: await Join() is mandatory on the normal path
rule: await Join() is mandatory on the normal path (compile error where provable, InvalidOperationException from DisposeAsync otherwise): the join-and-re-raise happens at a source-visible await, never at an unmarked end.

title: an await Join() call in the method body satisfies the mandatory-join rule
rule: await Join() is mandatory on the normal path (compile error where provable, InvalidOperationException from DisposeAsync otherwise).

title: a child's fault re-raises at await Join()
rule: await Join(): Task; // await all children; re-raise the FIRST fault (first-fault-wins, no aggregation)

title: Spawn after the scope has closed raises InvalidOperationException
rule: Spawn after close (after Join returned or disposal began) raises InvalidOperationException — deterministic, never a silent extension of the drain.

title: Spawn admits a capture-bearing body bounded by the scope
rule: method Spawn(scoped body: () -> Task); // start a child (§28.14 storage-bounded)

title: an owned TaskScope field is rejected
rule: Every other owning position is a compile error naming this rule, at the declaration that spells the position or at the expression that would place a `TaskScope` in one, `TaskScope?` reading as `TaskScope` throughout: ... any position language spec §28.1 admits `owned` at — a parameter (`out` and lambda parameters included), a return slot, a field, a choice payload, a function-type slot, an owning inline-array slot.

title: returning a new TaskScope through an owned Object return slot is rejected
rule: Every other owning position is a compile error naming this rule ... and an owning position of a wider static type reached by a language spec §5.1 reference conversion (an `owned Object` return, an `owned IAsyncDisposable` parameter, an `await using var` declared at `Object` or at an interface).

title: a TaskScope borrow passed at a generic parameter is an inferred type argument and is rejected
rule: `TaskScope` is admissible as no type argument at all, explicit or inferred, at any instantiation site ... a borrow passed to a generic parameter is the type-argument case above.

title: passing a new TaskScope to an owned IAsyncDisposable parameter is rejected
rule: Every other owning position is a compile error naming this rule ... and an owning position of a wider static type reached by a language spec §5.1 reference conversion (an `owned Object` return, an `owned IAsyncDisposable` parameter, an `await using var` declared at `Object` or at an interface).

title: an await using var declared at Object over a new TaskScope is rejected
rule: A `TaskScope` is minted only as the initializer of an `await using var` binding whose static type is `TaskScope` ... an owning position of a wider static type reached by a language spec §5.1 reference conversion (an `owned Object` return, an `owned IAsyncDisposable` parameter, an `await using var` declared at `Object` or at an interface).

title: a var borrow alias of the await using scope is admitted and usable
rule: Borrows are otherwise unrestricted — a plain parameter at `TaskScope`, at `Object` or at an interface, a pattern binding, a child body's self-capture.

title: a borrowing collection of class elements cannot be a Locked<T> interior
rule: borrowing collections of class elements do not (Locked<Dictionary<string, Session>> is rejected — own the values: Locked<OwningDictionary<string, Session>>).

title: an owning collection of sendable elements is an admitted Locked<T> interior
rule: owning collections the §4 statement makes sendable (`OwningSet<T>` at a sendable `T`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>` at a sendable `V` and a sendable-value or `string` key, …) ... qualify ... Locked<OwningDictionary<string, Session>> is the admitted spelling.

title: a lock guard's Value is a mutable borrow of the interior
rule: A guard's Value property is a borrow of the interior whose source is the guard ... so the borrow rules bound every interior borrow by the guard's life.

title: TryLock(timeout) returns null while the lock is already held
rule: TryLock(timeout: TimeSpan): owned LockGuard<T>?; // null on timeout (Try shape (b)). Non-reentrant: a holder re-acquiring waits on itself.

title: an explicit Dispose() of a live guard binding is rejected while a borrow of its Value is live
rule: a guard binding cannot be explicitly Dispose()d or discarded while a borrow from its Value is live.

title: disposing a guard after its last interior borrow use is admitted
rule: a guard binding cannot be explicitly Dispose()d or discarded while a borrow from its Value is live.

title: a static owned readonly Locked<T> registry compiles warning-free
rule: The canonical process-global registry — the static owned readonly idiom (rule-4 warning suppressed by §22.12 rule 4's warning-suppression set, the v0.186 ruling).

title: a store through a ReadGuard-sourced borrow is rejected
rule: In the body holding the guard, the compiler rejects all stores, move, and ref/out passing through a ReadGuard-sourced borrow.

title: a WriteGuard's Value carries no store restriction
rule: WriteGuard<T>.Value and LockGuard<T>.Value carry no restriction — those guards are exclusive.

title: a write guard's mutation is observed by a later read acquisition
rule: public method Read(): owned ReadGuard<T>; ... public method Write(): owned WriteGuard<T>;

title: Map reassembles results in input order
rule: Results in input order; first fault wins, surfaced at the await as DomainFaultedException.

title: Reduce over an associative combiner with an identity seed matches the serial fold
rule: The serial-fold correspondence holds exactly when the combiner is associative and the seed is its identity.

title: a capturing lambda body is rejected as a Parallel spawn position
rule: The body/selector/combiner parameters are spawn positions: capture-free (a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference).

title: a capture-free lambda is an admitted Parallel spawn position
rule: The body/selector/combiner parameters are spawn positions: capture-free (a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference).

title: ForEach invokes its body exactly once per element
rule: public static method ForEach<A>(items: Array<A>, body: (A) -> (), degree: int := 0): owned Task where A: sendable, notnull;

title: Stream has no async Span<byte> overload — only the windowed Array<byte> async form exists
rule: No async span overloads (v0.179, #1438). Asynchronous byte I/O uses the heap-owned windowed form — ReadAsync/WriteAsync(buffer: Array<byte>, offset, count, token); the async span overloads were removed.

title: FileStream(path, mode) resolves via the FileAccess.ReadWrite default
rule: access defaults to FileAccess.ReadWrite: new FileStream(path, mode) is new FileStream(path, mode, FileAccess.ReadWrite).

title: File.WriteAllBytes accepts a ReadOnlySpan<byte> for the zero-copy serializer path
rule: public static method WriteAllBytes(path: string, contents: ReadOnlySpan<byte>); // v0.165 (#1358): serializer-output path, zero-copy

title: Directory.Delete(path) resolves via the recursive := false default
rule: public static method Delete(path: string, recursive: bool := false); // IOException if non-empty and not recursive

title: Path.GetExtension returns "" when the path has no extension
rule: GetExtension(path): string; // "" when none

title: catching FileNotFoundException requires `import System.IO;`
rule: None are auto-imported; users import System.IO; to get them.

title: FileNotFoundException is unresolved without `import System.IO;`
rule: None are auto-imported; users import System.IO; to get them.

title: Reset() stops the stopwatch
rule: Reset() stops the stopwatch and zeroes Elapsed; a restart from zero is sw.Reset(); sw.Start();

title: StartNew() returns an already-running Stopwatch
rule: static method StartNew(): owned Stopwatch; ... StartNew() is the fresh-instance form.

title: Stopwatch is sendable and a moved running stopwatch keeps running
rule: `Stopwatch` is **sendable**, on the sendable form's copy-state ground. A moved running stopwatch keeps measuring.

title: Debug.Assert never throws — a true condition just continues
rule: Assert never throws; a failed assertion terminates the process, so a true condition simply continues execution.

title: int.Parse raises FormatException on non-numeric input
rule: The ParseOrNull note fixes Parse's own contract: absence of a valid integer literal in the input raises FormatException (the FormatException/OverflowException contract Parse establishes).

title: int.TryParse returns false and assigns default(int) on failure
rule: TryParse(s: string, out result: int): bool is Try shape (c) — false on failure, with the out slot assigned default(T) (here 0).

title: int.ParseOrNull returns null exactly where Parse raises
rule: ParseOrNull(s: string): int? — null exactly where Parse(s) raises (the FormatException/OverflowException contract); otherwise the parsed value.

title: int.MinValue and int.MaxValue are the exact compiler-provided constants
rule: public static const MinValue: int := -2_147_483_648; public static const MaxValue: int := 2_147_483_647;

title: int.Parse(s, radix) parses under the requested radix
rule: static pure method Parse(s: string, radix: int): int; radix in {2, 8, 10, 16}.

title: int.Parse with an unsupported radix raises ArgumentException
rule: radix in {2, 8, 10, 16}; any other radix raises ArgumentException — a caller bug, not input failure.

title: int.Parse raises OverflowException on an out-of-range value
rule: Parse establishes the FormatException/OverflowException contract that ParseOrNull and TryParse are defined against.

title: ToString(radix) emits the lower-case digits
rule: stdlib §9.1: "`ToString(radix)` emits the **lower-case** digits". The radix alphabet of radix 16 is `0`–`9` with `A`–`F`, and the rendering of 255 is the lower-case `ff`.

title: ToString(radix) renders a minus sign then the magnitude's digits
rule: stdlib §9.1: "`ToString(radix)` emits the **lower-case** digits — a `-` for a negative value followed by the magnitude's digits most significant first". The magnitude of -42 in radix 16 is `2a`.

title: ToString(radix) renders zero as a single 0
rule: stdlib §9.1: "`ToString(radix)` emits the **lower-case** digits — ... a single `0` for zero, never a leading zero otherwise".

title: Parse(s, radix) accepts either case of the letter digits
rule: stdlib §9.1: "`Parse(s, radix)` and `TryParse(s, radix, …)` accept **either case** of the letter digits — `int.Parse("ff", 16)` and `int.Parse("FF", 16)` are both `255`".

title: Parse(s, radix) raises FormatException on a digit outside the radix
rule: stdlib §9.1: the input grammar of the radix forms is "one or more digits of that radix, and nothing else; no whitespace, no `0x`/`0b` prefix, no digit separators, and any other input raises `FormatException`". `9` is not a digit of radix 8.

title: Parse(s, radix) and ToString(radix) are inverse
rule: stdlib §9.1: "The two are therefore inverse: `T.Parse(n.ToString(radix), radix)` is `n` for every value of every integer type and every admitted radix".

title: the no-format ToString emits the text ToString(10) emits
rule: stdlib §9.1: "The no-format `ToString()` ... emits the text `ToString(10)` emits: `(-42).ToString()` is `"-42"`".

title: TryParse(s, radix, out) is shape (c) where Parse raises
rule: stdlib §9.1 declares `TryParse(s: string, radix: int, out result: int): bool` — "shape (c): false (out = 0) exactly where Parse(s, radix) raises FormatException/OverflowException". `zz` is not a radix-16 digit string, so `Parse(s, radix)` raises `FormatException` and the `Try` form returns false with the out slot at 0.

title: TryParse(s, radix, out) raises ArgumentException on an invalid radix
rule: stdlib §9.1 declares `TryParse(s: string, radix: int, out result: int): bool` with the note "an invalid radix raises ArgumentException from both forms" — the radix set is {2, 8, 10, 16}.

title: Parse(s, radix) accepts an optional leading sign
rule: stdlib §9.1: the radix forms read "an optional leading `+` or `-`, then one or more digits of that radix, and nothing else".

title: Parse(s, radix) rejects leading whitespace
rule: stdlib §9.1: the input grammar of the radix forms is "an optional leading `+` or `-`, then one or more digits of that radix, and nothing else; no whitespace, no `0x`/`0b` prefix, no digit separators, and any other input raises `FormatException`".

title: the radix parse and render are inverse for the uint head
rule: stdlib §9.1 (v0.345) "The radix alphabet": "The two are therefore inverse: `T.Parse(n.ToString(radix), radix)` is `n` for every value of every integer type and every admitted radix."  The `uint` head is one of those integer types, so the round trip through `uint` must answer the `uint` value.

title: the radix parse grammar admits no digit separator
rule: stdlib §9.1 (v0.345) "The radix alphabet": "an optional leading `+` or `-`, then one or more digits of that radix, and nothing else; no whitespace, no `0x`/`0b` prefix, no digit separators, and any other input raises `FormatException`".

title: the radix parse grammar admits no 0x prefix
rule: stdlib §9.1 (v0.345) "The radix alphabet": "an optional leading `+` or `-`, then one or more digits of that radix, and nothing else; no whitespace, no `0x`/`0b` prefix, no digit separators, and any other input raises `FormatException`".

title: the radix parse form reaches the narrow integer types too
rule: stdlib §9.1 (v0.345): "Each integer type is declared as a record … The example below shows `Int32`; **the others have analogous shapes** with their respective `MinValue`/`MaxValue`." — the radix form is one of the analogous shapes.

title: a string radix argument matches no radix parameter and is a compile error
rule: stdlib §9.1 (v0.350) declares `public static pure method Parse(s: string, radix: int): int;`, so the second argument must be an int. Language spec §5.1 (v0.350): "A value of one type implicitly converts to another when no programmer-visible information is lost", and no implicit conversion has string as its source. Language spec §22.6 (v0.350): "with no applicable candidate at all, the no-candidate error".

title: the int radix form of the same parse call runs under radix 16
rule: stdlib §9.1 (v0.350) declares `public static pure method Parse(s: string, radix: int): int;` with radix in {2, 8, 10, 16}, so 16 is an admitted radix and "ff" parses to 255.

title: the radix parse admits a sign but no 0x prefix after the sign
rule: stdlib §9.1 (v0.350) "The radix alphabet": "an optional leading `+` or `-`, then one or more digits of that radix, and nothing else; no whitespace, no `0x`/`0b` prefix, no digit separators, and any other input raises `FormatException`".

title: the radix parse rejects the empty string
rule: stdlib §9.1 (v0.350) "The radix alphabet": the input is "an optional leading `+` or `-`, then one or more digits of that radix, and nothing else", and "any other input raises `FormatException`". The empty string has no digits, so it is other input.

title: at radix 16 the text 0b11 is four hex digits, with no prefix stripped
rule: stdlib §9.1 (v0.350) "The radix alphabet": the digits of radix 16 are "`0`–`9` with `A`–`F`", and the input is "an optional leading `+` or `-`, then one or more digits of that radix, and nothing else; no whitespace, no `0x`/`0b` prefix". `b` is a radix-16 digit, so "0b11" is the digits 0, b, 1, 1: 0xB11 = 2833.

title: TryParse(s, radix, out) returns false for a 0x prefix
rule: stdlib §9.1 (v0.350) "The radix alphabet": "`Parse(s, radix)` and `TryParse(s, radix, …)` … under the input grammar the string forms carry throughout: an optional leading `+` or `-`, then one or more digits of that radix, and nothing else; no whitespace, no `0x`/`0b` prefix". The `Try` form reports the same inputs `Parse` rejects by returning false.

title: a radix parse of a sign with no digits raises FormatException
rule: stdlib §9.1 (v0.350) "The radix alphabet": the input is "an optional leading `+` or `-`, then one or more digits of that radix, and nothing else". A bare `+` and a bare `-` have no digits, so each raises `FormatException`.

title: double.IsNaN reports the NaN constant true
rule: static pure method IsNaN(value: double): bool;

rule: IeeeEquals returns false for any pair involving NaN, including NaN-vs-NaN.

title: double.Parse admits the spellings the input grammar lists
rule: **Input grammar.** `Parse` accepts an optional sign (`+` or `-`), then one or more of the digits `0`–`9`, then optionally a `.` followed by one or more digits, then optionally an exponent — `e` or `E`, an optional sign, and one or more digits — and nothing else: `"5"`, `"+5"`, `"-0.25"`, `"007.5"` and `"6.02E+23"` are admitted.

title: double.Parse raises FormatException for the spellings the input grammar forbids
rule: There is no surrounding whitespace, no digit separator, no hexadecimal form and no bare point, so `" 5"`, `"5 "`, `"1_000"`, `"0x1p3"`, `".5"` and `"5."` raise `FormatException`, as does any other input apart from exactly `"NaN"`, `"Infinity"` and `"-Infinity"`.

title: a signed bare point is not in the input grammar and raises FormatException
rule: **Input grammar.** `Parse` accepts an optional sign (`+` or `-`), then one or more of the digits `0`–`9`, then optionally a `.` followed by one or more digits, then optionally an exponent — `e` or `E`, an optional sign, and one or more digits — and nothing else: `"5"`, `"+5"`, `"-0.25"`, `"007.5"` and `"6.02E+23"` are admitted.

title: double.Parse raises FormatException for every non-finite spelling but the three exact ones
rule: They are matched exactly, so `"nan"`, `"inf"`, `"infinity"`, `"INFINITY"`, `"+Infinity"` and `"-NaN"` raise `FormatException`.

title: double.Parse raises OverflowException on an input spelling an unrepresentable number
rule: So `double.Parse("1.7976931348623158e308")` is `double.MaxValue` and `float.Parse("3.4028235e38")` is `float.MaxValue`, while `double.Parse("1e999")`, `double.Parse("-1e999")` and `float.Parse("3.5e38")` raise.

title: an inadmissible input spelling a number raises FormatException, not OverflowException
rule: An input the grammar does not admit raises `FormatException` whatever number a part of it spells: `"1_000e999"` raises `FormatException`, not the `OverflowException` below.

title: double.TryParse returns false exactly where Parse raises
rule: `TryParse` returns `false` in every case where `Parse` would raise, and the span forms carry the string forms' contract.

title: double.ParseOrNull returns null exactly where Parse raises
rule: null exactly where Parse(s) raises; otherwise the parsed value

title: a point not followed by digits is not in the input grammar and raises FormatException
rule: **Input grammar.** `Parse` accepts an optional sign (`+` or `-`), then one or more of the digits `0`–`9`, then optionally a `.` followed by one or more digits, then optionally an exponent — `e` or `E`, an optional sign, and one or more digits — and nothing else: `"5"`, `"+5"`, `"-0.25"`, `"007.5"` and `"6.02E+23"` are admitted.

title: double.BitwiseEquals compares bit patterns of widened float operands and tells -0.0 from +0.0
rule: `BitwiseEquals` returns `true` only when the two `double` values have identical bit patterns; it distinguishes `+0.0` from `-0.0`.

title: double.IeeeEquals and BitwiseEquals widen integer and float arguments before comparing
rule: `IeeeEquals` returns `false` for any pair involving `NaN`; `BitwiseEquals` returns `true` only when the two `double` values have identical bit patterns; it distinguishes `+0.0` from `-0.0`. Both take `double` parameters, so a `uint` or `float` argument converts implicitly (spec 5.1) and a value above 2^31 keeps its sign.

title: float.IeeeEquals and BitwiseEquals follow the double distinction at binary32 width
rule: The same `IeeeEquals`/`BitwiseEquals` distinction described for `Double` applies to `Float` with the appropriate bit-pattern width.

title: Float.IsNaN accepts an int argument through the implicit int to float conversion
rule: Float.IsNaN takes a float parameter; an int converts implicitly to float (language spec 5.1 table, int row), so IsNaN(3) is admitted and 3 is not NaN.

title: Float.IsNaN accepts its parameter by name
rule: Float.IsNaN is declared IsNaN(value: float); named arguments bind to the declared parameter name (language spec 22.5), and an int converts to float implicitly (spec 5.1).

title: Float.IeeeEquals accepts a long and an int through implicit conversions to float
rule: Float.IeeeEquals takes two float parameters; long and int both convert implicitly to float (language spec 5.1 table), and 4L equals 4 as floats.

title: Float.IeeeEquals rejects double arguments
rule: Float.IeeeEquals takes two float parameters; double to float is not in the implicit-conversion table of language spec 5.1, so a double argument is rejected.

title: Float.IsFinite rejects a double literal argument
rule: Float.IsFinite takes a float parameter; double to float is not an implicit conversion (language spec 5.1), and 3.0 is a double literal.

title: Decimal.Round uses banker's rounding (round-half-to-even) at a midpoint
rule: pure method Round(digits: int): decimal; // banker's rounding (round-half-to-even), matching Math.Round.

title: Decimal.Round raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException outside 0..28 digits
rule: Round(digits: int): decimal; digits outside 0..28: ArgumentOutOfRangeException.

title: decimal.ParseOrNull returns null exactly where Parse raises
rule: ParseOrNull(s: string): decimal? — v0.231: null exactly where Parse(s) raises; otherwise the parsed value.

title: a decimal renders without trailing zeros because scale is not part of its value
rule: stdlib §9.3 (v0.345) "Rendering and range": "There is no exponent, no grouping separator, and no trailing-zero padding, because **scale is not part of a `decimal`'s value**: `1.50m` and `1.5m` are one value and both render `1.5`".

title: a whole decimal renders as its integer digits
rule: stdlib §9.3 (v0.345) "Rendering and range": "`10m` renders `10`, and `0m` renders `0`" — the exact decimal form of the value, with no trailing-zero padding.

title: zero renders as a single 0
rule: stdlib §9.3 (v0.345) "Rendering and range": "the integer digits (a single `0` when the magnitude is below one) … `0m` renders `0`".

title: decimal.MaxValue is the exact 29-digit constant
rule: stdlib §9.3 (v0.345) "Rendering and range": "`MaxValue` is `79228162514264337593543950335`".

title: decimal.MinValue is the exact negated 29-digit constant
rule: stdlib §9.3 (v0.345) "Rendering and range": "`MinValue` is `-79228162514264337593543950335`".

title: decimal.Zero and decimal.One are the constants 0m and 1m
rule: stdlib §9.3 (v0.345) "Rendering and range": "`Zero` is `0m` and `One` is `1m`".

title: decimal.Parse admits leading zeros and renders the exact value
rule: stdlib §9.3 (v0.345): "`007.50` [is] admitted" — the parsed value is the exact decimal value, which renders without trailing zeros.

title: decimal.Parse admits an optional leading plus sign
rule: stdlib §9.3 (v0.345): "`Parse` accepts an optional leading sign (`+` or `-`) … `"+5"` [is] admitted".

title: decimal.Parse admits a leading minus sign and a fractional part
rule: stdlib §9.3 (v0.345): "`Parse` accepts an optional leading sign (`+` or `-`) … `"-0.25"` [is] admitted".

title: decimal.Parse rejects a value with no integer digit
rule: stdlib §9.3 (v0.345): "`.5` … raise `FormatException`" — the grammar is one or more digits, then optionally a `.` and one or more digits.

title: decimal.Parse rejects an exponent
rule: stdlib §9.3 (v0.345): "§9.2's input grammar **without its exponent** … `"1e3"` [raises] `FormatException`".

title: decimal.Parse rejects surrounding whitespace
rule: stdlib §9.3 (v0.345): "**surrounding whitespace is not accepted** and raises `FormatException`".

title: decimal.Parse rejects a digit separator
rule: stdlib §9.3 (v0.345): "`"1_000"` [raises] `FormatException`" — the grammar admits the digits `0`–`9` and nothing else.

title: decimal.Parse rejects a second decimal point
rule: stdlib §9.3 (v0.345): "`"1.2.3"` [raises] `FormatException`" — the grammar admits at most one `.` followed by one or more digits.

title: decimal.Parse rounds an over-long in-range value
rule: stdlib §9.3 (v0.345): "An in-range value with more digits than a `decimal` holds is rounded … `"0.12345678901234567890123456785"` parses to `0.1234567890123456789012345678`".

title: a value that rounds into range at scale 0 parses to MaxValue
rule: stdlib §9.3 (v0.345): "a value outside `decimal`'s range — one whose rounding does not fit at scale 0 … so `"79228162514264337593543950335.4"` parses to `MaxValue`".

title: a value whose rounding does not fit at scale 0 raises OverflowException
rule: stdlib §9.3 (v0.345): "`"79228162514264337593543950335.5"` raises — raises `OverflowException`".

title: decimal.TryParse returns false exactly where Parse raises
rule: stdlib §9.3 (v0.345): "`TryParse` returns `false` in every case where `Parse` would raise" — and the out slot keeps the default value.

rule: static pure method Parse(s: string): bool; // "true"/"false", case-insensitive

title: bool.ToString renders exactly "True" or "False"
rule: pure method ToString(): string; // "True" or "False"

title: char.Parse raises FormatException on a multi-code-point string
rule: Parse accepts a string containing exactly one code point (s.Length = 1); any other input — the empty string or a multi-code-point string — raises FormatException.

title: char.IsDigit classifies a decimal digit
rule: static pure method IsDigit(c: char): bool;

title: char.ToUpper applies the simple case mapping to a character
rule: public static pure method ToUpper(c: char): char; — `ToUpper`/`ToLower` apply the simple case mapping — one code point to one, unconditional, no locale tailoring — and return the argument unchanged where it has none.

title: char declares no radix Parse, so a radix call reaches no candidate
rule: stdlib §9.5 declares the `char` members — `Parse(s: string): char`, `TryParse(s: string, out result: char): bool` and `ParseOrNull(s: string): char?` — and no radix form among them. §22.6: "If no candidate is applicable at all — no candidate is reachable: a conversion §5.1 does not admit as implicit ... the call is a compile error with no candidates cited".

title: char.ToUpper accepts its parameter by name
rule: char.ToUpper is declared ToUpper(c: char): char; a named argument binds to the declared parameter name (language spec 22.5).

title: char.IsDigit rejects an int argument
rule: char.IsDigit takes a char parameter; int to char is not in the implicit-conversion table of language spec 5.1 (char converts to int, not the reverse), so IsDigit(65) is rejected.

title: Split keeps every empty segment between separator occurrences
rule: Splitting yields every (possibly empty) segment between separator occurrences: adjacent separators yield an empty element between them. There is no remove-empty-entries option.

title: IndexOf("") is 0 — the vacuous-match convention
rule: IndexOf("", start) = start, so IndexOf("") = 0.

title: StartsWith("") is true — the vacuous-match convention
rule: Empty needle (v0.230): Contains("") = true; StartsWith("") = true; EndsWith("") = true.

title: PadCenter puts the odd extra padding character on the right
rule: PadCenter splits the padding evenly; when it is odd, the extra character goes to the RIGHT: "ab".PadCenter(5) = " ab  ".

title: IsNullOrWhiteSpace(null) is true
rule: static pure method IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value: string?): bool;

title: an int search value is rejected by string.IndexOf, which takes a char or a string
rule: `IndexOf(value: char, startIndex: int := 0): int` and `IndexOf(value: string, startIndex: int := 0): int` take a char or a string search value; "a conversion §5.1 does not admit as implicit" leaves no candidate reachable ([§22.6]), so the call is a compile error.

title: a narrowed int? search value is rejected by string.IndexOf, which takes a char or a string
rule: `IndexOf(value: char, startIndex: int := 0): int` and `IndexOf(value: string, startIndex: int := 0): int` take a char or a string search value; after `x is not null` (narrowing the true branch) the value is an int, and "a conversion §5.1 does not admit as implicit" leaves no candidate reachable ([§22.6]).

title: a narrowed char? search value is accepted by string.IndexOf as its char overload
rule: `IndexOf(value: char, startIndex: int := 0): int` takes a char search value and returns the index of the first occurrence, so `c` in `abc` is at index 2; the narrowing comes from "`x is not null` (narrowing the true branch)" ([§7.4]).

title: a narrowed string? receiver answers IndexOf with the char argument's first occurrence
rule: `IndexOf(value: char, startIndex: int := 0): int` returns the code-point index of the first occurrence, so `c` in `abc` is at index 2; the receiver is narrowed by "`x is not null` (narrowing the true branch)" ([§7.4]) before its member is used.

title: a narrowed string? search value is accepted by string.IndexOf as its string overload
rule: `IndexOf(value: string, startIndex: int := 0): int` returns the index of the first occurrence at or after startIndex, so `b` in `abc` is at index 1; the narrowing comes from "`x is not null` (narrowing the true branch)" ([§7.4]).

title: string.Repeat with a count of zero is the empty string
rule: public static pure method Repeat(c: char, count: int): string;  // count < 0 raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException; count = 0 is ""

title: PadCenter splits an even padding evenly
rule: PadCenter splits the padding evenly; when it is odd, the extra character goes to the RIGHT: "ab".PadCenter(5) = " ab  ".

title: PadCenter returns the string unchanged when the total width is its length
rule: Pad contract (all three Pad members): totalWidth <= Length returns the original string unchanged; totalWidth < 0 raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException.

title: PadCenter pads with the given padding character
rule: public pure method PadCenter(totalWidth: int, paddingChar: char := ' '): string; Pad contract (all three Pad members): totalWidth <= Length returns the original string unchanged; totalWidth < 0 raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException. PadCenter splits the padding evenly.

title: PadCenter with a negative total width raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException
rule: Pad contract (all three Pad members): totalWidth <= Length returns the original string unchanged; totalWidth < 0 raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException.

title: string.PadCenter has no static form
rule: public pure method PadCenter(totalWidth: int, paddingChar: char := ' '): string; — declared as an instance member of `String`, with no static form, so a static reference to it names no declared member and is a compile error.

title: a call to Substring supplying three arguments matches no declared form
rule: public pure method Substring(startIndex: int): string; public pure method Substring(startIndex: int, length: int): string; — the declared forms take one or two arguments, so a call supplying three binds neither; arity filtering leaves no candidate and the call is a compile error.

title: a call to TrimStart supplying an argument matches no declared form
rule: public pure method TrimStart(): string; — the declared form takes no argument, and every parameter that declares no default must be bound; a call supplying an argument binds no declared form and is a compile error.

title: a call to Substring supplying two arguments binds the two-argument form
rule: public pure method Substring(startIndex: int, length: int): string; — the call supplies exactly the declared form's arguments, so the member is applicable and the call is admitted.

title: string.Empty is not a declared member of String
rule: The `String` member list declares no `Empty` member — the empty-string member it declares is `IsEmpty` — so a static reference to `string.Empty` names no declared member and is a compile error.

title: an instance member named Empty is not a declared member of String
rule: The `String` member list declares no `Empty` member — the empty-string member it declares is `IsEmpty` — so a member access `.Empty` on a string names no declared member and is a compile error.

title: a call to PadCenter supplying three arguments matches no declared form
rule: public pure method PadCenter(totalWidth: int, paddingChar: char := ' '): string; — the declared form takes one or two arguments, the second declaring a default, so a call supplying three binds no declared form; arity filtering leaves no candidate and the call is a compile error.

title: string.IndexOf with a startIndex past the receiver's Length raises IndexOutOfRangeException
rule: public pure method IndexOf(value: char, startIndex: int := 0): int; code-point index of the first occurrence at or after startIndex, or -1; 0 <= startIndex <= Length (IndexOutOfRangeException otherwise)

title: string.IndexOf with a startIndex equal to the receiver's Length answers -1
rule: public pure method IndexOf(value: char, startIndex: int := 0): int; code-point index of the first occurrence at or after startIndex, or -1; 0 <= startIndex <= Length (IndexOutOfRangeException otherwise) — a startIndex equal to the receiver's Length is inside the bound, and the occurrence lies before it, so the answer is -1.

title: string.Repeat with a negative count raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException
rule: public static pure method Repeat(c: char, count: int): string;  // count < 0 raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException; count = 0 is ""

title: string.PadLeft and string.PadRight with a negative total width raise ArgumentOutOfRangeException
rule: Pad contract (all three Pad members): totalWidth <= Length returns the original string unchanged; totalWidth < 0 raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException.

title: string.Join rejects a string in the items slot
rule: public static method Join(separator: string, items: IEnumerable<string>): string; — the items parameter takes an IEnumerable<string>, and a value of one type implicitly converts to another when no programmer-visible information is lost; a `string` implements IEnumerable<char> (§4.6), not IEnumerable<string>, and §5.1's table lists no conversion from string to IEnumerable<string> — so the call is a compile error.

title: string.Join admits an array in the items slot
rule: public static method Join(separator: string, items: IEnumerable<string>): string; — an Array<string> is an IEnumerable<string> (§4.4), so the items argument converts to the parameter without loss and the call is admitted; this is the accepting twin of l9_6_0027, which differs by the items argument's type alone.

title: string.Join rejects a reordered named-argument call whose slots carry the wrong types
rule: public static method Join(separator: string, items: IEnumerable<string>): string; — a named argument binds the parameter it names (§22.5), so `items := "abc"` supplies a `string` to the `items: IEnumerable<string>` parameter and `separator := parts` supplies an `Array<string>` to the `separator: string` parameter; a value of one type implicitly converts to another when no programmer-visible information is lost, and §5.1's table lists neither conversion — so the call is a compile error.

title: string.Join binds a named argument to the parameter it names
rule: public static method Join(separator: string, items: IEnumerable<string>): string; — a named argument binds the parameter it names (§22.5), so `items := parts` supplies the Array<string> to the `items: IEnumerable<string>` parameter and `separator := "abc"` supplies the string to the `separator: string` parameter; an Array<string> is an IEnumerable<string> (§4.4) and a string is a string, so both arguments convert to their parameters without loss and the call is admitted.

title: string.Insert with a startIndex past the receiver's Length raises IndexOutOfRangeException
rule: public pure method Insert(startIndex: int, value: string): string; — §9.6 declares the member with no contract paragraph of its own, so the `StringBuilder` twin's Contracts paragraph decides it: "`Insert` and `Remove` raise `IndexOutOfRangeException` when the index or the `(startIndex, length)` window falls outside `0..Length`". A startIndex past the receiver's Length is outside `0..Length`, so the call raises rather than inserting at the end.

title: string.Insert with a startIndex equal to the receiver's Length is admitted
rule: public pure method Insert(startIndex: int, value: string): string; — §9.6 declares the member with no contract paragraph of its own, so the `StringBuilder` twin's Contracts paragraph decides it: "`Insert` and `Remove` raise `IndexOutOfRangeException` when the index or the `(startIndex, length)` window falls outside `0..Length`". The bound `0..Length` is INCLUSIVE at both ends, so a startIndex equal to the receiver's Length is inside it and the call is admitted rather than raising — this is the admitting twin of l9_6_0031, which differs by the index alone.

title: a string's Remove window counts code points, not bytes
rule: stdlib §9.6 (v0.345) "The window members: `Substring`, `Remove` and `Insert`": "Positions and lengths count code points (`Length`)."

title: a string's Remove window counts code points in a four-byte-wide string
rule: stdlib §9.6 (v0.345) "The window members: `Substring`, `Remove` and `Insert`": "Positions and lengths count code points (`Length`)" — the window is over the code-point sequence whatever the string's internal width is.

title: a to-the-end Remove window at Length yields the receiver unchanged
rule: stdlib §9.6 (v0.345) "The window members: `Substring`, `Remove` and `Insert`": "`startIndex` may equal `Length` and `length` may be `0`: … `"abc".Remove(3)` is `"abc"`".

title: an Insert at Length appends to the receiver
rule: stdlib §9.6 (v0.345) "The window members: `Substring`, `Remove` and `Insert`": "`startIndex` may equal `Length` … `"abc".Insert(3, "d")` is `"abcd"`".

title: a window reaching past the end of the string raises IndexOutOfRangeException
rule: stdlib §9.6 (v0.345) "The window members: `Substring`, `Remove` and `Insert`": "a window reaching past the end (`startIndex + length > Length`) raises `IndexOutOfRangeException` … `"abc".Substring(2, 2)` raises".

title: string.Repeat over the empty unit is the empty string for a positive count
rule: stdlib §9.6 (v0.350) declares `public static pure method Repeat(unit: string, count: int): string;` and states `Repeat("", n) = ""`, so the empty unit repeated three times has length 0.

title: string.Repeat over a non-empty unit with a count of zero is the empty string
rule: public static pure method Repeat(unit: string, count: int): string; // same count contract; the char overload's contract states count = 0 is "", and the unit overload declares the same count contract

title: string.Repeat over a non-empty unit with a negative count raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException
rule: public static pure method Repeat(unit: string, count: int): string; // same count contract; the char overload's contract states count < 0 raises ArgumentOutOfRangeException

title: named arguments unit and count bind the string overload of Repeat
rule: stdlib §9.6 declares `public static pure method Repeat(unit: string, count: int): string;`. Language spec §22.5: each supplied argument binds exactly one parameter, so `unit := "ab"` binds the parameter named unit and `count := 0` binds the parameter named count.

title: a call to string.Repeat supplying one argument matches no declared form
rule: stdlib §9.6 declares `Repeat(c: char, count: int): string` and `Repeat(unit: string, count: int): string`, both with no default for count. Language spec §22.5: every parameter that declares no default must be bound, positionally or by name.

title: Trim with a string literal as its chars argument is admitted
rule: stdlib §9.6 declares `public pure method Trim(chars: IEnumerable<char>): string;`. Language spec §4.6 states that `string` implements `IEnumerable<char>`, so a string value is an admitted chars argument.

title: Trim with a string-typed variable as its chars argument is admitted
rule: stdlib §9.6 declares `public pure method Trim(chars: IEnumerable<char>): string;`. Language spec §4.6 states that `string` implements `IEnumerable<char>`, so a string-typed variable is an admitted chars argument.

title: Trim with an int chars argument matches no declared form
rule: stdlib §9.6 declares `public pure method Trim(chars: IEnumerable<char>): string;`. An int is not an IEnumerable<char>, so the argument binds no declared form. Language spec §22.6 governs overload applicability.

title: string.Join over arrays of wide, narrow and empty strings
rule: string.Join(separator, items) concatenates the items with the separator between each adjacent pair (stdlib 9.6); an Array<string> is an IEnumerable<string>. Non-ASCII text joins like any other.

title: string.Join with a Latin-1 separator and a wide-string result compares equal to its literal
rule: string.Join(separator, items) concatenates the items with the separator between each adjacent pair (stdlib 9.6); an Array<string> is an IEnumerable<string>. The result equals the literal with the same code points.

title: string.Join called in a loop with named arguments and a user method taking IEnumerable<string>
rule: string.Join(separator, items) concatenates the items with the separator between each adjacent pair (stdlib 9.6); an Array<string> is an IEnumerable<string>. Named arguments bind by the declared parameter names separator and items (spec 22.5).

rule: public pure method CompareTo(other: string, ignoreCase: bool): int;

title: string LastIndexOf(string): last start index, -1 when absent, Length for the empty string
rule: -1 when absent; LastIndexOf("") = Length

title: string LastIndexOf(char) gives the index of the last occurrence
rule: public pure method LastIndexOf(value: char): int;   // last occurrence, or -1

title: the predicate count on an Array<T> receiver does not reach the same-named operator
rule: The LINQ extensions in §5 apply to `Array<T>` because it implements `IEnumerable<T>` — except the four whose names `Array<T>` itself declares: `Contains`, `Count`, `Reverse`, and `ToArray` resolve to the instance members and the same-named §5 operators are unreachable on an `Array<T>` receiver — `arr.Count(pred)` does not resolve to LINQ's predicate count. Under spec §26.5 rule 1 the instance member wins by name — of any arity, applicability, or accessibility — so the committed instance lookup is `Array<T>.Count`, which takes no argument; the predicate count supplies one, no candidate survives, and the call is a compile error.

title: the no-argument Count on an Array<T> receiver is the instance member
rule: The LINQ extensions in §5 apply to `Array<T>` because it implements `IEnumerable<T>` — except the four whose names `Array<T>` itself declares: `Contains`, `Count`, `Reverse`, and `ToArray` resolve to the instance members and the same-named §5 operators are unreachable on an `Array<T>` receiver. `Array<T>` declares `public pure readonly property Count: int` (stdlib §4.4), so the no-argument read is that instance member's own form and is admitted — it is the predicate count, not the instance member, that matches no declared form.

title: a null-conditional Contains on an Array reaches the declared Array.Contains, not a user extension
rule: `Contains`, `Count`, `Reverse`, and `ToArray` resolve to the instance members and the same-named

title: GetEnumerator on an open-ended range raises InvalidOperationException
rule: Calling GetEnumerator on an open-ended range (IsOpenEnded is true) raises InvalidOperationException.

title: IsEmpty is true for an empty exclusive-bound range
rule: public pure readonly property IsEmpty: bool; // true if the range contains no values

title: Range.Contains is a bool in conditions, boolean composition, comparisons, ternaries and lambdas
rule: Stdlib §9.8 (v0.340): "`Contains(v)` is `true` iff the range is nonempty under iteration and `v` lies within the endpoint extent (exclusive upper bound excluded) ... `Step` affects membership only through direction/emptiness." The result is a `bool`, so it composes with `not`, `or`, `and`, `= true`, an if-expression and a lambda body.

title: Range.Contains in a lambda is correct for long, uint, ulong, descending, stepped, empty ranges
rule: Stdlib §9.8 (v0.340): "`Contains(v)` is `true` iff the range is nonempty under iteration and `v` lies within the endpoint extent (exclusive upper bound excluded) ... `Step` affects membership only through direction/emptiness." So `1L..10L step 3L` contains 5L (the step skips it in iteration, not in membership), `10..1 step -3` contains 8, and `5..<5` is empty and contains nothing.

title: Range.Contains over a byte range, directly and through a lambda
rule: Stdlib §9.8 (v0.340): "`Contains(v)` is `true` iff the range is nonempty under iteration and `v` lies within the endpoint extent (exclusive upper bound excluded) ... `Step` affects membership only through direction/emptiness." For `Range<byte>` over `1..4`, 3 is a member and 9 is not, whether asked directly or through a capturing lambda.

title: Range.Contains through a Range<int> field, a method parameter and a call argument
rule: Stdlib §9.8 (v0.340): "`Contains(v)` is `true` iff the range is nonempty under iteration and `v` lies within the endpoint extent (exclusive upper bound excluded) ... `Step` affects membership only through direction/emptiness." A `Range<int>` held in a class field, passed as a parameter, or its `Contains` result passed on as a `bool` argument answers the same membership question.

title: the bool result of Range.Contains does not convert implicitly to int
rule: Stdlib §9.8 (v0.340): "`Contains(v)` is `true` iff the range is nonempty under iteration and `v` lies within the endpoint extent (exclusive upper bound excluded) ... `Step` affects membership only through direction/emptiness." The result is a `bool`; "No implicit conversion to or from any other type" (§4.1 `bool`, v0.340), so `var n: int := q.Contains(2);` is a type error: a `bool` is not implicitly convertible to `int`.

title: Range<int>.Contains rejects a uint argument
rule: Stdlib §9.8 (v0.340): "`Contains(v)` is `true` iff the range is nonempty under iteration and `v` lies within the endpoint extent (exclusive upper bound excluded) ... `Step` affects membership only through direction/emptiness." `Contains(v)` takes the range's element type `T`; §5.1 under "The following are **never implicit**" lists "Between signed and unsigned types of the same or narrower width (e.g. `int → uint`, `uint → int`"; so a `uint` argument to a `Range<int>` is rejected: a `uint` is not implicitly convertible to `int`.

title: a user record named Range keeps its own Contains, whatever its result type
rule: A non-generic `Range` is a different name from the always-available `Range<T>` (names are compared with their generic arity, §2.2 *Collisions*, v0.340), and a current-module declaration is found before an import (§2.7 rule 1), so `r.Contains(2)` calls the record's own `Contains`, which returns `int` (`x + Lo`) and is not typed `bool`.

title: a user generic class named Range<T> keeps its own Contains, called directly and through a lambda
rule: Names are compared with their generic arity (§2.2 *Collisions*, v0.340) and a current-module declaration is found before an import (§2.7 rule 1), so the module's own `Range<T>` hides the always-available stdlib `Range<T>` and `r.Contains(2)` calls the user's method, which returns `int`, not `bool`.

title: FromUnderlyingOrNull returns null for an undeclared underlying value
rule: It returns the declared constant whose underlying value equals value, or null when there is none — total, never raises.

title: NameOf returns the declared constant's own identifier
rule: NameOf(value) returns the constant's identifier — under duplicate values, the first-declared constant's; the pair round-trips up to aliasing.

title: IntPtr's explicitly-declared equality compares by address
rule: Equality for these types is therefore declared explicitly ... the = and <> overloads plus the Equals(T) and override GetHashCode that language spec §25.2's co-declaration rule requires.

title: CString.Length is the byte length excluding the null terminator
rule: public readonly property Length: int; // byte length, excluding the null terminator

title: CString has no public constructor — instances come from its factory methods
rule: public class CString // No public constructor; obtained via factory methods.

title: CString.From(s) is the sanctioned construction route
rule: public static method From(s: string): owned CString;

title: RawBytes.From copies the source buffer; later mutation does not affect it
rule: RawBytes.From(buffer) allocates a fresh, owned RawBytes containing a copy of the source bytes. Mutations to the source after construction do not affect the RawBytes; the buffer is independent.

title: CopyTo writes Length bytes starting at destOffset
rule: CopyTo(destination, destOffset) // copies Length bytes into destination[destOffset .. destOffset+Length).

title: a CopyTo window outside the destination's Count raises IndexOutOfRangeException
rule: a window outside destination's Count raises IndexOutOfRangeException (the §1/§7.1 window rule).

title: RawBytes is not sendable and cannot cross a domain boundary
rule: RawBytes is a class and not sendable (language spec §30.14's class rule — not sealed), so a FromForeign view never crosses a domain boundary; stated here so the invariant is explicit.

title: Ptr<T>.Zero compares equal to itself under the intrinsic address equality
rule: public static readonly property Zero: Ptr<T>; ... The intrinsic compares the address representation.

title: Ptr<Ptr<T>> nested pointer is not admitted
rule: Nested Ptr<Ptr<T>> is NOT admitted (language spec §32.12).

title: a single-level Ptr<T> over an admitted pointee type is admitted
rule: T is gated (per-instantiation ...) to the FFI-POINTEE SET: integer types, float, double, bool, IntPtr, UIntPtr, and C-compatible records.

title: Interop.CodeAddress accepts a capture-free static method reference
rule: F gated per-instantiation to FFI-compatible function types ... a static method reference or a non-capturing lambda.

title: Interop.CodeAddress rejects a capturing lambda argument
rule: a capture-bearing argument is rejected with §32.8's diagnostic; the env clause does not apply.
